section: Secondary information for rice: the proportional odds model
text:
Secondary information for rice: the proportional odds model
Grain arsenic is weakly structured in space, so data on their own inform a node only over a short distance. The. The first step is a proportional odds model (ordered logistic regression) that predicts, at any location, the probability of not exceeding each of the nine GAs thresholds from three covariates:
\[
P\big(\text{GAs} \le z_k \mid \mathbf{x}\big) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\big[-(\theta_k - \mathbf{x}^\top \boldsymbol\beta)\big]}, \qquad k = 1, \dots, 9.
\]
The intercepts \(\theta_1 < \dots < \theta_9\) are specific to the thresholds and the slopes \(\boldsymbol\beta\) are shared. A positive slope means that the covariate shifts the whole distribution of GAs upwards. The covariates are WAs, phosphate-extractable soil As (PAs) and oxalate-extractable Fe (AoFe). The model is fitted by maximum likelihood with scipy, and standard errors come from the numerical Hessian.


Code
# Well arsenic, phosphate-extractable arsenic, and oxalate iron: the covariates for grain arsenic.
COVARS = ["WAs", "PAs", "AoFe"]
X = df[COVARS].to_numpy(float)
class_g = np.searchsorted(THR_G, gas, side="left")       # class 0..9; class <= k  <=>  GAs <= z_k

# Cumulative probability at each threshold, from ordered intercepts and one slope per covariate.
def po_cdf(theta, beta, Xmat):
    return expit(theta[None, :] - (Xmat @ beta)[:, None])

# Negative log-likelihood of the observed grain-arsenic classes.
def po_negloglik(v, Xmat=X, cls=class_g):
    theta, beta = v[:K], v[K:]
    c = np.column_stack([np.zeros(len(Xmat)), po_cdf(theta, beta, Xmat), np.ones(len(Xmat))])
    p = c[np.arange(len(Xmat)), cls + 1] - c[np.arange(len(Xmat)), cls]
    return -np.sum(np.log(np.clip(p, 1e-12, None)))

def fit_proportional_odds(Xmat, cls):
    # Intercepts are parameterized as a first value plus positive increments so that they stay ordered
    unpack = lambda p: np.r_[np.cumsum(np.r_[p[0], np.exp(p[1:K])]), p[K:]]
    p0 = np.r_[-2.0, np.full(K - 1, np.log(0.5)), np.zeros(Xmat.shape[1])]
    res = minimize(lambda p: po_negloglik(unpack(p), Xmat, cls), p0, method="BFGS")
    return unpack(res.x)

# Numerical Hessian, used for the standard errors of the three slopes.
def numerical_hessian(f, v):
    n = len(v)
    h = 1e-4 * np.maximum(1.0, np.abs(v))
    H = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i, n):
            ei, ej = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n)
            ei[i], ej[j] = h[i], h[j]
            H[i, j] = H[j, i] = (f(v + ei + ej) - f(v + ei - ej) - f(v - ei + ej) + f(v - ei - ej)) / (4 * h[i] * h[j])
    return H

# Slope estimates and t statistics for the shift each covariate gives to grain arsenic.
po = fit_proportional_odds(X, class_g)
theta_hat, beta_hat = po[:K], po[K:]
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(numerical_hessian(po_negloglik, po))))[K:]

po_tbl = pd.DataFrame({"estimate": beta_hat, "SE": se, "t_value": beta_hat / se}, index=COVARS)
display(po_tbl.round(4))

# Prior probabilities at the data and at the grid nodes
prior_d = po_cdf(theta_hat, beta_hat, X)
prior_g = po_cdf(theta_hat, beta_hat, grid[COVARS].to_numpy(float))
ind_g = (gas[:, None] <= THR_G[None, :]).astype(float)
resid_g = ind_g - prior_d

# Share of indicator variance removed by the covariates, from the Brier score at each threshold.
fit_chk = pd.DataFrame({"threshold_ug_kg": THR_G, "observed_cdf": ind_g.mean(0), "mean_prior_at_data": prior_d.mean(0),
                        "mean_prior_at_grid": prior_g.mean(0),
                        "Brier_prior": (resid_g ** 2).mean(0), "Brier_no_covariates": ind_g.var(0)})
fit_chk["variance_explained_pct"] = 100 * (1 - fit_chk["Brier_prior"] / fit_chk["Brier_no_covariates"])
display(fit_chk.round(3))

# Covariate maps and the prior probability of grain arsenic above its median threshold.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 4.6))
for ax, c, lab in zip(axes[:3], COVARS, ["WAs (µg/L)", "PAs (mg/kg)", "AoFe (%)"]):
    plot_grid(ax, grid[c].to_numpy(), f"Covariate: {lab}", cmap="viridis")
plot_grid(axes[3], 1.0 - prior_g[:, 4], rf"Prior P(GAs > {THR_G[4]:.0f} µg/kg)", cmap="RdYlBu_r", vmin=0, vmax=1)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The second step treats what the covariates leave unexplained. The residual at a data location is the hard indicator minus the prior probability,

title: Arsenic Exposure and Cancer Risk from Groundwater and Rice
section: SIS with local prior means for grain arsenic
text:
SIS with local prior means for grain arsenic
At a node \(\mathbf{u}\) the local distribution is the prior from the proportional odds model, corrected by simple kriging of the residuals of the neighbours:
\[
F^*(\mathbf{u}; z_k) = p(\mathbf{u}; z_k) + \sum_{\alpha=1}^{n} \lambda_\alpha(\mathbf{u}; z_k)\,\big[i(\mathbf{u}_\alpha; z_k) - p(\mathbf{u}_\alpha; z_k)\big].
\]
The neighbours are the nearest data and previously simulated nodes. Far from any neighbour the weights go to zero and the node falls back on the prior. The rest of the algorithm is the same as in Section 4.
sklm_cdf and sis_local_means from geolattice.geostatistics apply the estimator at arbitrary points (cross-validation) and embed it in sequential simulation.


Code
# Residual variances and power-tail exponents for GAs, then SIS with local prior means.
var_g = resid_g.var(axis=0)
p_low_g, p_up_g = tails(gas, THR_G)

# Local prior means from the proportional-odds model, updated by kriging the indicator residuals.
t0 = time.perf_counter()
sim_g = sis_local_means(
    gxy,
    prior_g,
    xy,
    ind_g,
    prior_d,
    THR_G,
    models_g,
    var_g,
    # Simulated grain arsenic stays between the lowest and highest measured values.
    zmin=float(gas.min()),
    zmax=float(gas.max()),
    p_low=p_low_g,
    p_up=p_up_g,
    nsim=N_SIM,
    seed=SEED,
)
print(f"GAs: {sim_g.shape[0]} realizations x {sim_g.shape[1]} nodes in {(time.perf_counter() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")
print(f"Simulated range: {sim_g.min():.0f} to {sim_g.max():.0f} µg/kg   data range: {gas.min():.0f} to {gas.max():.0f} µg/kg")


GAs: 100 realizations x 1369 nodes in 0.4 min
Simulated range: 95 to 845 µg/kg   data range: 94 to 845 µg/kg



Does the secondary information help? Cross-validation for GAs
Three predictors of GAs are compared with the same 10 folds: indicator kriging without covariates, the proportional odds prior alone, and the prior corrected by kriging of the residuals (SKlm). The proportional odds model and the residuals are refitted in each fold. The variogram models are kept fixed.


Code
# Indicator variograms of GAs itself, for the comparison without covariates
models_g_ik = []
for k in range(K):
    lag, gamma, n_pairs = experimental_variogram(xy, ind_g[:, k])
    models_g_ik.append(fit_standardized_model(lag, gamma / ind_g[:, k].var(), n_pairs))

# Same ten folds as the water cross-validation. The proportional-odds model is refit inside each training fold.
cv_ik, cv_prior, cv_sklm = (np.full(len(gas), np.nan) for _ in range(3))
for tr, te in folds:
    cm = class_means(gas[tr], THR_G)
    cls_tr = np.searchsorted(THR_G, gas[tr], side="left")
    v = fit_proportional_odds(X[tr], cls_tr)
    pr_tr, pr_te = po_cdf(v[:K], v[K:], X[tr]), po_cdf(v[:K], v[K:], X[te])
    # (a) indicator kriging without covariates: constant prior equal to the global proportions
    glob = ind_g[tr].mean(axis=0)
    F = sklm_cdf(xy[te], np.tile(glob, (len(te), 1)), xy[tr], ind_g[tr] - glob, models_g_ik, ind_g[tr].var(axis=0))
    cv_ik[te] = etype_from_cdf(F, cm)
    # (b) proportional odds prior alone
    cv_prior[te] = etype_from_cdf(order_relations(pr_te), cm)
    # (c) prior + simple kriging of residuals
    F = sklm_cdf(xy[te], pr_te, xy[tr], ind_g[tr] - pr_tr, models_g, (ind_g[tr] - pr_tr).var(axis=0))
    cv_sklm[te] = etype_from_cdf(F, cm)

# Water indicator kriging from the earlier folds, and the three grain predictors on the same folds.
cv_tbl = pd.DataFrame([
    {"variable": "WAs", "predictor": "Indicator kriging", **cv_w_scores},
    {"variable": "GAs", "predictor": "Indicator kriging (no covariates)", **cv_scores(gas, cv_ik)},
    {"variable": "GAs", "predictor": "Proportional odds prior only", **cv_scores(gas, cv_prior)},
    {"variable": "GAs", "predictor": "Prior + kriged residuals (SKlm)", **cv_scores(gas, cv_sklm)},
])
display(cv_tbl.round(3))
rmse_gain = 100 * (1 - cv_tbl.loc[3, "RMSE"] / cv_tbl.loc[1, "RMSE"])
print(f"RMSE improvement of SKlm over indicator kriging for GAs: {rmse_gain:.0f}%")

# Measured values against the cross-validated E-type, for water and for the two grain models.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.8))
for ax, obs, pred, title in [(axes[0], was, cv_w, "WAs: indicator kriging"), (axes[1], gas, cv_ik, "GAs: indicator kriging"),
                             (axes[2], gas, cv_sklm, "GAs: SKlm")]:
    ax.scatter(obs, pred, s=12, c="0.3", alpha=0.6, linewidths=0)
    lim = [0, max(obs.max(), pred.max())]
    ax.plot(lim, lim, "k:")
    ax.set_xlabel("Observed")
    ax.set_ylabel("Cross-validated E-type")
    ax.set_title(f"{title} (R² = {np.corrcoef(obs, pred)[0, 1] ** 2:.2f})", fontsize=10)

text:
Realizations and summary maps
Four randomly selected realizations of each variable are shown first. Each one is a possible reality. The differences between them are the spatial uncertainty.


Code
# Four realizations of each variable. The colour scale stops at the 98th percentile so a few high values do not flatten the maps.
pick = np.sort(np.random.default_rng(SEED).choice(N_SIM, size=4, replace=False))
W_RANGE = (float(was.min()), float(np.quantile(was, 0.98)))
G_RANGE = (float(gas.min()), float(np.quantile(gas, 0.98)))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(19, 9))
for j, r in enumerate(pick):
    plot_grid(axes[0, j], sim_w[r], f"WAs, realization {r + 1}", vmin=W_RANGE[0], vmax=W_RANGE[1], label="µg/L")

The realizations are summarized node by node: the mean (E-type), the standard deviation, the interquartile range and the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles. Where the 0.1 quantile is high, arsenic is almost certainly high. Where the 0.9 quantile is low, it is almost certainly low.


Code
# Node-wise mean, standard deviation, interquartile range, and the 10th and 90th percentiles across realizations.
def summarize(sims):
    q10, q25, q75, q90 = np.quantile(sims, [0.10, 0.25, 0.75, 0.90], axis=0)
    return {"E-type": sims.mean(axis=0), "SD": sims.std(axis=0), "IQR": q75 - q25, "0.1 quantile": q10, "0.9 quantile": q90}

sum_w, sum_g = summarize(sim_w), summarize(sim_g)

# Concentration maps use the data colour scale. The spread maps start at zero.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(5, 2, figsize=(11, 23))
for i, key in enumerate(sum_w):
    level = key in ("E-type", "0.1 quantile", "0.9 quantile")
    plot_grid(axes[i, 0], sum_w[key], f"WAs: {key}", label="µg/L",
              vmin=W_RANGE[0] if level else 0, vmax=W_RANGE[1] if level else None,
              cmap="Spectral_r" if level else "magma_r")
    plot_grid(axes[i, 1], sum_g[key], f"GAs: {key}", label="µg/kg",
              vmin=G_RANGE[0] if level else 0, vmax=G_RANGE[1] if level else None,
              cmap="Spectral_r" if level else "magma_r")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Correlation between the E-type maps of WAs and GAs: {np.corrcoef(sum_w['E-type'], sum_g['E-type'])[0, 1]:.2f}")
print(f"Mean node SD as a share of the data SD:  WAs {sum_w['SD'].mean() / was.std():.2f}   GAs {sum_g['SD'].mean() / gas.std():.2f}")









Correlation between the E-type maps of WAs and GAs: 0.63
Mean node SD as a share of the data SD:  WAs 0.90   GAs 0.91


Reading the results. The single realizations are noisy, and they should be. Each one reproduces the variability of the data, which a kriged or E-type map smooths away. The E-type maps recover the regional patterns: high WAs in the south-centre and low WAs in the north-east. The 0.1 quantile map shows where WAs is high with confidence, and the 0.9 quantile map shows that the north-east is the only area where WAs is low with confidence.
The uncertainty maps are sobering. The mean standard deviation across realizations is about 90% of the standard deviation of the data for both variables, so the data constrain the value at an unsampled node only weakly. The E-type maps of WAs and GAs are correlated (r = 0.63) because the kriged WAs map is one of the covariates of the GAs prior.

Checking the simulations
A set of realizations is valid if it reproduces the statistics it was built from. Two checks follow: the histogram (through its quantiles) and the variogram. The E-type map is included in the first check to show what kriging-type smoothing does to the distribution.


Code
# Quantiles used to compare the data, the realizations, and the smoothed E-type map.
qs = [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9]

for name, data, sims, summ in [("WAs", was, sim_w, sum_w), ("GAs", gas, sim_g, sum_g)]:

    rows.append({"variable": name, "source": "data", "mean": data.mean(), "SD": data.std(), **dict(zip(map(str, qs), np.quantile(data, qs)))})

    rows.append({"variable": name, "source": "E-type map", "mean": summ["E-type"].mean(), "SD": summ["E-type"].std(), **dict(zip(map(str, qs), np.quantile(summ["E-type"], qs)))})

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 9.5))

    # Rescaled variograms check that the realizations reproduce the spatial structure of the data.
    for r in rng_v.choice(N_SIM, size=min(25, N_SIM), replace=False):

Reading the results.

Histogram. The realizations reproduce the distribution of the data. For WAs the average realization has a mean of 135 and a median of 125 µg/L against 130 and 119 in the data. For GAs the mean is 319 against 326 µg/kg. The E-type maps do not: their standard deviations are 39 µg/L and 25 µg/kg against 79 and 120 in the data. A risk calculation run on the E-type map alone would miss both tails.
Variogram. The realizations match the data variogram at long lags but are too variable at short lags. At the first lag the rescaled semivariance of the WAs realizations is about 0.65 against 0.35 for the data, and for GAs about 0.9 against 0.65. This is a known property of SIS for continuous variables. A value is drawn at random inside its class, so correlation within a class is lost, and the indicator nugget is added at every threshold.

The second point matters for interpretation. Simulated maps are somewhat noisier at short range than reality, which widens the local distributions. More thresholds or a smaller nugget in the indicator models would reduce the effect.

title: Arsenic Exposure and Cancer Risk from Groundwater and Rice
section: Arsenic intake from water and rice
text:
Arsenic intake from water and rice
Daily intake of inorganic As by an adult is
\[
\text{Intake} = \frac{C_{iAs} \times I \times B_{iAs}}{BW} \qquad [\mu\text{g As / kg body weight / day}],
\]
where \(C_{iAs}\) is the inorganic As concentration, \(I\) the daily consumption, \(B_{iAs}\) the bioavailability and \(BW\) the body weight (60 kg).

Water. All As in groundwater is taken as inorganic and fully bioavailable. Water intake follows a log-normal distribution fitted to published surveys, with a median of about 3.3 L/day.
Rice. Inorganic As is predicted from total grain As with the regression \(\text{GAs}_i = 19.6 + 0.67\,\text{GAs}\). Bioavailability is 90%. Rice intake follows a Cauchy distribution centred on 0.46 kg/day. A Cauchy distribution has unbounded tails, so draws are restricted here to the range of the published values, 0.33 to 0.78 kg/day.

The assumptions are that people drink shallow tube-well water, eat locally grown rice and cook it in As-free water. For each node of each realization one consumption value is drawn, so the result describes a randomly chosen adult living at that node.
Intake is compared with 2.1 µg As/kg body weight/day, the former WHO maximum tolerable daily intake (MTDI), and with half of it. The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has withdrawn this value, so it serves here as a reference level, not as a safe limit.


Code
# One consumption draw per realization and node, from the published water and rice intake distributions.
rng_mc = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 1)

water_l = rng_mc.lognormal(WATER_LOGN_MU, WATER_LOGN_SIGMA, size=sim_w.shape)

# Cauchy draws restricted to the range of rice intakes in the published study.
def truncated_cauchy(rng, loc, scale, low, high, size):
    cdf = lambda v: 0.5 + np.arctan((v - loc) / scale) / np.pi
    u = rng.uniform(cdf(low), cdf(high), size=size)
    return loc + scale * np.tan(np.pi * (u - 0.5))

rice_kg = truncated_cauchy(rng_mc, RICE_CAUCHY_LOC, RICE_CAUCHY_SCALE, RICE_MIN, RICE_MAX, sim_g.shape)

# Intake in µg of arsenic per kg of body weight per day. Grain total arsenic is converted to inorganic arsenic first.
intake_w = sim_w * water_l * BIOAVAIL_WATER / BODY_WEIGHT
intake_g = (IAS_INTERCEPT + IAS_SLOPE * sim_g) * rice_kg * BIOAVAIL_RICE / BODY_WEIGHT

print(f"Water consumption draws: median {np.median(water_l):.2f} L/day (5th to 95th percentile {np.percentile(water_l, 5):.2f} to {np.percentile(water_l, 95):.2f})")
print(f"Rice consumption draws:  median {np.median(rice_kg):.2f} kg/day (5th to 95th percentile {np.percentile(rice_kg, 5):.2f} to {np.percentile(rice_kg, 95):.2f})")

# The same calculation at the sampled fields with median consumption, 's text
obs_w = was * np.exp(WATER_LOGN_MU) * BIOAVAIL_WATER / BODY_WEIGHT
obs_g = (IAS_INTERCEPT + IAS_SLOPE * gas) * RICE_CAUCHY_LOC * BIOAVAIL_RICE / BODY_WEIGHT
obs_tbl = pd.DataFrame({
    "median_intake": [np.median(obs_w), np.median(obs_g)],
    "pct_fields_ge_50pct_MTDI": [100 * (obs_w >= 0.5 * MTDI).mean(), 100 * (obs_g >= 0.5 * MTDI).mean()],
    "pct_fields_ge_MTDI": [100 * (obs_w >= MTDI).mean(), 100 * (obs_g >= MTDI).mean()],
    "pct_fields_ge_2x_MTDI": [100 * (obs_w >= 2 * MTDI).mean(), 100 * (obs_g >= 2 * MTDI).mean()],
}, index=["Water", "Rice"])
print("\nIntake at the 263 sampled fields with median consumption (µg As/kg body weight/day):")
display(obs_tbl.round(1))

# Probability, over the realizations, that intake reaches the reference levels
P = {("Water", "MTDI"): (intake_w >= MTDI).mean(axis=0), ("Rice", "MTDI"): (intake_g >= MTDI).mean(axis=0),
     ("Water", "50% MTDI"): (intake_w >= 0.5 * MTDI).mean(axis=0), ("Rice", "50% MTDI"): (intake_g >= 0.5 * MTDI).mean(axis=0)}
p_rice_gt_water = (intake_g > intake_w).mean(axis=0)
rice_share = np.median(intake_g / (intake_g + intake_w), axis=0)

# Maps of those probabilities, including half the reference intake and the share coming from rice.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(17, 10.5))
plot_grid(axes[0, 0], P[("Water", "MTDI")], "Water: P(intake >= 2.1 µg/kg/day)", cmap="RdYlBu_r", vmin=0, vmax=1, label="Probability")

plot_grid(axes[0, 2], p_rice_gt_water, "P(intake from rice > intake from water)", cmap="PuOr_r", vmin=0, vmax=1, label="Probability")
plot_grid(axes[1, 0], P[("Water", "50% MTDI")], "Water: P(intake >= 1.05 µg/kg/day)", cmap="RdYlBu_r", vmin=0, vmax=1, label="Probability")
plot_grid(axes[1, 1], P[("Rice", "50% MTDI")], "Rice: P(intake >= 1.05 µg/kg/day)", cmap="RdYlBu_r", vmin=0, vmax=1, label="Probability")
plot_grid(axes[1, 2], 100 * rice_share, "Median share of rice in total intake", cmap="YlGn", vmin=0, vmax=100, label="%")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Median intake over all nodes and realizations:  water {np.median(intake_w):.2f}   rice {np.median(intake_g):.2f} µg As/kg body weight/day")
print(f"Area where rice is more likely than water to be the larger source: {100 * (p_rice_gt_water > 0.5).mean():.1f}%")

Reading the results.

Water dominates. At the sampled fields with median consumption, intake from water has a median of 6.5 µg As/kg body weight/day, about three times the MTDI. It reaches the MTDI at 88% of the wells and twice the MTDI at 74%. Rice gives a median of 1.6 µg/kg/day and reaches the MTDI at 17% of the fields, but it reaches half of the MTDI at 88%.
Maps. The probability that water intake reaches the MTDI is above 0.9 on 68% of the area. For rice it stays below 0.4 on more than 99% of the area. Half of the MTDI is reached from rice alone with a probability of at least 0.5 almost everywhere.

title: Arsenic Exposure and Cancer Risk from Groundwater and Rice
text:
Lifetime cancer risk
The incremental lifetime cancer risk is
\[
CR = \text{Intake} \times \frac{ED \times EF \times CPS}{AT_c} \times 10^{-3},
\]
with exposure duration \(ED\) = 28 years, exposure frequency \(EF\) = 350 days per year, averaging time \(AT_c\) = 70 years (25,550 days) and a cancer potency slope \(CPS\) of 1.5 per mg/kg body weight/day for ingested inorganic arsenic. The factor \(10^{-3}\) converts µg to mg. A risk of \(10^{-4}\), one additional case per 10,000 people, is taken as the acceptable level.
The median of the realizations at each node is the central estimate and the 95th percentile is the reasonable maximum estimate.


Code
# Lifetime risk per unit intake: duration, frequency, and potency, divided by the averaging time, with µg converted to mg.
RISK_FACTOR = ED * EF * CPS / AT * 1.0e-3
risk_w = intake_w * RISK_FACTOR
risk_g = intake_g * RISK_FACTOR
PER = 1.0e4      # express risk per 10,000 people

# Median and 95th percentile at each node, expressed as cases per 10,000 people.

Reading the results.

Level of risk. The median lifetime cancer risk is 3.9 x 10⁻³ from water and 9.1 x 10⁻⁴ from rice, or about 39 and 9 additional cases per 10,000 people. The.6 x 10⁻⁴ for rice. Both media exceed the 10⁻⁴ level at every node, rice by a factor of about nine.
Unions. Median water risk ranges from 21 per 10,000 in Tala to 51 in Magura. Rice risk is nearly uniform, between 8.3 and 9.6 per 10,000. Water therefore drives the differences between unions, and rice adds a floor of risk that would remain even where safe drinking water is supplied.
Scale. With the stated assumptions, the expected number of additional lifetime cancer cases among the 221,219 people in the union file is about 950 from water and 210 from rice.

Comparison with the. The union values agree with the draft Table 2 only when its rows are matched to the polygons by the UID field of tala_union.shp. On that key the correlation of the water medians is 1.00 (0.96 for the rice medians and for the 95th percentile of water). Matched on the union names printed in the draft, the correlation is -0.61. The draft table appears to list the values in UID order beside names in alphabetical order, so its row labels should be checked before publication. For example, the lowest water risk in the draft (18.6) is printed beside Khalishkhali but belongs to the polygon of Tala union, which is also the lowest here (20.5).
After matching, the rice values are within about 5% of the draft. The water medians here are lower than the draft in most unions, by 10% to 20% where risk is high. The lower number of realizations, the coarser grid and the single-structure variogram models are possible reasons.

title: Arsenic Exposure and Cancer Risk from Groundwater and Rice
text:
Conclusions and limitations
What the analysis shows

Groundwater As is high almost everywhere in Tala Upazila. Drinking shallow tube-well water gives a median intake of about three times the former tolerable daily intake, and about 95% of the population lives where exceeding it is more likely than not.
Rice alone rarely reaches the tolerable intake, but it reaches half of it almost everywhere. Its lifetime cancer risk of about 9 per 10,000 is nearly the same in every union and is about nine times the acceptable level.
Spatial prediction is much weaker for rice grain than for water. Covariates (WAs, phosphate-extractable soil As, oxalate-extractable Fe) raise the cross-validated R² for GAs from 0.05 to 0.17. Spatial correlation of the residuals adds very little.
Simulation, not kriging, is the right tool for the risk calculation. The realizations reproduce the histogram of the data, while the E-type map loses more than half of the standard deviation.
Mitigation of drinking water has the largest effect on risk. Where safe water is supplied, rice becomes the main remaining source.

Limitations

The notebook uses 100 realizations on a 500 m grid. The 95th percentiles are the least stable results.
Each indicator variogram has a nugget and one structure.
SIS realizations are too variable at short lags (Section 9).
The GAs prior uses one kriged map of WAs, so the uncertainty of WAs is not carried into the rice simulation. WAs and GAs are simulated independently.
The wells sampled are irrigation wells. Using them for drinking-water exposure assumes that domestic wells nearby draw the same water.
The intake model takes one adult body weight, cooking in As-free water and locally grown rice all year. The bioavailability of As from rice is uncertain.
The MTDI of 2.1 µg/kg body weight/day has been withdrawn, and the cancer risk model is linear with a single potency slope.
Population is spread evenly within each union.

title: Correlation Functions (correlation_function)
text:
Overview
Every kriging and Gaussian simulation method rests on a model of how correlation decays with distance. correlation_function(h, model, range_, nu=1.5, alpha=1.0) returns that correlation, \(\rho(h)\), for the six models GeoLattice supports. It is the building block of all the Bayesian kriging classes, and it is useful on its own for building covariance matrices, simulating fields and comparing models.

The range_ parameter follows the Variogram convention of each model, so a fitted variogram’s parameters can be used directly. In the Bayesian kriging classes, nu is passed as the Matérn smoothness or as the stable exponent.
The notebook:

defines the models and their properties: positive definiteness, smoothness at the origin, practical range and numerical conditioning;
checks those properties numerically;
shows what each model’s fields look like;
chooses a model for real data by marginal likelihood.

title: Correlation Functions (correlation_function)
text:
Theory

Correlation, covariance and variogram
For a second-order stationary field \(Z(\mathbf{x})\) with partial sill \(\sigma^2\) and nugget \(c_0\):
\[
C(\mathbf{h}) = \sigma^2\rho(\mathbf{h}) + c_0\,\mathbf{1}[\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}],
\qquad
\gamma(\mathbf{h}) = c_0 + \sigma^2\bigl(1 - \rho(\mathbf{h})\bigr) \quad (\mathbf{h} \ne \mathbf{0}).
\]
So \(\rho(h) = 1 - \gamma(h)\) for a variogram with unit partial sill and no nugget, which is exactly how correlation_function evaluates it, from the variogram models in geolattice.geostatistics.core.variogram_models. In Bayesian kriging the covariance matrix is \(\sigma^2[\mathbf{R}(\phi) + \tau\mathbf{I}]\), with \(\mathbf{R}_{ij} = \rho(\lVert\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\rVert)\) and \(\tau = c_0/\sigma^2\).


The models
With range parameter \(a\) and \(r = h/a\):







Model
\(\rho(h)\)




spherical
\(1 - \tfrac32 r + \tfrac12 r^3\) for \(r < 1\); \(0\) for \(r \ge 1\)


exponential
\(e^{-r}\)


Gaussian
\(e^{-r^2}\)


Matérn
\(\dfrac{2^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma(\nu)}\, r^\nu K_\nu(r)\), with \(K_\nu\) the modified Bessel function of the second kind


cubic
\(1 - (7r^2 - 8.75r^3 + 3.5r^5 - 0.75r^7)\) for \(r < 1\); \(0\) for \(r \ge 1\)


stable
\(e^{-r^\alpha}\), \(0 < \alpha \le 2\)



The spherical and cubic models have compact support: the correlation is exactly 0 beyond \(a\). The others only decay toward 0.


Valid correlation functions: positive definiteness
Not every decreasing function is a correlation function. For any locations and weights, the variance of a linear combination must be non-negative:
\[
\operatorname{Var}\Bigl(\sum_i \lambda_i Z(\mathbf{x}_i)\Bigr) = \sigma^2 \sum_{i,j} \lambda_i\lambda_j\, \rho(\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j) \ge 0 .
\]
So \(\rho\) must be positive definite. By Bochner’s theorem this holds exactly when \(\rho\) is the Fourier transform of a non-negative spectral density. Validity depends on the dimension:

all six models are valid in 1, 2 and 3 dimensions;
the “triangular” function \(\max(1 - h/a, 0)\) is valid in 1 dimension only.

An invalid function can make kriging variances negative and Cholesky factorizations fail (Section 9).


Behaviour at the origin and smoothness
The behaviour of \(\rho\) near \(h = 0\) sets how rough the field is (Stein, 1999):

Linear at the origin (\(1 - \rho(h) \propto h\)): exponential, spherical, Matérn \(\nu = 1/2\), stable \(\alpha = 1\). The field is continuous but not differentiable; its sample paths are rough.
Parabolic at the origin (\(1 - \rho(h) \propto h^2\)): Gaussian, cubic, Matérn \(\nu > 1\), stable \(\alpha = 2\). The field is mean-square differentiable, with smooth sample paths.
In general, a Matérn field is \(\lceil\nu\rceil - 1\) times mean-square differentiable, and a stable field with \(\alpha < 2\) is not differentiable, with roughness increasing as \(\alpha\) decreases.

The behaviour near the origin matters far more for kriging than the shape at large lags (Stein, 1999).


The Matérn family
The Matérn model has a smoothness parameter \(\nu > 0\) and contains the most common models:

\(\nu = 1/2\): the exponential, \(\rho = e^{-r}\);
\(\nu = 3/2\): \(\rho = (1 + r)\,e^{-r}\);
\(\nu = 5/2\): \(\rho = (1 + r + r^2/3)\,e^{-r}\);
\(\nu \to \infty\): the Gaussian. With \(a = a_G / (2\sqrt{\nu})\), the Matérn correlation tends to \(e^{-(h/a_G)^2}\).

Its spectral density decays like \(\lVert\boldsymbol\omega\rVert^{-(2\nu + d)}\), which is why \(\nu\) controls the smoothness. Because it spans rough to smooth fields with one extra parameter, it is the default recommendation of much of the modern literature.


The stable family
\(\rho(h) = e^{-(h/a)^\alpha}\), with \(0 < \alpha \le 2\):

\(\alpha = 1\) is the exponential and \(\alpha = 2\) the Gaussian;
\(\alpha < 1\) gives a sharper drop at the origin and a heavier tail;
\(\alpha > 2\) is not positive definite.

In correlation_function the exponent is alpha, and the Bayesian kriging classes pass their nu argument as \(\alpha\) when model="stable".


Range parameter and practical range
The parameter \(a\) is not comparable across models. The practical range is the distance where \(\rho\) falls to 0.05 (where the variogram reaches 95% of its sill):



Model
Practical range




spherical
\(0.81\,a\); correlation 0 at \(a\)


exponential
\(\ln 20\,a \approx 3a\)


Gaussian
\(\sqrt{\ln 20}\,a \approx 1.73a\)


stable
\((\ln 20)^{1/\alpha}a \approx 3^{1/\alpha}a\)


Matérn
depends on \(\nu\)



When models are compared, their range grids should cover comparable practical ranges.


Numerical conditioning
Kriging solves systems with the correlation matrix \(\mathbf{R}\). Models that are very smooth at the origin (Gaussian, Matérn with large \(\nu\)) make neighbouring rows of \(\mathbf{R}\) nearly identical when points are close relative to the range, so \(\mathbf{R}\) becomes ill-conditioned: its condition number explodes. GeoLattice adds a tiny diagonal jitter (\(10^{-10}\) relative); in practice a small nugget, or a less smooth model, is the robust remedy.

text:
Practical Ranges
The distance where each model’s correlation falls below 0.05, found numerically, against the formulas of Section 2.7.


Code
hf = np.linspace(0, 20, 200001)


def practical(model, **kw):
    return hf[np.argmax(correlation_function(hf, model, 1.0, **kw) < 0.05)]


rows = [
    {"model": "spherical", "numerical": practical("spherical"), "formula": 0.81},
    {"model": "exponential", "numerical": practical("exponential"), "formula": np.log(20)},
    {"model": "gaussian", "numerical": practical("gaussian"), "formula": np.sqrt(np.log(20))},
    {"model": "cubic", "numerical": practical("cubic"), "formula": np.nan},
]
for a_ in [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0]:
    rows.append({"model": f"stable, alpha = {a_}", "numerical": practical("stable", alpha=a_), "formula": np.log(20) ** (1 / a_)})
for nu in [0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 5.0]:
    rows.append({"model": f"matern, nu = {nu}", "numerical": practical("matern", nu=nu), "formula": np.log(20) if nu == 0.5 else np.nan})
pr = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model")
display(pr.round(3))
ok = pr.dropna()

title: Correlation Functions (correlation_function)
section: Smoothness: Behaviour at the Origin and Sample Paths
text:
Smoothness: Behaviour at the Origin and Sample Paths
Close to \(h = 0\), \(1 - \rho(h)\) grows linearly for the exponential and spherical models and quadratically for the Gaussian and cubic. On log-log axes the slope is the power: 1 for linear, 2 for parabolic. One-dimensional Gaussian fields simulated with each model (the same random numbers, practical range 1) show what that means for the data.


Code
hs = np.geomspace(1e-3, 1e-1, 50)
slopes = {}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 4.8))
for m, kw in [("exponential", {}), ("spherical", {}), ("matern", dict(nu=1.5)), ("gaussian", {}), ("cubic", {}),
              ("stable", dict(alpha=0.5))]:
    v = 1 - correlation_function(hs, m, 1.0, **kw)
    slope = np.polyfit(np.log(hs), np.log(v), 1)[0]
    label = m + (" nu=1.5" if m == "matern" else " alpha=0.5" if m == "stable" else "")
    slopes[label] = slope
    axes[0].loglog(hs, v, label=f"{label}: slope {slope:.2f}")
axes[0].set_xlabel("h")
axes[0].set_ylabel("1 - rho(h)")
axes[0].set_title("Behaviour at the origin (log-log)")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 600)
d = np.abs(x[:, None] - x[None, :])
eps = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(len(x))
scale = {"exponential": 1 / 3, "spherical": 1 / 0.81, "gaussian": 1 / np.sqrt(3), "matern": 1 / 3}
for i, (m, kw) in enumerate([("exponential", {}), ("spherical", {}), ("matern", dict(nu=1.5)), ("gaussian", {})]):
    R = correlation_function(d, m, scale[m], **kw)
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(R + 1e-8 * np.eye(len(x)))
    axes[1].plot(x, L @ eps + 3 * i, label=m + (" nu=1.5" if m == "matern" else ""))
axes[1].set_title("1-D sample paths (same random numbers, offset for display)")
axes[1].set_yticks([])
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
display(pd.Series(slopes, name="log-log slope near 0").round(2).to_frame())
record("exponential slope ~1, gaussian slope ~2", "PASS" if abs(slopes["exponential"] - 1) < 0.05 and abs(slopes["gaussian"] - 2) < 0.05 else "FAIL",
       f"exponential {slopes['exponential']:.2f}, gaussian {slopes['gaussian']:.2f}")

The log-log slopes confirm the classification of Section 2.4:

exponential (0.99) and spherical (1.00) are linear at the origin;
Matérn \(\nu = 1.5\) (1.99), Gaussian (2.00) and cubic (1.98) are parabolic;

The sample paths use the same random numbers and the same practical range, so they differ only in texture. The exponential and spherical paths are jagged at every scale. Matérn \(\nu = 1.5\) is smooth with visible changes of slope. The Gaussian path is very smooth, which is rarely realistic for soil or ore data.

The Matérn Family
The closed forms of Section 2.5 for \(\nu = 0.5, 1.5, 2.5\) are checked, then the limit to the Gaussian with the rescaled range \(a = a_G/(2\sqrt{\nu})\).

closed = {0.5: np.exp(-r_), 1.5: (1 + r_) * np.exp(-r_), 2.5: (1 + r_ + r_ ** 2 / 3) * np.exp(-r_)}

title: Correlation Functions (correlation_function)
text:
Positive Definiteness in Practice
The smallest eigenvalue of the correlation matrix on 400 random points in the unit square, for each model with practical range about 0.5. A valid model gives eigenvalues \(\ge 0\) (up to rounding). For contrast, two invalid functions:

the triangular function \(\max(1 - h/a, 0)\), valid only in one dimension;
a stable model with \(\alpha = 2.5\), built by hand.



Code
pts = np.random.default_rng(1).uniform(0, 1, (400, 2))
D = np.sqrt(((pts[:, None] - pts[None]) ** 2).sum(-1))
mats = {"spherical": correlation_function(D, "spherical", 0.5 / 0.81),
        "exponential": correlation_function(D, "exponential", 0.5 / 3),
        "gaussian": correlation_function(D, "gaussian", 0.5 / np.sqrt(3)),
        "matern nu=1.5": correlation_function(D, "matern", 0.5 / 4.75, nu=1.5),
        "cubic": correlation_function(D, "cubic", 0.5),
        "stable alpha=1.5": correlation_function(D, "stable", 0.5 / 3 ** (1 / 1.5), alpha=1.5),
        "INVALID triangular (1-D only)": np.maximum(1 - D / 0.5, 0.0),
        "INVALID stable alpha=2.5": np.exp(-(D / 0.3) ** 2.5)}
eig = pd.Series({k: np.linalg.eigvalsh(v).min() for k, v in mats.items()}, name="smallest eigenvalue")
display(eig.to_frame())
valid_ok = all(eig[k] > -1e-8 for k in mats if not k.startswith("INVALID"))
invalid_neg = all(eig[k] < -1e-6 for k in mats if k.startswith("INVALID"))
record("valid models positive semi-definite, invalid ones not", "PASS" if valid_ok and invalid_neg else "FAIL")

All six GeoLattice models give a non-negative smallest eigenvalue. The values run from \(1.3 \times 10^{-2}\) (exponential) down to \(5 \times 10^{-5}\) (Matérn) and \(-1.3 \times 10^{-14}\) for the Gaussian. The Gaussian value is rounding error: the matrix is valid but numerically singular, which Section 10 looks at.
The two invalid functions give clearly negative eigenvalues: −0.42 for the triangular function, which is valid only in one dimension, and −1.02 for the stable model with \(\alpha = 2.5\). Kriging with either matrix can produce negative variances, and Cholesky-based simulation fails. This is why correlation_function rejects \(\alpha > 2\).

title: Correlation Functions (correlation_function)
text:
Numerical Conditioning
The condition number of \(\mathbf{R}\) for 300 random points in the unit square, as the practical range grows from 0.1 to 2, for a rough model (exponential), a moderately smooth one (Matérn \(\nu = 1.5\)) and a very smooth one (Gaussian). Adding a relative nugget of 0.01 shows the usual remedy.


Code
pts = np.random.default_rng(2).uniform(0, 1, (300, 2))
D = np.sqrt(((pts[:, None] - pts[None]) ** 2).sum(-1))
prs = np.geomspace(0.1, 2.0, 12)
rows = []
for pr_ in prs:
    row = {"practical range": pr_}
    for name, model, a_fac, kw in [("exponential", "exponential", 1 / 3, {}), ("matern 1.5", "matern", 1 / 4.75, dict(nu=1.5)),
                                   ("gaussian", "gaussian", 1 / np.sqrt(3), {})]:
        R = correlation_function(D, model, pr_ * a_fac, **kw)
        row[name] = np.linalg.cond(R)
        row[name + " + nugget 0.01"] = np.linalg.cond(R + 0.01 * np.eye(len(D)))
    rows.append(row)
cond = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("practical range")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.8))
for col, st in [("exponential", "-"), ("matern 1.5", "-"), ("gaussian", "-"), ("gaussian + nugget 0.01", "--")]:
    ax.semilogy(cond.index, cond[col], st, marker="o", ms=3, label=col)
ax.axhline(1e16, color="k", ls=":", lw=1, label="1 / machine epsilon")
ax.set_xlabel("practical range (unit square)")
ax.set_ylabel("condition number of R")
ax.legend()

The smoothness of the model, more than the range, drives conditioning:

Practical range 0.1. The condition numbers are 61 (exponential), \(1.2 \times 10^3\) (Matérn 1.5) and \(1.1 \times 10^5\) (Gaussian).
Practical range 0.39. The Gaussian matrix reaches \(7 \times 10^{17}\). That is beyond \(1/\varepsilon \approx 10^{16}\), so its solution has no correct digits.
Practical range 2. The values are \(4.7 \times 10^4\) (exponential), \(2.7 \times 10^8\) (Matérn) and \(9.7 \times 10^{19}\) (Gaussian).

A relative nugget of 0.01 brings the Gaussian down to \(4.1 \times 10^3\) and \(2.4 \times 10^4\) for the last two ranges, similar to the exponential. A Gaussian model therefore needs a nugget in practice, even when the data seem to have none.

title: Correlation Functions (correlation_function)
text:
Simulated Two-Dimensional Fields
correlation_function is all that is needed to simulate a Gaussian field: build \(\mathbf{R}\), factor it, and multiply white noise. Fields on a 60 × 60 grid, with the same random numbers and a practical range of 0.3 for every model, show the texture each model implies.


Code
n = 60
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, 1, n), np.linspace(0, 1, n))
P = np.column_stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()])
Dg = np.sqrt(((P[:, None] - P[None]) ** 2).sum(-1))
eps = np.random.default_rng(3).standard_normal(len(P))
specs = [("exponential", "exponential", 0.3 / 3, {}), ("spherical", "spherical", 0.3 / 0.81, {}),
         ("matern nu = 1.5", "matern", 0.3 / 4.75, dict(nu=1.5)), ("gaussian", "gaussian", 0.3 / np.sqrt(3), {}),
         ("stable alpha = 0.5", "stable", 0.3 / 9.0, dict(alpha=0.5)), ("cubic", "cubic", 0.3 / 0.6, {})]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(17, 11))
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for ax, (title, model, a_, kw) in zip(axes.flat, specs):
    R = correlation_function(Dg, model, a_, **kw)
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(R + 1e-6 * np.eye(len(P)))
    im = ax.imshow((L @ eps).reshape(n, n), origin="lower", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-2.5, vmax=2.5)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
print(f"6 fields of {len(P)} nodes in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


6 fields of 3600 nodes in 3.9 s









All six fields share the same random numbers and the same practical range, so their large features sit in the same places. The differences are in the short-scale texture:

the exponential and stable \(\alpha = 0.5\) fields are speckled, and the stable one has the most fine detail;
the spherical field is also rough at short scale;
the Matérn \(\nu = 1.5\) and cubic fields show smooth blobs;
the Gaussian field is the smoothest.

Each field took about 0.7 s, because a dense Cholesky factorization costs \(O(n^3)\). For grids much beyond a few thousand nodes, use the sequential simulators of Section 05_07 instead.

title: Correlation Functions (correlation_function)
text:
Choosing a Model from Data
Which correlation model fits a real variable? BayesianKriging computes the marginal likelihood of each model, integrated over a grid of ranges and nugget ratios. The sum over the grid, weighted by the prior, is the model evidence, and differences of log evidence are log Bayes factors. For log-cadmium in the Jura, the candidates are:

the spherical, exponential, Gaussian and cubic models;
Matérn with \(\nu \in \{1, 1.5, 2.5\}\);
stable with \(\alpha \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.5\}\).

Matérn \(\nu = 0.5\) and stable \(\alpha = 1\) are left out because they are the exponential model; including them would count the same model three times in the posterior probabilities. Each range grid covers practical ranges from 0.1 to 4 km, and all models share the same flat trend and \(\sigma^2\) priors, so their evidences are comparable. The model prior is uniform over the list.


Code
DATA = "../../../../Data/00_shared/data_geostatistics/"
jura = pd.read_csv(DATA + "jura_data.csv", index_col=0)
xyj = jura[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
zj = np.log(jura["Cd"].to_numpy(float))
PRAC = np.geomspace(0.1, 4.0, 25)
NUG = [0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0]
candidates = [("spherical", "spherical", 1.5, 1 / 0.81), ("exponential", "exponential", 1.5, 1 / 3),
              ("gaussian", "gaussian", 1.5, 1 / np.sqrt(3)), ("cubic", "cubic", 1.5, 1 / 0.6)]
for nu in [1.0, 1.5, 2.5]:
    candidates.append((f"matern nu = {nu}", "matern", nu, 1 / practical("matern", nu=nu)))
for a_ in [0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.5]:
    candidates.append((f"stable alpha = {a_}", "stable", a_, 1 / np.log(20) ** (1 / a_)))
rows = []
for name, model, shape, fac in candidates:
    m = BayesianKriging(model, nu=shape, range_grid=PRAC * fac, nugget_grid=NUG).fit(xyj, zj)
    p_ = m.posterior_
    rows.append({"model": name, "log evidence": logsumexp(p_.log_marginal + p_.log_prior),
                 "posterior mean practical range (km)": float((p_.weight * p_.range).sum() / fac),
                 "posterior mean nugget ratio": float((p_.weight * p_.nugget_ratio).sum())})
ev = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model")
ev["log Bayes factor vs best"] = ev["log evidence"] - ev["log evidence"].max()
ev["posterior probability"] = np.exp(ev["log Bayes factor vs best"]) / np.exp(ev["log Bayes factor vs best"]).sum()
display(ev.sort_values("log evidence", ascending=False).round(3))

The evidence ranks the models by their behaviour at the origin. The rough models come first:

stable \(\alpha = 0.5\), posterior probability 0.69;
stable \(\alpha = 0.75\), 0.28;
exponential, 0.026.

Every model that is parabolic at the origin has a log Bayes factor of −6 or worse (Matérn \(\nu \ge 1\), stable \(\alpha = 1.5\), cubic), and the Gaussian is at −11.0. Log-cadmium in the Jura is a rough variable.
The two stable models win by changing how the variance is split. Stable \(\alpha = 0.5\) has a posterior mean nugget ratio of 0.036 and a practical range of 1.6 km, against 0.25 and 0.49 km for the exponential. Its correlation drops steeply near the origin and then decays slowly, so it treats as spatial structure much of what the exponential model calls nugget. Going further, to \(\alpha = 0.25\), is strongly rejected (−12.7), and its practical range of 3.5 km is close to the top of the 4 km grid.
Evidence measures how well a model predicts the data as a whole. A hold-out check asks the practical question directly. The models are fitted on a 70% training set, stratified by land use (random_state=42), and the 30% test set is predicted as new observations (signal=False, which includes the nugget). The scores are RMSE, the coverage of the 90% predictive interval, and the mean log predictive density (MLPD; higher is better), computed from the Student-t mixture.


Code
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedShuffleSplit

tr, te = next(StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.3, random_state=42).split(xyj, jura["Landuse"]))
rows = []
for name, model, shape, fac in candidates:
    m = BayesianKriging(model, nu=shape, range_grid=PRAC * fac, nugget_grid=NUG).fit(xyj[tr], zj[tr])
    mean = m.predict(xyj[te], signal=False)
    q = m.predict_quantiles(xyj[te], [0.05, 0.95], signal=False)
    loc, sc, dof = m._component_predictions(xyj[te], signal=False)
    dens = (m._weights[:, None] * stats.t.pdf((zj[te][None] - loc) / sc, dof[:, None]) / sc).sum(0)
    rows.append({"model": name, "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((mean - zj[te]) ** 2)),
                 "90% coverage": np.mean((zj[te] >= q[:, 0]) & (zj[te] <= q[:, 1])),
                 "MLPD": np.mean(np.log(dens))})
ho = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model").sort_values("MLPD", ascending=False)
display(ho.round(3))
print(f"test points: {len(te)}")
record("hold-out 90% intervals cover 80-97% for every model",
       "PASS" if ho["90% coverage"].between(0.80, 0.97).all() else "FAIL",
       f"range {ho['90% coverage'].min():.2f}-{ho['90% coverage'].max():.2f}")

On the 108 test points, the hold-out comparison splits the models into the same two groups as the evidence:

Rough models. Stable \(\alpha = 0.75\), the exponential and stable \(\alpha = 0.5\) are nearly tied, with RMSE 0.528 to 0.531, MLPD −0.742 to −0.749 and 90% coverage 0.944.

correlation_function(h, model, range_, nu, alpha) returns \(\rho(h) = 1 - \gamma(h)\) for six models in the Variogram parametrization, with \(\rho(0) = 1\), and it rejects a stable \(\alpha\) outside \((0, 2]\). In the Bayesian kriging classes, nu is the Matérn smoothness or the stable exponent.
The behaviour at the origin sets the smoothness of the field: slope 1 for the exponential and spherical, 2 for the Gaussian, cubic and Matérn \(\nu > 1\), and \(\alpha\) for the stable model. It also matters most for prediction.
range_ is not comparable across models. The practical range is \(\ln 20\,a\) for the exponential, \(1.73a\) for the Gaussian, \(0.81a\) for the spherical and \(4.74a\) for Matérn \(\nu = 1.5\).
The Matérn closed forms and the Gaussian limit check out to machine precision and to 0.005 respectively. Stable \(\alpha = 1\) and \(2\) reproduce the exponential and the Gaussian exactly.
All six models are positive definite in 2D; the triangular function and stable \(\alpha > 2\) are not.
Smooth models make the correlation matrix ill-conditioned: the Gaussian passes \(10^{17}\) at a moderate range. A small nugget fixes it.
For Jura log-cadmium, both the marginal likelihood and a hold-out test favour models that are rough at the origin over smooth ones. Comparing correlation models by evidence in BayesianKriging is a quick, principled way to choose.

title: Conjugate Bayesian Kriging (ConjugateBayesianKriging)
Conjugate Bayesian Kriging (ConjugateBayesianKriging)
text:
Theory

The model with a known correlation
\[
\mathbf{z} \mid \boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\bigl(\mathbf{F}\boldsymbol\beta,\; \sigma^2\mathbf{V}\bigr),
\qquad
\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{R}(\phi) + \tau\mathbf{I},
\]
with:

\(\mathbf{F}\) the \(n \times p\) trend matrix (a constant, a polynomial in the coordinates, covariates);
\(\mathbf{R}(\phi)\) the correlation matrix of the chosen model at the fixed range \(\phi\);
\(\tau\) the fixed relative nugget (nugget / partial sill);
\(\sigma^2\) the unknown partial sill.



The normal-inverse-gamma prior
The conjugate prior is
\[
\boldsymbol\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}, \sigma^2\mathbf{V}_\beta),
\qquad
\sigma^2 \sim \text{Scale-inv-}\chi^2(n_0, s_0^2),
\]

\(n_0\) acts as a number of “prior observations” of the variance, with prior guess \(s_0^2\);
\(\mathbf{V}_\beta\) expresses how sure the prior is about the trend, in units of the sill.

The reference prior, \(p(\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2\) (beta_prior="flat", sigma2_prior="reciprocal"), is the limit \(\mathbf{V}_\beta^{-1} \to 0\), \(n_0 \to 0\).


The posterior
With \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{F}\):
\[
\mathbf{V}_\beta^* = \bigl(\mathbf{V}_\beta^{-1} + \mathbf{A}\bigr)^{-1},
\qquad
\boldsymbol\beta^* = \mathbf{V}_\beta^*\bigl(\mathbf{V}_\beta^{-1}\mathbf{m} + \mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{z}\bigr),
\]
\[
\boldsymbol\beta \mid \sigma^2, \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\beta^*, \sigma^2\mathbf{V}_\beta^*),
\qquad
\sigma^2 \mid \mathbf{z} \sim \text{Scale-inv-}\chi^2(\nu^*, S^{*2}),
\qquad
\nu^* = n_0 + n,
\qquad
\nu^* S^{*2} = n_0 s_0^2 + Q,
\]
where \(Q = (\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{F}\mathbf{m})^\top(\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{F}\mathbf{V}_\beta\mathbf{F}^\top)^{-1}(\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{F}\mathbf{m})\).

The posterior trend is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean \(\mathbf{m}\) and the GLS estimate \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{z}\).
The posterior sill pools the prior guess \(s_0^2\) (weight \(n_0\)) with what the data say.
Under the reference prior, \(\boldsymbol\beta^*\) is the GLS estimate, \(\nu^* = n - p\), and \(S^{*2}\) is the GLS residual variance.



The Student-t predictive
At a new location \(\mathbf{x}_0\), with \(\mathbf{r}_0\) its correlations to the data, \(\mathbf{f}_0\) its trend row and \(\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{f}_0 - \mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}_0\), integrating out \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\) gives
\[
z(\mathbf{x}_0) \mid \mathbf{z} \;\sim\; t_{\nu^*}\Bigl(
\underbrace{\mathbf{f}_0^\top\boldsymbol\beta^* + \mathbf{r}_0^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{F}\boldsymbol\beta^*)}_{\text{kriging predictor}},\;\;
S^{*2}\bigl[\underbrace{v_{00} - \mathbf{r}_0^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}_0}_{\text{simple-kriging part}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{g}^\top\mathbf{V}_\beta^*\mathbf{g}}_{\text{trend uncertainty}}\bigr]\Bigr),
\]
with \(v_{00} = 1\) for the noise-free signal and \(1 + \tau\) for a new observation. Three sources of uncertainty are visible:

the field itself, the simple-kriging variance, small near data;
the trend, \(\mathbf{g}^\top\mathbf{V}_\beta^*\mathbf{g}\), which grows as \(\mathbf{f}_0\) moves away from the data’s trend values, so it matters most when extrapolating a polynomial trend;
the sill, through the Student-t: with few data \(\nu^*\) is small, so the tails are heavy and intervals wider than Gaussian ones with the same scale.



Special cases: ordinary, universal and simple kriging

Flat trend prior: the location is the universal kriging predictor (ordinary kriging for trend=0), and the bracket is the universal kriging variance in correlation units.
\(\mathbf{V}_\beta \to \mathbf{0}\), a known trend \(\mathbf{m}\): the trend term vanishes, the location is simple kriging with mean \(\mathbf{m}\), and the variance is the simple-kriging variance.

In between, an informative \(\mathbf{V}_\beta\) gives a predictor between simple and ordinary kriging, weighting the prior mean against the data.


What the conjugate model does not cover
The range, the correlation model and the nugget ratio are treated as known. Their uncertainty is not in the intervals. BayesianKriging puts them on a grid and averages over their posterior; Section 10 measures the difference.

Data and the Fixed Variogram
The Jura cadmium data on the log scale, with the same 70/30 split by land use as the other Bayesian kriging notebooks. A spherical variogram is fitted to the 251 training samples. Its range and relative nugget are then fixed for the conjugate model.


Code
DATA = "../../../../Data/00_shared/data_geostatistics/"
jura = pd.read_csv(DATA + "jura_data.csv", index_col=0)
jura["logCd"] = np.log(jura["Cd"])
sss = StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.30, random_state=42)
tr, te = next(sss.split(jura, jura["Landuse"]))
train, test = jura.iloc[tr].reset_index(drop=True), jura.iloc[te].reset_index(drop=True)
xy, xy_test = train[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float), test[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
z, z_test = train["logCd"].to_numpy(float), test["logCd"].to_numpy(float)

vg = Variogram(xy, z, model="spherical", n_lags=15, estimator="matheron", use_gpu=False).fit()
NUG, PSILL, RANGE = (float(v) for v in vg.fitted_params[:3])
TAU = NUG / PSILL
print(f"spherical variogram: nugget {NUG:.3f}, partial sill {PSILL:.3f}, range {RANGE:.2f} km  ->  relative nugget {TAU:.2f}")
hh = np.linspace(0, 3, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(vg.lags, vg.experimental, "o", label="experimental")
ax.plot(hh, vg(hh), "r-", label="fitted spherical")
ax.set_xlabel("h (km)")
ax.set_ylabel("semivariance of log(Cd)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Conjugate Bayesian Kriging (ConjugateBayesianKriging)
section: From a Fitted Variogram to a Bayesian Predictor
text:
From a Fitted Variogram to a Bayesian Predictor
BayesianKriging.from_variogram(vg) builds a ConjugateBayesianKriging with the variogram’s range and relative nugget and the reference prior. Its predictive mean should equal ordinary kriging with the same variogram, and its predictive scale should be the ordinary kriging variance with the sill replaced by the posterior estimate.


Code
cbk = BayesianKriging.from_variogram(vg).fit(xy, z)
print(type(cbk).__name__, "| range", cbk.range_grid, "| nugget ratio", np.round(cbk.nugget_grid, 3))
c = cbk._comps[0]
print(f"posterior: beta* = {c['beta'][0]:.3f}, S^2 = {c['s2']:.3f} (fitted partial sill {PSILL:.3f}), dof = {c['dof']:.0f}")

ok = OrdinaryKriging(vg, use_gpu=False).fit(xy, z)
ok_mean, ok_se = ok.predict(xy_test, return_variance=True)
c_mean, c_sd = cbk.predict(xy_test, return_std=True, signal=False)
loc, scale, dof = cbk._component_predictions(xy_test, signal=False)
record("conjugate mean == ordinary kriging", "PASS" if np.allclose(c_mean, ok_mean, atol=1e-4) else "FAIL",
       f"max |diff| {np.abs(c_mean - ok_mean).max():.1e}")
ratio = (scale[0] ** 2 / c["s2"]) / (ok_se ** 2 / (NUG + PSILL) * (1 + TAU))
print(f"(Student-t scale^2 / S^2) / (OK variance / sill, observation scale): mean {ratio.mean():.4f}")


ConjugateBayesianKriging | range [1.33409093] | nugget ratio [1.164]
posterior: beta* = 0.071, S^2 = 0.213 (fitted partial sill 0.210), dof = 250
✅ [PASS] conjugate mean == ordinary kriging  max |diff| 9.5e-09
(Student-t scale^2 / S^2) / (OK variance / sill, observation scale): mean 1.0000


Both identities hold exactly:

Location. The predictive mean equals ordinary kriging to \(10^{-8}\).
Scale. Student-t scale² / \(S^2\) equals the ordinary kriging variance divided by the partial sill (ratio 1.0000).

The conjugate model is ordinary kriging, with two changes:

the sill is estimated from the data in the same pass, \(S^2 = 0.213\) against the fitted 0.210;
the distribution is a Student-t with \(n - 1 = 250\) degrees of freedom.

With 251 samples the t is practically Gaussian, so the intervals are the same. The next section shows when they differ.

title: Conjugate Bayesian Kriging (ConjugateBayesianKriging)
section: Small Samples: Why the Student-t Matters
text:
Small Samples: Why the Student-t Matters
With 251 samples the Student-t has 250 degrees of freedom and is a Gaussian. Its value shows with few samples. The experiment repeats, 60 times for each sample size \(n \in \{8, 12, 20, 40, 80, 160\}\):

draw \(n\) random training sites from all 359;
predict 100 other random sites with the variogram fixed (range and relative nugget from the full data set; only the sill is estimated);
score the 90% intervals of three predictors:

conjugate Bayesian: Student-t with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom and scale from \(S^2\);
plug-in Gaussian: the same location and scale, but Gaussian quantiles, which is what a kriging analysis with an estimated sill reports;
oracle Gaussian: Gaussian with the sill estimated from all 359 samples, which no real analysis has.




Code
all_xy = jura[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
all_z = jura["logCd"].to_numpy(float)
vg_all = Variogram(all_xy, all_z, model="spherical", n_lags=15, estimator="matheron", use_gpu=False).fit()
nug_a, psill_a, range_a = (float(v) for v in vg_all.fitted_params[:3])
tau_a = nug_a / psill_a
oracle_s2 = ConjugateBayesianKriging("spherical", range_=range_a, nugget_ratio=tau_a).fit(all_xy, all_z)._comps[0]["s2"]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
rows = []
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for n in [8, 12, 20, 40, 80, 160]:
    cov_t, cov_g, cov_o, w_t, w_g = [], [], [], [], []
    for rep in range(60):
        idx = rng.permutation(len(all_z))
        trn, tst = idx[:n], idx[n:n + 100]
        m = ConjugateBayesianKriging("spherical", range_=range_a, nugget_ratio=tau_a).fit(all_xy[trn], all_z[trn])
        loc_, sc_, df_ = m._component_predictions(all_xy[tst], signal=False)
        loc_, sc_, df_ = loc_[0], sc_[0], df_[0]
        unit = sc_ / np.sqrt(m._comps[0]["s2"])
        yt = all_z[tst]
        qt, qg = stats.t.ppf(0.95, df_), stats.norm.ppf(0.95)
        cov_t.append(np.mean(np.abs(yt - loc_) <= qt * sc_))
        cov_g.append(np.mean(np.abs(yt - loc_) <= qg * sc_))
        cov_o.append(np.mean(np.abs(yt - loc_) <= qg * unit * np.sqrt(oracle_s2)))
        w_t.append(np.mean(2 * qt * sc_))
        w_g.append(np.mean(2 * qg * sc_))
    rows.append({"n": n, "dof": n - 1, "coverage: conjugate t": np.mean(cov_t), "coverage: plug-in Gaussian": np.mean(cov_g),
                 "coverage: oracle Gaussian": np.mean(cov_o), "width: t": np.mean(w_t), "width: Gaussian": np.mean(w_g),
                 "t / Gaussian width": np.mean(w_t) / np.mean(w_g)})
small = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("n")
print(f"{6 * 60} fits in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
display(small.round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.5))
for col, c_ in [("coverage: conjugate t", "tab:blue"), ("coverage: plug-in Gaussian", "tab:red"), ("coverage: oracle Gaussian", "0.5")]:
    ax.plot(small.index, small[col], "o-", c=c_, label=col.replace("coverage: ", ""))
ax.axhline(0.9, color="k", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xticks(small.index, small.index)
ax.set_xlabel("number of training samples n")
ax.set_ylabel("coverage of nominal 90% intervals")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
record("Student-t closer to 90% than plug-in Gaussian at n = 8",
       "PASS" if abs(small.loc[8, "coverage: conjugate t"] - 0.9) < abs(small.loc[8, "coverage: plug-in Gaussian"] - 0.9) else "FAIL",

Few samples: the Student-t keeps its promise. With 8 samples, the Student-t intervals cover 90.2% of the held-out values, while the Gaussian intervals with the same estimated sill cover only 86.4%. The t intervals are 15% wider at \(n = 8\) and 9% wider at \(n = 12\), and that extra width is exactly what is needed to account for estimating the sill from a handful of values.

Speed. The 360 fits took half a second: the conjugate model is as cheap as kriging.

title: Conjugate Bayesian Kriging (ConjugateBayesianKriging)
section: Between Simple and Ordinary Kriging: the Trend Prior
text:
Between Simple and Ordinary Kriging: the Trend Prior
With trend=0, the trend is a single mean \(\beta_0\). A normal prior \(\beta_0 \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(m, \sigma^2 v_\beta)\) moves the predictor between two classical estimators:

\(v_\beta \to \infty\) gives ordinary kriging;
\(v_\beta \to 0\) gives simple kriging with mean \(m\).

The prior mean here is \(m = 0\) on the log scale, i.e. Cd = 1 mg/kg, a plausible regional value. The limits are checked against OrdinaryKriging and SimpleKriging(mean=0), and the posterior mean of \(\beta_0\) is traced along the way.


Code
M0 = 0.0
sk = SimpleKriging(vg, mean=M0, use_gpu=False).fit(xy, z)
sk_mean = sk.predict(xy_test)
rows = []
for vb in [1e-8, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0, 10.0, 1e8]:
    m = ConjugateBayesianKriging("spherical", range_=RANGE, nugget_ratio=TAU,
                                 beta_prior=("normal", [M0], [[vb]])).fit(xy, z)
    pm, ps = m.predict(xy_test, return_std=True, signal=False)
    rows.append({"prior variance v_beta": vb, "posterior beta0": m._comps[0]["beta"][0],
                 "max |mean - SK|": np.abs(pm - sk_mean).max(), "max |mean - OK|": np.abs(pm - ok_mean).max(),
                 "mean predictive sd": ps.mean(), "test RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((pm - z_test) ** 2))})
limits = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("prior variance v_beta")
display(limits.round(4))
record("tiny prior variance reproduces simple kriging", "PASS" if limits.iloc[0]["max |mean - SK|"] < 1e-3 else "FAIL",
       f"max diff {limits.iloc[0]['max |mean - SK|']:.1e}")
record("huge prior variance reproduces ordinary kriging", "PASS" if limits.iloc[-1]["max |mean - OK|"] < 1e-3 else "FAIL",
       f"max diff {limits.iloc[-1]['max |mean - OK|']:.1e}")

title: Conjugate Bayesian Kriging (ConjugateBayesianKriging)
section: Trend Uncertainty Away from the Data
text:
Trend Uncertainty Away from the Data
The trend term \(\mathbf{g}^\top\mathbf{V}_\beta^*\mathbf{g}\) in the predictive variance grows as the prediction point moves away from where the trend was estimated. Along an east-west transect through the study area, extended 3 km beyond it on both sides, the predictive sd is compared for a constant (trend=0), linear (trend=1) and quadratic (trend=2) trend. The test-set accuracy of the three is also compared.


Code
tx = np.linspace(xy[:, 0].min() - 3, xy[:, 0].max() + 3, 300)
transect = np.column_stack([tx, np.full_like(tx, np.median(xy[:, 1]))])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(17, 4.6))
rows = []
for deg, c_ in [(0, "tab:blue"), (1, "tab:orange"), (2, "tab:green")]:

    mu_, sd_ = m.predict(transect, return_std=True)
    axes[0].plot(tx, sd_, c=c_, label=f"trend = {deg}")
    axes[1].plot(tx, mu_, c=c_, label=f"trend = {deg}")
    pm, ps = m.predict(xy_test, return_std=True, signal=False)

Inside the study area, the three trend models give nearly the same predictive sd: test RMSE 0.558-0.562, coverage 0.91-0.93. A polynomial trend adds nothing to these data, and the quadratic model’s six coefficients cost a little coverage.
Outside the data, they differ sharply:

with a constant trend, the sd levels off at the sill, because the prediction reverts to the estimated mean;
with a linear trend, it grows linearly with distance;
with a quadratic trend, it grows quadratically.

The trend term \(\mathbf{g}^\top\mathbf{V}_\beta^*\mathbf{g}\) measures how far the trend is being extrapolated, and the predictive means diverge accordingly. Plug-in universal kriging includes the same term in its variance, but a polynomial trend should never be extrapolated far without strong reasons.

title: Conjugate Bayesian Kriging (ConjugateBayesianKriging)
section: Informative Priors from an Earlier Survey
text:
Informative Priors from an Earlier Survey
A common situation: a new survey has only a few samples, but an earlier survey nearby gives a fair idea of the mean and variability. The Jura is split at its median x coordinate:

the western samples play the earlier survey;
in the east, 15 sites are drawn as the new survey, and the remaining eastern sites are predicted.

The earlier survey’s posterior becomes the prior for the new one:

trend: \(\mathbf{m}\) = its \(\beta^*\), and \(\mathbf{V}_\beta\) = its \(\mathbf{V}_\beta^*\) inflated 5× as a discount, because two areas are not identical;
variance: \(n_0 = 10\) prior “observations” of the variance at its \(S^2\).

Three priors are compared on 40 random draws of the 15 eastern sites:

the reference prior;
the earlier survey’s prior;
a deliberately wrong, confident prior: a mean 1.5 log units too high with a small \(\mathbf{V}_\beta\).



Code
west = jura["Xloc"] < jura["Xloc"].median()
xy_w, z_w = jura.loc[west, ["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float), jura.loc[west, "logCd"].to_numpy(float)
xy_e, z_e = jura.loc[~west, ["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float), jura.loc[~west, "logCd"].to_numpy(float)
old = ConjugateBayesianKriging("spherical", range_=range_a, nugget_ratio=tau_a).fit(xy_w, z_w)._comps[0]
print(f"earlier survey (west, n = {len(z_w)}): beta* {old['beta'][0]:.3f}, S^2 {old['s2']:.3f};  "
      f"east mean log(Cd) {z_e.mean():.3f}, variance {z_e.var():.3f}")
priors = {
    "reference (flat, 1/sigma^2)": dict(),
    "earlier survey": dict(beta_prior=("normal", old["beta"], 5 * old["Vbeta"]),
                           sigma2_prior=("scaled_inv_chi2", 10.0, old["s2"])),
    "wrong and confident": dict(beta_prior=("normal", old["beta"] + 1.5, 0.01 * np.eye(1)),
                                sigma2_prior=("scaled_inv_chi2", 10.0, old["s2"])),
}
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
res = {k: {"rmse": [], "cover": [], "width": [], "beta": []} for k in priors}
for rep in range(40):
    idx = rng.permutation(len(z_e))
    trn, tst = idx[:15], idx[15:]
    for k, kw in priors.items():
        m = ConjugateBayesianKriging("spherical", range_=range_a, nugget_ratio=tau_a, **kw).fit(xy_e[trn], z_e[trn])
        pm = m.predict(xy_e[tst], signal=False)
        q = m.predict_quantiles(xy_e[tst], [0.05, 0.95], signal=False)
        res[k]["rmse"].append(np.sqrt(np.mean((pm - z_e[tst]) ** 2)))
        res[k]["cover"].append(np.mean((z_e[tst] >= q[:, 0]) & (z_e[tst] <= q[:, 1])))
        res[k]["width"].append(np.mean(q[:, 1] - q[:, 0]))
        res[k]["beta"].append(m._comps[0]["beta"][0])
prior_tab = pd.DataFrame({k: {"RMSE": np.mean(v["rmse"]), "coverage 90%": np.mean(v["cover"]),
                              "width 90%": np.mean(v["width"]), "posterior beta0 (mean)": np.mean(v["beta"]),
                              "posterior beta0 (sd over draws)": np.std(v["beta"])} for k, v in res.items()}).T
display(prior_tab.round(3))
record("earlier-survey prior beats the reference prior with 15 samples (RMSE)",
       "PASS" if prior_tab.loc["earlier survey", "RMSE"] < prior_tab.loc["reference (flat, 1/sigma^2)", "RMSE"] else "FAIL",
       f"{prior_tab.loc['reference (flat, 1/sigma^2)', 'RMSE']:.3f} -> {prior_tab.loc['earlier survey', 'RMSE']:.3f}")

The east and the west differ: the earlier survey’s mean is −0.02 in log(Cd), the east’s 0.21. That is a realistic test of borrowing information.

The earlier-survey prior helps, modestly. The posterior of \(\beta_0\) varies less between draws of the 15 sites (sd 0.095 against 0.141), RMSE improves slightly (0.578 against 0.583), and coverage rises to 0.93. The prior pulls \(\beta_0\) toward the west’s lower mean (0.14 against 0.22), the cost of borrowing from a different area. The 5× discount on \(\mathbf{V}_\beta\) keeps that pull moderate.
The wrong, confident prior hurts the predictions (RMSE 0.89), since it fixes \(\beta_0\) at 1.42, far from the data. Yet its intervals still cover 93%. In the conjugate model, a conflict between prior and data inflates \(Q\) and with it the posterior sill \(S^{*2}\), so the intervals widen (3.1 against 2.0 log units). The model signals its own conflict, and it is worth checking: a posterior sill far above the prior’s \(s_0^2\), or \(\beta^*\) far from the GLS estimate, means the prior and the data disagree.

title: Conjugate Bayesian Kriging (ConjugateBayesianKriging)
section: The Weak Point: a Fixed Range
text:
The Weak Point: a Fixed Range
The conjugate model is only as good as the fixed range and nugget. The same predictor is run on the 70/30 split with the range multiplied by 0.25 to 4 (the relative nugget kept), and compared with BayesianKriging, which averages over a grid of ranges and nugget ratios instead of fixing them.


Code
rows = []
for f in [0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0]:
    m = ConjugateBayesianKriging("spherical", range_=RANGE * f, nugget_ratio=TAU).fit(xy, z)
    pm = m.predict(xy_test, signal=False)
    q = m.predict_quantiles(xy_test, [0.05, 0.95], signal=False)
    rows.append({"model": f"conjugate, range x {f}", "range (km)": RANGE * f, "test RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((pm - z_test) ** 2)),
                 "coverage 90%": np.mean((z_test >= q[:, 0]) & (z_test <= q[:, 1])), "width 90%": np.mean(q[:, 1] - q[:, 0])})
bk = BayesianKriging("spherical", range_grid=np.geomspace(0.1, 4, 25), nugget_grid=[0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5]).fit(xy, z)
pm = bk.predict(xy_test, signal=False)
q = bk.predict_quantiles(xy_test, [0.05, 0.95], signal=False)
rows.append({"model": "BayesianKriging (grid over range and nugget)", "range (km)": float((bk.posterior_.weight * bk.posterior_.range).sum()),
             "test RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((pm - z_test) ** 2)), "coverage 90%": np.mean((z_test >= q[:, 0]) & (z_test <= q[:, 1])),
             "width 90%": np.mean(q[:, 1] - q[:, 0])})

The predictions are fairly robust to the fixed range. Halving or doubling the range changes test RMSE by about 0.01, and coverage stays between 0.91 and 0.94. Even a 4× error costs only 0.03 in RMSE.
But nothing in the conjugate output warns about a wrong range. The intervals are about equally wide whatever the range: the conjugate model reports uncertainty given the range.
BayesianKriging, which averages over the range and the nugget (posterior mean range 0.49 km, much shorter than the fitted 1.33 km), matches the best fixed range on RMSE (0.556) and coverage (0.935) without having to know it.

With this many well-spread data, the fixed-range model loses little. With sparse data, or when the variogram fit is uncertain, the difference grows, and that is the case for BayesianKriging.

title: Conjugate Bayesian Kriging (ConjugateBayesianKriging)
text:
Maps
On a 100 m version of the Jura grid (1,540 nodes), the conjugate model with the fitted variogram gives exact Student-t summaries at every node:

the predictive median of log(Cd), back-transformed as exp(median), which is the median Cd;
the width of the 90% interval;
\(P(\text{Cd} > 0.8 \text{ mg/kg})\).



Code
grid_df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "jura_grid.csv", index_col=0)
g = grid_df[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
i50 = np.rint((g[:, 0] - g[:, 0].min()) / 0.05).astype(int)
j50 = np.rint((g[:, 1] - g[:, 1].min()) / 0.05).astype(int)
grid = g[(i50 % 2 == 0) & (j50 % 2 == 0)]
gi = np.rint((grid[:, 0] - grid[:, 0].min()) / 0.1).astype(int)
gj = np.rint((grid[:, 1] - grid[:, 1].min()) / 0.1).astype(int)
EXT = [grid[:, 0].min() - 0.05, grid[:, 0].max() + 0.05, grid[:, 1].min() - 0.05, grid[:, 1].max() + 0.05]
t0 = time.perf_counter()
qg = cbk.predict_quantiles(grid, [0.05, 0.5, 0.95])
pg = cbk.predict_proba(grid, np.log(0.8))
print(f"{len(grid)} nodes in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(22, 6.5))
for ax, (v, title, cm, lo_, hi_) in zip(axes, [
        (np.exp(qg[:, 1]), "Median Cd = exp(median of log Cd) (mg/kg)", "YlOrRd", 0.3, 3),
        (qg[:, 2] - qg[:, 0], "Width of the 90% interval (log units)", "magma", None, None),
        (pg, "P(Cd > 0.8 mg/kg)", "RdYlBu_r", 0, 1)]):
    img = np.full((gj.max() + 1, gi.max() + 1), np.nan)
    img[gj, gi] = v
    im = ax.imshow(img, origin="lower", extent=EXT, cmap=cm, vmin=lo_, vmax=hi_, interpolation="nearest")
    ax.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], s=4, facecolors="none", edgecolors="k", linewidths=0.4)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


1540 nodes in 0.11 s










Exact and fast. The Student-t summaries are computed exactly at 1,540 nodes in about 0.1 s.
The median Cd map shows the smooth ordinary-kriging pattern.
Interval width. The 90% interval width is smallest at the samples and largest in gaps and along the edges.
Exceedance. \(P(\text{Cd} > 0.8)\) is high over most of the area (most samples exceed the guide value), and drops only where predicted cadmium is clearly low.

ConjugateBayesianKriging fixes the correlation (range, model, nugget ratio) and integrates the trend and sill out exactly. Its predictive mean equals ordinary (or universal) kriging, and its predictive distribution is a Student-t with the kriging variance scaled by the posterior sill: both identities hold to \(10^{-8}\) on the Jura data.
With few samples, the Student-t matters. With 8 samples its 90% intervals covered 90.2% of held-out values, against 86.4% for Gaussian intervals with the same estimated sill. From about 40 samples the two agree.
The trend prior spans the classical estimators: a tiny prior variance reproduces simple kriging, a huge one ordinary kriging, both exactly, with compromises in between.
Trend uncertainty is small inside the data but grows fast when a linear or quadratic trend is extrapolated.
Informative priors from an earlier survey reduced the spread of the estimated mean with only 15 new samples. A wrong, confident prior gave poor predictions, but the conjugate model widened its intervals in response to the prior-data conflict.
The fixed range is the model’s blind spot. Here the predictions were robust to it, and BayesianKriging, which averages over the range, matched the best fixed choice without knowing it.


When to use which







Situation
Choice




A trusted variogram (from a large earlier survey, or a well-established model)
ConjugateBayesianKriging / from_variogram: exact, fast, Student-t intervals


Few samples
the conjugate model at least; its t intervals stay calibrated where Gaussian plug-in intervals do not


Prior knowledge of the mean or the variability
beta_prior=("normal", m, Vb) and sigma2_prior=("scaled_inv_chi2", n0, s0sq), discounted; check for prior-data conflict


A known mean
a small Vb reproduces simple kriging with Student-t intervals


A polynomial trend
expect wide intervals outside the data, where the trend is extrapolated


Range or nugget uncertain
BayesianKriging, which averages over them
