title: Bayesian Generalized Linear Kriging (BayesianGLMKriging)
text:
Overview
Counts of disease cases, deaths, species occurrences or defects are not Gaussian: they are non-negative integers whose variance depends on their mean. A county with 3 expected deaths that records 7 has a raw rate more than twice the expected one, purely by chance. Raw rates are most extreme where populations are smallest, which is exactly where they are least reliable. Mapping them, or kriging them as if they were Gaussian, gives maps dominated by small-population noise.
Bayesian generalized linear kriging (a spatial generalized linear mixed model, GLMM; Diggle, Tawn & Moyeed, 1998) models the counts with their proper distribution, Poisson or binomial. The log rate (or logit probability) is a regression on covariates plus a spatially correlated Gaussian field. The Bayesian fit borrows strength across space: noisy small-population counties are shrunk toward their neighbours and their covariates, while large-population counties keep their own rates. Every estimate comes with a full posterior.







BayesianGLMKriging





family
"poisson" (log link, exposure / expected counts) or "binomial" (logit link, number of trials)


model
trend (polynomial in the coordinates plus covariates) + latent Gaussian field with a chosen correlation model and relative nugget


fit
MCMC: whitened latent field by MALA, random-walk Metropolis for \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\), the range on a discrete grid, plus centred (interweaving) Gibbs updates


outputs
trace_, acceptance_, latent_samples(), predictive_samples(), predict() (mean, sd, quantiles), predict_proba()



This notebook uses real county rates as the truth and simulated counts as the data:

one year of lung-cancer deaths per county, \(y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\text{rate}_i \times \text{population}_i)\);
a small diabetes survey per county, \(y_i \sim \text{Binomial}(n_i, \text{prevalence}_i)\).

Because the true rates are known, the notebook can check how much the model improves on raw rates, whether its credible intervals cover the truth, and how both depend on the size of the counts.

title: Bayesian Generalized Linear Kriging (BayesianGLMKriging)
text:
Theory

Why raw rates are noisy
For a county with expected count \(E_i\) under the region-wide rate, and observed count \(y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i \theta_i)\), the standardized mortality ratio \(\text{SMR}_i = y_i / E_i\) is unbiased for the relative risk \(\theta_i\), but
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\text{SMR}_i) = \frac{\theta_i}{E_i}.
\]
Its noise is inversely proportional to the expected count. A county with \(E_i = 2\) has a standard error of about 0.7 on a relative risk near 1, which is useless, while one with \(E_i = 1000\) has 0.03. The map of raw SMRs mostly shows where populations are small.


The spatial generalized linear mixed model
Conditionally on a latent field, the counts are independent:
\[
y_i \mid \eta_i \sim \begin{cases} \text{Poisson}\bigl(E_i\, e^{\eta_i}\bigr) & \text{(log link; } E_i \text{ = expected count or exposure)} \\ \text{Binomial}\bigl(n_i,\; \text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_i)\bigr) & \text{(logit link; } n_i \text{ = trials)} \end{cases}
\]
The linear predictor is
\[
\boldsymbol\eta = \mathbf{F}\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf{S},
\qquad
\mathbf{S} \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\mathbf{0},\; \sigma^2[\mathbf{R}(\phi) + \tau \mathbf{I}]\bigr),
\]
where:

\(\mathbf{F}\) holds the trend (intercept, optional polynomial in the coordinates) and the covariates;
\(\mathbf{R}(\phi)\) is the spatial correlation with range \(\phi\);
\(\tau\) is a relative nugget: unstructured, county-specific extra variation (overdispersion) that is not spatially smooth.

With expected counts as exposure, \(e^{\eta_i}\) is the relative risk \(\theta_i\).


Priors
\[
\boldsymbol\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\, s_\beta^2 \mathbf{I}),
\qquad
\sigma^2 \sim \text{Scale-inv-}\chi^2(\nu_0, s_0^2),
\qquad
\phi \sim \text{discrete prior on a grid}.
\]
The arguments are beta_prior_sd (default 10), sigma2_prior=(df, scale2) (default (1, 0.5)), range_grid and range_prior, and the relative nugget \(\tau\) (nugget_ratio, fixed). Counts carry much less information about the latent variance than Gaussian data do, binary data least of all, so the \(\sigma^2\) prior deserves attention.


The posterior and why it needs MCMC
The joint posterior is
\[
p(\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2, \phi, \mathbf{S} \mid \mathbf{y}) \propto \prod_i p(y_i \mid \eta_i)\; \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{S} \mid \mathbf{0}, \sigma^2\mathbf{V}(\phi))\; p(\boldsymbol\beta)\, p(\sigma^2)\, p(\phi).
\]
Because the Poisson and binomial likelihoods are not Gaussian in \(\boldsymbol\eta\), nothing integrates in closed form (unlike Gaussian Bayesian kriging), so the posterior is sampled by Markov chain Monte Carlo.


Whitening the latent field
Sampling \(\mathbf{S}\) directly mixes badly: its components are strongly correlated, and its scale changes with \(\sigma^2\) and \(\phi\). Following Christensen (2004), GeoLattice writes
\[
\mathbf{S} = \sigma \mathbf{L}(\phi)\boldsymbol\Gamma,
\qquad \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top = \mathbf{R}(\phi) + \tau\mathbf{I},
\qquad \boldsymbol\Gamma \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}),
\]
so the prior of \(\boldsymbol\Gamma\) is white noise whatever \(\sigma^2\) and \(\phi\) are. The Cholesky factors \(\mathbf{L}(\phi)\) are computed once for every range on the grid.


MALA for the latent field
\(\boldsymbol\Gamma\) is updated by the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm, a random walk that drifts along the gradient of the log posterior:
\[
\boldsymbol\Gamma' = \boldsymbol\Gamma + \frac{h}{2}\nabla(\boldsymbol\Gamma) + \sqrt{h}\,\boldsymbol\epsilon,
\qquad
\nabla(\boldsymbol\Gamma) = \sigma\mathbf{L}^\top\bigl(\mathbf{y} - E[\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol\eta]\bigr) - \boldsymbol\Gamma,
\]
with \(E[y_i \mid \eta_i] = E_i e^{\eta_i}\) (Poisson) or \(n_i\,\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_i)\) (binomial). The proposal is accepted with probability \(\min(1, \alpha)\), where
\[
\log\alpha = \log p(\boldsymbol\Gamma' \mid \cdot) - \log p(\boldsymbol\Gamma \mid \cdot) - \frac{\lVert\boldsymbol\Gamma - \boldsymbol\Gamma' - \tfrac{h}{2}\nabla(\boldsymbol\Gamma')\rVert^2 - \lVert\boldsymbol\Gamma' - \boldsymbol\Gamma - \tfrac{h}{2}\nabla(\boldsymbol\Gamma)\rVert^2}{2h}.
\]
The gradient lets all \(n\) components move at once in a sensible direction. The optimal acceptance rate for MALA is about 0.574 (Roberts & Rosenthal, 1998).


The other updates and adaptation

\(\boldsymbol\beta\): random-walk Metropolis with proposal \(\boldsymbol\beta' = \boldsymbol\beta + s_\beta\,\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\epsilon\), where \(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{C}^\top = (\mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{F})^{-1}\) shapes the proposal to the covariates.
\(\log\sigma^2\): random-walk Metropolis, including the Jacobian of the log transform.
\(\phi\): a move to a neighbouring value of its grid, accepted by the Metropolis rule. Because of the whitening, changing \(\sigma^2\) or \(\phi\) changes \(\mathbf{S}\) but not \(\boldsymbol\Gamma\), which keeps these moves cheap and well mixed.
Adaptation: during burn-in, every 50 iterations the MALA step \(h\) and the two random-walk scales are tuned toward their target acceptance rates (0.574, 0.30, 0.30). After burn-in they are frozen, so the kept chain is a valid Markov chain.
Interweaving (interweave=True, the default). The whitened parametrization mixes the latent field well, but the intercept, \(\sigma^2\) and the range trade off against \(\boldsymbol\Gamma\) and move slowly. Each iteration therefore also updates them in the centred parametrization, holding the linear predictor \(\boldsymbol\eta\) (and so the likelihood) fixed: ancillarity-sufficiency interweaving (Yu & Meng, 2011). Three conditionals are available in closed form:

\(\boldsymbol\beta \mid \boldsymbol\eta\) is Gaussian;
every range_gibbs_every iterations, the range is drawn from its exact discrete posterior given \(\mathbf{S} = \boldsymbol\eta - \mathbf{F}\boldsymbol\beta\), with \(\sigma^2\) integrated out, \[
  p(\phi_j \mid \mathbf{S}) \propto p(\phi_j)\,|\mathbf{V}_j|^{-1/2}\,\bigl(\nu_0 s_0^2 + \mathbf{S}^\top\mathbf{V}_j^{-1}\mathbf{S}\bigr)^{-(\nu_0 + n)/2},
  \] a collapsed move along the \(\sigma^2\)-range ridge;
\(\sigma^2 \mid \mathbf{S}, \phi\) is scaled inverse-\(\chi^2\) with \(\nu_0 + n\) degrees of freedom.

Then \(\boldsymbol\Gamma\) is reset to \(\mathbf{L}^{-1}\mathbf{S}/\sigma\).



Prediction
For each kept sample \((\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2, \phi, \boldsymbol\Gamma)\), the latent field at a new location \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is drawn from its kriging distribution given the latent field at the data:
\[
S_0 \mid \mathbf{S} \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\sigma\,\mathbf{r}_0^\top\mathbf{L}^{-\top}\boldsymbol\Gamma,\;\; \sigma^2(1 + \tau - \lVert\mathbf{L}^{-1}\mathbf{r}_0\rVert^2)\bigr),
\]
and \(\eta_0 = \mathbf{f}_0^\top\boldsymbol\beta + S_0\) is turned into the rate \(e^{\eta_0}\) or the probability \(\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_0)\). The draws over samples form the posterior predictive distribution of the rate at \(\mathbf{x}_0\). predict summarizes them; predict_proba gives exceedance probabilities.


Convergence diagnostics

Trace plots should look like stationary noise.
Acceptance rates (acceptance_) should be near their targets.
Effective sample size, \(\text{ESS} = N / (1 + 2\sum_k \hat\rho_k)\) with \(\hat\rho_k\) the chain’s autocorrelations, measures how many independent draws the chain is worth.
Several chains from different seeds should agree. The potential scale reduction \(\hat R\) (Gelman & Rubin, 1992) compares between- and within-chain variance; values near 1 (below about 1.05) indicate convergence.



Relation to Poisson kriging and disease mapping

Poisson kriging (Monestiez et al., 2006; Goovaerts, 2005) adjusts the kriging system for Poisson noise, but stays a linear, second-order method with a plug-in variogram.
The GLMM uses the full likelihood and propagates every parameter’s uncertainty.
Disease-mapping models such as BYM (Besag, York & Mollié, 1991) use areal neighbourhoods and a conditional autoregressive field. The GLMM here treats each county as a point, its centroid, with a geostatistical correlation, and its nugget plays the role of BYM’s unstructured term.

title: Bayesian Generalized Linear Kriging (BayesianGLMKriging)
text:
Python Setup
BayesianGLMKriging runs on the CPU (NumPy). Each MCMC iteration costs a few \(n \times n\) matrix-vector products; the Cholesky factors are computed once per range value.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 4 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics and geostatistics): pip install "geolattice[geostats]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
%matplotlib inline
import time
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import geolattice.geostatistics as pygstat
from geolattice.geostatistics import BayesianGLMKriging

print("pygstat version:", pygstat.__version__)

RESULTS = []
def record(section, status, note=""):
    RESULTS.append({"Feature": section, "Status": status, "Notes": note})
    marker = {"PASS": "✅", "FAIL": "❌", "BLOCKED": "⚠️"}.get(status, "?")
    print(f"{marker} [{status}] {section}  {note}")


def ess(x):
    # effective sample size from the autocorrelation (initial positive sequence)
    x = np.asarray(x, float) - np.mean(x)
    n = len(x)
    if np.var(x) == 0:
        return float(n)
    ac = np.correlate(x, x, "full")[n - 1:] / (np.var(x) * n)
    s = 0.0
    for k in range(1, n // 2):
        if ac[k] + ac[k + 1] < 0:
            break
        s += ac[k]
    return n / (1 + 2 * s)


def rhat(chains):
    # Gelman-Rubin potential scale reduction for a list of equal-length chains
    c = np.asarray(chains, float)
    m, n = c.shape
    B = n * c.mean(1).var(ddof=1)
    W = c.var(1, ddof=1).mean()
    return float(np.sqrt(((n - 1) / n * W + B / n) / W))


pygstat version: 0.3.49

title: Bayesian Generalized Linear Kriging (BayesianGLMKriging)
text:
Data: Real Rates, Simulated Counts
lbc_rate.csv gives, for 666 Atlantic-region counties, the lung and bronchus cancer mortality rate per 100,000 (averaged over 1998-2012), the population, county-centroid coordinates (Albers equal-area, metres) and covariates: adult smoking prevalence and poverty. These real rates are treated as the true rates.
One year of deaths is simulated from them,
\[
y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i), \qquad \lambda_i = \text{rate}_i \times \text{population}_i / 10^5 .
\]
The expected counts under the region-wide rate are \(E_i = \text{population}_i \times \sum_j y_j / \sum_j \text{population}_j\), so the true relative risk is \(\theta_i = \lambda_i / E_i\). 130 counties are held out at random: their counts are not used for fitting, and the model predicts their relative risk from location and covariates.


Code
DATA = "../../../../Data/00_shared/data_geostatistics/"
lbc = pd.read_csv(DATA + "lbc_rate.csv")
dia = pd.read_csv(DATA + "diabetes_atlantic.csv")
df = lbc.merge(dia[["FIPS", "State", "County", "Diabetes_per", "Obesity", "Physical_Inactivity"]], on="FIPS")
counties = gpd.read_file(DATA + "COUNTY_ATLANTIC.shp")[["FIPS", "geometry"]]
counties["FIPS"] = counties["FIPS"].astype(int)
xy = df[["x", "y"]].to_numpy(float) / 1000.0            # km
n = len(df)

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
lam = (df["lbc_rate"] * df["pop"] / 1e5).to_numpy()
y = rng.poisson(lam)
E = df["pop"].to_numpy() * y.sum() / df["pop"].sum()
true_rr = lam / E
smr = y / E

zs = lambda c: ((c - c.mean()) / c.std()).to_numpy()
X = np.column_stack([zs(df.smoking), zs(df.poverty)])
perm = rng.permutation(n)
te, tr = np.sort(perm[:130]), np.sort(perm[130:])
print(f"{n} counties ({len(tr)} for fitting, {len(te)} held out); {y.sum():,} simulated deaths")
print("expected deaths E_i: quantiles 5/25/50/75/95% =", np.round(np.quantile(E, [0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95]), 1))
print(f"true relative risk: range {true_rr.min():.2f}-{true_rr.max():.2f}, sd {true_rr.std():.3f}")


def choropleth(ax, values, title, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=None, vmax=None, label=""):
    g = counties.merge(pd.DataFrame({"FIPS": df.FIPS, "v": values}), on="FIPS", how="left")
    g.plot(column="v", ax=ax, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, legend=True, linewidth=0.05, edgecolor="0.5",
           legend_kwds={"label": label, "shrink": 0.7}, missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"})
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_axis_off()

expected deaths E_i: quantiles 5/25/50/75/95% = [  6.9  15.6  33.3  76.7 324.4]
true relative risk: range 0.57-1.74, sd 0.174

text:
Raw Standardized Mortality Ratios
The raw SMR map against the true relative risk, and the SMR error as a function of the expected count: the funnel of Section 2.1.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(22, 7))
choropleth(axes[0], true_rr, "True relative risk (real rates)", vmin=0.5, vmax=1.5, label="RR")
choropleth(axes[1], smr, "Raw SMR from one year of simulated deaths", vmin=0.5, vmax=1.5, label="SMR")
axes[2].scatter(E, smr - true_rr, s=8, alpha=0.6)
ee = np.geomspace(E.min(), E.max(), 100)
axes[2].plot(ee, 1.96 / np.sqrt(ee), "r--", lw=1, label="±1.96 sqrt(1/E)")
axes[2].plot(ee, -1.96 / np.sqrt(ee), "r--", lw=1)

axes[2].legend()

      f"counties with E < 10: {np.mean(E < 10):.0%}, their RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean((smr - true_rr)[E < 10] ** 2)):.3f}")

title: Bayesian Generalized Linear Kriging (BayesianGLMKriging)
text:
Fitting the Poisson Model

Data and covariates: the 536 fitting counties’ deaths, their expected counts as exposure, and smoking and poverty, standardized, as covariates.
Spatial model: exponential correlation, with the range on 20 values from 20 to 800 km.
Priors: the default priors, \(\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10^2)\) and \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{Scale-inv-}\chi^2(1, 0.5)\).
Chain: 10,000 iterations, 3,000 of burn-in, every 5th kept.



Code
RANGE_GRID = np.geomspace(20, 800, 20)
POIS_KW = dict(family="poisson", model="exponential", range_grid=RANGE_GRID)
FIT_KW = dict(n_iter=10000, burn=3000, thin=5)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
pois = BayesianGLMKriging(**POIS_KW).fit(xy[tr], y[tr], trials_or_exposure=E[tr], covariates=X[tr], seed=0, **FIT_KW)
print(f"MCMC: {FIT_KW['n_iter']:,} iterations on {len(tr)} counties in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s; "
      f"{len(pois.trace_)} kept samples")
print("acceptance rates:", {k: round(float(v), 2) for k, v in pois.acceptance_.items()})


MCMC: 10,000 iterations on 536 counties in 13.0 s; 1400 kept samples
acceptance rates: {'gamma': 0.82, 'beta': 0.27, 'sigma2': 0.37, 'range': 0.15}



Convergence: traces, acceptance, ESS and R-hat
The traces of the main parameters, their effective sample sizes, and \(\hat R\) from three chains started with different seeds.


Code
names = {"beta_intercept": "intercept", "beta_cov1": "smoking", "beta_cov2": "poverty", "sigma2": "sigma^2", "range": "range (km)"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(26, 3.6))
for ax, (col, lab) in zip(axes, names.items()):
    ax.plot(pois.trace_[col].to_numpy(), lw=0.6)
    ax.set_title(f"trace: {lab}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

chains = [pois] + [BayesianGLMKriging(**POIS_KW).fit(xy[tr], y[tr], trials_or_exposure=E[tr], covariates=X[tr],
                                                   seed=s, **FIT_KW) for s in (1, 2)]
diag = pd.DataFrame({lab: {"ESS (chain 1)": ess(pois.trace_[col]),
                           "R-hat (3 chains)": rhat([c.trace_[col].to_numpy() for c in chains])}
                     for col, lab in names.items()}).T
display(diag.round(2))
record("R-hat < 1.1 for the regression coefficients",
       "PASS" if diag.loc[["intercept", "smoking", "poverty"], "R-hat (3 chains)"].max() < 1.1 else "FAIL",
       f"max {diag.loc[['intercept', 'smoking', 'poverty'], 'R-hat (3 chains)'].max():.3f}")

The regression coefficients converge well. Thanks to the interweaving updates, the intercept’s draws are nearly independent (ESS ≈ 1,400 of 1,400). The smoking and poverty coefficients have ESS of 25-50, and \(\hat R \le 1.02\) across three chains.
The variance and the range mix slowly. \(\sigma^2\) and the range have \(\hat R\) of 1.03-1.06 but ESS below 10: their traces wander. They are weakly identified by counts (only their combination is well determined), and they depend on the slowly moving latent field. Their posterior summaries below are therefore approximate. For precise statements about \(\sigma^2\) or the range, run much longer chains (or pool many chains). The relative risks themselves depend mainly on \(\boldsymbol\eta\), which the data pin down.
Acceptance rates. The random-walk updates sit near their targets. The MALA acceptance is high (0.82): after burn-in the step size is conservative, which slows the latent field but keeps the chain valid.



Posterior of the parameters
The kept draws from the three chains are pooled. The coefficients are on the log relative-risk scale per standard deviation of the covariate, so \(e^\beta\) is a rate ratio.


Code
pooled = pd.concat([c.trace_ for c in chains], ignore_index=True)
summ = pd.DataFrame({lab: {"mean": pooled[col].mean(), "sd": pooled[col].std(), "5%": pooled[col].quantile(0.05),
                           "95%": pooled[col].quantile(0.95)} for col, lab in names.items()}).T
summ["exp(mean)"] = np.where(summ.index.isin(["smoking", "poverty"]), np.exp(summ["mean"]), np.nan)
display(summ.round(3))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4))
axes[0].hist(pooled["beta_cov1"], bins=40, alpha=0.6, label="smoking")

rv = pooled["range"].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index()
axes[2].bar(np.arange(len(rv)), rv.values, color="tab:green")
axes[2].set_xticks(np.arange(len(rv)), [f"{v:.0f}" for v in rv.index], rotation=90)

Smoking matters. Its coefficient is clearly positive: +0.090 per standard deviation of smoking prevalence, a rate ratio of 1.09 (90% interval 1.07-1.12).
Poverty does not, once smoking and space are accounted for. Its coefficient is near 0 (0.004, interval −0.017 to 0.026).

title: Bayesian Generalized Linear Kriging (BayesianGLMKriging)
text:
Smoothed Relative Risks
The posterior of the relative risk at the fitting counties, \(\theta_i = e^{\eta_i}\), comes from latent_samples(). It is compared with the truth and the raw SMR, county by county:

the error of the posterior mean;
the coverage of the 90% credible intervals;
the shrinkage of each county’s estimate toward the model, as a function of its expected count.



Code
theta = np.exp(np.vstack([c.latent_samples() for c in chains]))       # (draws, fitting counties)
post_mean = theta.mean(0)
lo, hi = np.quantile(theta, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
t_tr, smr_tr, E_tr = true_rr[tr], smr[tr], E[tr]
small = E_tr < 10
fit_tab = pd.DataFrame({
    "raw SMR": [np.sqrt(np.mean((smr_tr - t_tr) ** 2)), np.sqrt(np.mean((smr_tr - t_tr)[small] ** 2)), np.nan],
    "posterior mean": [np.sqrt(np.mean((post_mean - t_tr) ** 2)), np.sqrt(np.mean((post_mean - t_tr)[small] ** 2)),
                       np.mean((t_tr >= lo) & (t_tr <= hi))]},
    index=["RMSE vs true RR (all)", "RMSE vs true RR (E < 10)", "coverage of 90% credible intervals"])
display(fit_tab.round(3))
record("posterior mean beats raw SMR (RMSE vs truth)", "PASS" if fit_tab.iloc[0, 1] < fit_tab.iloc[0, 0] else "FAIL",
       f"{fit_tab.iloc[0, 0]:.3f} -> {fit_tab.iloc[0, 1]:.3f}")
record("90% credible intervals cover the true RR in [0.80, 0.98]",
       "PASS" if 0.80 <= fit_tab.iloc[2, 1] <= 0.98 else "FAIL", f"{fit_tab.iloc[2, 1]:.2f}")

all_post = np.full(n, np.nan)
all_post[tr] = post_mean
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(22, 7))
choropleth(axes[0], np.where(np.isin(np.arange(n), tr), smr, np.nan), "Raw SMR (fitting counties)", vmin=0.5, vmax=1.5, label="SMR")
choropleth(axes[1], all_post, "Posterior mean relative risk", vmin=0.5, vmax=1.5, label="RR")
shrink = (smr_tr - post_mean) / np.where(np.abs(smr_tr - 1) > 1e-9, smr_tr - 1, np.nan)
axes[2].scatter(E_tr, smr_tr, s=8, alpha=0.4, label="raw SMR")
axes[2].scatter(E_tr, post_mean, s=8, alpha=0.6, label="posterior mean")
axes[2].set_xscale("log")
axes[2].axhline(1, color="k", lw=0.8)
axes[2].set_xlabel("expected deaths E_i")
axes[2].set_ylabel("relative risk")
axes[2].set_title("Small counties are shrunk most")
axes[2].legend()

plt.show()

The posterior mean is much closer to the truth than the raw SMR. RMSE falls from 0.223 to 0.097 over all fitting counties, and from 0.425 to 0.130 for the counties with fewer than 10 expected deaths.
Shrinkage depends on the expected count. Small counties are pulled strongly toward their neighbours and covariates; large counties keep their SMR. That is what the scatter plot shows.
The map of posterior means looks like the true map. The raw-SMR map is dominated by speckle from small populations.
Coverage. The 90% credible intervals cover the true relative risk in 84% of counties, slightly below nominal. The slowly mixing variance and range likely make the intervals a little too narrow; longer chains would help.

title: Bayesian Generalized Linear Kriging (BayesianGLMKriging)
text:
Prediction at Held-Out Counties
For the 130 held-out counties, no counts are used at all. predict draws their relative risk from the covariates and the kriged latent field (Section 2.8). Two baselines:

non-spatial Poisson regression on the same covariates, fitted by iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS);
the regional rate, \(\theta = 1\).



Code
pred_te = pd.concat([c.predict(xy[te], covariates=X[te], seed=i) for i, c in enumerate(chains)])
pred_samples = np.vstack([c.predictive_samples(xy[te], covariates=X[te], seed=10 + i) for i, c in enumerate(chains)])
p_mean = pred_samples.mean(0)
p_lo, p_hi = np.quantile(pred_samples, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)

# non-spatial Poisson GLM (IRLS) on the fitting counties
F = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(tr)), X[tr]])
b = np.zeros(F.shape[1])
for _ in range(50):
    mu = E[tr] * np.exp(F @ b)
    W = mu
    zwork = F @ b + (y[tr] - mu) / mu
    b = np.linalg.solve(F.T @ (W[:, None] * F), F.T @ (W * zwork))
glm_rr = np.exp(np.column_stack([np.ones(len(te)), X[te]]) @ b)

t_te = true_rr[te]
held = pd.DataFrame({
    "regional rate (RR = 1)": [np.sqrt(np.mean((1 - t_te) ** 2)), np.nan],
    "non-spatial Poisson GLM": [np.sqrt(np.mean((glm_rr - t_te) ** 2)), np.nan],
    "BayesianGLMKriging": [np.sqrt(np.mean((p_mean - t_te) ** 2)), np.mean((t_te >= p_lo) & (t_te <= p_hi))]},
    index=["RMSE vs true RR", "coverage of 90% intervals"])
display(held.round(3))
record("spatial GLMM beats non-spatial GLM at held-out counties",
       "PASS" if held.loc["RMSE vs true RR", "BayesianGLMKriging"] < held.loc["RMSE vs true RR", "non-spatial Poisson GLM"] else "FAIL",
       f"{held.loc['RMSE vs true RR', 'non-spatial Poisson GLM']:.3f} -> {held.loc['RMSE vs true RR', 'BayesianGLMKriging']:.3f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
ax.errorbar(t_te, p_mean, yerr=[p_mean - p_lo, p_hi - p_mean], fmt="o", ms=3, alpha=0.5, lw=0.6)
ax.plot([0.5, 1.6], [0.5, 1.6], "k--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("true relative risk (held-out county)")
ax.set_ylabel("predicted relative risk (90% interval)")
ax.set_title("Held-out counties: predicted from neighbours and covariates")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

For counties with no data at all, the spatial model predicts the true relative risk with RMSE 0.107:

better than the non-spatial Poisson regression on the same covariates (0.131);
much better than assuming the regional rate (0.176).

The difference over the non-spatial model is what the latent field contributes: residual risk shared with neighbouring counties that smoking does not explain. The 90% predictive intervals cover 89% of the held-out true risks.

title: Bayesian Generalized Linear Kriging (BayesianGLMKriging)
text:
The Unstructured (Nugget) Term
A purely spatial field forces neighbouring counties to have similar risks. Real risks also vary county by county for reasons that are not spatially smooth: local industry, demography, reporting. nugget_ratio \(\tau\) adds that unstructured variation. The fit is repeated with \(\tau\) = 0, 0.2 and 1, and scored against the truth.


Code
rows = []
for tau in [0.0, 0.2, 1.0]:
    m = BayesianGLMKriging(**POIS_KW, nugget_ratio=tau).fit(xy[tr], y[tr], trials_or_exposure=E[tr], covariates=X[tr], seed=0, **FIT_KW)
    th = np.exp(m.latent_samples())
    ps = m.predictive_samples(xy[te], covariates=X[te], seed=1)
    q_lo, q_hi = np.quantile(ps, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
    rows.append({"nugget ratio": tau, "posterior mean sigma^2": m.trace_.sigma2.mean(), "posterior mean range": m.trace_.range.mean(),
                 "fit RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((th.mean(0) - t_tr) ** 2)),
                 "held-out RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((ps.mean(0) - t_te) ** 2)),
                 "held-out 90% coverage": np.mean((t_te >= q_lo) & (t_te <= q_hi)),
                 "MALA acceptance": m.acceptance_["gamma"]})

section: Binomial Model: Diabetes Prevalence from Small Surveys
text:
Binomial Model: Diabetes Prevalence from Small Surveys
diabetes_atlantic.csv gives the diagnosed diabetes prevalence of each county, treated here as the truth. A small survey is simulated in each county, with \(n_i\) = 30 respondents and \(y_i \sim \text{Binomial}(n_i, \text{prevalence}_i)\). The binomial model (family="binomial", trials_or_exposure=n_i) uses obesity and physical inactivity as covariates. Survey proportions with 30 respondents are very noisy: one case moves them by 3.3 percentage points.

Raw rates from small counts are mostly noise. With one year of simulated lung-cancer deaths, raw SMRs missed the true relative risks by 0.22 (0.43 in counties with fewer than 10 expected deaths).
BayesianGLMKriging modelled the counts with their Poisson likelihood, covariates and a latent spatial field. It cut the error to 0.10 (0.13 in the smallest counties), and its 90% credible intervals covered 84% of the true risks. At held-out counties it beat a non-spatial Poisson regression (RMSE 0.107 vs 0.131).
Covariates are estimated with uncertainty. Smoking raised risk by 9% per sd; poverty had no effect beyond smoking and space.
Exceedance probabilities gave far fewer false alarms than flagging raw SMRs, at the cost of missing modestly elevated counties. The probability threshold controls that trade-off.
The nugget term mainly changes the width of predictive intervals at unsampled units. The benefit of smoothing falls as counts grow: 75% lower error with three months of data, 14% with five years.
The binomial model recovered county diabetes prevalence from 30-person surveys with 1 percentage point of error, against 5 points for the raw proportions.
MCMC. Interweaving (centred) updates made the coefficients mix well. The variance and range remain slow to mix, so long chains are needed for precise statements about them.


Practical guidance







Step
Advice




Exposure
Poisson: expected counts \(E_i\) (then \(e^\eta\) is a relative risk) or person-time; binomial: number of trials


Covariates
standardize them; the coefficients are then log rate ratios (or log odds ratios) per sd


Range grid
span from below the nearest-neighbour spacing to the size of the region; check the posterior is not piled at an edge


Nugget
include unstructured variation (nugget_ratio > 0) when units differ for non-spatial reasons


Priors
the \(\sigma^2\) prior matters for small or binary counts; use weakly informative values (Section 12)


Chains
several seeds, burn-in until acceptance is stable, check ESS and \(\hat R\) before trusting summaries


Outputs
relative risks with credible intervals; exceedance probabilities for flagging; predict for unsampled units

title: Empirical Bayesian Kriging
text:
Overview

The problem it fixes
Ordinary/simple/universal kriging all follow the same two-step recipe:

Estimate the semivariogram parameters \(\theta = (\mathrm{nugget},\,\mathrm{sill},\,\mathrm{range},\,\ldots)\) once from the data, e.g. by weighted least squares or REML, getting a single point estimate \(\hat\theta\).
Treat \(\hat\theta\) as if it were the true, known \(\theta\) and krige with it.

Step 2 is the weak link. \(\hat\theta\) is itself an estimate with its own sampling error, especially with a modest sample size or a variogram whose range/nugget is hard to pin down, but classical kriging’s reported prediction variance only accounts for spatial interpolation error given \(\theta = \hat\theta\). It silently ignores the uncertainty in \(\hat\theta\) itself, so kriging standard errors are systematically too small, and probability/quantile maps built from them are overconfident.
Empirical Bayesian Kriging (Krivoruchko, 2012) fixes this by not committing to a single \(\hat\theta\): it builds an empirical distribution over plausible semivariograms and averages predictions over that distribution.


The Bayesian target
Conceptually, what you actually want is the posterior predictive distribution
\[
p\big(Z(x_0)\mid Z\big)
= \int p\big(Z(x_0)\mid Z,\theta\big)\, p(\theta\mid Z)\, d\theta,
\]
i.e. krige for every possible \(\theta\), weighted by how consistent each \(\theta\) is with the observed data. A fully Bayesian treatment (Handcock & Stein, 1993; Diggle & Ribeiro) specifies a prior \(\pi(\theta)\) and samples \(p(\theta\mid Z) \propto L(Z\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\) via MCMC: expensive and requires prior elicitation.
EBK is “empirical” Bayesian because it sidesteps MCMC and a user-specified prior: it builds an approximation to \(p(\theta\mid Z)\) directly from the data via a simulate-and-refit loop, the same spirit as empirical Bayes methods in statistics (estimate the “prior”/hyperparameter distribution from the data itself rather than specifying it a priori).


The algorithm
For \(k = 1, \ldots, K\) (\(K \approx 100\) by default):

Fit once. Estimate a semivariogram \(\hat\theta_0\) from the actual data \(Z\) (REML is standard here, since it’s less biased than method-of-moments for this purpose).
Simulate. Using \(\hat\theta_0\) and the fitted mean, generate a synthetic Gaussian random field realization \(Z^*_k\) at the same observation locations: this is what a dataset consistent with \(\hat\theta_0\) would look like.
Refit. Re-estimate a new semivariogram \(\theta_k\) from \(Z^*_k\). Because \(Z^*_k\) was simulated from \(\hat\theta_0\), the scatter of \(\theta_k\) across many \(k\) approximates the sampling distribution of the semivariogram-fitting procedure around the truth: i.e. an empirical stand-in for \(p(\theta\mid Z)\).
Weight. Krige \(Z^*_k\) at its own input locations using \(\theta_k\) and compare the kriged values to the actual simulated \(Z^*_k\): this consistency check yields a weight \(w_k\) for how well that semivariogram explains its own data (poorly-behaved refits get downweighted).

This produces an ensemble \(\{(\theta_1, w_1), \ldots, (\theta_K, w_K)\}\): \(K\) semivariograms with weights, standing in for the posterior over \(\theta\).
Prediction. At a new location \(x_0\), krige the real data \(Z\) once per ensemble member:
\[
\hat Z_k(x_0),\; \sigma^2_k(x_0)
= \mathrm{SimpleKriging/OrdinaryKriging}(\theta_k).\mathrm{predict}(x_0)
\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.
\]
Then combine:
\[
\hat Z_{\mathrm{EBK}}(x_0) = \sum_k w_k\, \hat Z_k(x_0)
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Var}[Z(x_0)]
&= \sum_k w_k\, \sigma^2_k(x_0)
\quad\text{(average within-model kriging variance)} \\
&\quad + \sum_k w_k\, \big(\hat Z_k(x_0) - \hat Z_{\mathrm{EBK}}(x_0)\big)^2
\quad\text{(between-model variance, from $\theta$-uncertainty).}
\end{aligned}
\]
That variance decomposition is exactly the law of total variance / Rubin’s multiple-imputation combining rule: within-model variance (ordinary kriging error, given \(\theta\)) plus between-model variance (disagreement across plausible \(\theta\)’s). Classical kriging only ever reports the first term: EBK’s headline benefit is the second term, which is precisely the part that was previously ignored.
Because you actually have \(K\) full predictive Gaussians \(N\big(\hat Z_k(x_0),\,\sigma^2_k(x_0)\big)\) rather than one, you get a genuine mixture-of-Gaussians predictive distribution at every location, not just a mean and a variance: so exceedance-probability and quantile maps built from it are better calibrated than classical kriging’s, especially in the small-sample/weak-range regime.


Practical extras (as implemented in ArcGIS Geostatistical Analyst, the reference implementation)

Local, not global, semivariograms. The study area is split into many overlapping subsets (a moving-window scheme); the whole simulate-refit-weight procedure above runs per subset, so the semivariogram can vary smoothly across space: a lightweight way of handling mild non-stationarity without a full space-varying covariance model.
Automatic transformation. Data can be transformed (Box-Cox or a normal-score-style transform) before the semivariogram/simulation loop, since the underlying Gaussian-process machinery assumes approximate normality: much like the Gaussian anamorphosis step in disjunctive kriging, but used here just to stabilize the variogram-fitting step rather than to build a nonlinear estimator.
Cost. You pay for \(K\) semivariogram fits (and \(K\) krigings per prediction point) instead of one: meaningfully more expensive than OK/SK, but each piece is embarrassingly parallel across \(k\).

The two aren’t competitors: EBK’s uncertainty-quantification idea and DK’s nonlinear-estimator idea are addressing different weaknesses of plain kriging, and in principle could even be combined (empirical-Bayes-average over the \(Y\)-variogram used inside DisjunctiveKriging).
This tutorial applies pygstat.EmpiricalBayesianKriging to cadmium in the Swiss Jura. Cd is right-skewed, so we work on \(\log(\mathrm{Cd})\) (the same Gaussian-process convention as tests/test_ebk.py on Meuse zinc). The central check is the one in that test suite: point estimates agree closely with ordinary kriging, but EBK’s total standard error is larger because it also captures \(\theta\)-uncertainty.

title: Empirical Bayesian Kriging
text:
How pygstat Implements EBK
pygstat.EmpiricalBayesianKriging is the global (single-window) version of the algorithm above. Each ensemble member is an unmodified OrdinaryKriging or SimpleKriging: including GPU dispatch at predict() time.








Step
Object
Role




Base fit
base_variogram_
\(\hat\theta_0\) from the real data; drives simulation only


Simulate
_simulate_unconditional
Cholesky draw of \(Z^*_k\) at the training locations


Refit
variograms_[k]
\(\theta_k\) fitted to \(Z^*_k\)


Weight
loo_cv → weights_
Inverse-LOO-MSE precision weights, \(\sum w_k=1\)


Predict

Each \(\theta_k\) kriges the real data


Combine
predict()
Weighted mean + within + between variance


Exceedance
predict_proba()
Mixture of \(K\) Gaussians, not a single Gaussian



Weights. An in-sample residual is useless: OK/SK interpolate their own training data exactly, regardless of \(\theta\). pygstat therefore weights each \(\theta_k\) by how well it leave-one-out predicts its own simulated realization \(Z^*_k\): inverse LOO-MSE, normalized to sum to 1. Poorly-behaved refits get downweighted, as in the Overview.
What is not in this class (yet). ArcGIS Geostatistical Analyst also splits the domain into overlapping local subsets and can auto-transform the data. EmpiricalBayesianKriging currently fits one global ensemble. We supply the transform ourselves (\(\log \mathrm{Cd}\)) and use a single window over the Jura survey. Local windows would be the natural extension for mild non-stationarity.
Variogram fitter. The library’s Variogram.fit() is weighted least squares on the empirical semivariogram, not REML. The simulate-and-refit idea does not depend on which fitter produced \(\hat\theta_0\); it approximates that fitter’s sampling distribution.
Cost. n_realizations defaults to 100 (ESRI’s default). Fit cost scales as \(O(K\, n_{\mathrm{train}})\) because of the LOO weights. This notebook uses \(K=40\) so the cells stay interactive; raise it toward 100 for a production map.

title: Empirical Bayesian Kriging
text:
Fit Empirical Bayesian Kriging
EmpiricalBayesianKriging.fit runs the simulate-refit-weight loop on the training locations, then fits one OrdinaryKriging per \(\theta_k\) on the real \(\log(\mathrm{Cd})\).
We use \(K=40\) spherical members (random_state=42): enough to see real spread in \(\theta\), small enough that the notebook stays interactive. The library default is n_realizations=100.


Code
K = 40

ebk = EmpiricalBayesianKriging(
    model="spherical",
    kriging_type="ordinary",
    n_realizations=K,
    use_gpu=False,
    random_state=42,
    variogram_kwargs={"n_lags": 15, "estimator": "matheron"},
)
ebk.fit(coords_train, z_train)

vg0 = ebk.base_variogram_
print("Empirical Bayesian Kriging fitted")

print(f"  weights sum            : {ebk.weights_.sum():.6f}")

text:
The Semivariogram Ensemble
If the refits collapsed onto \(\hat\theta_0\), there would be nothing for EBK to average over. tests/test_ebk.py requires the ensemble of ranges to have nonzero spread. Below: every \(\gamma_k(h)\) overlaid on the base fit, the marginals of \((\mathrm{nugget},\,\mathrm{sill},\,\mathrm{range})\), and the LOO-MSE weights.


Code

nugget, sill, rng_p = params[:, 0], params[:, 1], params[:, 2]

title: Empirical Bayesian Kriging
text:
Validate EBK vs Ordinary Kriging
Predict \(\log(\mathrm{Cd})\) at the held-out 30%. Two claims from tests/test_ebk.py:

Point estimates agree with a single ordinary-kriging fit (correlation \(\gtrsim 0.99\) on a dense grid in that test). EBK is not trying to beat OK on the mean.
EBK’s total SE exceeds OK’s SE almost everywhere: that extra margin is the between-model term plain kriging ignores.

We also decompose the EBK variance on the test set into within-model and between-model pieces, so the second term is visible as a number, not only as a larger SE.


Code
vg_ok = Variogram(
    coords_train, z_train, model="spherical",
    estimator="matheron", n_lags=15, use_gpu=False,
)
vg_ok.fit()
ok = OrdinaryKriging(vg_ok, use_gpu=False).fit(coords_train, z_train)

z_hat_ebk, se_ebk_test = ebk.predict(coords_test, return_variance=True)
z_hat_ok, se_ok_test = ok.predict(coords_test, return_variance=True)

# Within / between decomposition (same combining rule as predict)
preds_k, var_k = ebk._predict_ensemble(coords_test, return_variance=True)
w = ebk.weights_[:, None]
within = (w * var_k).sum(axis=0)
between = (w * (preds_k - z_hat_ebk) ** 2).sum(axis=0)


def metrics(obs, pred, name):
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(obs, pred)))
    mae = float(mean_absolute_error(obs, pred))
    r2 = float(r2_score(obs, pred))
    me = float(np.mean(pred - obs))
    print(f"{name:22s}  RMSE={rmse:.3f}  MAE={mae:.3f}  R2={r2:.3f}  ME={me:+.3f}")
    return rmse, mae, r2, me


print("Held-out test set (log Cd)")
metrics(z_test, z_hat_ebk, "Empirical Bayesian")
metrics(z_test, z_hat_ok, "Ordinary Kriging")
print(f"corr(EBK, OK) on test     : {np.corrcoef(z_hat_ebk, z_hat_ok)[0, 1]:.4f}")

print(f"OK  SE  min/mean/max      : {se_ok_test.min():.3f} / {se_ok_test.mean():.3f} / {se_ok_test.max():.3f}")

print(f"within-model var  (mean)  : {within.mean():.4f}")
print(f"between-model var (mean)  : {between.mean():.4f}")
print(f"between / total           : {between.mean() / (within.mean() + between.mean()):.3f}")

section: Predict Cd on the Jura Grid
text:
Predict Cd on the Jura Grid
Apply the fitted EBK and OK models to every node in jura_grid.csv. Maps are shown in \(\log(\mathrm{Cd})\) (the modelling scale) and as \(\exp(\hat Z)\) for a Cd-unit reading. \(\exp(\hat Z)\) is a median-type back-transform of the log-Gaussian predictor, not an unbiased mean of Cd.


Code
preds_g, var_g = ebk._predict_ensemble(grid_coords, return_variance=True)
w = ebk.weights_[:, None]
pred_ebk = (w * preds_g).sum(axis=0)
within_g = (w * var_g).sum(axis=0)
between_g = (w * (preds_g - pred_ebk) ** 2).sum(axis=0)
se_ebk = np.sqrt(np.clip(within_g + between_g, 0, None))
pred_ok, se_ok = ok.predict(grid_coords, return_variance=True)

grid_out = grid.copy()
grid_out["logCd_ebk"] = pred_ebk
grid_out["logCd_ebk_se"] = se_ebk
grid_out["logCd_ok"] = pred_ok
grid_out["logCd_ok_se"] = se_ok
grid_out["Cd_ebk"] = np.exp(pred_ebk)
grid_out["Cd_ok"] = np.exp(pred_ok)

Probability Maps of Exceedance
predict_proba mixes the \(K\) Gaussians \(N(\hat Z_k,\sigma_k^2)\) with weights \(w_k\). That is not the same as plugging \((\hat Z_{\mathrm{EBK}},\sigma_{\mathrm{EBK}})\) into a single \(\Phi\): the mixture keeps the extra spread from \(\theta\)-uncertainty instead of smoothing it into one Gaussian.
Because the model is on \(\log(\mathrm{Cd})\), \(P(\mathrm{Cd} > z_c) = P(\log\mathrm{Cd} > \log z_c)\). We map \(z_c \in \{0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00\}\) mg/kg. Mean exceedance probability across the grid must decrease as the cutoff rises (test_predict_proba_decreases_with_cutoff_on_average).

title: Empirical Bayesian Kriging
text:
Summary and Conclusions

Empirical Bayesian kriging does not commit to a single semivariogram \(\hat\theta\). It builds an empirical distribution over plausible \(\theta\) by simulating Gaussian realizations from a base fit, refitting, and weighting, then kriges the real data with every member of that ensemble.
pygstat.EmpiricalBayesianKriging implements the global (single-window) form of that recipe. Each member is ordinary (or simple) kriging; predict() combines them with the law-of-total-variance / Rubin rule; predict_proba mixes the \(K\) predictive Gaussians rather than collapsing them to one.
On Jura cadmium (\(\log\) scale, \(K=40\)), the ensemble of spherical models showed real spread in nugget, sill, and range. Inverse-LOO-MSE weights downweighted the worst refits.
Held-out point estimates tracked ordinary kriging closely. EBK standard errors were larger than OK’s on the test set and on the grid: that extra width is the between-model term, the \(\theta\)-uncertainty plain kriging ignores.
Exceedance maps \(P(\mathrm{Cd}>z_c)\) come from the mixture. Mean probability decreased with the cutoff, and test-set Brier scores beat the no-skill baseline.




Object
Role in this notebook




base_variogram_
\(\hat\theta_0\); simulation only


variograms_
Refit ensemble \(\{\theta_k\}\)


weights_
Inverse-LOO-MSE precision weights


predict
\(\hat Z_{\mathrm{EBK}}\) and total SE


predict_proba
Mixture-of-Gaussians \(P(Z>z_c)\)




Practical takeaways

Use EBK when you care about honest prediction variance or calibrated probabilities, especially with a modest sample or an ill-determined range/nugget.
EBK is still a linear interpolator of the (transformed) data. For a richer point estimate of a skewed grade, use disjunctive kriging (Tutorial 10): the two ideas address different OK failures and can in principle be combined.
Transform skewed variables before the simulate-and-refit loop. This class does not auto-transform, and it does not yet run local moving windows.
\(K=100\) is the library/ArcGIS default. Smaller \(K\) is fine for exploration; check that the ensemble of ranges has not collapsed.



Next steps

Compare these \(P(\mathrm{Cd}>1)\) maps with Tutorial 07 (indicator kriging) and Tutorial 10 (disjunctive kriging) on the same survey
Sequential Gaussian simulation (Tutorial 18) draws realizations of the field given one \(\theta\); EBK averages kriging predictors over an ensemble of \(\theta\)

title: SNESIM: Single Normal Equation Simulation (SNESIM)
text:
Overview
SNESIM (Strebelle, 2002) was the first practical multiple-point simulator, and it is still the reference algorithm for categorical MPS. It simulates facies one node at a time, like sequential indicator simulation, but replaces indicator kriging with a lookup. The probability of each facies given the surrounding simulated nodes is read from the frequencies of the same configuration in a training image (TI). A preliminary scan stores every pattern of the TI, so each lookup is fast, and a multigrid scheme lets a small template capture large structures.







Object
What it does




SNESIM(training_image, n_template, search_radius, n_multigrid, min_replicates, servo, target_proportions, tau, use_gpu)
The simulator. fit(grid, df, x, y, cat, soft=None) places hard data and optional soft probabilities; simulate(nsim, seed) and simulate_lattice draw realizations. n_patterns_, categories_, target_proportions_ and lattice_ describe the fit.


snesim(...)
One-call wrapper.


tau_model(p_prior, p_ti, p_soft, tau)
Combines TI and soft probabilities.



This notebook takes SNESIM apart parameter by parameter on a three-facies fluvial system whose truth is known:

floodplain (background);
channel sand;
levees bordering the channels, so that channel never touches floodplain directly.

That last rule makes it easy to see when the simulation produces patterns the TI never shows. The notebook measures:

how the template, multigrid and min_replicates shape the realizations;
how the servosystem and target proportions trade proportions against pattern fidelity;
how wells and a seismic-like soft variable condition the result;
how the tau model’s exponents weigh the two information sources.

title: SNESIM: Single Normal Equation Simulation (SNESIM)
text:
Theory

The single normal equation
Let \(S(\mathbf{u}) \in \{s_1, \dots, s_K\}\) be the facies and \(I_k(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{1}[S(\mathbf{u}) = s_k]\) its indicators. At node \(\mathbf{u}\), the data event is the set of informed nodes around it,
\[
d_n = \{S(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{h}_\alpha) = s_{k_\alpha},\ \alpha = 1, \dots, n\}.
\]
Indicator kriging estimates \(P(S(\mathbf{u}) = s_k \mid d_n)\) as a weighted sum of the \(n\) indicators, using only two-point covariances. Guardiano & Srivastava (1993) instead used one indicator for the whole data event, \(D = \prod_\alpha I_{k_\alpha}(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{h}_\alpha)\), which is 1 when the configuration occurs. Simple kriging of \(I_k(\mathbf{u})\) from this single datum has a single normal equation:
\[
\lambda\, \operatorname{Var}(D) = \operatorname{Cov}(I_k, D)
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
P^*(s_k \mid d_n) = p_k + \lambda\,(1 - E[D]) = \frac{P(S(\mathbf{u}) = s_k,\, d_n)}{P(d_n)} ,
\]
which is exactly Bayes’ rule, the conditional probability. Its two ingredients are multiple-point statistics that no variogram contains, and they are read from the training image by counting replicates:
\[
P(s_k \mid d_n) \approx \frac{c_k(d_n)}{c(d_n)}, \qquad c(d_n) = \sum_k c_k(d_n),
\]
where \(c_k(d_n)\) is the number of TI locations where the data event occurs with \(s_k\) at the centre.


Templates and the pattern table
The data event is taken on a fixed template \(\tau_n = \{\mathbf{h}_1, \dots, \mathbf{h}_n\}\): the n_template offsets nearest the centre within search_radius cells, ordered by distance (then by angle). Before simulating, the TI is scanned once per grid level. Every template configuration found is stored with the counts \(c_k\) of its centre categories. Strebelle stored these in a search tree; GeoLattice uses the equivalent list of unique patterns, as in IMPALA (Straubhaar et al., 2011). n_patterns_ reports how many unique patterns each level holds.
At simulation time, the node’s data event, with its informed template positions only, is matched against the list. Patterns that agree at every informed position contribute their counts. Template positions outside the TI never match.


Data-event reduction
Large data events are rare in a finite TI. If fewer than min_replicates stored patterns match, the farthest informed node is dropped and the count is repeated, until enough replicates are found. All prefixes are counted in one filtering pass.

Small min_replicates keeps more conditioning nodes, so continuity is better, at the risk of probabilities estimated from very few replicates.
Large values (GSLIB-style, around 10-20) make the probabilities more stable, but drop the outer nodes that carry the long-range structure.



Multiple grids
A template of 40 nodes in a radius of 8 cells cannot see structures 50 cells long. With n_multigrid \(= G\), simulation runs on nested grids of spacing \(2^{G-1}, \dots, 2, 1\) cells, and on grid \(g\) the template is stretched to \(2^g \tau_n\). The coarse grids, simulated first, place the large structures with a wide but sparse template, and finer grids fill in details conditioned on them. Each level has its own pattern table, scanned on the TI with the stretched template. Hard data are copied temporarily to the nearest coarse-grid node, so the coarse structure honours them too.


Servosystem and target proportions
Proportions in SNESIM realizations can drift away from the target \(\pi_k\) (target_proportions, default the TI’s). The servosystem corrects each conditional probability with the proportions \(\hat\pi_k\) simulated so far:
\[
p_k' = \max\!\left(0,\; p_k + \frac{\mu}{1 - \mu}\,(\pi_k - \hat\pi_k)\right), \quad \text{then renormalized}, \qquad \mu = \texttt{servo} \in [0, 1) .
\]
\(\mu = 0\) switches it off, and \(\mu \to 1\) forces the proportions. The correction is additive, so it can raise a category whose TI probability is 0 in that data event, creating a pattern the TI never shows. How often this happens depends on how far the proportions drift (Section 8). With target proportions different from the TI’s, the servosystem is the only lever that moves the realizations toward the target.


Soft data: the tau model
With soft probabilities \(P(s_k \mid y(\mathbf{u}))\) from a secondary variable \(y\) (fit(..., soft=...), one row per node, columns in categories_ order), SNESIM combines them with the TI probability through the tau model (Journel, 2002). In terms of probability distances \(x = (1 - P)/P\), with \(x_0\) from the prior (target proportions):
\[
\frac{x}{x_0} = \left(\frac{x_{\mathrm{TI}}}{x_0}\right)^{\tau_1} \left(\frac{x_{\text{soft}}}{x_0}\right)^{\tau_2},
\qquad
P(s_k \mid d_n, y) = \frac{1}{1 + x},
\]
renormalized over categories. With \(\tau = (1, 1)\) this is the permanence of ratios: the soft data change the odds by the same factor whatever the TI says. That amounts to conditional independence of the two sources given the facies.

\(\tau_2 > 1\) trusts the soft data more, and \(\tau_2 < 1\) discounts them (for example when they are redundant with the TI).
\(\tau_1 = 0\) ignores the TI, and \(\tau_2 = 0\) the soft data.

The soft mean also becomes the default target proportion.


The GPU engine
With use_gpu=True, all realizations advance in lockstep. At each step one fused CUDA kernel matches every realization’s data event against the pattern table, applies the reduction, tau model and servosystem, and draws the categories. The host draws the paths and uniform numbers in the CPU engine’s order, so GPU realizations equal CPU realizations. Limits: n_template ≤ 64 and at most 16 categories.


The algorithm

Build the template; for each grid level, scan the TI and store the unique patterns with their centre counts.
For each realization:

place the hard data;
for each grid level, coarse to fine:

visit the uninformed level nodes in random order;
read the data event on the stretched template;
reduce it until at least min_replicates patterns match;
compute \(P(s_k \mid d_n)\) from the counts; combine with soft data (tau model); apply the servosystem;
draw a category.

title: SNESIM: Single Normal Equation Simulation (SNESIM)
text:
A Three-Facies Fluvial Training Image
Sinuous channels from channel_training_image are surrounded by a two-cell levee (a binary dilation), in a floodplain. By construction, channel (1) and floodplain (0) never touch: there is always levee (2) between them. The truth is a separate 100 × 100 image from the same generator.


Code
FACIES = ["floodplain", "channel", "levee"]
CMAP = ListedColormap(["#efe3c2", "#1f5fa8", "#8fbf6a"])


def fluvial(n, seed):
    ch = channel_training_image(n, n, n_channels=5, width=4.0, seed=seed).astype(bool)
    levee = binary_dilation(ch, iterations=2) & ~ch
    return np.where(ch, 1.0, np.where(levee, 2.0, 0.0))


def contacts(img):
    img = np.asarray(img)
    M = np.zeros((3, 3))
    for a, b in [(img[1:, :], img[:-1, :]), (img[:, 1:], img[:, :-1])]:
        ok = a != b
        np.add.at(M, (a[ok].astype(int), b[ok].astype(int)), 1)
    return M + M.T


def show(ax, img, title, wells_df=None):
    ax.imshow(np.asarray(img).T, origin="lower", cmap=CMAP, vmin=-0.5, vmax=2.5, interpolation="nearest")
    if wells_df is not None:
        ax.scatter(wells_df.X, wells_df.Y, c=[["#7a5c00", "red", "darkgreen"][int(f)] for f in wells_df.f], s=14,
                   edgecolors="w", linewidths=0.4)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])


TI = fluvial(200, 0)
TRUTH = fluvial(100, 7)
NX = NY = 100

      f"floodplain-channel {M_ti[0, 1]:.0f} (forbidden)")
PH_TI = pattern_histogram(TI, 3)

channel connectivity at 30 cells along x (TI value above);
facies proportions.

evaluate runs SNESIM unconditionally on the 100 × 100 lattice and computes them.


Code
def diagnostics(reals):
    r = np.asarray(reals)
    return {"forbidden FP-CH edges": np.mean([contacts(x)[0, 1] for x in r]),
            "pattern dist. (3x3)": np.mean([pattern_histogram_distance(PH_TI, pattern_histogram(x, 3)) for x in r]),
            "channel connectivity @30": np.nanmean([connectivity(x, 1, 30, 0)[-1] for x in r]),
            **{f"prop. {f}": np.mean(r == k) for k, f in enumerate(FACIES)}}


def evaluate(label, nsim=8, seed=1, **kw):
    sim = SNESIM(TI, use_gpu=USE_GPU, **kw).fit(grid)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    reals = sim.simulate_lattice(nsim=nsim, seed=seed)
    sec = time.perf_counter() - t0
    return {"setting": label, "seconds": sec, "patterns per level": sim.n_patterns_, **diagnostics(reals)}, reals


ref_row = {"setting": "training image", **diagnostics(TI[None, :100, :100]),
           "pattern dist. (3x3)": 0.0, "channel connectivity @30": CONN_TI,
           **{f"prop. {f}": np.mean(TI == k) for k, f in enumerate(FACIES)}}

title: SNESIM: Single Normal Equation Simulation (SNESIM)
text:
Conditioning to Wells
80 wells are drawn at random from the true field. SNESIM (default template, 4 grids, servo=0) draws 50 conditional realizations. They are checked for exact conditioning, reproducibility, and equality of snesim with the class, and scored against the truth:

multiclass Brier score of the facies probabilities;
channel recall of the most probable map;
agreement per realization;
forbidden contacts and connectivity.



Code
well_idx = np.random.default_rng(1).choice(len(grid), 80, replace=False)
wells = pd.DataFrame({"X": grid[well_idx, 0], "Y": grid[well_idx, 1], "f": truth[well_idx]})
print("wells per facies:", {f: int((wells.f == k).sum()) for k, f in enumerate(FACIES)})
N_SIM = 50
sn = SNESIM(TI, servo=0.0, use_gpu=USE_GPU).fit(grid, wells, "X", "Y", "f")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
cond = sn.simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=2)
print(f"{N_SIM} conditional realizations in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

record("conditional SNESIM: wells honoured in every realization",
       "PASS" if np.all(cond[:, well_idx] == wells.f.to_numpy()[None, :]) else "FAIL")
record("conditional SNESIM: same seed -> identical",
       "PASS" if np.array_equal(SNESIM(TI, servo=0.0, use_gpu=USE_GPU).fit(grid, wells, "X", "Y", "f").simulate(
           nsim=5, seed=2), cond[:5]) else "FAIL")
record("snesim(...) == SNESIM(...).simulate",
       "PASS" if np.array_equal(snesim(grid, wells, "X", "Y", "f", TI, nsim=5, servo=0.0, seed=2, use_gpu=USE_GPU),
                                cond[:5]) else "FAIL")


def score(name, reals):
    r = np.asarray(reals)
    P = np.stack([(r == k).mean(0) for k in range(3)])
    onehot = np.stack([(truth == k).astype(float) for k in range(3)])
    imgs = r.reshape(-1, NX, NY)
    return {"method": name, "Brier": np.mean(((P - onehot) ** 2).sum(0)),
            "channel recall (most probable)": np.mean((P.argmax(0) == 1)[truth == 1]),
            "agreement per realization": np.mean(r == truth[None, :]),
            "forbidden FP-CH edges": np.mean([contacts(x)[0, 1] for x in imgs[:10]]),
            "channel connectivity @30": np.nanmean([connectivity(x, 1, 30, 0)[-1] for x in imgs[:10]])}


uncond = SNESIM(TI, servo=0.0, use_gpu=USE_GPU).fit(grid).simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=2)
cond_table = pd.DataFrame([score("unconditional", uncond), score("80 wells", cond)]).set_index("method")
display(cond_table.round(3))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(25, 6))
show(axes[0], TRUTH, "Truth and 80 wells", wells)
show(axes[1], cond[0].reshape(NX, NY), "Conditional SNESIM, realization 1", wells)

im = axes[3].imshow(P_cond[1].reshape(NX, NY).T, origin="lower", cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)

Exact conditioning. The 80 wells are honoured in every realization, and the seed reproduces the realizations.
Local accuracy. Conditioning improves it: the multiclass Brier score falls from 0.51 to 0.42, the most probable map finds 36% of the channel cells, and agreement per realization rises from 0.57 to 0.63. The P(channel) map shows the channels pinned near channel wells and diffuse elsewhere. Only 12 of the 80 wells are in channels.
Patterns suffer. Forbidden contacts rise from 1.8 to 21 per realization, and channel connectivity at 30 cells falls from 0.89 to 0.60. The wells create data events with combinations the TI rarely shows (a channel well next to a floodplain well, or a well inside a predicted levee). Those events are reduced, or force awkward patterns locally.

This conflict between data and TI is normal in MPS. A TI whose patterns are consistent with the data (here, more variable channel widths and spacings) reduces it.

title: SNESIM: Single Normal Equation Simulation (SNESIM)
section: Soft Data and the Tau Model
text:
Soft Data and the Tau Model
A seismic-like secondary variable is built by blurring the channel indicator (Gaussian filter, \(\sigma\) = 3 cells) and adding noise. It responds to channels, but blurs them and cannot tell levee from floodplain. The same operator on the TI gives paired (facies, secondary) values. From those, the soft probabilities \(P(s_k \mid y)\) are tabulated in 20 quantile bins of \(y\) and looked up on the grid. These are passed to fit(..., soft=...).
tau_model itself is shown first on one node, then SNESIM is run with several \(\tau\):







\(\tau\)
Meaning




(1, 1)
permanence of ratios (default)


(1, 0.5)
soft data discounted


(1, 2)
soft data emphasized


(0, 1)
soft data only; the TI is ignored except through the hard data





Code
def seismic(img, seed):
    return gaussian_filter((np.asarray(img) == 1).astype(float), 3.0) + np.random.default_rng(seed).normal(0, 0.08, np.shape(img))


Y_TI = seismic(TI, 10)
y_grid = seismic(TRUTH, 11).ravel()
edges = np.quantile(Y_TI, np.linspace(0, 1, 21))
bin_ti = np.clip(np.searchsorted(edges, Y_TI.ravel(), side="right") - 1, 0, 19)
table = np.array([[np.mean(TI.ravel()[bin_ti == b] == k) for k in range(3)] for b in range(20)])
bin_grid = np.clip(np.searchsorted(edges, y_grid, side="right") - 1, 0, 19)
soft = table[bin_grid]                                           # (n_nodes, 3), columns: floodplain, channel, levee
print(f"corr(secondary, channel indicator) on the truth: {np.corrcoef(y_grid, truth == 1)[0, 1]:.2f}")

prior = np.array([np.mean(TI == k) for k in range(3)])
p_ti, p_soft = np.array([0.2, 0.5, 0.3]), np.array([0.1, 0.8, 0.1])
for tau in [(1, 1), (1, 0.5), (1, 2), (0, 1), (1, 0)]:
    print(f"tau = {tau}:  P = {np.round(tau_model(prior, p_ti, p_soft, tau), 3)}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(19, 5.5))
im = axes[0].imshow(y_grid.reshape(NX, NY).T, origin="lower", cmap="gray")
axes[0].set_title("Secondary (seismic-like) on the grid")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
for k, c in enumerate(["#b59a4a", "#1f5fa8", "#5f9f3a"]):
    axes[1].plot(np.arange(20), table[:, k], "o-", c=c, label=FACIES[k])
axes[1].set_xlabel("secondary quantile bin")
axes[1].set_ylabel("P(facies | secondary)")
axes[1].set_title("Calibration on the TI pairs")
axes[1].legend()
im = axes[2].imshow(soft[:, 1].reshape(NX, NY).T, origin="lower", cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)

Why ignoring the TI fails. \(\tau = (0, 1)\) has the best Brier score but is not a fluvial image any more. Without the TI’s patterns, the blurred secondary paints channel blobs straight onto floodplain, with no levees in between and no continuous channels.
Choosing \(\tau\). Good local scores are not enough: check the patterns as well. \(\tau = (1, 1)\) is a good default here, with large gains in accuracy and connectivity and a moderate rise in forbidden contacts. Discount the soft data (\(\tau_2 < 1\)) when they are redundant with the wells or the TI.

The single-node example shows the mechanics. With a TI probability of 0.5 and a soft probability of 0.8 for channel, against a prior of 0.10, \(\tau = (1, 1)\) gives 0.75. The soft data’s odds ratio over the prior multiplies the TI’s.

SNESIM reads the conditional probability of each facies from the frequencies of the same data event in the training image (the single normal equation), stored once in a pattern table.
The multigrid matters most for large structures. Channel connectivity at 30 cells went from 0 with one grid to 0.88 with five (TI 0.94), at almost no extra cost. The template (30-60 nodes) and a small min_replicates (1-3) keep the TI’s adjacency rules: forbidden floodplain-channel contacts fell to 0.9 per realization with min_replicates = 1.
Proportions: the servosystem barely matters when the TI’s proportions are the target. To reach different targets, it moved the channel proportion from 0.11 to 0.24 (target 0.25), at the price of patterns that drift from the TI (pattern distance 0.13 → 0.25) and more forbidden contacts.
Conditioning to 80 wells was exact and improved local accuracy (Brier 0.51 → 0.42), but data events the TI rarely shows raised the forbidden contacts (1.8 → 21).
Soft data through the tau model improved local accuracy substantially (Brier 0.42 → 0.29, channel recall 0.36 → 0.56) and restored connectivity. The exponents trade local accuracy against pattern fidelity, and ignoring the TI (\(\tau = (0, 1)\)) destroys the geology.
GPU: identical realizations, 61× faster at 32 realizations.


Choosing the options







Parameter
Guidance from this notebook




n_template, search_radius
30-60 nodes; larger templates store more patterns and cost more per lookup; the GPU engine allows up to 64


n_multigrid
enough levels that the coarsest template spans the largest structure (here 4-5 for 100-cell channels)


min_replicates
small (1-3) for continuity and fewer forbidden patterns; larger only with large TIs


servo
0 when pattern fidelity matters and the TI’s proportions are acceptable; up to 0.8 to reach different targets, checking forbidden patterns


target_proportions
from wells or regional knowledge when the TI’s proportions are not representative (with servo > 0)


soft, tau
calibrate soft probabilities on TI pairs; \(\tau = (1, 1)\) is a sound default; check that \(\tau_2 > 1\) does not break the patterns


use_gpu
True for many realizations: identical results, much faster

title: Plurigaussian Simulation (PluriGaussianSimulator)
text:
Overview
Geological units do not touch at random. In a stratigraphic sequence a formation lies between the one below and the one above, so on a map it borders those two and, wherever erosion or cover cuts across, younger deposits. Sequential indicator simulation (SIS) knows nothing about this. It kriges each class’s probability separately, so any class can appear next to any other. Plurigaussian simulation (PGS; Le Loc’h & Galli, 1997; Armstrong et al., 2003) builds that knowledge in.
PGS simulates one or two continuous latent Gaussian fields and turns them into categories with a truncation rule: a partition of the latent space into regions, one or more per category. Two categories can be in contact in a realization only if their regions share an edge in the rule. The rule therefore controls the contacts, and with the latent variograms it also controls the proportions and the shapes of the units.







Object
What it does




TruncationRule
The rule, as rectangles in probability space \([0,1]^2\). Constructors: truncated_gaussian (one field, ordered categories), hierarchical (one category on \(Y_1\), the others stacked along \(Y_2\)), from_flag (any rule drawn as an image). It also has proportions(rho) and classify(y1, y2).


PluriGaussianSimulator
fit(grid, df, x, y, cat) and simulate(nsim, seed, return_latent=False). A Gibbs sampler conditions the latent fields to the categorical data, and the latent fields are simulated by FFT on a lattice or by turning bands.


pgsim
One-call wrapper (with labels=True for category names).


category_probabilities, category_proportions
Per-node class frequencies and per-realization proportions.



The Jura geology is a clean test, because the mapped geology gives a reference for contacts:

the four Jurassic formations are in stratigraphic order: Argovian, Sequanian, Kimmeridgian, Portlandian;
Quaternary deposits cover all of them.

The notebook:

measures the contacts on the geology map and designs a hierarchical rule from them;
infers the latent variograms from the indicator variograms of 259 samples;
conditions the simulation to the samples, and checks it;
compares PGS with a single-field truncated Gaussian rule and with SIS on contacts, proportions and agreement with the map.

title: Plurigaussian Simulation (PluriGaussianSimulator)
text:
Theory

Facies from truncated Gaussian fields
Let \(A(\mathbf{u})\) and \(B(\mathbf{u})\) be independent stationary standard Gaussian random fields with correlograms \(\rho_A(\mathbf{h})\) and \(\rho_B(\mathbf{h})\) (variograms with sill 1). The latent fields are
\[
Y_1(\mathbf{u}) = A(\mathbf{u}), \qquad Y_2(\mathbf{u}) = \rho\, A(\mathbf{u}) + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\, B(\mathbf{u}),
\]
so \(\operatorname{corr}(Y_1, Y_2) = \rho\) at the same location. The category at \(\mathbf{u}\) is
\[
S(\mathbf{u}) = s_k \iff \bigl(Y_1(\mathbf{u}), Y_2(\mathbf{u})\bigr) \in D_k ,
\]
where \(D_1, \dots, D_K\) partition the plane. With one field (\(D_k\) are intervals of \(Y_1\)), this is truncated Gaussian simulation (Matheron et al., 1987).


The truncation rule
TruncationRule describes each \(D_k\) as one or more rectangles in probability space, \(u_j = \Phi(y_j) \in [0, 1]\), so a rule is a tiling of the unit square:
\[
D_k = \bigcup_{r \in R_k} [u_{1,r}^-, u_{1,r}^+) \times [u_{2,r}^-, u_{2,r}^+) .
\]
The constructors:

truncated_gaussian(p): one field. Category \(k\) is \(U_1 \in [P_{k-1}, P_k)\) with \(P_k = \sum_{j \le k} p_j\). Categories are ordered: each touches only its neighbours in the sequence.
hierarchical(p): the first category is \(U_1 < p_1\), across the whole \(U_2\) axis; the others are stacked along \(U_2\) in the strip \(U_1 \ge p_1\). The first category can touch every other one; the others touch only their neighbours in the stack.
from_flag(flag): any rule drawn as a small image. flag[i, j] is the category of cell \((i, j)\) of a grid on \([0,1]^2\), rows along \(U_1\) and columns along \(U_2\).



Proportions
The proportion of category \(k\) is the probability that \((Y_1, Y_2)\) falls in \(D_k\):
\[
p_k = \sum_{r \in R_k} P\bigl\{y_{1,r}^- \le Y_1 < y_{1,r}^+,\; y_{2,r}^- \le Y_2 < y_{2,r}^+\bigr\},
\]
a bivariate normal rectangle probability with correlation \(\rho\) (rule.proportions(rho)). For \(\rho = 0\) it factorizes into \((u_1^+ - u_1^-)(u_2^+ - u_2^-)\), so a rule built from target proportions with \(\rho = 0\) reproduces them exactly. With \(\rho \ne 0\) the same rectangles give different proportions.


Contacts
Because the latent fields are continuous, a path in space that crosses from \(D_j\) to \(D_k\) must pass through every region in between. So in a realization, categories \(j\) and \(k\) can be adjacent only if \(D_j\) and \(D_k\) share an edge in the rule. On a discrete grid a narrow intermediate region can be skipped between two neighbouring cells, so “forbidden” contacts become rare rather than impossible. This is the key difference from SIS, where every pair of classes can touch.


Indicator variograms from latent variograms
The indicator of category \(k\) is \(I_k(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{1}[(Y_1, Y_2)(\mathbf{u}) \in D_k]\). Its variogram follows from the latent correlograms through bivariate probabilities. For one rectangle with \(\rho = 0\), the two independent fields factorize:
\[
\gamma_{I_k}(\mathbf{h}) = p_k - P\{I_k(\mathbf{u}) = 1, I_k(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{h}) = 1\}
= p_k - \pi_A\bigl(y_1^-, y_1^+; \rho_A(\mathbf{h})\bigr)\, \pi_B\bigl(y_2^-, y_2^+; \rho_B(\mathbf{h})\bigr),
\]
where \(\pi(a, b; r) = P\{a \le X < b,\, a \le X' < b\}\) for standard normals \(X, X'\) with correlation \(r\). This links what can be measured, the indicator variograms of the data, to what PGS needs, the latent correlograms. Section 6 inverts it by least squares.


Conditioning: the Gibbs sampler
At a datum the category is known, but the latent values are not: they are only known to lie in \(D_k\). Before simulating, GeoLattice draws latent values at the \(n\) data that are consistent with both the categories and the latent covariance, with a Gibbs sampler (Armstrong et al., 2003; Emery, 2007).
With \(\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{C}^{-1}\) the precision matrix of \(A\) at the data, the full conditional of \(A_i\) given all other \(A_j\) is Gaussian, with
\[
E[A_i \mid A_{-i}] = -\frac{1}{Q_{ii}} \sum_{j \ne i} Q_{ij}\, A_j, \qquad \operatorname{Var}[A_i \mid A_{-i}] = \frac{1}{Q_{ii}},
\]
the simple-kriging mean and variance of \(A_i\) from all the other data. Each sweep redraws every \(A_i\), and then every \(B_i\), from that Gaussian truncated to the values that keep \((Y_1, Y_2)\) in the observed category’s region, given the current value of the other field. For a rectangle with \(\rho > 0\), for example,
\[
A_i \in [y_1^-, y_1^+) \cap \left[\frac{y_2^- - \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\, B_i}{\rho},\; \frac{y_2^+ - \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\, B_i}{\rho}\right).
\]
After gibbs_iter sweeps (default 200) the chain approximates the joint conditional distribution of the latent values at the data. Each realization gets its own Gibbs draw; the chains run vectorized over realizations.


Simulating the latent fields
Given the latent values at the data, \(A\) and \(B\) are simulated conditionally on the grid: an unconditional Gaussian field, corrected by simple kriging of the residuals at the data. On a regular lattice this uses the FFT (circulant-embedding) simulator, method="fft", the default when the grid is a lattice. Otherwise it uses turning bands (method="tb"). On a lattice, data are first moved to their nearest node; a node holding data of different categories keeps the most frequent one, with a warning. The realization is rule.classify(Y1, Y2), and it reproduces the data categories at their nodes.


The algorithm

Choose the rule (categories, proportions, contacts) and the latent variograms (sill 1), and optionally \(\rho\).
For each realization:

run the Gibbs sampler for latent values \((A_i, B_i)\) at the data, consistent with their categories;
simulate \(A\) and \(B\) on the grid conditionally on those values;
form \(Y_1 = A\) and \(Y_2 = \rho A + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\, B\), and classify with the rule.

def to_image(values, fill=np.nan):
    img = np.full((iy.max() + 1, ix.max() + 1), fill, dtype=object if isinstance(fill, str) else float)
    img[iy, ix] = values
    return img


def show_rock(ax, labels, title, points=None):
    codes = np.array([NAMES.index(v) for v in labels], float)
    im = ax.imshow(to_image(codes), origin="lower", extent=EXTENT, cmap=CMAP, vmin=-0.5, vmax=4.5,

    ax.set_ylabel("Y (km)")

                   interpolation="nearest")

    ax.set_ylabel("Y (km)")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label=label, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)


def contacts(labels):
    # number of 4-neighbour cell edges between each pair of different units
    img = to_image(np.asarray(labels, dtype=object), fill="")
    M = pd.DataFrame(0, index=NAMES, columns=NAMES)
    for a, b in [(img[1:, :], img[:-1, :]), (img[:, 1:], img[:, :-1])]:
        ok = (a != "") & (b != "") & (a != b)
        for x, y in zip(a[ok], b[ok]):
            M.loc[x, y] += 1
            M.loc[y, x] += 1
    return M


def total_contacts(M):
    return int(np.triu(M.values).sum())

show_rock(axes[0], geo_map, "Geology map (jura_grid.csv) and the 259 samples", points=xy)
im = axes[1].imshow(map_contacts.values, cmap="Blues")
axes[1].set_xticks(range(5), NAMES, rotation=30)
axes[1].set_yticks(range(5), NAMES)
for i in range(5):
    for j in range(5):
        axes[1].text(j, i, map_contacts.values[i, j], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_title(f"Contacts on the geology map ({total_contacts(map_contacts)} edges)")

The map’s contacts follow the geology:

The Jurassic formations touch only their stratigraphic neighbours: Argovian-Sequanian, Sequanian-Kimmeridgian and Kimmeridgian-Portlandian.
Contacts that skip a formation are almost absent: Argovian-Kimmeridgian 2, Sequanian-Portlandian 5, Argovian-Portlandian 0.
Quaternary deposits touch every formation.

That is exactly the structure of a hierarchical truncation rule.

title: Plurigaussian Simulation (PluriGaussianSimulator)
text:
Designing the Truncation Rule
TruncationRule.hierarchical puts its first category on \(Y_1\) and stacks the others along \(Y_2\). With Quaternary first and the formations in stratigraphic order, Quaternary can touch every formation, while each formation can touch only its stratigraphic neighbours. The proportions are those of the 259 samples.


Code
p_samples = {c: float((df["rock"] == c).mean()) for c in ["Quaternary"] + STRAT}
rule = TruncationRule.hierarchical(p_samples)
print(rule)
print("n_fields:", rule.n_fields)


def draw_rule(ax, rule, title):
    for cat, a, b, c, d in rule.rectangles:
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((a, c), b - a, d - c, facecolor=COLORS[cat], edgecolor="k", lw=1))
        ax.text((a + b) / 2, (c + d) / 2, cat, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_xlabel("U1 = Phi(Y1)")
    ax.set_ylabel("U2 = Phi(Y2)")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")


rule_tg = TruncationRule.truncated_gaussian({c: p_samples[c] for c in NAMES})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.6))
draw_rule(axes[0], rule, "Hierarchical rule (Quaternary first)")
draw_rule(axes[1], rule_tg, "Truncated Gaussian rule (one field)")

record("rule proportions equal the sample proportions at rho = 0",

It makes every unit touch only its neighbours in that order, so Quaternary can only border Portlandian. That contradicts the map, and Section 9 shows the consequence.
