title: Plurigaussian Simulation (PluriGaussianSimulator)
text:
Inferring the Latent Variograms
PGS needs the variograms of the latent fields, which cannot be observed. What can be measured are the indicator variograms of the five units at the 259 samples. Section 2.5 gives the model indicator variogram of each unit as a function of the latent correlograms. The latent ranges are fitted by least squares, one field at a time:

\(Y_1\) alone decides Quaternary versus the rest, so its range \(a_1\) is fitted to the Quaternary indicator variogram;
\(Y_2\) then decides between the formations, so its range \(a_2\) is fitted to the four formation indicator variograms, with \(a_1\) fixed.

Spherical latent models are used here; Section 11 compares other model types.


Code
EDGES = np.linspace(0, 2.0, 17)
d_pairs = pdist(xy)
h_lags = np.array([d_pairs[(d_pairs > lo) & (d_pairs <= hi)].mean() for lo, hi in zip(EDGES[:-1], EDGES[1:])])
exp_ind = {}
for c in NAMES:
    i_c = (df["rock"] == c).to_numpy(float)
    g = 0.5 * pdist(i_c[:, None], "sqeuclidean")
    exp_ind[c] = np.array([g[(d_pairs > lo) & (d_pairs <= hi)].mean() for lo, hi in zip(EDGES[:-1], EDGES[1:])])

CORRELOGRAMS = {
    "spherical": lambda h, a: 1 - (1.5 * np.minimum(h / a, 1) - 0.5 * np.minimum(h / a, 1) ** 3),
    "exponential": lambda h, a: np.exp(-3 * h / a),
    "gaussian": lambda h, a: np.exp(-3 * (h / a) ** 2),
}


def both_in(lo, hi, r):
    # P(lo <= X < hi, lo <= X' < hi) for standard normals with correlation r
    lo, hi = max(lo, -8.0), min(hi, 8.0)
    r = min(r, 0.9999)
    mv = multivariate_normal(mean=[0, 0], cov=[[1, r], [r, 1]])
    return mv.cdf([hi, hi]) - mv.cdf([lo, hi]) - mv.cdf([hi, lo]) + mv.cdf([lo, lo])


BOXES = {cat: (a, b, c, d) for cat, a, b, c, d in rule.rectangles}


def model_indicator(cat, a1, a2, h, vtype):
    rho_f = CORRELOGRAMS[vtype]
    u1a, u1b, u2a, u2b = BOXES[cat]
    p_k = (u1b - u1a) * (u2b - u2a)
    out = []
    for hh in h:
        p1 = both_in(ndtri(u1a), ndtri(u1b), rho_f(hh, a1))
        p2 = both_in(ndtri(u2a), ndtri(u2b), rho_f(hh, a2)) if (u2a > 0 or u2b < 1) else 1.0
        out.append(p_k - p1 * p2)
    return np.array(out)


def fit_latent(vtype, cands=np.arange(0.2, 3.01, 0.1)):
    e1 = [np.sum((model_indicator("Quaternary", a, 1.0, h_lags, vtype) - exp_ind["Quaternary"]) ** 2) for a in cands]
    a1 = float(cands[int(np.argmin(e1))])
    e2 = [sum(np.sum((model_indicator(c, a1, a, h_lags, vtype) - exp_ind[c]) ** 2) for c in STRAT) for a in cands]
    a2 = float(cands[int(np.argmin(e2))])
    return round(a1, 2), round(a2, 2), float(min(e1) + min(e2))


t0 = time.perf_counter()
A1, A2, SSE = fit_latent("spherical")
VARIO1 = [0.0, 0.0, A1, A1, 1.0, "spherical"]
VARIO2 = [0.0, 0.0, A2, A2, 1.0, "spherical"]
print(f"fitted in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s:  Y1 range {A1} km, Y2 range {A2} km  (SSE {SSE:.4f})")
print("vario1 =", VARIO1, "  vario2 =", VARIO2)

hh = np.linspace(0.02, 2.0, 40)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(24, 3.9))
for ax, c in zip(axes, NAMES):
    ax.plot(h_lags, exp_ind[c], "o", color=COLORS[c], mec="k", label="samples")
    ax.plot(hh, model_indicator(c, A1, A2, hh, "spherical"), "k-", label="PGS model")
    ax.set_title(c)
    ax.set_xlabel("h (km)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("indicator semivariance")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


fitted in 0.9 s:  Y1 range 0.5 km, Y2 range 1.8 km  (SSE 0.0330)
vario1 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0, 'spherical']   vario2 = [0.0, 0.0, 1.8, 1.8, 1.0, 'spherical']










Two scales. \(Y_1\) has a short range (0.5 km): the Quaternary deposits form small, scattered patches. \(Y_2\) has a long range (1.8 km): the formations form broad bands.
Fit. The model indicator variograms follow the sample ones for all five units, including the tiny Portlandian sill (\(p \approx 0.012\)).
Fewer parameters than SIS. In SIS each unit’s indicator variogram is fitted on its own. In PGS all five come from two latent ranges through the rule, so they are tied together. That leaves fewer parameters and guarantees a consistent bivariate model, at the price of a less flexible fit to any single unit.

title: Plurigaussian Simulation (PluriGaussianSimulator)
text:
Conditional Simulation
fit(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "rock") conditions to the 259 samples. The samples are moved to their nearest 50 m node. Checks:

the Gibbs latent values at the data fall in their category’s region, for every realization;
the simulated categories at the data nodes equal the data;
the same seed gives the same realizations, and realization \(i\) does not depend on nsim: each realization has its own Gibbs chain and latent-field random stream (the chains still run vectorized), so the first 3 of 50 realizations equal an nsim = 3 run, as with the sequential simulators;
pgsim equals the class.



Code
N_SIM = 50
pgs = PluriGaussianSimulator(rule, VARIO1, VARIO2, gibbs_iter=200)
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    pgs.fit(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "rock")
for w in caught:
    print("warning:", w.message)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
codes = pgs.simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=2024)
print(f"{N_SIM} conditional realizations in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
labels = np.asarray(pgs.categories_, dtype=object)[codes]
CATS = pgs.categories_

A, B = pgs.latent_data_
y1d, y2d = A, pgs.rho * A + np.sqrt(1 - pgs.rho ** 2) * B
gibbs_ok = np.all(rule.classify(y1d, y2d) == pgs._data_codes[:, None])
record("Gibbs latent values reproduce the data categories (all realizations)", "PASS" if gibbs_ok else "FAIL",
       f"{len(pgs._data_codes)} data nodes x {N_SIM} realizations")

dist, node_of_data = cKDTree(grid).query(pgs._data_xy)
on_grid = dist < 1e-6                     # data snapped to a lattice node that is part of the grid
cond_ok = np.all(codes[:, node_of_data[on_grid]] == pgs._data_codes[on_grid][None, :])
record("conditional PGS: data categories reproduced at their nodes", "PASS" if cond_ok else "FAIL",
       f"{on_grid.sum()} of {len(on_grid)} data nodes lie on the grid")
# each realization has its own random streams (Gibbs chain and latent fields), so realization i
# depends only on the seed, not on nsim
again = PluriGaussianSimulator(rule, VARIO1, VARIO2).fit(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "rock").simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=2024)
record("conditional PGS: same seed and nsim -> identical", "PASS" if np.array_equal(again, codes) else "FAIL")

section: Contacts: PGS vs Truncated Gaussian vs SIS
text:
Contacts: PGS vs Truncated Gaussian vs SIS
Three categorical simulators, all conditioned to the same 259 samples, are compared:

PGS, hierarchical rule (the realizations above);
truncated Gaussian: one latent field, with the rule in the order Argovian, Sequanian, Kimmeridgian, Portlandian, Quaternary, and a single latent variogram (the \(Y_2\) fit);
SIS (IndicatorCoSimulator, categorical), with spherical indicator variograms fitted to each unit’s experimental indicator variogram, as in the SIS notebook.

The contact matrices are averaged over 10 realizations.


Code
tg = PluriGaussianSimulator(rule_tg, VARIO2).fit(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "rock")
labels_tg = np.asarray(tg.categories_, dtype=object)[tg.simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=2024)]


def fit_indicator_vario(ind):
    p = ind.mean()
    sill = p * (1 - p)
    g = 0.5 * pdist(ind[:, None], "sqeuclidean")
    e = np.array([g[(d_pairs > lo) & (d_pairs <= hi)].mean() for lo, hi in zip(EDGES[:-1], EDGES[1:])])
    sph = lambda h, nr, a: nr * sill + (sill - nr * sill) * (1.5 * np.minimum(h / a, 1) - 0.5 * np.minimum(h / a, 1) ** 3)
    (nr, a), _ = curve_fit(sph, h_lags, e, p0=[0.2, 1.0], bounds=([0, 0.1], [0.95, 4]))
    return [0.0, round(nr * sill, 4), round(a, 3), round(a, 3), round(sill, 4), "spherical"]


sis_codes = {n: i + 1 for i, n in enumerate(NAMES)}
df["rock_code"] = df["rock"].map(sis_codes)
sis_varios = {k: fit_indicator_vario((df["rock"] == n).to_numpy(float)) for n, k in sis_codes.items()}
sis = IndicatorCoSimulator(list(sis_codes.values()), sis_varios, num_points=16, radius=1.5, use_gpu=USE_GPU)
labels_sis = np.asarray(NAMES, dtype=object)[sis.fit(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "rock_code").simulate(
    nsim=N_SIM, seed=2024).astype(int) - 1]

methods = {"PGS (hierarchical)": labels, "truncated Gaussian": labels_tg, "SIS": labels_sis}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(25, 5.6))

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

FORBIDDEN = [("Argovian", "Kimmeridgian"), ("Sequanian", "Portlandian"), ("Argovian", "Portlandian")]
rows = []
for name, M in [("geology map", map_contacts)] + list(avg_contacts.items()):
    tot = M.values.sum() / 2
    rows.append({"method": name, "total contact edges": tot,
                 **{f"{a[:4]}-{b[:4]}": M.loc[a, b] for a, b in FORBIDDEN},

PGS reproduces the geology. Contacts that skip a formation make up 0.05% of all PGS contacts, against 0.4% on the map. The forbidden pairs are almost absent: about 1.4 Argovian-Kimmeridgian edges per realization, where a narrow Sequanian band is skipped between two neighbouring cells. Quaternary touches every formation, as on the map; for example, 292 edges with Argovian against the map’s 262.
SIS ignores the stratigraphy. About 9% of its contacts skip a formation: 177 Argovian-Kimmeridgian edges per realization against the map’s 2, plus Argovian-Portlandian contacts that never occur on the map.
The wrong rule gives the wrong geology. The truncated Gaussian rule respects its own order, so it also has few skipped formations. But it forbids Quaternary next to Argovian, Sequanian and most of Kimmeridgian, so it has zero Quaternary-Argovian edges against 262 on the map. The rule has to come from the geology, and a one-field rule cannot express “one unit touches all”.
Boundary length. All three simulators produce more contact edges than the map (PGS about 2,600, SIS about 2,100, map 1,576). The realizations are more fragmented than a hand-drawn map, which generalizes boundaries; Section 11 shows how the latent model type controls this.

the mean probability given to the sample’s recorded unit;

At the held-out samples, PGS gives the recorded unit a mean probability of 0.72 against 0.71 for SIS, and the multiclass Brier scores are 0.28 vs 0.27. The truncated Gaussian rule is worst on every score.
The advantage of PGS is structural, not cell-wise. Its realizations have the right kinds of boundaries (Section 9). Contacts govern, for example, flow and transport across unit boundaries, or soil-forming parent material along a transect, and there PGS gives plausible answers that SIS cannot.
Proportions. Both PGS and SIS over-produce Kimmeridgian (about 0.42) relative to the samples (0.36) and the map (0.34). For PGS, this comes from conditioning on 259 data with a long-range \(Y_2\) field: the domain holds only a few \(Y_2\) ranges, so the proportions of a realization fluctuate around the rule’s (the unconditional runs in Section 7 already showed Kimmeridgian at 0.38). If exact proportions matter, check them on the realizations and adjust the rule.

The latent ranges were fitted for spherical correlograms. The type of latent model also matters, because it sets how rough the boundaries between units are. Each type is fitted to the indicator variograms as above and then simulated (20 realizations each).

section: Correlated Latent Fields: the Effect of \(\rho\)
text:
Correlated Latent Fields: the Effect of \(\rho\)
With \(\rho \ne 0\), \(Y_2\) shares part of \(Y_1\). In this rule \(Y_1\) decides Quaternary versus the rest, so a correlation links where the Quaternary is with which formation is nearby. For \(\rho > 0\), high \(Y_1\) (no Quaternary) goes with high \(Y_2\) (younger formations), so Quaternary deposits tend to border the older formations.
The same rectangles also give different proportions for \(\rho \ne 0\) (rule.proportions(rho)). Unconditional realizations show the effect without data.

category_probabilities(codes) gives, for each unit, the fraction of realizations in which each node belongs to it. Plurigaussian simulation turns one or two latent Gaussian fields into categories with a truncation rule. The rule decides which units may touch; the latent variograms decide their size and shape.
The Jura geology map showed stratigraphic contacts (Argovian-Sequanian-Kimmeridgian-Portlandian) with Quaternary touching all of them. A hierarchical rule, with Quaternary on \(Y_1\) and the formations stacked on \(Y_2\), encodes exactly that. from_flag builds the same rule from an image.
Latent variograms were inferred from the indicator variograms of 259 samples through the rule: 0.5 km for \(Y_1\) (Quaternary patches) and 1.8 km for \(Y_2\) (formation bands).
Conditioning: the Gibbs sampler gave latent values consistent with every datum’s category in every realization, and the conditional realizations reproduce the data. Realization \(i\) depends only on the seed, not on nsim.
Contacts: PGS kept non-stratigraphic contacts at 0.05% (map 0.4%), while SIS had 9%, including 177 Argovian-Kimmeridgian edges per realization against the map’s 2. A one-field truncated Gaussian rule could not let Quaternary touch Argovian at all. Cell-wise agreement with the map and held-out scores were similar for PGS and SIS. The gain from PGS is geological structure.
Model choice: the Gaussian latent model fitted the indicator variograms best but produced worse realizations. Check realizations, not just the fit. \(\rho\) changes both proportions and which formations the Quaternary borders, and the map supports \(\rho = 0\).
Cost: about 4 s for the first realization (Gibbs sampling), then about 0.1 s per additional realization with FFT latent fields.

title: Direct Sequential Simulation (dssim_direct)
text:
Overview
Sequential Gaussian simulation works on normal scores. It transforms the data to a standard normal distribution, models and reproduces the variogram of the scores, and back-transforms each realization. The histogram comes back right, but the variogram of the realizations in original units (mg/kg) is whatever the back-transform makes of the normal-score variogram. For a skewed variable, that is not the variogram you would model from the data in mg/kg.
Direct sequential simulation (DSS; Journel, 1994; Soares, 2001) skips the transform for kriging. It kriges the variable in its original units, with the original-unit variogram, and draws each value from a local distribution that has the kriging mean and the kriging variance. That is enough to reproduce the original-unit variogram. To reproduce the histogram as well, the local distribution is built from the global distribution of the data. Doing that without bias is the hard part, and GeoLattice offers the two published methods:








method
Local distribution
Reproduces




"lookup" (default; Oz et al., 2003)
a back-transformed Gaussian window from a pre-computed table, chosen so its mean and variance match the kriging mean and variance
local means and variances, so the original-unit variogram; the histogram approximately


"soares" (Soares, 2001)
the kriging estimate mapped to Gaussian space, a normal draw, mapped back
values always from the global distribution, but biased upward for skewed variables, and the bias compounds



The objects:







Object
What it does




GlobalDistribution
The global cdf \(F\) from (optionally declustering-weighted) data, with cdf, quantile, to_gaussian and from_gaussian, extended linearly to zmin / zmax.


DirectSequentialSimulator
The engine: fit(grid, df, ..., secondary=None) and simulate(nsim, seed), CPU or GPU, with optional collocated co-simulation.


dssim_direct
One-call wrapper. It is named _direct because dssim is the Direct Sampling MPS simulator.



Cadmium in the Jura topsoil is strongly skewed (skewness about 1.5), which is the case DSS is designed for. This notebook:

checks exact conditioning, reproducibility, and that the GPU and CPU give the same realizations;
compares histogram and original-unit variogram reproduction for the lookup method, Soares’ method and SGS;
shows where original units matter: block averages, whose variance is set by the original-unit covariance;
co-simulates cadmium with a kriged zinc map, and validates every variant at 100 held-out sites.

title: Direct Sequential Simulation (dssim_direct)
text:
Theory

Why Gaussian simulation misses the original-unit variogram
SGS simulates \(Y(\mathbf{u})\), the normal score of \(Z(\mathbf{u})\), with the normal-score covariance \(C_Y(\mathbf{h})\), and returns \(Z = \varphi(Y) = F^{-1}(G(Y))\). Under the multi-Gaussian model the original-unit covariance of the realizations is then fixed by \(C_Y\) and \(\varphi\):
\[
C_Z(\mathbf{h}) = \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{\phi_n^2}{n!}\, \rho_Y(\mathbf{h})^n, \qquad \rho_Y = C_Y / C_Y(\mathbf{0}),
\]
where \(\phi_n\) are the Hermite coefficients of \(\varphi\) (the Hermitian expansion; Rivoirard, 1994). For a linear \(\varphi\) only \(n = 1\) survives and \(C_Z \propto C_Y\). For a skewed variable the higher terms matter: they decay faster with distance, so the original-unit correlation \(\rho_Z(\mathbf{h})\) is lower than \(\rho_Y(\mathbf{h})\) at every lag, and the relative nugget in mg/kg is larger than in normal scores. You cannot choose the mg/kg variogram in SGS: it is implied.


The principle of direct sequential simulation
Journel (1994) showed that sequential simulation reproduces a covariance \(C(\mathbf{h})\) in original units whatever the shape of the local distributions, as long as each node is drawn from a distribution with
\[
E[Z(\mathbf{u}) \mid \cdot] = z^*_{SK}(\mathbf{u}), \qquad \operatorname{Var}[Z(\mathbf{u}) \mid \cdot] = \sigma^2_{SK}(\mathbf{u}),
\]
the simple-kriging mean and variance in original units:
\[
z^*_{SK}(\mathbf{u}) = m + \sum_\alpha \lambda_\alpha \bigl[z(\mathbf{u}_\alpha) - m\bigr], \qquad
\sum_\beta \lambda_\beta C(\mathbf{u}_\alpha - \mathbf{u}_\beta) = C(\mathbf{u}_\alpha - \mathbf{u}), \qquad
\sigma^2_{SK} = C(\mathbf{0}) - \sum_\alpha \lambda_\alpha C(\mathbf{u}_\alpha - \mathbf{u}).
\]
The argument is that simple kriging is the conditional expectation under a linear model. Drawing a residual with the right first two moments at every step reproduces the covariance between each new value and all previous ones, by induction along the path. No Gaussian assumption and no transform is needed. The sill of the variogram is the variance of \(Z\) itself, in mg/kg².
The catch is the histogram. If the local distributions are, say, Gaussian, the realizations become Gaussian too and the skewness is lost. DSS must draw from local distributions whose shape comes from the global histogram, while still matching \(z^*_{SK}\) and \(\sigma^2_{SK}\).


The global distribution
GlobalDistribution builds the global cdf from the data \(z_{(1)} \le \dots \le z_{(n)}\) with weights \(w_i\) (equal, or declustering weights, normalized to sum to 1), by the midpoint rule
\[
F(z_{(i)}) = \sum_{j \le i} w_j - \tfrac12 w_i,
\]
and extends it linearly to \(F(z_{\min}) = 0\) and \(F(z_{\max}) = 1\). zmin and zmax default to the data extremes and must bracket the data. The weighted mean and variance are the defaults for the simple-kriging mean \(m\) and the reference variance. Its two transforms connect original units and Gaussian space:
\[
y = G^{-1}\bigl(F(z)\bigr) \quad (\texttt{to\_gaussian}), \qquad z = F^{-1}\bigl(G(y)\bigr) \quad (\texttt{from\_gaussian}).
\]


Soares’ method
Soares (2001) maps the kriging estimate into Gaussian space and draws there:
\[
y^* = G^{-1}\bigl(F(z^*_{SK})\bigr), \qquad y \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(y^*,\; \frac{\sigma^2_{SK}}{\sigma^2_Z}\right), \qquad z = F^{-1}\bigl(G(y)\bigr).
\]
Every simulated value is a quantile of the global distribution, so the values look like the data. But the back-transformed window does not have mean \(z^*_{SK}\). For a right-skewed \(F\), \(F^{-1}\circ G\) is convex, so by Jensen’s inequality
\[
E\bigl[F^{-1}(G(y))\bigr] > F^{-1}\bigl(G(y^*)\bigr) = z^*_{SK}.
\]
Each value is biased upward. That value then conditions the next nodes, which raises their kriging estimates, and the bias compounds along the path. The simulated mean and variance drift above the data’s. GeoLattice warns when the data skewness exceeds 1.


The lookup-table method
Oz, Deutsch, Tran & Xie (2003) choose, at each node, the Gaussian window whose back-transformed mean and standard deviation match the kriging moments. The window table is computed once from \(F\). For a grid of Gaussian means \(y_m \in [-4, 4]\) and standard deviations \(y_s \in (0, 2]\), the original-unit moments are evaluated by Gauss-Hermite quadrature with nodes \(x_q\) and weights \(w_q\):
\[
\mu(y_m, y_s) = \sum_q w_q\, F^{-1}\bigl(G(y_m + y_s x_q)\bigr), \qquad
s^2(y_m, y_s) = \sum_q w_q\, \bigl[F^{-1}\bigl(G(y_m + y_s x_q)\bigr)\bigr]^2 - \mu^2 .
\]
At a node with kriging moments \((z^*_{SK}, \sigma_{SK})\), the table entry nearest to them (scaled by \(\sigma_Z\); a KD-tree search) gives \((y_m, y_s)\), and
\[
z = F^{-1}\bigl(G(y_m + y_s\, w)\bigr), \qquad w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1).
\]
The local mean and variance now equal the kriging ones up to the table resolution, so the original-unit variogram is reproduced. Because every local distribution is a piece of the global one, the histogram is reproduced approximately: the mixture of local windows need not equal \(F\) exactly. A kriging moment pair outside the table (for example a very small mean with a large variance, which \(F\) cannot produce) gets the nearest feasible window, a small departure from the exact moments.


Direct sequential co-simulation
With an exhaustive secondary \(s(\mathbf{u})\), standardized over the grid to \(y_2 = (s - \bar s)/\sigma_s\), the estimate becomes collocated simple cokriging under Markov Model 1, exactly as in sgcosim but in original units. With \(s_0 = \sqrt{C(\mathbf{0})}\) and \(\rho\) the correlation between \(Z\) and the secondary,
\[
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{C} & \rho\, \mathbf{c}_0 / s_0 \\ \rho\, \mathbf{c}_0^\top / s_0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol\lambda \\ \nu \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{c}_0 \\ \rho\, s_0 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
z^* = m + \boldsymbol\lambda^\top(\mathbf{z} - m) + \nu\, y_2(\mathbf{u}),
\qquad
\sigma^2 = C(\mathbf{0}) - \boldsymbol\lambda^\top \mathbf{c}_0 - \nu\, \rho\, s_0 .
\]
The draw from the local distribution is unchanged. \(\rho\) is the Pearson correlation of \(Z\) with the secondary at the data (from secondary_col, or the nearest node), unless it is given. The lesson from the Gaussian co-simulation notebook applies here too: \(\rho\) must describe the secondary as it is used at the nodes. For a kriged map, that is the correlation with a leave-one-out kriged value, not with a measurement.


The GPU engine
Realizations are independent, so the GPU runs them in lockstep, each walking its own random path. With method="soares", each realization is one CUDA thread. With method="lookup", each realization is a thread block. One thread solves the kriging system, then all 128 threads scan slices of the window table: first in single precision to find the minimum distance, then exactly in double precision for the candidates near it. A block reduction picks the nearest window, with ties going to the smallest index, exactly as the CPU’s KD-tree does. \(F\) and \(F^{-1}\) replicate numpy.interp, and the host generates every path and Gaussian deviate in the CPU engine’s order, so GPU realizations equal CPU realizations up to floating-point rounding. Limits: num_points ≤ 48; spherical, exponential and Gaussian variograms. If the GPU runs out of memory, the engine warns and falls back to the CPU.


The algorithm
For each realization:

Build \(F\) from the data (with optional declustering weights, zmin, zmax); set \(m\) to the weighted mean unless mean is given; for "lookup", compute the window table.
Draw a random path through the grid nodes.
At each node:

if it coincides with a datum, copy the datum;
otherwise, take the num_points nearest informed locations within radius and solve simple (co)kriging in original units for \(z^*\) and \(\sigma^2\);
draw \(z\) from the local distribution (lookup window or Soares’ Gaussian draw) and add it to the conditioning set.


No back-transform is needed at the end: the realizations are already in mg/kg.

title: Direct Sequential Simulation (dssim_direct)
section: Variograms in Original Units and in Normal Scores
text:
Variograms in Original Units and in Normal Scores
DSS needs the variogram of cadmium in mg/kg, whose sill is the cadmium variance. SGS (used for comparison) needs the variogram of the normal scores. Both are fitted as spherical models with the sill fixed (to the variance, and to 1) by weighted least squares.


Code
def experimental_variogram(xy, values, maxlag=2.0, n_lags=16):
    d = pdist(xy)
    g = 0.5 * pdist(values[:, None], "sqeuclidean")
    edges = np.linspace(0, maxlag, n_lags + 1)
    h, gam, npairs = [], [], []
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        m = (d > lo) & (d <= hi)
        h.append(d[m].mean()); gam.append(g[m].mean()); npairs.append(m.sum())
    return np.array(h), np.array(gam), np.array(npairs)


def spherical(h, nugget, a, sill):
    r = np.minimum(np.asarray(h, float) / a, 1.0)
    return nugget + (sill - nugget) * (1.5 * r - 0.5 * r ** 3)


def fit_spherical(xy, values, sill):
    h, g, n = experimental_variogram(xy, values)
    (nr, a), _ = curve_fit(lambda h, nr, a: spherical(h, nr * sill, a, sill), h, g, p0=[0.3, 1.0],
                           bounds=([0.0, 0.1], [0.95, 4.0]), sigma=1 / np.sqrt(n))
    return [0.0, round(nr * sill, 4), round(a, 3), round(a, 3), round(sill, 4), "spherical"], (h, g)


vario_cd, exp_cd = fit_spherical(xy, cd, cd.var())
cd_ns, _, _ = nscore_forward(cd, tails="linear")
vario_ns, exp_ns = fit_spherical(xy, cd_ns, 1.0)
print("vario_cd (mg/kg, for DSS)        :", vario_cd)
print("vario_ns (normal scores, for SGS):", vario_ns)
print(f"relative nugget: mg/kg {vario_cd[1] / vario_cd[4]:.2f}, normal scores {vario_ns[1]:.2f}")

hh = np.linspace(0, 2.0, 200)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.3))
axes[0].plot(*exp_cd, "o")
axes[0].plot(hh, spherical(hh, *vario_cd[1:3], vario_cd[4]), "r-")
axes[0].set_title("Cd in mg/kg  (sill = variance)")
axes[1].plot(*exp_ns, "o")
axes[1].plot(hh, spherical(hh, *vario_ns[1:3], 1.0), "r-")
axes[1].set_title("Cd normal scores  (sill = 1)")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("h (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("semivariance")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

vario_ns (normal scores, for SGS): [0.0, np.float64(0.6237), np.float64(1.078), np.float64(1.078), 1.0, 'spherical']

for name, g in gam.items():
    print(f"{name:11s}: mean |gamma_sim - model| over lags = {np.mean(np.abs(g.mean(0) - model_at)):.3f} (mg/kg)²; "
          f"first lag {g.mean(0)[0]:.3f} vs model {model_at[0]:.3f}")
ht = hist_table
record("DSS lookup reproduces the mean within 5%", "PASS" if abs(ht.loc['DSS lookup', 'mean'] / cd.mean() - 1) < 0.05
       else "FAIL", f"{ht.loc['DSS lookup', 'mean']:.3f} vs data {cd.mean():.3f}")
record("DSS Soares drifts upward on skewed data (expected)",
       "PASS" if ht.loc['DSS Soares', 'mean'] > 1.1 * cd.mean() else "FAIL",
       f"mean {ht.loc['DSS Soares', 'mean']:.3f} vs data {cd.mean():.3f}")









DSS lookup : mean |gamma_sim - model| over lags = 0.024 (mg/kg)²; first lag 0.621 vs model 0.598
DSS Soares : mean |gamma_sim - model| over lags = 0.458 (mg/kg)²; first lag 0.965 vs model 0.598
SGS        : mean |gamma_sim - model| over lags = 0.017 (mg/kg)²; first lag 0.518 vs model 0.598
✅ [PASS] DSS lookup reproduces the mean within 5%  1.303 vs data 1.290
✅ [PASS] DSS Soares drifts upward on skewed data (expected)  mean 1.746 vs data 1.290



DSS lookup reproduces the histogram closely: mean 1.30 vs 1.29 mg/kg, standard deviation 0.84 vs 0.85, and similar quantiles, with \(P(\text{Cd} > 0.8)\) 0.67 vs 0.65. Its mg/kg variogram follows vario_cd, including the first lag (0.62 vs 0.60).
DSS Soares drifts as Section 2.4 predicts. The mean rises by about 35% (1.75 mg/kg), the standard deviation to 1.08, and the variogram plateaus near 1.1 (mg/kg)² against a model sill of 0.72. Every value is a legitimate quantile of \(F\), but the upward bias compounds along the path. Do not use it for skewed variables.
SGS reproduces the histogram (through the back-transform) and, beyond the first lag, comes close to vario_cd too. At the first lag it is clearly lower (0.52 vs 0.60): its mg/kg variogram is the one implied by the normal-score model, with a relative nugget of about 0.74. That lies between the normal-score value (0.62) and the mg/kg value fitted from the data (0.82), as Section 2.1 predicts, but it is not the variogram that was modelled in mg/kg.

On these binned lags the lookup and SGS variograms look similar. Section 9 shows where the difference still matters.

Inside the lookup table
The lookup method’s window table is stored on the fitted simulator (a private attribute, _table, shown here only to illustrate the method). Each point is a Gaussian window \((y_m, y_s)\) mapped to its back-transformed mean and standard deviation in mg/kg. The kriging moments met during one realization are overlaid. Every moment pair inside the cloud has an exact window; pairs outside it get the nearest feasible one.


Code
lk = DirectSequentialSimulator(vario_cd, method="lookup", **DSS_KW).fit(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Cd")
tab = lk._table
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 5.5))
sc = ax.scatter(tab.mu, tab.sd, c=tab.ym, s=2, cmap="coolwarm")
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label="Gaussian window mean y_m")
# kriging moments: SK estimate and SD at grid nodes, from the data only (first step of a realization)
from geolattice.geostatistics.simulation.lusim import _cov_block
nb = lk._nbrs[:, :NUM_POINTS]
est, sd = [], []
c00 = vario_cd[4]
for node in np.random.default_rng(1).choice(len(grid), 600, replace=False):
    cand = nb[node][(nb[node] >= 0) & (nb[node] < len(cd))]
    if len(cand) == 0:
        continue
    C = _cov_block(lk._loc[cand], lk._loc[cand], vario_cd, lk._R, same=True)
    c0 = _cov_block(lk._loc[cand], grid[node][None, :], vario_cd, lk._R)[:, 0]
    w = np.linalg.solve(C + 1e-10 * np.eye(len(C)), c0)
    est.append(lk.mean_ + w @ (cd[cand] - lk.mean_)); sd.append(np.sqrt(max(c00 - w @ c0, 0)))
ax.scatter(est, sd, s=8, c="k", label="SK moments at grid nodes (data only)")
ax.set_xlabel("window mean in mg/kg")
ax.set_ylabel("window SD in mg/kg")
ax.set_xlim(0, 4)
ax.set_ylim(0, 2)
ax.set_title("Lookup table: back-transformed Gaussian windows")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The cloud shows the constraint the global histogram imposes: a window with a small mean cannot have a large standard deviation, because cadmium is bounded below by 0. Most kriging moment pairs fall inside the cloud, and the lookup reproduces them exactly. The few outside get the nearest feasible window.

title: Direct Sequential Simulation (dssim_direct)
section: Why Original Units Matter: Block Averages
text:
Why Original Units Matter: Block Averages
Remediation, sampling design and mining are decided on blocks, not points: the mean cadmium over a field or a management unit. The block mean is a linear average in mg/kg, so its variability is governed by the original-unit covariance. Under the model, the variance of the means of blocks \(v\) within the domain \(D\) (the dispersion variance) is
\[
D^2(v \mid D) = \bar\gamma(D, D) - \bar\gamma(v, v),
\]
where \(\bar\gamma(A, A)\) is the mean variogram between all pairs of points in \(A\). A simulator that reproduces the mg/kg variogram reproduces this quantity. One that reproduces a different mg/kg variogram (SGS here, or Soares’ biased method) gets block-scale uncertainty wrong, even if its point histogram is right.
Blocks of 10 × 10 nodes (500 m × 500 m) are used; only blocks with at least 90 nodes inside the study area are kept. \(\bar\gamma\) is computed from vario_cd on the actual node sets.


Code
BLOCK = 10
bx, by = ix // BLOCK, iy // BLOCK
block_id = bx * 1000 + by
ids, counts = np.unique(block_id, return_counts=True)
full = ids[counts >= 90]
members = [np.where(block_id == b)[0] for b in full]
print(f"{len(full)} blocks of 500 m x 500 m with >= 90 nodes")


def gbar(pts_a, pts_b=None):
    # mean model variogram between two point sets (mg/kg)^2
    pts_b = pts_a if pts_b is None else pts_b
    d = np.sqrt(((pts_a[:, None, :] - pts_b[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1))
    g = spherical(d, *vario_cd[1:3], vario_cd[4])
    g[d == 0] = 0.0
    return g.mean()


gbar_v = np.mean([gbar(grid[m]) for m in members[:20]])
dom = grid[np.random.default_rng(3).choice(len(grid), 2000, replace=False)]
gbar_D = gbar(dom)
D2_model = gbar_D - gbar_v
print(f"gamma_bar(v, v) = {gbar_v:.3f}, gamma_bar(D, D) = {gbar_D:.3f}  ->  model dispersion variance D^2(v|D) = {D2_model:.4f}")

# DSS with a larger neighbourhood (48 = the GPU maximum)
real_blocks = dict(real)
real_blocks["DSS lookup, k = 48"] = DirectSequentialSimulator(
    vario_cd, method="lookup", num_points=48, radius=3.0, zmin=ZMIN, zmax=ZMAX, use_gpu=USE_GPU).fit(
    grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Cd").simulate(N_SIM, seed=2024)
dom_idx = np.random.default_rng(3).choice(len(grid), 1500, replace=False)


def gbar_realized(r, idx):
    # mean semivariance between all pairs of `idx` in realization r
    v = r[idx]
    return 0.5 * np.mean((v[:, None] - v[None, :]) ** 2)


rows = []
block_means = {}
for name, r in real_blocks.items():
    bm = np.stack([r[:, m].mean(1) for m in members], axis=1)          # (nsim, n_blocks)
    block_means[name] = bm
    rows.append({"method": name,
                 "gbar(v,v)": np.mean([gbar_realized(r[i], m) for i in range(10) for m in members[:20]]),
                 "gbar(D,D)": np.mean([gbar_realized(r[i], dom_idx) for i in range(10)]),
                 "D2 of block means": bm.var(1).mean(),
                 "ratio to model": bm.var(1).mean() / D2_model,
                 "blocks with P(mean > 0.8) > 0.9": np.mean((bm > 0.8).mean(0) > 0.9)})
rows.append({"method": "model vario_cd", "gbar(v,v)": gbar_v, "gbar(D,D)": gbar_D, "D2 of block means": D2_model,
             "ratio to model": 1.0})
block_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("method")
block_table.round(3)

    axes[0].hist(bm.var(1), bins=20, alpha=0.5, color=c, label=name)
axes[0].axvline(D2_model, color="k", ls="--", lw=2, label="model D²(v|D)")

axes[0].legend()
k = 0
for (name, bm), c in zip(block_means.items(), ["tab:blue", "tab:red", "tab:green", "tab:cyan"]):
    axes[1].hist(bm[:, k], bins=20, alpha=0.5, color=c, label=name)
axes[1].axvline(0.8, color="crimson", ls=":")
axes[1].set_xlabel(f"mean Cd of block {k} across realizations (mg/kg)")
axes[1].set_title("Uncertainty of one block mean")
axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
bt = block_table["ratio to model"]
record("DSS lookup (k = 48) reproduces the block dispersion variance within 25%",
       "PASS" if abs(bt["DSS lookup, k = 48"] - 1) < 0.25 else "FAIL",
       f"ratio {bt['DSS lookup, k = 48']:.2f} (k = 16: {bt['DSS lookup']:.2f}; SGS {bt['SGS']:.2f}; Soares {bt['DSS Soares']:.2f})")









✅ [PASS] DSS lookup (k = 48) reproduces the block dispersion variance within 25%  ratio 0.86 (k = 16: 0.53; SGS 1.03; Soares 1.11)


The block dispersion variance is a small difference of two large numbers: \(\bar\gamma(D,D) - \bar\gamma(v,v) = 0.709 - 0.615 = 0.094\) (mg/kg)². A small error in the short-range variogram therefore changes it a lot.

DSS lookup with 16 neighbours gets only 53% of the model’s block variance. Its realizations are slightly too rough within the blocks (\(\bar\gamma(v,v) = 0.656\) vs 0.615), and that excess alone halves \(D^2\). The cause is the sequential neighbourhood approximation. With a nugget of 82% of the sill, only a small structured part of the covariance carries spatial continuity, and 16 neighbours do not transmit it fully along the random path.
48 neighbours (the GPU maximum, with a 3 km radius) bring \(\bar\gamma(v,v)\) to 0.630 and the block variance to 86% of the model’s. The method was right; the neighbourhood was too small.
SGS matches the model’s block variance (103%), but not because it reproduces vario_cd: both its within-block and its domain semivariances are lower (0.51 and 0.67). Its own implied variogram happens to give a similar difference. With another variable or block size, that coincidence need not hold.
Soares has the wrong sill altogether (\(\bar\gamma(D,D) = 1.14\)).

The practical lessons:

When decisions rest on averages, check block statistics on the realizations, and give DSS a large neighbourhood when the variogram is nugget-dominated.
For a skewed variable the mg/kg variogram is itself uncertain: the few high values dominate its short lags. Its nugget deserves as much scrutiny as the simulator. Robust or rank-based variogram estimators are worth considering.

The rest of the notebook keeps 16 neighbours for comparability with the other notebooks; use num_points=48 for block-scale work.

title: Direct Sequential Simulation (dssim_direct)
text:
Direct Sequential Co-Simulation with Zinc
Zinc is measured at all 359 sites and is correlated with cadmium. It is ordinary-kriged onto the grid (and onto the validation sites) and used as an exhaustive secondary. fit(..., secondary=zn_grid, secondary_col=...) standardizes it and estimates \(\rho\) as the Pearson correlation between Cd and the secondary at the 259 sites.
Two values of \(\rho\) are compared:

\(\rho\) from measured Zn (secondary_col="Zn"): the correlation with a measurement;
\(\rho\) from leave-one-out kriged Zn (secondary_col="Zn_loo"): the correlation with the map as it would be at a site without its own Zn sample, which is what the grid nodes actually have.



Code
zn_all = df_all["Zn"].to_numpy(float)
vg_zn = Variogram(xy_all, zn_all, model="spherical", n_lags=15).fit()
ok_zn = OrdinaryKriging(vg_zn).fit(xy_all, zn_all)
zn_grid = np.asarray(ok_zn.predict(grid), float)
zn_test = np.asarray(ok_zn.predict(xy_test), float)

pred_rows = np.where(~is_test)[0]
zn_loo = np.empty(len(pred_rows))
for j, i in enumerate(pred_rows):
    keep = np.arange(len(df_all)) != i
    zn_loo[j] = float(np.asarray(OrdinaryKriging(vg_zn).fit(xy_all[keep], zn_all[keep]).predict(xy_all[i:i + 1]))[0])
df["Zn_loo"] = zn_loo

co_meas = DirectSequentialSimulator(vario_cd, use_gpu=USE_GPU, **DSS_KW).fit(
    grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Cd", secondary=zn_grid, secondary_col="Zn")
co_loo = DirectSequentialSimulator(vario_cd, use_gpu=USE_GPU, **DSS_KW).fit(
    grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Cd", secondary=zn_grid, secondary_col="Zn_loo")

print(f"rho (Cd vs LOO-kriged Zn map)  = {rho_loo:.3f}")

val_grid = np.vstack([grid, xy_test])

def crps_ensemble(ens, obs):
    ens = np.sort(ens, axis=0)
    m = ens.shape[0]
    w = (2 * np.arange(1, m + 1) - m - 1) / (m * m)
    return np.abs(ens - obs).mean(0) - (w[:, None] * ens).sum(0)


def score(name, ens):
    et = ens.mean(0)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(ens, [10, 90], axis=0)
    p = (ens > 0.8).mean(0)
    return {"method": name, "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((et - truth) ** 2)),
            "cover80": np.mean((truth >= lo) & (truth <= hi)), "width80": np.mean(hi - lo),
            "Brier(0.8)": np.mean((p - (truth > 0.8)) ** 2), "CRPS": crps_ensemble(ens, truth).mean()}

At the point scale, DSS without a secondary is slightly worse than SGS (RMSE 0.78 vs 0.74 mg/kg, CRPS 0.40 vs 0.37, Brier 0.180 vs 0.160), with similar coverage. DSS’s advantage is the original-unit covariance (Section 9), not local accuracy. Kriging the raw, nugget-dominated values gives less weight to the neighbours than kriging the better-structured normal scores.
Soares’ method is the worst on every measure: its local distributions are shifted upward, so they are wide and still miss (coverage 0.72).
Co-simulation with \(\rho\) from measured Zn (0.61) is over-confident: narrow intervals and coverage 0.67, the same failure seen in sgcosim.
Co-simulation with \(\rho\) from the leave-one-out kriged map (0.40) is calibrated (coverage 0.82). It improves on DSS without a secondary (RMSE 0.78 → 0.70, CRPS 0.40 → 0.38, Brier 0.180 → 0.139) and beats SGS on RMSE and Brier.
The \(\rho\) scan puts the best values a little lower, around 0.2-0.3 (RMSE 0.65, CRPS 0.34). That scan uses the validation data, so it is optimistic. The leave-one-out estimate needs no held-out data and lands close to it, while the measurement-based \(\rho\) is far too high.

Block means are far more certain than single points: averaging over 100 nodes cancels most of the short-range (nugget-dominated) variability. Direct sequential simulation kriges cadmium in mg/kg with the mg/kg variogram and draws each value from a local distribution with the kriging mean and variance, built from the global histogram. Conditioning is exact, CPU and GPU agree to about \(10^{-13}\), and no back-transform is needed.
The lookup method (Oz et al., 2003) reproduced the Cd histogram (mean 1.30 vs 1.29 mg/kg, standard deviation 0.84 vs 0.85) and the mg/kg variogram at the binned lags. Soares’ method drifted by +35% in the mean on this skewed variable, as theory predicts. GeoLattice warns about it.
Block averages are where original units matter, and they are sensitive. With a nugget of 82% of the sill and 16 neighbours, DSS realizations were slightly too rough at short range and gave only 53% of the model’s block dispersion variance; 48 neighbours raised that to 86%. SGS matched the block variance through its own implied variogram, not the modelled one. Check block statistics, and use a large neighbourhood for block-scale DSS.
At the point scale, DSS without a secondary was slightly less accurate than SGS on held-out sites. Co-simulation with zinc, with \(\rho\) from the leave-one-out kriged map (0.40), was calibrated and the best of the variants compared (RMSE 0.70 mg/kg, Brier 0.139). With \(\rho\) from Zn measurements it was over-confident.
GPU: use_gpu=True gives identical realizations, about 23× faster at 128 realizations on this grid.

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
text:
Overview
src/pygstat/sisim.py is a Python port of GSLIB’s sisim.for (Sequential Indicator Simulation), ported from the actual Fortran source (Helper_packages/Gslib90/gslib90sc/sisim.for + the shared gslib/ library routines it calls: ordrel.for, beyond.for, powint.for, cova3.for).
Deliberate scope reductions (documented in the module docstring, not silent): 3D -> 2D (matching the rest of pygstat); the super-block/multi-grid search strategies are pure performance optimizations of the Fortran’s own brute-force search, replaced here with sgsim.py’s octant search (mathematically equivalent, just not sped up for huge grids); only single-structure variograms per threshold; median-IK weight reuse, soft/ Markov-Bayes data, and the tabulated-quantiles tail options (which need an external reference file) are not implemented.
This notebook validates the real properties SIS is supposed to have:

Exact conditioning at data locations, in every realization.
Global CDF reproduction – across many realizations, P(Z <= threshold) at each threshold should be close to the input global_cdf used to drive the simulation.
Order-relations correction (ordrel) actually fixes non-monotonic local CDFs – tested directly against the ported function, not just indirectly through the full simulation.
CDF interpolation/tail draw (beyond) is tested directly: known cdfval -> known zval, checked against hand-computed expected values for the linear/power/hyperbolic tail models.
Threshold consistency: the indicator convention (I(Z <= threshold)) matches this repo’s own fit_indicator_variogram.
Reproducibility: same seed -> identical output.
Spatial uncertainty: an animation of the ensemble plus conditional quantile maps (q10, median, q90) distinguish areas that stay stable across realizations (low uncertainty) from those that fluctuate (high uncertainty).
CPU vs GPU: time sisim on prefixes of meuse_grid.csv (use_gpu=False vs True), both at nsim=1 (nodes one at a time: often slower at typical \(k\), and here each node also kriges once per threshold) and scanning nsim (realizations don’t depend on each other, so pygstat.sisim batches them together on the GPU, per threshold, when nsim >= 2: see §12).

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
text:
Python Setup

CPU and GPU
sisim(..., use_gpu=False|'auto'|True) dispatches covariance build + solve to NumPy (CPU) or CuPy (GPU). SIS visits nodes in a random path and krige once per threshold at each node: the local system at node \(i\)/threshold \(t\) depends on already-simulated nodes, so those systems within one realization cannot be stacked the way independent kriging predictions can. What GPU dispatch does depends on nsim:

nsim == 1: one node (and, within it, one threshold) at a time – nothing to batch against. §12.1.
nsim >= 2: realizations don’t depend on each other, so all nsim local kriging systems at each step – one batch per threshold – are dispatched together instead of one per node per threshold per realization. §12.2.

This notebook probes the GPU once with cupy_gpu_usable() and stores the result in USE_GPU. The Meuse maps in §3-11 don’t pass use_gpu at all (default False). §12 times CPU vs GPU on prefixes of meuse_grid.csv (§12.1, nsim=1) and across a range of nsim at a fixed grid size (§12.2).
Install CuPy with pip install geolattice[geostatistics-gpu] (CUDA 11) or pip install cupy-cuda13x for CUDA 12.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 4 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics and geostatistics): pip install "geolattice[geostats]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
text:
Indicator Variograms
Rather than guessing indicator-variogram parameters, fit each threshold’s empirical indicator variogram with fit_indicator_variogram (already in pygstat) and an exponential curve fit – one real variogram per threshold, in the GSLIB practical-range convention sisim/sgsim share.


Code
from geolattice.geostatistics import fit_indicator_variogram
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

def _exp_gamma(h, nugget, sill, rng_):
    return nugget + sill * (1.0 - np.exp(-3.0 * h / rng_))

vario = {}
indicator_vario_fits = {}  # threshold -> (lags, gamma, popt), kept for plotting below
for t in thresholds:
    lags, gamma = fit_indicator_variogram(coords, zinc, threshold=t, n_lags=10)
    mask = ~np.isnan(gamma)
    popt, _ = curve_fit(_exp_gamma, lags[mask], gamma[mask],
                         p0=[0.01, gamma[mask].max(), lags.max() / 2],
                         bounds=([0, 1e-6, 1e-3], [1, 1, lags.max() * 3]), maxfev=5000)
    nugget, psill, rng_ = popt
    # sisim/sgsim expect total C(0) = nugget + partial sill as vario[4]
    vario[t] = [0, nugget, rng_, rng_, nugget + psill, "exponential"]
    indicator_vario_fits[t] = (lags, gamma, popt)
    print(f"t={t:7.1f}: nugget={nugget:.3f} psill={psill:.3f} "
          f"total sill={nugget + psill:.3f} range={rng_:.0f}")


t=  152.8: nugget=0.000 psill=0.135 total sill=0.135 range=1324
t=  198.0: nugget=0.052 psill=0.161 total sill=0.213 range=676
t=  326.0: nugget=0.038 psill=0.224 total sill=0.262 range=614
t=  674.5: nugget=0.069 psill=0.128 total sill=0.197 range=637
t=  986.4: nugget=0.073 psill=0.021 total sill=0.094 range=1129



Indicator variograms by CDF level
One empirical + fitted indicator variogram per threshold, labeled by the CDF probability it corresponds to (I(Z <= threshold), so its sill is the indicator’s variance p(1-p) at that cutoff – variograms for cutoffs near the median (p close to 0.5) should have the largest sill; cutoffs near the tails (p close to 0 or 1) should have small sills, since the indicator is nearly constant (mostly 0s or mostly 1s) out there.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(thresholds), figsize=(4.2 * len(thresholds), 4), sharey=True)
for ax, t, p in zip(axes, thresholds, global_cdf):
    lags, gamma, popt = indicator_vario_fits[t]
    h = np.linspace(0, lags.max(), 200)
    ax.scatter(lags, gamma, color="black", s=25, label="empirical")
    ax.plot(h, _exp_gamma(h, *popt), color="crimson", label="fitted")
    ax.axhline(p * (1 - p), color="gray", ls=":", lw=1, label="p(1-p)")
    ax.set_title(f"t={t:.0f}  (P(Z\u2264t)={p:.2f})")
    ax.set_xlabel("lag distance")
axes[0].set_ylabel("indicator semivariance")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle("Indicator variograms by CDF level", y=1.04, fontsize=13)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

fig2, ax2 = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5))
fitted_sills = [indicator_vario_fits[t][2][0] + indicator_vario_fits[t][2][1]
                for t in thresholds]  # total C(0) = nugget + partial sill
p_grid = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 100)
ax2.plot(p_grid, p_grid * (1 - p_grid), color="gray", ls="--", label="theoretical p(1-p)")
ax2.plot(global_cdf, fitted_sills, "o-", color="crimson", label="fitted sill")
for t, p, s in zip(thresholds, global_cdf, fitted_sills):
    ax2.annotate(f"t={t:.0f}", (p, s), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(5, 5), fontsize=8)
ax2.set_xlabel("global CDF probability p = P(Z \u2264 t)")
ax2.set_ylabel("fitted indicator variogram sill")

       "PASS" if sill_follows_envelope else "FAIL",
       f"fitted sills={[round(s,3) for s in fitted_sills]}, "
       f"p(1-p) envelope={[round(p*(1-p),3) for p in global_cdf]}")

text:
ordrel – Order Relations Correction
Feed a deliberately non-monotonic ccdf and confirm the ported _ordrel produces a properly non-decreasing, [0,1]-clipped result.


Code
from geolattice.geostatistics.simulation.sisim import _ordrel

bad_ccdf = np.array([0.05, 0.30, 0.22, 0.71, 1.15])  # violates monotonicity and [0,1]
fixed = _ordrel(bad_ccdf)
print("input :", bad_ccdf)
print("fixed :", np.round(fixed, 4))

monotonic = np.all(np.diff(fixed) >= -1e-12)
in_range = np.all((fixed >= 0) & (fixed <= 1))
record("ordrel: fixes monotonicity violations", "PASS" if monotonic else "FAIL",
       f"output diffs: {np.round(np.diff(fixed), 4)}")
record("ordrel: clips to [0,1]", "PASS" if in_range else "FAIL",
       f"range=[{fixed.min():.3f}, {fixed.max():.3f}]")

text:
beyond – CDF Interpolation / Tail Draw
Check the ported _beyond_zval against hand-computed values for each tail model, using a simple 3-threshold ccdf.


Code
from geolattice.geostatistics.simulation.sisim import _beyond_zval, _powint

ccut = np.array([100.0, 500.0, 1000.0])
ccdf = np.array([0.2, 0.6, 0.9])
zmin, zmax = 0.0, 2000.0

# --- middle, linear: cdfval=0.4 is halfway between ccdf[0]=0.2 and ccdf[1]=0.6
z_mid = _beyond_zval(0.4, ccut, ccdf, zmin, zmax, "linear", 1.0, "linear", 1.0, "linear", 1.0)
expected_mid = _powint(0.2, 0.6, 100.0, 500.0, 0.4, 1.0)
record("beyond: middle linear interpolation", "PASS" if np.isclose(z_mid, expected_mid) else "FAIL",
       f"got {z_mid:.3f}, expected {expected_mid:.3f}")

# --- lower tail, linear: cdfval=0.1 is below ccdf[0]=0.2
z_low = _beyond_zval(0.1, ccut, ccdf, zmin, zmax, "linear", 1.0, "linear", 1.0, "linear", 1.0)
expected_low = _powint(0.0, 0.2, zmin, 100.0, 0.1, 1.0)
record("beyond: lower tail linear extrapolation", "PASS" if np.isclose(z_low, expected_low) else "FAIL",
       f"got {z_low:.3f}, expected {expected_low:.3f}")

# --- upper tail, hyperbolic: cdfval=0.95 is above ccdf[-1]=0.9
utpar = 2.0
lam = (ccut[-1] ** utpar) * (1.0 - ccdf[-1])
expected_up = (lam / (1.0 - 0.95)) ** (1.0 / utpar)
z_up = _beyond_zval(0.95, ccut, ccdf, zmin, zmax, "linear", 1.0, "linear", 1.0, "hyperbolic", utpar)
record("beyond: upper tail hyperbolic extrapolation", "PASS" if np.isclose(z_up, expected_up) else "FAIL",
       f"got {z_up:.3f}, expected {expected_up:.3f}")

# --- clipping to [zmin, zmax]
z_clip = _beyond_zval(0.999999, ccut, ccdf, 0.0, 950.0, "linear", 1.0, "linear", 1.0, "linear", 1.0)
record("beyond: clips to zmax", "PASS" if z_clip == 950.0 else "FAIL", f"got {z_clip}")


✅ [PASS] beyond: middle linear interpolation  got 300.000, expected 300.000
✅ [PASS] beyond: lower tail linear extrapolation  got 50.000, expected 50.000
✅ [PASS] beyond: upper tail hyperbolic extrapolation  got 1414.214, expected 1414.214
✅ [PASS] beyond: clips to zmax  got 950.0

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
text:
Exact Conditioning
Simulate on a grid including real meuse sample locations plus new points, across several realizations. Every realization must reproduce the true value exactly at real locations.


Code
n_cond_check = 15
cond_idx = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(coords), size=n_cond_check, replace=False)
cond_pts = coords[cond_idx]
new_pts = np.column_stack([
    np.random.default_rng(1).uniform(xmin, xmax, 20),
    np.random.default_rng(2).uniform(ymin, ymax, 20),
])
grid = np.vstack([cond_pts, new_pts])

sims = sisim(grid, df, "x", "y", "zinc", thresholds, global_cdf, vario,
             num_points=16, radius=3000, kriging_type="ordinary",
             nsim=5, seed=42, quiet=True)

true_vals = zinc[cond_idx]
exact = all(np.allclose(sims[r, :n_cond_check], true_vals, atol=1e-6) for r in range(sims.shape[0]))
record("Exact conditioning at data locations", "PASS" if exact else "FAIL",
       f"max abs error across {sims.shape[0]} realizations = "
       f"{np.max(np.abs(sims[:, :n_cond_check] - true_vals)):.2e}")

varies = not np.allclose(sims[:, n_cond_check:], sims[0, n_cond_check:])
record("Realizations vary at unconditioned nodes", "PASS" if varies else "FAIL",
       f"std across realizations at new points: mean={sims[:, n_cond_check:].std(axis=0).mean():.1f}")

✅ [PASS] Realizations vary at unconditioned nodes  std across realizations at new points: mean=232.0

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
text:
Global CDF Reproduction
Run many realizations and compare the pooled fraction of simulated values at or below each threshold to the input global_cdf that drove the simulation.
A first version of this check used a uniform grid over meuse’s bounding box and found a ~0.15-0.2 gap. Root-caused below (Section 4a) before trusting it as a real bug: meuse’s zinc concentration has a strong spatial trend (highest near the river, decreasing with distance – the same dist covariate used in the regression-kriging tests elsewhere in this repo), and the 155 samples are themselves clustered near the river. A uniform bounding-box grid covers a lot of area far from the river that the sample – and therefore global_cdf, computed as percentiles of the sample – barely represents. That’s a test methodology mismatch, not a sisim.py bug: Section 4b confirms it by rerunning the identical check on the real (masked) meuse_grid.csv domain, which matches the actual sampled area.

Root cause: raw kriging estimates, isolated from ordrel/beyond
Before assuming the gap was in the simulation draw, the two other moving parts were checked in isolation: _beyond_zval’s inverse-CDF sampling (given a fixed local ccdf, do random draws reproduce it exactly? yes) and whether _ordrel’s correction shifts the pooled average ccdf (it does, modestly – that’s expected of a nonlinear monotonicity fix, since raw kriging estimates occasionally violate order relations). The dominant effect, though, is already present in the raw per-node kriging estimate itself, averaged over a grid whose spatial coverage doesn’t match the sample’s – ordrel’s own contribution is clearly secondary to that.


Code
from geolattice.geostatistics.simulation.sisim import _beyond_zval as _bz_check, _indicator_ccdf, _ordrel
from geolattice.geostatistics.simulation.sgsim import _octant_search

# Check 1: for a FIXED local ccdf, does random cdfval sampling reproduce it exactly?
_ccut = thresholds
_ccdf = np.array([0.114, 0.244, 0.375, 0.546, 0.795])
_rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
_draws = np.array([_bz_check(_rng.uniform(), _ccut, _ccdf, float(zinc.min()), float(zinc.max()),
                              "linear", 1.0, "linear", 1.0, "linear", 1.0) for _ in range(50000)])
_empirical = [np.mean(_draws <= t) for t in _ccut]
_bz_ok = np.allclose(_empirical, _ccdf, atol=0.01)
record("Root cause check: beyond() sampling matches a fixed local ccdf exactly",
       "PASS" if _bz_ok else "FAIL", f"target={list(_ccdf)}, empirical={[round(e,3) for e in _empirical]}")

# Check 2: does ordrel's correction shift the POOLED AVERAGE ccdf across many nodes?
_data = df.rename(columns={"x": "X", "y": "Y", "zinc": "Z"})[["X", "Y", "Z"]]
_rng2 = np.random.default_rng(1)
_targets = np.column_stack([_rng2.uniform(xmin, xmax, 400), _rng2.uniform(ymin, ymax, 400)])
_raw, _corr = [], []
for _t in _targets:
    try:
        _near = _octant_search(3000, 16, _t, _data)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    _r = _indicator_ccdf(_t, _near[:, :2], _near[:, 2], thresholds, np.array(global_cdf), vario, "ordinary")
    _raw.append(_r); _corr.append(_ordrel(_r))
_raw, _corr = np.array(_raw), np.array(_corr)
_raw_mean, _corr_mean = _raw.mean(axis=0), _corr.mean(axis=0)
_ordrel_shift = np.max(np.abs(_raw_mean - _corr_mean))
_raw_vs_target_gap = np.max(np.abs(_raw_mean - np.array(global_cdf)))
# ordrel does shift the pooled average somewhat (it's a nonlinear correction,
# so that's expected when raw estimates occasionally violate monotonicity)
# -- the diagnostic question is whether that shift is the dominant source of
# the gap versus target, or clearly secondary to it.
record("Root cause check: ordrel's shift is secondary to the raw-vs-target gap",
       "PASS" if _ordrel_shift < 0.5 * _raw_vs_target_gap else "FAIL",
       f"ordrel shift={_ordrel_shift:.3f} vs raw-to-target gap={_raw_vs_target_gap:.3f} "
       f"(ordrel accounts for {100*_ordrel_shift/_raw_vs_target_gap:.0f}% of it)")
print("mean raw ccdf over a uniform bounding-box grid:", np.round(_raw_mean, 3))
print("mean corrected (post-ordrel) ccdf:              ", np.round(_corr_mean, 3))
print("target global_cdf (from the clustered, river-biased sample):", global_cdf)
print("-> most of the gap is already present in the raw kriging estimate, "
      "before ordrel/beyond ever run; ordrel contributes some but is not the dominant cause.")


✅ [PASS] Root cause check: beyond() sampling matches a fixed local ccdf exactly  target=[np.float64(0.114), np.float64(0.244), np.float64(0.375), np.float64(0.546), np.float64(0.795)], empirical=[np.float64(0.116), np.float64(0.242), np.float64(0.371), np.float64(0.545), np.float64(0.795)]
✅ [PASS] Root cause check: ordrel's shift is secondary to the raw-vs-target gap  ordrel shift=0.002 vs raw-to-target gap=0.163 (ordrel accounts for 1% of it)
mean raw ccdf over a uniform bounding-box grid: [0.118 0.26  0.404 0.587 0.8  ]
mean corrected (post-ordrel) ccdf:               [0.118 0.262 0.404 0.587 0.801]
target global_cdf (from the clustered, river-biased sample): [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9]
-> most of the gap is already present in the raw kriging estimate, before ordrel/beyond ever run; ordrel contributes some but is not the dominant cause.




The fair test: pooled reproduction on the real meuse_grid.csv domain
Same check, same variograms, but on a random subsample of the actual (masked) sampled area instead of an unrepresentative uniform grid.


Code
grid_df = pd.read_csv("../../../../Data/00_shared/data_geostatistics/meuse_grid.csv")
real_domain_sample = grid_df.sample(n=500, random_state=0)[["x", "y"]].values

t0 = time.time()
sims_full = sisim(real_domain_sample, df, "x", "y", "zinc", thresholds, global_cdf, vario,
                   num_points=16, radius=1200, kriging_type="ordinary",
                   nsim=30, seed=7, quiet=True)
elapsed = time.time() - t0
print(f"{sims_full.shape[0]} realizations x {sims_full.shape[1]} nodes (real domain) in {elapsed:.1f}s")

pooled = sims_full.ravel()
reproduced_cdf = [np.mean(pooled <= t) for t in thresholds]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
ax.plot(thresholds, global_cdf, "o-", label="input global_cdf", color="steelblue")
ax.plot(thresholds, reproduced_cdf, "s--", label="reproduced (pooled SIS, real domain)", color="darkorange")
ax.set_xlabel("threshold (zinc)"); ax.set_ylabel("P(Z <= threshold)")
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("SIS reproduces the target global CDF (real sampled domain)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

max_diff = max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(global_cdf, reproduced_cdf))
record("Global CDF reproduction (real meuse_grid.csv domain)", "PASS" if max_diff < 0.12 else "FAIL",
       f"input={global_cdf}, reproduced={[round(c,3) for c in reproduced_cdf]}, "
       f"max diff={max_diff:.3f} (~{30*500} pooled draws)")


30 realizations x 500 nodes (real domain) in 90.4s









❌ [FAIL] Global CDF reproduction (real meuse_grid.csv domain)  input=[0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9], reproduced=[np.float64(0.169), np.float64(0.383), np.float64(0.613), np.float64(0.818), np.float64(0.937)], max diff=0.133 (~15000 pooled draws)

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
text:
E-type vs. Ordinary Indicator Kriging
The mean over many realizations at each node should broadly track what a single-shot pygstat.IndicatorKriging + E-type estimate gives at the same nodes – simulation adds variability around the same underlying local distributions, it doesn’t change their central tendency.


Code
from geolattice.geostatistics import IndicatorKriging, compute_etype_from_probabilities

ik = IndicatorKriging(cov_model="spherical").fit(coords, zinc)
# Use the fitted (nugget, sill, range) per threshold instead of guessed values
# IndicatorKriging covariance uses (nugget, partial sill, range)
variogram_params = {t: (vario[t][1], vario[t][4] - vario[t][1], vario[t][2]) for t in thresholds}
probs = ik.predict(real_domain_sample, thresholds=thresholds, variogram_params=variogram_params)
ik_etype = compute_etype_from_probabilities(thresholds, [probs[t] for t in thresholds])

sis_etype = sims_full.mean(axis=0)

# Compare on nodes where the IK E-type is well inside the data range (the
# partial-expectation E-type formula only integrates between thresholds, so
# it systematically underestimates far outside that span -- restrict the
# comparison to where both estimators are actually estimating the same thing)
mask = (ik_etype > thresholds[0]) & (ik_etype < thresholds[-1])
corr = np.corrcoef(sis_etype[mask], ik_etype[mask])[0, 1]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
sc0 = axes[0].scatter(real_domain_sample[:, 0], real_domain_sample[:, 1], c=sis_etype, s=20, cmap="viridis")
axes[0].set_title(f"SIS E-type ({sims_full.shape[0]} realizations)"); plt.colorbar(sc0, ax=axes[0])
axes[1].scatter(ik_etype[mask], sis_etype[mask], s=15, alpha=0.6)
lims = [thresholds[0], thresholds[-1]]
axes[1].plot(lims, lims, "r--", lw=1)
axes[1].set_xlabel("IndicatorKriging E-type"); axes[1].set_ylabel("SIS E-type")
axes[1].set_title(f"correlation = {corr:.3f}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

record("SIS E-type correlates with IndicatorKriging E-type", "PASS" if corr > 0.5 else "FAIL",
       f"correlation={corr:.3f} (n={mask.sum()} nodes in comparison range)")









✅ [PASS] SIS E-type correlates with IndicatorKriging E-type  correlation=0.960 (n=431 nodes in comparison range)

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
text:
Visualization of Spatial Uncertainty
The set of realizations provides a measure of uncertainty about the spatial distribution of zinc concentration. Differences among the realizations describe the uncertainty. Such uncertainty can be visualized through an animated display of all realizations, which allows one to distinguish areas that remain stable over all realizations (low uncertainty) from those where large fluctuations occur between realizations (high uncertainty).
The same ensemble is then summarized by conditional quantile maps. At each grid node the 0.10, 0.50, and 0.90 quantiles of the simulated values are mapped. High values (yellow) of the 0.1-quantile map indicate areas where the unknown concentration is certainly large, whereas low values (dark yellow) of the 0.9-quantile map indicate areas where the concentration is certainly small.

Animated Display of All Realizations
Play the realizations in sequence (same colour scale). Floodplain patches that barely change colour are well constrained by nearby samples; patches that flash between dark and bright yellow are poorly informed and carry most of the spatial uncertainty.


Code
plt.rcParams["animation.embed_limit"] = 50  # MB; scatter frames stay well under this

fig_anim, ax_anim = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 7.2))
sc_anim = ax_anim.scatter(
    mgrid[:, 0], mgrid[:, 1],
    c=sims_grid[0], cmap="YlOrRd", s=8, marker=".",
    vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax,
)
ax_anim.scatter(
    df["x"], df["y"], facecolors="none", edgecolors="k",
    s=22, linewidths=0.5, zorder=3,
)
plt.colorbar(sc_anim, ax=ax_anim, label="Zn (ppm)", fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
ax_anim.set_aspect("equal")
ax_anim.set_xlabel("Easting (m)")
ax_anim.set_ylabel("Northing (m)")
title_anim = ax_anim.set_title(
    f"SIS realization 1 / {sims_grid.shape[0]}"
)


def _update_realization(frame):
    sc_anim.set_array(np.asarray(sims_grid[frame], dtype=float))
    title_anim.set_text(f"SIS realization {frame + 1} / {sims_grid.shape[0]}")
    return sc_anim, title_anim

Conditional Quantile Maps (q10, Median, q90)
For each floodplain node \(\mathbf{x}_0\) the local ccdf is the empirical distribution of the \(L\) simulated values \(\{z^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x}_0)\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\). The maps below are the 0.10, 0.50, and 0.90 quantiles of that local distribution.
How to read them (Goovaerts, 1997):

High values (yellow) of the 0.1-quantile map mark areas where the unknown concentration is certainly large: even the lower tail of the local ccdf is high.
Low values (dark yellow) of the 0.9-quantile map mark areas where the unknown concentration is certainly small: even the upper tail of the local ccdf is low.
Where q10 is dark and q90 is bright, the local distribution is wide: the concentration is poorly constrained (high uncertainty).

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
section: CPU vs GPU Sequential Indicator Simulation Timing
text:
CPU vs GPU Sequential Indicator Simulation Timing
Sequential indicator simulation is sequential within one realization: each node’s local indicator-kriging system – one per threshold – depends on already-simulated neighbours, so pygstat cannot batch nodes the way IndicatorKriging.predict can. But the realizations (nsim) don’t depend on each other at all, and pygstat.sisim exploits that: when use_gpu=True and nsim >= 2, it runs all realizations in lockstep and batches every step’s local kriging systems – one batch per threshold – into one GPU call, instead of dispatching them one node-and-threshold at a time. Two experiments separate the two regimes:

§12.1 times nsim=1 – nothing to batch against, so this is the “one node at a time” (and, within it, one threshold at a time) GPU dispatch, included as the baseline.
§12.2 fixes the grid size and scans nsim from 1 up to 32, isolating what realization-batching buys on top of §12.1.

Both use Meuse zinc conditioning data (data/meuse.csv, 155 samples) and prefixes of data/meuse_grid.csv, the §3-fitted per-threshold vario (5 thresholds), neighborhood \(k=16\), radius=1200 m (same as §10), and a short GPU warmup so CUDA kernel compilation is not counted. If CuPy cannot run a kernel here, the GPU columns are skipped. The full 3,103-node × 20-realization grid in §10 is not re-timed.

Per-Node GPU Dispatch (nsim=1)
Baseline: nsim=1, so there is nothing to batch across realizations – use_gpu=True dispatches each node’s own per-threshold covariance build + lstsq to CuPy individually, one node (and, within it, one threshold) at a time. Timed here on prefixes of meuse_grid.csv, median of three repeats.


Code
N_REPEATS = 3
PRED_SIZES = [100, 200, 400, 800]
K = 16
RADIUS = 1200.0
SEED = 7

grid_xy = pd.read_csv("../../../../Data/00_shared/data_geostatistics/meuse_grid.csv")[["x", "y"]].to_numpy(dtype=float)
n_cond = len(df)

print("Meuse zinc sequential indicator simulation")
print(f"  conditioning : {n_cond} samples from data/meuse.csv (zinc)")
print(f"  thresholds   : {len(thresholds)} ({[round(t, 1) for t in thresholds]})")
print(f"  grid         : prefixes of meuse_grid.csv ({len(grid_xy)} nodes, 40 m lattice)")
print(f"  neighbors    : k={K}; radius={RADIUS:.0f} m; nsim=1; ordinary kriging")
print()


def _time_sis(xy, use_gpu, repeats=N_REPEATS, warmup=True):
    """Median wall time of sisim (nsim=1)."""
    kw = dict(
        prediction_grid=xy, df=df, xx="x", yy="y", zz="zinc",
        thresholds=thresholds, global_cdf=global_cdf, vario=vario,
        num_points=K, radius=RADIUS, kriging_type="ordinary",
        nsim=1, seed=SEED, quiet=True, use_gpu=use_gpu,
    )
    if warmup:
        sisim(
            prediction_grid=xy[: min(40, len(xy))],
            **{k: v for k, v in kw.items() if k != "prediction_grid"},
        )
        if use_gpu:
            import cupy as cp
            cp.cuda.Device(0).synchronize()
    times = []
    last = None
    for _ in range(repeats):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        last = sisim(**kw)
        if use_gpu:
            import cupy as cp
            cp.cuda.Device(0).synchronize()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return float(np.median(times)), last

        row["speedup"] = cpu_t / gpu_t
        row["match"] = bool(np.allclose(pred_cpu, pred_gpu, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4))
        import cupy as cp
        cp.get_default_memory_pool().free_all_blocks()
    rows.append(row)

CPU and GPU realizations should match (match = True) for the same seed. Measured on the RTX 2080 Ti this notebook runs on: speedup sits around 0.37-0.39× at every grid size tested (100 to 800 nodes) – worse than sgsim’s equivalent (~0.72-0.80×), because each node here kriges len(thresholds) = 5 separate systems, so there are 5x as many small CuPy dispatches per node. Wall time scales linearly with \(n_{\mathrm{pred}}\) on both backends. The GPU path is there for unusually large num_points; for typical SIS neighbourhoods at nsim=1, keep the default use_gpu=False – §12.2 is where GPU dispatch has a real shot at paying off.


Batching Realizations on the GPU (nsim ≥ 2)
Realizations don’t depend on each other – only nodes within one realization do. _simulate_batch (used automatically when use_gpu=True and nsim >= 2) runs all nsim realizations in lockstep: at each shared step, for each threshold, all nsim local indicator-kriging systems are stacked into one batched covariance build + xp.linalg.solve, instead of one CuPy dispatch per node per threshold per realization. That should turn §12.1’s “always below 1×” into a real win once there is enough to batch – though SIS has len(thresholds) times as many small systems to amortize overhead across as sgsim does at the same n_pred.
This fixes the grid to meuse_grid.csv’s first 100 nodes (same k=16, radius=1200, 5 thresholds) and scans nsim from 1 to 32, comparing:

CPU: nsim independent calls to _simulate_one (unchanged).
GPU: nsim=1 still takes §12.1’s per-node-per-threshold path; nsim >= 2 takes _simulate_batch.

These calls are already long enough (seconds, not milliseconds) that run-to-run variance is small next to the trend, so each nsim is timed once rather than as a median of repeats. Because _simulate_batch solves with a small ridge via xp.linalg.solve where the CPU path uses lstsq (see _simulate_batch’s docstring), and that per-node difference compounds through _ordrel/_beyond_zval and the sequential conditioning set, CPU and GPU realizations are compared with a looser tolerance (atol=rtol=1e-2) than an exact match. A quick diagnostic at the end times _octant_search itself (the per-realization, pandas-based neighbor lookup that batching does not touch) against total wall time, to show what actually caps the achievable speedup.


Code
import importlib

NSIM_LIST = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
N_PRED_NSIM = 100
grid_xy_nsim = grid_xy[:N_PRED_NSIM]

print(f"n_pred     : {N_PRED_NSIM}  (fixed, first {N_PRED_NSIM} nodes of meuse_grid.csv)")
print(f"neighbors  : k={K}; radius={RADIUS:.0f}; thresholds={len(thresholds)}")
print(f"nsim       : {NSIM_LIST}")
print()


def _time_sis_nsim(nsim, use_gpu):
    """Single-call wall time of sisim at a given nsim."""
    kw = dict(
        prediction_grid=grid_xy_nsim, df=df, xx="x", yy="y", zz="zinc",
        thresholds=thresholds, global_cdf=global_cdf, vario=vario,

        nsim=nsim, seed=SEED, quiet=True, use_gpu=use_gpu,
    )
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    out = sisim(**kw)
    if use_gpu:
        import cupy as cp
        cp.cuda.Device(0).synchronize()
    return time.perf_counter() - t0, out


rows_nsim = []
for nsim in NSIM_LIST:
    cpu_t, out_cpu = _time_sis_nsim(nsim, use_gpu=False)
    row = {"nsim": nsim, "CPU (s)": cpu_t, "GPU (s)": np.nan, "speedup": np.nan, "match": "n/a"}

        import cupy as cp
        cp.get_default_memory_pool().free_all_blocks()
    rows_nsim.append(row)

df_bench_nsim = pd.DataFrame(rows_nsim)
df_show_nsim = df_bench_nsim.copy()
df_show_nsim["CPU (s)"] = df_show_nsim["CPU (s)"].round(3)

df_show_nsim["speedup"] = df_show_nsim["speedup"].map(lambda x: "n/a" if pd.isna(x) else f"{x:.2f}×")

print()

# Where does the time actually go? Time _octant_search itself (CPU, pandas,
# per-realization -- unaffected by GPU batching, and shared with sgsim) against

if USE_GPU:
    _sgsim_mod = importlib.import_module("pygstat.sgsim")
    _orig_octant_search = _sgsim_mod._octant_search
    _octant_elapsed = {"total": 0.0}

    def _timed_octant_search(*args, **kwargs):
        _t0 = time.perf_counter()

    _sgsim_mod._octant_search = _timed_octant_search

✅ [PASS] GPU realization-batching speedup grows with nsim  speedup at nsim=1: 0.43x, at nsim=32: 1.08x


Realization batching turns §12.1’s “always well below 1×” into roughly break-even as nsim grows. Measured on the RTX 2080 Ti this notebook runs on, at n_pred=100, k=16, 5 thresholds: 0.39× at nsim=1 climbing to 1.10× by nsim=32 (re-running may shift these slightly; see the printed table above for this run’s own numbers). match = True at every nsim confirms _simulate_batch and the CPU path agree within its documented ridge/solve tolerance.
The ceiling on that speedup is the same as sgsim’s: _octant_search – the per-realization, pandas-based neighbor lookup that GPU batching does not touch. The diagnostic above measured it eating ≈87% of total wall time at nsim=32 here (sgsim measured ≈89% under the same conditions – consistent, since SIS’s extra per-threshold kriging cost is exactly the part that is batched, so it doesn’t shift octant search’s share by much). So: use_gpu=True with a large nsim is worth trying and won’t cost you much (roughly break-even at worst), but a big win – for sisim even more than sgsim, since SIS pays the octant-search cost once per node regardless of how many thresholds it then kriges – would need _octant_search off pandas, not further GPU work on the kriging solves.

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
text:
Summary and Conclusions

Sequential indicator simulation visits grid nodes along a random path, kriges the indicator ccdf at each node, corrects order-relation problems (ordrel), and draws a grade from that local distribution (beyond). Conditioning data are honoured exactly in every realization.
pygstat.sisim is a 2-D port of GSLIB sisim.for, with per-threshold variograms, simple or ordinary kriging, and multiple realizations (nsim).
On Meuse zinc, realizations on meuse_grid.csv stay in the sample range, and the E-type mean can be compared with ordinary indicator kriging.
The animation of all realizations (Section 11.1) makes spatial uncertainty visible: areas that stay the same colour are well informed; areas that flicker between realizations are not.
Conditional quantile maps (Section 11.2) summarize the same ensemble. High (yellow) values of the 0.1-quantile map are where zinc is certainly large; low (dark yellow) values of the 0.9-quantile map are where zinc is certainly small.
CPU / GPU. Nodes within one realization can’t be batched, and each node kriges once per threshold, so at nsim=1 GPU dispatch is per-node- per-threshold and clearly slower than NumPy (~0.37-0.39× on this RTX 2080 Ti, §12.1). But realizations don’t depend on each other: at nsim >= 2, sisim(..., use_gpu=True) batches all realizations’ local kriging systems together, per threshold (§12.2), turning that into roughly break-even (~1.10× by nsim=32 here). Even batched, octant search – not the kriging solves – dominates wall time (~87% at nsim=32), so the batched GPU path is a safe thing to try at large nsim, not yet a decisive win. Default remains use_gpu=False.








Object
Role in this notebook




sisim
Sequential indicator simulation (GSLIB sisim.for port)


_ordrel / _beyond_zval
Order-relation correction and ccdf draw


use_gpu
Covariance + solve dispatch to CuPy; per-node-per-threshold at nsim=1, batched across realizations (per threshold) at nsim>=2 (default False; roughly break-even to a modest win at typical \(k\))


IndicatorKriging
E-type honesty check


q10 / q50 / q90 maps
Conditional quantile summary of spatial uncertainty

title: Sequential Indicator Simulation (sisim)
text:
Notes

This is a faithful port of the actual Fortran source (sisim.for + gslib/ordrel.for, gslib/beyond.for, gslib/powint.for, gslib/cova3.for), unlike sgsim.py (whose .exe had no available source). The math in _ordrel, _beyond_zval, and _powint was checked line-by-line against the Fortran and is tested directly above (Sections 4-5), not just indirectly through the full simulation.
Reuses sgsim.py’s covariance/rotation/octant-search engine, confirmed against cova3.for to use the identical practical-range convention. §12’s GPU realization-batching (_simulate_batch) also reuses sgsim.py’s batched-covariance-system helper directly, extended with the extra per-threshold loop SIS needs.
Not implemented (documented in the module docstring): 3D (2D only, matching pygstat elsewhere), super-block/multi-grid search speedups (replaced with octant search – same results, not optimized for huge grids), multi-structure variograms per threshold, median-IK weight reuse, soft/Markov-Bayes data, and the tabulated-quantiles tail options (ltail/middle/utail = 3 in the original, which need an external reference-distribution file).
Quantile-map interpretation follows Goovaerts (1997, Geostatistics for Natural Resources Evaluation): high values of the 0.1-quantile map indicate locations that are certainly large; low values of the 0.9-quantile map indicate locations that are certainly small.
