Sequential Gaussian co-simulation draws the primary at each node from its collocated simple-cokriging distribution under Markov Model 1. It needs only the primary variogram and the correlation \(\rho\). \(\rho = 0\) gives plain SGS (checked exactly), and \(\rho \to 1\) copies the secondary.
On the Jura data, nickel was co-simulated with a kriged chromium map as the exhaustive secondary. Conditioning is exact, the Ni histogram and short-range variogram are reproduced, and the realizations carry the Cr pattern.
\(\rho\) must match the secondary as used at the nodes. The correlation with measured Cr (0.70) over-weights a kriged map: 80% intervals then cover only 64% of the held-out values. The leave-one-out correlation with the kriged map (0.40) gives the lowest error (RMSE 4.91 vs 5.67 mg/kg for SGS, CRPS 2.61 vs 3.05) with well-calibrated intervals (coverage 0.85). A scan over \(\rho\) puts the optimum at the same place.
mm1_nugget_ratio_ correctly flagged the kriged map as too smooth for multi-collocated cokriging, which performed worse than the collocated default.
sgcosim_hierarchical reproduces the Ni-Cr correlation when Cr is known only at the data (0.71 vs 0.75). Independent simulations do not (0.24), and they underestimate joint exceedance areas (0.28 vs 0.68 km² with both Ni > 30 and Cr > 45 mg/kg).
The realizations turn into uncertainty maps: conditional quantiles, exceedance probabilities, and the distribution of the area with Ni > 30 mg/kg. Co-simulation shifts that area estimate (1.31 vs 1.00 km² for SGS) because the Cr map raises Ni away from the Ni samples.
GPU: use_gpu=True and sgsim_gpu run one CUDA thread per realization and reproduce the CPU realizations to about \(10^{-13}\). They are slower than the CPU for one realization and about 12× faster at 128 realizations on this grid.

title: Sequential Indicator Co-Simulation (sicosim)
text:
Overview
Sequential indicator simulation (SIS) simulates a variable through indicators: 0/1 codes for “this class” (categorical) or “below this threshold” (continuous). At each node it kriges the probability of every class or threshold from nearby indicators, then draws a class or a value from those probabilities. Unlike Gaussian simulation it needs no normal-score transform and no multi-Gaussian assumption, and each class or threshold can have its own variogram. That is why it is the usual choice for facies, soil or land-cover classes, and for skewed variables whose high values are connected differently from the low ones.
Sequential indicator co-simulation adds soft data: probabilities that come from a secondary source rather than from a measurement at the node. A remote-sensing index, a geophysical survey, a geology map or a cheaper co-measured variable can all be turned into soft indicators \(y_k(\mathbf{u}) = P(\text{class } k \text{ at } \mathbf{u} \mid \text{secondary})\). The Markov-Bayes model (Zhu & Journel, 1993) says how much weight those probabilities get, through one calibration parameter \(B_k\) per class.







Object
What it does




SoftCalibration
Turns a continuous secondary variable into soft indicators: quantile bins of the secondary, class frequencies of the hard data in each bin, shrunk toward the global proportions, and the Markov-Bayes \(B_k\).


IndicatorCoSimulator
The engine. Categorical (classes) or continuous (ascending thresholds). fit(grid, df, ..., secondary=...) calibrates a secondary variable, or fit(..., soft=..., soft_data=... / B=...) takes soft probabilities directly. simulate(nsim, seed) runs on the CPU or the GPU.


sicosim
One-call wrapper: build, fit with a secondary variable, and simulate. Without a secondary it is plain SIS.



The Markov-Bayes co-simulation is approximate. The soft data are not reproduced exactly, the Markov-Bayes covariances are a model, and with a spatially smooth secondary the collocated system counts the soft information more than once (Section 2.8). This notebook measures the consequences on real data and shows a simple remedy.
On the Jura data:

Continuous: cadmium, simulated through six thresholds including the Swiss guide value of 0.8 mg/kg, with soft indicators from a kriged zinc map (Cd and Zn are strongly related) and, alternatively, from the geology map.
Categorical: rock type (five units), simulated from the samples, with soft indicators from a kriged cobalt map, and checked against the mapped geology.

What is checked:

exact conditioning, reproducibility, and GPU = CPU;
reproduction of the threshold proportions and the indicator variogram;
local accuracy at 100 held-out sites: E-type error, coverage of probability intervals, and the Brier score of the probability of exceeding 0.8 mg/kg.

title: Sequential Indicator Co-Simulation (sicosim)
text:
Theory

Indicator coding
For a continuous variable \(Z(\mathbf{u})\) and \(K\) ascending thresholds \(z_1 < \dots < z_K\), the indicator at threshold \(k\) is
\[
i(\mathbf{u}; z_k) = \begin{cases} 1 & Z(\mathbf{u}) \le z_k \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
\]
Its expected value is the cumulative distribution at \(z_k\), \(E[I(\mathbf{u}; z_k)] = F(z_k) = m_k\). For a categorical variable with classes \(s_1, \dots, s_K\),
\[
i(\mathbf{u}; s_k) = \begin{cases} 1 & S(\mathbf{u}) = s_k \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}
\qquad E[I(\mathbf{u}; s_k)] = p_k,
\]
the class proportion. In both cases the indicator has variance \(m_k(1 - m_k)\), and that is the sill of its variogram \(\gamma_I(\mathbf{h}; k)\). Each threshold or class has its own variogram, so the spatial continuity of high values can differ from that of low values. A Gaussian model cannot do that.


Indicator kriging of the conditional distribution
The conditional probability of class \(k\) at \(\mathbf{u}\), given the \(n\) nearest informed indicators, is estimated by simple indicator kriging:
\[
p_k^*(\mathbf{u}) = m_k + \sum_{\alpha=1}^{n} \lambda_\alpha \bigl[i(\mathbf{u}_\alpha; k) - m_k\bigr],
\qquad
\sum_{\beta=1}^{n} \lambda_\beta\, C_I(\mathbf{u}_\alpha - \mathbf{u}_\beta; k) = C_I(\mathbf{u}_\alpha - \mathbf{u}; k)\quad(\alpha = 1..n),
\]
with \(C_I(\mathbf{h}; k) = m_k(1-m_k) - \gamma_I(\mathbf{h}; k)\). For continuous variables the \(K\) values \(p_k^*\) are a discretized conditional cumulative distribution function (ccdf), \(F^*(\mathbf{u}; z_k \mid (n))\); for categorical ones they are class probabilities. One kriging system is solved per class or threshold at each node.
The variograms use the GSLIB list form with practical ranges, [azimuth, nugget, major_range, minor_range, sill, vtype], one per class or threshold (a dict {class: vario}) or one shared by all.


Sequential indicator simulation
As in every sequential method, the joint distribution of the \(N\) nodes is factored into conditionals along a random path:
\[
f(z_1, \dots, z_N \mid (n)) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} f\bigl(z_i \mid (n), z_1, \dots, z_{i-1}\bigr).
\]
At each node the ccdf (or class probabilities) is kriged from the data and the previously simulated nodes, a value is drawn from it, and the value joins the conditioning set as a hard indicator. Indicator kriging only approximates the true conditional distributions (it uses only two-point statistics), so SIS reproduces the indicator variograms and proportions approximately, not exactly.


Order relations, interpolation and tails
Kriging each threshold separately does not guarantee a valid distribution. The estimates can fall outside \([0, 1]\) and, for a ccdf, can decrease between thresholds. These are order-relation problems, and they are corrected before drawing:

Categorical: probabilities are clipped to \([0, 1]\) and renormalized to sum to 1.
Continuous: GSLIB ordrel. The ccdf is clipped to \([0, 1]\) and made non-decreasing by averaging an upward and a downward correction.

For a continuous variable a uniform number \(u\) is drawn, and \(z = F^{*-1}(u)\) is found by interpolating the corrected ccdf between thresholds (middle: linear or power). Outside the first and last thresholds it extrapolates with tail models (ltail, utail: linear, power or hyperbolic) bounded by zmin and zmax. A hyperbolic upper tail suits skewed variables such as metal concentrations:
\[
1 - F(z) = \bigl(1 - F(z_K)\bigr) \left(\frac{z_K}{z}\right)^{\omega}, \qquad z > z_K,
\]
with \(\omega\) = utpar.


Soft indicators and their calibration
A soft indicator is a prior probability from a secondary source:
\[
y(\mathbf{u}; k) = P\bigl\{I(\mathbf{u}; k) = 1 \mid s(\mathbf{u})\bigr\} \in [0, 1].
\]
SoftCalibration builds it from a continuous secondary variable \(s\) known at the hard data. The secondary values are split into n_bins quantile bins. In each bin \(b\), the soft indicator is the frequency of class \(k\) among the \(n_b\) hard data in that bin, pulled toward the global proportion \(m_k\) by a pseudo-count \(\kappa\) (smoothing):
\[
y_b(k) = \frac{\sum_{\alpha \in b} i(\mathbf{u}_\alpha; k) + \kappa\, m_k}{n_b + \kappa}.
\]
At any node the soft indicator is the table value of the bin its secondary value falls in. Soft probabilities from elsewhere, such as a classifier, an expert map or a categorical secondary like geology, can be passed directly with soft=.


The Markov-Bayes model
How informative is the soft indicator? The calibration parameter of class \(k\) is the difference between the mean soft value where the class is present and where it is absent:
\[
B_k = E\bigl[Y(\mathbf{u}; k) \mid I(\mathbf{u}; k) = 1\bigr] - E\bigl[Y(\mathbf{u}; k) \mid I(\mathbf{u}; k) = 0\bigr] \in [0, 1].
\]
\(B_k = 1\) means the soft indicator separates the class perfectly, and \(B_k = 0\) means it is useless. The Markov-Bayes model (Zhu & Journel, 1993) assumes the hard indicator screens the soft one. Under that hypothesis every covariance involving the soft indicator is the hard indicator covariance, rescaled:
\[
C_{IY}(\mathbf{h}; k) = B_k\, C_I(\mathbf{h}; k),
\qquad
C_Y(\mathbf{h}; k) = \begin{cases} |B_k|\, C_I(\mathbf{0}; k) & \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0} \\ B_k^2\, C_I(\mathbf{h}; k) & \mathbf{h} \ne \mathbf{0}. \end{cases}
\]
So no cross-variogram has to be modelled: the hard indicator variograms and one number per class are enough. When the soft indicators are the conditional expectations \(E[I \mid s]\), as SoftCalibration builds them, \(B_k = \operatorname{Var}(Y)/\operatorname{Var}(I)\), and \(B_k\) also measures how much of the indicator variance the secondary explains.


Collocated indicator cokriging
IndicatorCoSimulator uses the soft indicator at the node only (collocated), together with the \(n\) nearest hard or simulated indicators. The simple cokriging system for class \(k\), with \(\mathbf{C}\) the \(n \times n\) indicator covariances, \(\mathbf{c}_0\) the covariances to the node and \(\sigma^2_k = C_I(\mathbf{0}; k) = m_k(1-m_k)\), is
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{C} & B_k\, \mathbf{c}_0 \\[2pt]
B_k\, \mathbf{c}_0^\top & B_k\, \sigma^2_k
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\boldsymbol\lambda \\ \mu
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{c}_0 \\ B_k\, \sigma^2_k
\end{bmatrix},
\]
\[
p_k^*(\mathbf{u}) = m_k + \boldsymbol\lambda^\top (\mathbf{i} - m_k) + \mu\, \bigl[y(\mathbf{u}; k) - m_k\bigr].
\]
It helps to look at the solution with a single neighbour at covariance \(c\) (\(\rho = c / \sigma^2_k\)):
\[
\lambda = \rho\, \frac{1 - B_k}{1 - B_k \rho^2},
\qquad
\mu = 1 - \rho\, \lambda .
\]

No neighbours (\(\rho = 0\)): \(\mu = 1\) and \(p_k^* = y(\mathbf{u}; k)\), the soft probability.
\(B_k = 1\): \(\lambda = 0\), \(\mu = 1\). A perfect soft datum overrides the hard data.
\(B_k = 0\): with soft indicators calibrated as conditional expectations, \(y = m_k\) everywhere and the soft term vanishes, giving plain SIS. The weight \(\mu\) itself does not vanish; it is the soft values that carry \(B_k\).

Without soft data sicosim is plain SIS on this engine (simple indicator kriging, nearest-neighbour search without octants).


Why it is approximate: double counting a smooth secondary
The Markov-Bayes model treats the soft indicator like a noisy measurement of the hard one. Its cross-covariance with a hard indicator at distance \(\mathbf{h}\) is \(B_k C_I(\mathbf{h})\), which decays as fast as the indicator itself. A kriged map, a classified image or a geology map is the opposite: spatially smooth, so neighbouring nodes have almost the same soft value.
During sequential simulation, every previously simulated neighbour was drawn using its own soft value, so it already carries the secondary information. The collocated soft datum then adds that information again. With one neighbour that was drawn from the soft probability \(y\) itself, the expected probability at the next node, which has nearly the same \(y\), is
\[
E[p_k^*] = m_k + (\lambda + \mu)(y - m_k), \qquad \lambda + \mu = 1 + \lambda(1 - \rho) > 1 .
\]
So the probabilities overshoot the calibrated soft values. The realizations then become too confident, and the error is largest where the soft data are most informative. This is the indicator counterpart of over-weighting a smooth secondary in Gaussian co-simulation (see 05_07_02_sgcosim).
A simple remedy, used in Section 9.1, is to shrink the soft indicators toward the prior before simulation,
\[
y_f(\mathbf{u}; k) = m_k + f\,\bigl[y(\mathbf{u}; k) - m_k\bigr], \qquad 0 \le f \le 1,
\]
which scales the calibrated \(B_k\) by \(f\). Choose \(f\) by validation or cross-validation. \(f = 1\) is the plain Markov-Bayes model, and \(f = 0\) is SIS without soft data.


The GPU engine
Nodes within one realization depend on each other, but realizations do not. With use_gpu=True each realization is one CUDA thread walking its own random path. At each node the thread collects its informed neighbours, builds and solves one (co)kriging system per class or threshold by Gaussian elimination, applies the order-relation correction, and draws a class or a value with the same interpolation and tail rules. The host generates each realization’s path and uniform numbers in exactly the order the CPU engine uses them, so GPU and CPU realizations are identical up to floating-point rounding. Limits: num_points ≤ 48, at most 16 classes or thresholds, and spherical, exponential or Gaussian variograms. If the GPU runs out of memory, the engine warns and falls back to the CPU.


The algorithm
For each realization:

Code the hard data as indicators. Compute the global proportions \(m_k\) (or take declustered ones from proportions). Build the soft indicators and \(B_k\) from the secondary (SoftCalibration), or take them from soft and B / soft_data.
Draw a random path through the grid nodes.
At each node:

if it coincides with a datum, copy the datum;
otherwise, take the num_points nearest informed locations within radius and, for each class or threshold, solve the collocated indicator cokriging system for \(p_k^*\);
correct order relations, draw a class (categorical) or a value from the interpolated ccdf (continuous), and add it to the conditioning set.

title: Sequential Indicator Co-Simulation (sicosim)
section: Indicator Coding and Indicator Variograms of Cadmium
text:
Indicator Coding and Indicator Variograms of Cadmium
Six thresholds discretize the cadmium distribution: the 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 0.9 quantiles of the prediction set, plus the guide value 0.8 mg/kg, so that \(P(\text{Cd} > 0.8)\) is read directly from each simulated ccdf.
For each threshold the experimental indicator variogram is computed and a spherical model is fitted by weighted least squares. The sill is fixed at \(m_k(1 - m_k)\), the variance of the indicator, so only the nugget and the range are fitted.


Code
cd = df["Cd"].to_numpy(float)
THRESH = sorted(set(np.round(np.quantile(cd, [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9]), 2).tolist()) | {0.8})
print("thresholds (mg/kg):", THRESH)


def experimental_variogram(xy, values, maxlag=2.0, n_lags=16):
    d = pdist(xy)
    g = 0.5 * pdist(values[:, None], "sqeuclidean")
    edges = np.linspace(0, maxlag, n_lags + 1)
    h, gam, npairs = [], [], []
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        m = (d > lo) & (d <= hi)
        h.append(d[m].mean()); gam.append(g[m].mean()); npairs.append(m.sum())
    return np.array(h), np.array(gam), np.array(npairs)


def spherical(h, nugget, a, sill):
    r = np.minimum(np.asarray(h) / a, 1.0)
    return nugget + (sill - nugget) * (1.5 * r - 0.5 * r ** 3)


def fit_indicator_vario(xy, ind):
    # spherical model with sill p(1-p); returns the GSLIB list, the experimental points
    p = ind.mean()
    sill = p * (1 - p)
    h, g, n = experimental_variogram(xy, ind)
    (nr, a), _ = curve_fit(lambda h, nr, a: spherical(h, nr * sill, a, sill), h, g, p0=[0.3, 1.0],
                           bounds=([0.0, 0.1], [0.95, 4.0]), sigma=1 / np.sqrt(n))
    return [0.0, round(nr * sill, 4), round(a, 3), round(a, 3), round(sill, 4), "spherical"], (h, g)


vario_cd, exp_cd = {}, {}
for t in THRESH:
    vario_cd[t], exp_cd[t] = fit_indicator_vario(xy, (cd <= t).astype(float))

pd.DataFrame({t: {"P(Cd<=t)": (cd <= t).mean(), "nugget": v[1], "range (km)": v[2], "sill": v[4],

section: Soft Indicators from Zinc with SoftCalibration
text:
Soft Indicators from Zinc with SoftCalibration
The secondary must be known at every grid node and at the validation sites. Zinc is measured at all 359 sites, so it is ordinary-kriged onto the grid and to the validation sites (where the kriged value is close to the measured Zn, because those samples are used).
SoftCalibration then pairs the Cd indicators at the 259 prediction sites with the measured Zn there, splits Zn into 10 quantile bins, and tabulates \(P(\text{Cd} \le z_k \mid \text{Zn bin})\), shrunk toward the global proportions with one pseudo-count.


Code
zn_all = df_all["Zn"].to_numpy(float)
vg_zn = Variogram(xy_all, zn_all, model="spherical", n_lags=15).fit()
ok_zn = OrdinaryKriging(vg_zn).fit(xy_all, zn_all)
zn_grid = np.asarray(ok_zn.predict(grid), float)
zn_test = np.asarray(ok_zn.predict(xy_test), float)
print(f"Zn kriged on the grid: {zn_grid.min():.0f}: {zn_grid.max():.0f} mg/kg")

ind_cd = (cd[:, None] <= np.array(THRESH)[None, :]).astype(float)
cal = SoftCalibration(n_bins=10, smoothing=1.0).fit(ind_cd, df["Zn"].to_numpy(float), prior=PRIOR)
print("Markov-Bayes B per threshold:", dict(zip(THRESH, np.round(cal.B_, 3))))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(19, 4.6))
centers = np.r_[df.Zn.min(), cal.edges_[1:-1]]
for k, t in enumerate(THRESH):
    axes[0].step(np.arange(len(cal.table_)), cal.table_[:, k], where="mid", label=f"Cd <= {t}")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Zn bin (quantile class)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("soft indicator  P(Cd <= t | Zn bin)")
axes[0].set_title("Calibration table")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].bar([str(t) for t in THRESH], cal.B_, color="teal")
axes[1].set_xlabel("threshold (mg/kg)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("B")
axes[1].set_title("Markov-Bayes calibration parameter")
soft_zn_grid = cal.transform(zn_grid)
show_map(axes[2], 1 - soft_zn_grid[:, THRESH.index(0.8)], "Soft P(Cd > 0.8) from the Zn map",
         cmap="RdYlBu_r", vmin=0, vmax=1, label="probability")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Zn kriged on the grid: 26: 254 mg/kg
Markov-Bayes B per threshold: {0.45: np.float64(0.356), 0.68: np.float64(0.39), 0.8: np.float64(0.304), 1.1: np.float64(0.32), 1.67: np.float64(0.226), 2.34: np.float64(0.136)}









The table moves the way it should: the higher the zinc, the smaller the probability of being below a cadmium threshold. \(B_k\) is around 0.3-0.4 for the middle thresholds and smaller for the extreme ones. Zinc is a useful but far from perfect predictor of cadmium, and it says least about the rare very high values.

title: Sequential Indicator Co-Simulation (sicosim)
text:
Baseline: Plain SIS with IndicatorCoSimulator
Without a secondary, IndicatorCoSimulator is plain SIS. First, the properties every conditional simulation must have, checked on a small grid made of the 259 prediction sites plus 200 random nodes:

exact conditioning;
variability away from the data;
reproducibility with a fixed seed;
identical CPU and GPU realizations.



Code
pick = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(grid), 200, replace=False)
small_grid = np.vstack([xy, grid[pick]])

sis = IndicatorCoSimulator(THRESH, vario_cd, use_gpu=USE_GPU, **CONT_KW).fit(small_grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Cd")
sims_a = sis.simulate(nsim=8, seed=11)
sims_b = sis.simulate(nsim=8, seed=11)
sims_c = sis.simulate(nsim=8, seed=12)

err = np.abs(sims_a[:, :len(df)] - cd).max()
record("SIS: exact conditioning", "PASS" if err < 1e-9 else "FAIL", f"max |sim - data| = {err:.1e}")
spread = sims_a[:, len(df):].std(axis=0).mean()
record("SIS: realizations vary away from data", "PASS" if spread > 0.1 else "FAIL",
       f"mean std across realizations = {spread:.2f} mg/kg")
record("SIS: same seed -> identical", "PASS" if np.array_equal(sims_a, sims_b) else "FAIL")
record("SIS: different seed -> different", "PASS" if not np.allclose(sims_a, sims_c) else "FAIL")

sims_cpu = IndicatorCoSimulator(THRESH, vario_cd, **CONT_KW).fit(small_grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Cd").simulate(
    nsim=8, seed=11)
diff = np.abs(sims_cpu - sims_a).max()
record("SIS: GPU = CPU for the same seed", "PASS" if diff < 1e-6 else "FAIL",
       f"max |GPU - CPU| = {diff:.1e} mg/kg" + ("" if USE_GPU else " (no GPU: both ran on CPU)"))

text:
Validation at 100 Held-Out Sites
The realizations are drawn on the grid plus the 100 validation sites (with their kriged Zn), and scored on the true cadmium there:

Meaning

The accuracy plot extends the coverage check to all symmetric probability intervals.


Code
N_VAL = 300
val_grid = np.vstack([grid, xy_test])
zn_val = np.r_[zn_grid, zn_test]
VAL = slice(len(grid), None)


def score(name, ens):
    et = ens.mean(0)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(ens, [10, 90], axis=0)
    p = (ens > 0.8).mean(0)
    o = (truth > 0.8).astype(float)
    return {"method": name, "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((et - truth) ** 2)),
            "cover80": np.mean((truth >= lo) & (truth <= hi)), "width80": np.mean(hi - lo),
            "Brier(0.8)": np.mean((p - o) ** 2), "misclass(0.8)": np.mean((p > 0.5) != (o > 0.5))}


def accuracy_curve(ens, ps=np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19)):
    return ps, [np.mean((truth >= np.percentile(ens, 50 - 50 * p, axis=0)) &
                        (truth <= np.percentile(ens, 50 + 50 * p, axis=0))) for p in ps]


def shrink(soft, f, prior=PRIOR):
    # pull soft indicators toward the prior: y_f = m + f (y - m)
    return prior + f * (soft - prior)


sis_val = IndicatorCoSimulator(THRESH, vario_cd, use_gpu=USE_GPU, **CONT_KW).fit(val_grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Cd")
ens_sis = sis_val.simulate(nsim=N_VAL, seed=1)[:, VAL]

soft_val = cal.transform(zn_val)

    val_grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Cd", soft=soft_val, soft_data=soft_data_zn)
ens_mb = mb_val.simulate(nsim=N_VAL, seed=1)[:, VAL]

The full Markov-Bayes co-simulation (\(f = 1\)) improves the probability of exceeding the guide value (Brier score 0.153 → 0.129), and slightly improves the E-type (RMSE 0.721 → 0.705 mg/kg). But its 80% intervals are narrower (1.85 vs 2.00 mg/kg) and cover only 76% of the true values: the local distributions are over-confident. That is the double counting of a smooth secondary predicted in Section 2.8. The kriged Zn map is smooth, and each node uses it again on top of neighbours that already used it.

Shrinking the soft indicators
Section 2.8 predicted that a smooth secondary is counted more than once. The remedy is to shrink the soft indicators toward the prior, \(y_f = m_k + f(y - m_k)\), which also scales the calibrated \(B_k\) by \(f\). Scan \(f\) on the validation sites:

Shrinking the soft indicators halfway (\(f = 0.5\)) gives the best result on every measure. E-type RMSE falls from 0.721 to 0.624 mg/kg (−13%) and the Brier score from 0.153 to 0.123 (−20%), while coverage stays at 0.88 with intervals as wide as SIS’s. In other words, the intervals are better placed, not narrower. \(f = 0.25\) and \(f = 0.75\) are nearly as good, so the choice is not delicate; \(f = 1\) overshoots. The misclassification rate at the 0.5 probability cut barely moves (0.22 → 0.21). That rule throws away most of the probability information, which the Brier score keeps.
\(f = 0.5\) is used for the cadmium maps below.

title: Sequential Indicator Co-Simulation (sicosim)
section: Soft Probabilities from the Geology Map
text:
Soft Probabilities from the Geology Map
Geology is a categorical secondary known at every grid node, so it cannot go through the binning of SoftCalibration. Instead, the soft indicators are the conditional proportions \(P(\text{Cd} \le z_k \mid \text{rock type})\) from the 259 prediction sites, and they are passed with fit(soft=..., soft_data=...). soft_data (the same table looked up at the data) is used to estimate \(B_k\).
The rock type used is the one on the geology map at each site (the nearest grid node), not the one recorded in the field, because the map is what is available at the grid nodes. The two agree at about 86% of the sites.

The geology map is a weak secondary for cadmium at this sampling density. Its \(B_k\) are small (at most 0.21, near 0 for the high thresholds). On its own the geology table is better than knowing nothing (Brier 0.208 vs 0.231 for the global proportion), but it is much worse than SIS (0.153). The 259 nearby cadmium samples already carry what geology says about cadmium.
Used as full Markov-Bayes soft data, geology hurts: RMSE 0.721 → 0.787, Brier 0.153 → 0.174, coverage 0.78. A geology map is piecewise constant, the extreme case of a smooth secondary, so it is double-counted the most. Shrinking brings the result back toward SIS (\(f = 0.25\) matches it) but never beats it.
The lesson: soft data help only when they carry information that the hard data in the neighbourhood do not, and the only way to know is to validate.

title: Sequential Indicator Co-Simulation (sicosim)
text:
Categorical Co-Simulation: Rock Type
The same engine simulates classes. Here the variable is rock type at the 259 prediction sites, and the geology map is the reference to check against. The field classification of the samples and the map disagree at about 15% of the sites, so perfect agreement with the map is not expected.
The soft secondary is cobalt. Its concentration depends on the parent rock (soils on Argovian rocks are clearly poorer in Co), and a kriged Co map from all 359 sites gives soft class probabilities through SoftCalibration.
The indicator variogram of each class is fitted as before, with sill \(p_k(1 - p_k)\). classes=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and variable="categorical". Portlandian has only a few samples, so its variogram and proportion are poorly known.

vario_rock = {c: fit_indicator_vario(xy, (rock == c).astype(float))[0] for c in CLASSES}

                    for c, v in vario_rock.items()}).T.round(3))

Agreement with the map. The most probable class from SIS matches the geology map at 70% of the nodes; individual realizations match at 57-58%, as they should, since a realization is a plausible map, not the most likely one. Cobalt mainly identifies the Argovian unit (\(B = 0.41\); at most 0.14 for the others). As full soft data it lowers the agreement (0.67), and shrunk (\(f = 0.5\)) it is about level with SIS (0.69). The pattern is the same as for cadmium with geology: a smooth kriged map that adds little beyond 259 nearby class observations.
Realizations have patchy, map-like units that honour the samples. The probability of the most probable class is high near the samples and low along unit boundaries, which is where the uncertainty is.
Class proportions are not reproduced exactly. Kimmeridgian is over-produced (0.44 against 0.36 in the samples) at the expense of Sequanian and Quaternary. Kimmeridgian has the longest indicator range (1.35 km), so its kriged probabilities stay high far from the data, and clipping and renormalizing them favours it. Portlandian, with 3 samples, comes out at 1.5% against 5.3% on the map: a class that is barely sampled cannot be recovered. Categorical SIS controls proportions only through the kriging means \(m_k\). When target proportions matter, check them on the realizations, as here, and consider declustered proportions or a method that enforces them (e.g. simulated annealing).

The CPU engine needs about 2 s per realization, because it solves six cokriging systems at every node. Its time grows linearly with nsim (125 s for 64).

CPU and GPU realizations agree to about \(10^{-13}\) mg/kg at every nsim.

Use the GPU for tens of realizations or more; use the CPU for one or a few.

Sequential indicator (co-)simulation kriges the probability of every class or threshold at each node and draws from the corrected distribution. It handles categorical variables and skewed continuous ones, with one variogram per class or threshold and no Gaussian assumption. On cadmium it reproduced the six threshold proportions within 0.03 and honoured the data exactly. The GPU and CPU engines agree to about \(10^{-13}\).
Soft data enter through Markov-Bayes collocated indicator cokriging. SoftCalibration turns a continuous secondary (kriged Zn) into soft indicators and calibration parameters \(B_k\). fit(soft=..., soft_data=...) takes any probabilities, such as those from a geology map.
The Markov-Bayes co-simulation is approximate. With a smooth secondary the collocated system counts the soft information more than once (Section 2.8). On held-out cadmium the full model sharpened the exceedance probabilities but under-covered (76% for an 80% interval).
Shrinking the soft indicators halfway toward the prior fixed that. Co-simulation with zinc then beat plain SIS on every measure: E-type RMSE −13%, Brier score of \(P(\text{Cd} > 0.8)\) −20%, coverage 0.88. It also made the contamination map far more decisive: 20% of nodes with \(P < 0.1\) or \(P > 0.9\), against 2% for SIS.
Not every secondary helps. Geology for cadmium and cobalt for rock type carried little that the nearby hard data did not already have. Both hurt as full soft data and at best matched SIS when shrunk. Validate soft data before relying on them.
Categorical SIS produced realistic geology-like realizations (70% agreement of the most probable class with the map) but did not hold the class proportions exactly: the long-range class grew and a barely sampled class vanished.

title: Simulated Annealing Simulation (sasim)
text:
Overview
Sequential, spectral and turning-band simulators all construct a realization from a random-function model. Simulated annealing works the other way round. It starts from any image that already has the right histogram, and rearranges it until the image matches a list of target statistics. The targets can be the variogram, indicator variograms for each class, and the correlation with a secondary variable. The rearrangement is a stochastic optimization borrowed from statistical physics (Kirkpatrick et al., 1983), adapted to geostatistics by Deutsch (1992) and Deutsch & Journel (GSLIB sasim / anneal).
Its strengths and weaknesses follow from that design:




Simulated annealing




Histogram
reproduced exactly: the image is a permutation of the target values


Variogram(s)
reproduced as closely as the optimization allows, at the lags and directions in the objective


Categorical proportions
exact (contrast with SIS)


Several criteria at once
yes: any statistic that can be written as an objective component


Data conditioning
hard data are fixed, but their influence on nearby nodes comes only through the variogram pairs


Uncertainty model
none explicit: the spread between realizations depends on the objective and the schedule, not on a random-function model


Cost
many swaps (hundreds per node); CPU only in GeoLattice



The objects:







Object
What it does




SimulatedAnnealing
fit(grid, df, ..., secondary=None) sets up the lattice, hard data, targets and secondary. simulate(nsim, seed) returns realizations at the grid nodes; simulate_lattice returns the full lattice. history_, objective_ and n_swaps_ record the optimization, and experimental_variogram / target_variogram evaluate an image at the objective lags.


sasim
One-call wrapper.



On the Jura data the notebook:

simulates nickel with a variogram objective, and checks exact histogram reproduction, variogram reproduction by direction, the effect of the annealing schedule, and local accuracy at 100 held-out sites against SGS;
adds a correlation component with a kriged chromium map;
simulates rock type with indicator variograms, with exact proportions, checked against the geology map.

title: Simulated Annealing Simulation (sasim)
text:
Theory

Simulation as optimization
A realization is any image \(\{z(\mathbf{u}_j)\}_{j=1}^{N}\) on the lattice. Annealing defines an objective function \(O \ge 0\) that is 0 when the image has every target statistic, and searches for images with small \(O\). Different random starting images and random swap sequences lead to different low-\(O\) images: the realizations. There is no explicit random-function model. The set of realizations is “all images that match the targets well”, sampled by a randomized search. Two consequences follow:

anything that can be measured on an image can be a target;
the uncertainty between realizations is not calibrated by a probability model.



The objective function
The variogram component compares the image’s experimental variogram with the target model at a set of lag vectors. GeoLattice uses \(K\) = n_lags multiples of each direction \(\mathbf{d}\) in directions (default: the two axes and both diagonals, in cells):
\[
O_\gamma = \sum_{\mathbf{d}} \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\, \frac{\bigl[\hat\gamma(k\mathbf{d}) - \gamma(k\mathbf{d})\bigr]^2}{\gamma(k\mathbf{d})^2},
\qquad w_k \propto \frac{1}{k},
\qquad
\hat\gamma(\mathbf{h}) = \frac{1}{2N(\mathbf{h})} \sum_{N(\mathbf{h})} \bigl[z(\mathbf{u}) - z(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{h})\bigr]^2 .
\]
Dividing by \(\gamma^2\) makes every lag count in relative terms, so short lags (small \(\gamma\)) are matched as carefully as long ones. The weights \(1/k\) give extra emphasis to the short lags, which control the look of the image. \(\gamma\) is the model vario in original units, [azimuth, nugget, major_range, minor_range, sill, vtype], evaluated at the lag vectors in coordinate units.
For a categorical variable with classes \(s_1, \dots, s_C\), the indicator component is the same sum over each class’s indicator variogram \(\gamma_I(\mathbf{h}; s_c)\) from indicator_varios.
With an exhaustive secondary \(y(\mathbf{u})\), the correlation component is
\[
O_\rho = \bigl(\hat\rho_{zy} - \rho^{\text{target}}\bigr)^2 ,
\]
with \(\hat\rho_{zy}\) the correlation of the image with the secondary over the lattice, and \(\rho^{\text{target}}\) = target_correlation (default: the correlation of the data with the secondary).
Components live on different scales. As in GSLIB sasim, each is divided by the mean absolute change it undergoes over a set of random swaps of the starting image, \(\overline{|\Delta O_c|}\):
\[
O = \sum_c \frac{\omega_c}{\overline{|\Delta O_c|}}\, O_c ,
\]
so the user weights \(\omega_c\) (component_weights, e.g. {"variogram": 1, "correlation": 5}) are relative importances.


Swaps: the histogram for free
The starting image puts the stratified quantiles of the target histogram (target_values, by default the data) at the free nodes in random order:
\[
z_j = F^{-1}\!\left(\frac{j - 1/2}{N_{\text{free}}}\right), \qquad j = 1, \dots, N_{\text{free}}, \quad \text{randomly permuted.}
\]
Every perturbation is a swap of the values at two free nodes. A swap never changes the set of values, so the histogram is reproduced exactly, in every realization, at every step. For categorical variables this means the class proportions are exact, which sequential indicator simulation cannot guarantee.


The Metropolis rule and the annealing schedule
A swap that changes the objective from \(O\) to \(O'\) is accepted with probability
\[
P(\text{accept}) = \begin{cases} 1 & O' \le O \\ \exp\bigl(-(O' - O)/t\bigr) & O' > O, \end{cases}
\]
the Metropolis rule at temperature \(t\). Accepting some bad swaps early lets the search escape poor local minima. As \(t\) falls, the search becomes greedy. The schedule:








Parameter
Meaning
Default




t0
initial temperature, in units of the mean objective increase of a random swap (1 accepts a typical bad swap with probability \(e^{-1} \approx 0.37\))
1.0


reduction
\(t \leftarrow \lambda\, t\) after each temperature step
0.1


k_accept
accepted swaps per temperature
\(5\,N_{\text{free}}\)


k_max
attempted swaps per temperature
\(50\,N_{\text{free}}\)


max_swaps
total budget
\(500\,N_{\text{free}}\)


tol
stop when \(O \le \text{tol} \cdot O_{\text{init}}\)
\(10^{-3}\)


n_stop
stop after this many temperatures with no accepted swap
3



A fast schedule (small t0, small reduction) is close to a greedy descent: quick, but it can freeze in a poor arrangement. A slow schedule explores more. In GSLIB practice a fairly fast schedule works for variogram objectives because the objective landscape is benign (Deutsch & Journel, 1998).


Incremental updates
Recomputing the variogram after each swap would cost \(O(N)\) per lag. A swap only changes the pairs that involve the two swapped nodes, so GeoLattice updates the per-lag sums of squared differences from those pairs alone: \(O(L)\) per swap, with \(L\) the number of lag vectors. The lattice is padded with missing values so that pairs leaving the lattice are simply skipped. The correlation component is updated in \(O(1)\) from the change in \(\sum z y\).


Hard data, the lattice, and what annealing does not guarantee

Lattice. Annealing works on a regular lattice. fit infers it from the grid (or spacing), and it spans the bounding box of the grid and the data. Lattice nodes outside an irregular study area are simulated too, and they enter the objective, but simulate returns only the requested grid nodes.
Hard data are moved to their nearest lattice node. Several data at one node are averaged (continuous) or take their most frequent class (categorical). Those nodes are never swapped, so the data are honoured exactly at their nodes.
Conditioning is weak. A datum influences its neighbours only through the variogram pairs it belongs to. One pair among thousands at each lag carries almost no weight in \(O\), so nothing forces the nodes next to a high datum to be high. Annealed realizations can show discontinuities around the data, and their spread near the data can be too large. Sequential methods condition through kriging and do not have this problem. Section 9 measures it.
No probability model. The spread between realizations reflects the many images that fit the targets, not a posterior distribution. It is not guaranteed to be calibrated.



The algorithm
For each realization:

Place the hard data on the lattice; fill the free nodes with stratified quantiles of the target histogram in random order.
Compute the objective components, their scaling from random swaps, and the initial temperature.
Repeat until \(O \le \text{tol} \cdot O_{\text{init}}\), the swap budget is spent, or n_stop temperatures pass with no accepted swap:

at temperature \(t\), propose swaps of two random free nodes, update \(O\) incrementally, and accept by the Metropolis rule, until k_accept acceptances or k_max attempts;
record \(O / O_{\text{init}}\) in history_ and set \(t \leftarrow\) reduction \(\cdot\, t\).

Return the image at the grid nodes.

title: Simulated Annealing Simulation (sasim)
text:
Python Setup
SimulatedAnnealing runs on the CPU only. Each swap is a small NumPy update, and realizations run one after another. The cost grows with the number of lattice nodes, because the default swap budget and the swaps per temperature are proportional to it. The notebook therefore anneals on a 100 m lattice; Section 13 times the 50 m lattice too. Plain SGS (sgsim_gpu) is used for comparison, on the GPU when one is available.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 4 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics and geostatistics): pip install "geolattice[geostats]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
%matplotlib inline
import time
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
from IPython.display import HTML, display
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
from scipy.spatial import cKDTree

title: Simulated Annealing Simulation (sasim)
section: Jura Data and the Annealing Lattice
text:
Jura Data and the Annealing Lattice
The Jura data (Atteia et al., 1994; Goovaerts, 1997) are 359 topsoil samples from a 14.5 km² area of the Swiss Jura. jura_grid.csv holds 5,957 nodes on a 50 m lattice, with the mapped geology. Coordinates are in kilometres. Every second row and column gives a 100 m grid of 1,540 nodes; its lattice (the bounding box) has 49 × 59 = 2,891 nodes.
As in the earlier notebooks, 100 samples are held out at random as a validation set, and the other 259 are the conditioning data.


Code

title: Simulated Annealing Simulation (sasim)
text:
Target Variograms
Annealing matches a variogram in original units, so the target is the variogram of nickel in mg/kg, with the sill equal to its variance. SGS, used for comparison, needs the variogram of the normal scores. Both are spherical models fitted by weighted least squares with the sill fixed.


Code
def experimental_variogram(xy, values, maxlag=2.5, n_lags=20):
    d = pdist(xy)
    g = 0.5 * pdist(values[:, None], "sqeuclidean")
    edges = np.linspace(0, maxlag, n_lags + 1)
    h, gam, npairs = [], [], []
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        m = (d > lo) & (d <= hi)
        h.append(d[m].mean()); gam.append(g[m].mean()); npairs.append(m.sum())
    return np.array(h), np.array(gam), np.array(npairs)


def spherical(h, nugget, a, sill):
    r = np.minimum(np.asarray(h, float) / a, 1.0)
    return nugget + (sill - nugget) * (1.5 * r - 0.5 * r ** 3)


def fit_spherical(xy, values, sill):
    h, g, n = experimental_variogram(xy, values)
    (nr, a), _ = curve_fit(lambda h, nr, a: spherical(h, nr * sill, a, sill), h, g, p0=[0.3, 1.0],
                           bounds=([0.0, 0.1], [0.95, 4.0]), sigma=1 / np.sqrt(n))
    return [0.0, round(nr * sill, 3), round(a, 3), round(a, 3), round(sill, 3), "spherical"], (h, g)


vario_ni, exp_ni = fit_spherical(xy, ni, ni.var())
ni_ns, _, _ = nscore_forward(ni, tails="linear")
vario_ns, _ = fit_spherical(xy, ni_ns, 1.0)
print("vario_ni (mg/kg, annealing target):", vario_ni)
print("vario_ns (normal scores, SGS)      :", vario_ns)

hh = np.linspace(0, 2.5, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.3))
ax.plot(*exp_ni, "o", label="experimental (259 data)")
ax.plot(hh, spherical(hh, *vario_ni[1:3], vario_ni[4]), "r-", label="target model vario_ni")
ax.set_xlabel("h (km)")
ax.set_ylabel("semivariance (mg/kg)²")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


vario_ni (mg/kg, annealing target): [0.0, np.float64(10.057), np.float64(0.94), np.float64(0.94), np.float64(59.796), 'spherical']
vario_ns (normal scores, SGS)      : [0.0, np.float64(0.216), np.float64(0.944), np.float64(0.944), 1.0, 'spherical']









The objective uses 10 lags of one cell (100 m) along each of the four default directions, so it controls the variogram up to 1 km along the axes and 1.4 km along the diagonals. That covers the range of about 0.9 km.


Code
N_LAGS = 10
SA_KW = dict(n_lags=N_LAGS)

title: Simulated Annealing Simulation (sasim)
text:
A First Run with SimulatedAnnealing
Fit, simulate one realization, and look at what the optimizer did. history_ holds \(O / O_{\text{init}}\) after each temperature, n_swaps_ the swaps attempted, and objective_ the final relative objective.


Code
sa = SimulatedAnnealing(vario=vario_ni, **SA_KW).fit(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Ni")
lat = sa.lattice_
print(f"lattice: {lat['nx']} x {lat['ny']} = {lat['nx'] * lat['ny']} nodes, spacing {lat['dx']:.2f} km; "
      f"hard-data nodes: {np.isfinite(sa._hard).sum()} (259 data, some share a node)")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
img = sa.simulate_lattice(nsim=1, seed=1)[0]
print(f"one realization: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s, {sa.n_swaps_[0]:,} swaps, "
      f"final O / O_init = {sa.objective_[0]:.1e}, {len(sa.history_[0]) - 1} temperatures")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(19, 5.2))
axes[0].semilogy(sa.history_[0], "o-")
axes[0].set_xlabel("temperature step")
axes[0].set_ylabel("O / O_init")
axes[0].set_title("Convergence")
start = SimulatedAnnealing(vario=vario_ni, **SA_KW, max_swaps=1).fit(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Ni")
img0 = start.simulate_lattice(nsim=1, seed=1)[0]          # one swap only: essentially the start image
for ax, im_, title in [(axes[1], img0, "Starting image (random quantiles)"), (axes[2], img, "After annealing")]:
    h_ = ax.imshow(im_.T, origin="lower", cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=45,
                   extent=[lat["x0"], lat["x0"] + lat["nx"] * lat["dx"], lat["y0"], lat["y0"] + lat["ny"] * lat["dy"]])
    ax.set_title(title + ": full lattice")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    plt.colorbar(h_, ax=ax, label="Ni (mg/kg)", fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


lattice: 49 x 59 = 2891 nodes, spacing 0.10 km; hard-data nodes: 205 (259 data, some share a node)
one realization: 2.1 s, 57,001 swaps, final O / O_init = 9.9e-04, 3 temperatures









The full lattice includes the nodes outside the irregular study area (the corners of the bounding box); simulate drops them. The starting image is white noise with the right histogram, and annealing rearranges it into a spatially continuous field.
Checks on 20 realizations:

the histogram is exact (each image is a permutation of the start);
hard data are reproduced at their nodes;
the same seed reproduces the image;
sasim equals the class.

title: Simulated Annealing Simulation (sasim)
text:
Variogram Reproduction by Direction
experimental_variogram(image) and target_variogram() evaluate an image and the target at exactly the lag vectors in the objective: four directions × 10 lags. The realizations should follow the target in every direction, because every direction is in the objective. Between the controlled lags, and beyond them, nothing is enforced.


Code
target = sa.target_variogram()[0].reshape(4, N_LAGS)
emp = np.stack([sa.experimental_variogram(lat_reals[r])[0].reshape(4, N_LAGS) for r in range(N_SIM)])
names = ["E-W (1, 0)", "N-S (0, 1)", "diagonal (1, 1)", "diagonal (1, −1)"]
steps = [1.0, 1.0, np.sqrt(2), np.sqrt(2)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(21, 4.2), sharey=True)
for d, ax in enumerate(axes):
    h = np.arange(1, N_LAGS + 1) * steps[d] * CELL
    for r in range(N_SIM):
        ax.plot(h, emp[r, d], color="0.7", lw=0.8)
    ax.plot(h, target[d], "ro-", ms=4, label="target")
    ax.set_title(names[d])
    ax.set_xlabel("h (km)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("semivariance (mg/kg)²")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
rel = np.abs(emp.mean(0) - target) / target
worst = np.unravel_index(rel.argmax(), rel.shape)
print(f"relative error: median {np.median(rel):.3f}, max {rel.max():.3f} ({names[worst[0]]}, lag {worst[1] + 1})")
record("annealing: variogram within 10% of target at every controlled lag (mean of realizations)",
       "PASS" if rel.max() < 0.10 else "FAIL", f"max relative error {rel.max():.3f}")









relative error: median 0.032, max 0.072 (E-W (1, 0), lag 7)
✅ [PASS] annealing: variogram within 10% of target at every controlled lag (mean of realizations)  max relative error 0.072


At the controlled lags the realizations sit almost exactly on the target, in all four directions, with very little spread between realizations. That is the optimizer at work, and it is the main thing annealing does well. The remaining error (a few per cent, largest at the shortest lags) is set by the stopping rule: annealing stops when \(O\) falls to tol \(= 10^{-3}\) of its initial value. Section 8 tightens it. The narrow spread is also a reminder: the realizations agree with the model, not with the data. Sequential methods reproduce the model variogram only on average, with realistic ergodic fluctuations between realizations.

All four schedules reach the stopping tolerance. For a variogram objective the landscape is benign, so even an almost greedy quench (one temperature step, 0.6 s) gets there, about 4× faster than the default. The schedule does affect how well the variogram is matched at the end:

Both a slower schedule and a stricter tol buy precision with time. The stopping rule is the more direct lever: the default schedule with tol = 1e-4 was more precise than the slow schedule and took half the time.
For objectives with competing components (Section 10), or for categorical images, where swaps can create isolated pixels that a greedy search never removes, a slower schedule is worth more.

title: Simulated Annealing Simulation (sasim)
section: Conditioning and Local Accuracy: Annealing vs SGS
text:
Conditioning and Local Accuracy: Annealing vs SGS
The data are fixed at their nodes, but Section 2.6 warned that their influence on the neighbouring nodes is weak. Three diagnostics compare 20 annealed realizations with 20 SGS realizations on the same 100 m grid:

Continuity across the data: the mean squared difference between a hard-data node and its four lattice neighbours, against the same quantity between other nodes. In a realization without conditioning artefacts the two agree, at about \(2\gamma(100\text{ m})\).
E-type maps: does the mean of the realizations reflect the data?
Held-out sites: RMSE of the E-type and coverage of the 80% interval at the 100 validation sites, each read at its nearest grid node.



Code
sgs_reals = sgsim_gpu(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Ni", vario_ns, num_points=16, radius=1.5, nsim=N_SIM,
                      seed=2024, zmin=0.0, use_gpu=USE_GPU)
sgs_lat = np.full_like(lat_reals, np.nan)
sgs_lat[:, sa._grid_idx[:, 0], sa._grid_idx[:, 1]] = sgs_reals
in_grid = np.zeros(sa._hard.shape, bool)
in_grid[sa._grid_idx[:, 0], sa._grid_idx[:, 1]] = True


def neighbour_msd(images, mask):
    # mean squared difference between masked nodes and their 4 lattice neighbours (inside the grid)
    out = []
    for im_ in images:
        d2 = []
        for di, dj in [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]:
            nb = np.roll(np.roll(im_, di, 0), dj, 1)
            ok = mask & np.roll(np.roll(in_grid, di, 0), dj, 1) & in_grid
            d2.append((im_[ok] - nb[ok]) ** 2)
        out.append(np.concatenate(d2).mean())
    return np.mean(out)


hard_mask = hard & in_grid
free_mask = free & in_grid

    "around hard data": [neighbour_msd(lat_reals, hard_mask), neighbour_msd(sgs_lat, hard_mask)],
    "elsewhere": [neighbour_msd(lat_reals, free_mask), neighbour_msd(sgs_lat, free_mask)]},
    index=["annealing", "SGS"])

the intervals are equally wide, but SGS’s cover 74% of the true values against annealing’s 60%.

Annealing’s local distributions are both less accurate and less calibrated, because nothing in the objective ties them to the data the way kriging does.
E-type maps. The annealed E-type is noisier, with isolated spots at the data, while the SGS E-type is a smooth, kriging-like surface.

section: A Secondary Variable: the Correlation Component
text:
A Secondary Variable: the Correlation Component
Chromium is strongly related to nickel in the Jura soils. A kriged chromium map (from all 359 samples) is passed as secondary, which adds the correlation component \(O_\rho\). The target correlation defaults to the correlation between Ni and Cr at the data (secondary_col="Cr"). The weight of the correlation component relative to the variogram is varied with component_weights.


Code
xy_all = df_all[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
cr_all = df_all["Cr"].to_numpy(float)
vg_cr = Variogram(xy_all, cr_all, model="spherical", n_lags=15).fit()
cr_grid = np.asarray(OrdinaryKriging(vg_cr).fit(xy_all, cr_all).predict(grid), float)

rows, corr_reals = [], {}
for w in [0.0, 1.0, 5.0]:
    s = SimulatedAnnealing(vario=vario_ni, **SA_KW, component_weights={"variogram": 1.0, "correlation": w})
    s.fit(grid, df, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Ni", secondary=cr_grid, secondary_col="Cr")
    r_ = s.simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=11)
    corr_reals[w] = r_
    rho_real = np.array([np.corrcoef(r_[i], cr_grid)[0, 1] for i in range(len(r_))])
    lat_r = s.simulate_lattice(nsim=1, seed=5)[0]
    vg_err = np.abs(s.experimental_variogram(lat_r)[0] / s.target_variogram()[0] - 1).max()
    rows.append({"correlation weight": w, "target rho": s.rho_target_, "realized rho (mean)": rho_real.mean(),
                 "realized rho (sd)": rho_real.std(), "max rel. variogram error": vg_err,
                 **{k: v for k, v in score("", r_, ~on_hard).items() if k not in ("method", "n sites")}})

title: Simulated Annealing Simulation (sasim)
text:
Categorical Annealing: Rock Type
With indicator_varios={class: vario} the objective becomes the sum of the indicator-variogram mismatches of the five rock types. Because swaps keep the starting values, the class proportions are exact. In sequential indicator simulation the same rock types drifted (Kimmeridgian 0.44 against 0.36 in the samples).
The indicator variogram of each class is fitted with sill \(p_c(1 - p_c)\). The geology map is the reference, as in the SIS notebook.

rock = df["Rock"].to_numpy(float)
ind_varios = {c: fit_spherical(xy, (rock == c).astype(float), (rock == c).mean() * (1 - (rock == c).mean()))[0]

for c, v in ind_varios.items():
    print(f"{ROCKS[c]:13s} p = {(rock == c).mean():.3f}  vario = {v}")

Proportions are exact. On the free lattice nodes every realization has exactly the target proportions (standard deviation over realizations about \(10^{-17}\)). Sequential indicator simulation cannot guarantee that. Over the study-area nodes alone the proportions differ a little: Kimmeridgian 0.38 against 0.36, because the lattice nodes outside the irregular boundary also take part of the histogram. If the proportions must hold inside an irregular area, use a grid that fills the lattice, or pass a mask by simulating on the bounding box and discarding the outside.
Patterns. The realizations have patchy, map-like units with the target indicator variograms (E-W shown). The most probable class matches the geology map at 64% of the nodes, and single realizations at 57%. Portlandian keeps its sample proportion (1.1%), far below its 5.6% on the map, because annealing can only reproduce the proportions it is given. A better target (for example from the map, through target_values) would have to come from outside the samples.
Cost. Categorical annealing took about 26 s per realization, roughly ten times more than the continuous case on the same lattice: five indicator variograms per swap, and more swaps to converge.

Simulated annealing treats simulation as optimization. It swaps values of a random image until an objective made of target statistics is small. Swaps keep the histogram exactly, and hard data are fixed at their nodes. Both were checked on every realization.
Variograms are matched closely at the controlled lags and directions, in every realization, with very little ergodic spread. The precision is set by the stopping rule: about 11% maximum error with tol = 1e-3, and 4.5% with tol = 1e-4. For a variogram objective, even a quench converges; it was about 4× faster than the default schedule.
Conditioning is weak. Annealed realizations show discontinuities around the data (24% larger neighbour differences than elsewhere). At held-out sites away from the data they were less accurate than SGS (RMSE 6.36 vs 5.88 mg/kg) and poorly calibrated (80% intervals covered 60%, against 74% for SGS). Do not use annealing realizations as calibrated local uncertainty.
Extra statistics are easy to add. A correlation component brought the Ni-Cr map correlation from 0.46 to 0.74 (target 0.70) and improved the E-type. Its weight trades off against variogram precision.
Categorical annealing reproduced the rock-type proportions exactly in every realization, which SIS cannot do. Lattice nodes outside an irregular study area take part of the histogram.
Cost: about 36 µs per swap and hundreds of swaps per node: 2 s per continuous realization on the 100 m lattice, 9 s at 50 m, and about ten times more for five-class categorical objectives. CPU only.

title: Multiple-Point Statistics Simulation (DirectSampling, SNESIM)
text:
Overview
Every simulator in the earlier notebooks (SGS, SIS, DSS, PGS) is driven by two-point statistics: variograms or covariances, which describe how two locations at a given separation relate. Many geological structures are defined by relations among many points at once: a channel is a continuous, curving, connected body, and a sequence of units has a specific arrangement. Very different images can share the same variogram, and a two-point simulator will produce the most disordered of them. Multiple-point statistics (MPS) simulation takes those relations from a training image (TI): a conceptual picture of the expected patterns, such as a sketch, an outcrop, a process-based model, or a mapped analogue area. Each simulated node is drawn according to what the TI shows in the same neighbourhood configuration.
GeoLattice provides the two best-known MPS algorithms:









Algorithm
Idea
Variables
Notes




SNESIM (Strebelle, 2002)
scan the TI once, store every pattern with counts of its centre category; at each node read \(P(c \mid \text{data event})\) from the counts
categorical
multigrid; servosystem for proportions; soft data by the tau model


Direct Sampling (Mariethoz et al., 2010)
at each node, scan the TI from a random position for a pattern close enough to the data event and paste its centre
categorical and continuous
no pattern database; threshold controls fidelity; secondary TI for co-simulation



The objects:







Object
What it does




DirectSampling, dssim
Direct Sampling simulator and one-call wrapper


SNESIM, snesim
SNESIM simulator and one-call wrapper


tau_model
Combines TI and soft probabilities (Journel, 2002)


pattern_histogram, pattern_histogram_distance
Multiple-point histogram of an image, and the distance between two


connectivity
Probability that two cells of a category at a given lag belong to the same connected body


channel_training_image
Synthetic sinuous-channel TI



The notebook first uses a synthetic channel system, where the true field is known. It shows why SIS fails on channels, how the parameters of each MPS algorithm act, how conditioning and secondary data help, and how MPS handles continuous variables. It then turns to real data: the northern half of the Jura geology map is used as the training image for the southern half. That raises the practical question of every MPS study: is the TI representative?

title: Multiple-Point Statistics Simulation (DirectSampling, SNESIM)
text:
Theory

Beyond two-point statistics
A variogram \(\gamma(\mathbf{h}) = \tfrac12 E[(Z(\mathbf{u}) - Z(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{h}))^2]\) involves two points at a time. The multiple-point statistics of a categorical image are the probabilities of joint configurations of \(n\) points,
\[
P\bigl\{S(\mathbf{u}) = c,\; S(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{h}_1) = s_1,\; \dots,\; S(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{h}_n) = s_n\bigr\},
\]
which no variogram model can specify. Two-point simulators fill the gap with the maximum-entropy choice implied by kriging, which disperses high values instead of connecting them. Connectivity is precisely what controls flow, contamination pathways or drainage, so this matters in practice.


Training images and data events
A training image \(\mathrm{TI}\) is an exhaustive image on the simulation cell size (ti[ix, iy], axis 0 = x). It is assumed stationary: its patterns are replicated across it, and it describes the patterns expected in the study area. It need not be conditioned to any data.
At a node \(\mathbf{u}\), the data event \(d_n\) is the set of the \(n\) nearest informed nodes, hard data or previously simulated, with their offsets \(\mathbf{h}_\alpha\) and values \(s_\alpha\). MPS reads the conditional distribution of \(S(\mathbf{u})\) from the TI replicates of \(d_n\):
\[
P\bigl(S(\mathbf{u}) = c \mid d_n\bigr) = \frac{P(c,\, d_n)}{P(d_n)} \approx \frac{\#\{\mathbf{v} \in \mathrm{TI}: \mathrm{TI}(\mathbf{v}) = c,\; \mathrm{TI}(\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{h}_\alpha) = s_\alpha\ \forall \alpha\}}{\#\{\mathbf{v} \in \mathrm{TI}: \mathrm{TI}(\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{h}_\alpha) = s_\alpha\ \forall \alpha\}} ,
\]
the “single normal equation” of Guardiano & Srivastava (1993). It is the indicator-kriging system written for one \(n\)-point indicator, whose solution is just this ratio of counts. Sequential simulation along a random path then draws a realization, as in SIS, but with the conditional distribution borrowed from the TI instead of kriged from variograms.


SNESIM
SNESIM (Strebelle, 2002) makes that practical.

Template. The data event is restricted to a fixed template of the n_template nodes nearest the centre within search_radius cells.
Pattern storage. For each grid level the TI is scanned once, and every unique template pattern is stored with the counts of its centre categories. GeoLattice uses a list-based equivalent of Strebelle’s search tree, as in IMPALA (Straubhaar et al., 2011). n_patterns_ reports how many unique patterns were stored per level.
Data-event reduction. If fewer than min_replicates TI patterns match, the farthest informed nodes are dropped until enough do.
Multigrid. Simulation runs from the coarsest grid (spacing \(2^{G-1}\) cells, with \(G\) = n_multigrid) to the finest, with the template stretched by the grid spacing. Large structures are fixed early by a small template, and finer grids fill in details.
Servosystem. To keep the global proportions near the targets \(\pi_c\) (target_proportions, default the TI proportions), each conditional probability is corrected with the current simulated proportions \(\hat\pi_c\):

\[
p_c' = \begin{cases} \max\!\left(0,\; p_c + \frac{\mu}{1 - \mu}\bigl(\pi_c - \hat\pi_c\bigr)\right) & p_c > 0 \\ 0 & p_c = 0 \end{cases}, \quad \text{renormalized}, \qquad \mu = \texttt{servo} \in [0, 1).
\]
The correction is additive, so applied to every category it would give positive probability to a category that the TI says is impossible in that data event (\(p_c = 0\)), creating patterns the TI never shows. GeoLattice therefore corrects only the categories with \(p_c > 0\); if nothing is left after clipping, the uncorrected \(p_c\) is used. Section 7 checks this on a TI with a strict adjacency rule.


Direct Sampling
Direct Sampling (Mariethoz, Renard & Straubhaar, 2010) builds no database. At each node it takes the data event (up to n_neighbors informed nodes within search_radius), then scans the TI from a random position, computing a distance between the data event and the TI pattern at each candidate location \(\mathbf{v}\):
\[
d\bigl(d_n, \mathrm{TI}(\mathbf{v})\bigr) = \frac{\sum_\alpha w_\alpha\, \delta_\alpha}{\sum_\alpha w_\alpha},
\qquad
\delta_\alpha = \begin{cases} \mathbf{1}[\mathrm{TI}(\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{h}_\alpha) \ne s_\alpha] & \text{categorical} \\ |\mathrm{TI}(\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{h}_\alpha) - s_\alpha| / \text{range}(\mathrm{TI}) & \text{continuous,} \end{cases}
\]
with weights \(w_\alpha = |\mathbf{h}_\alpha|^{-\text{distance\_power}}\). The first location with \(d \le\) threshold is accepted, and its centre value is pasted at \(\mathbf{u}\). If max_scan_fraction of the TI has been scanned without success, the best match seen is used.

Scanning from a random start and accepting the first good-enough match amounts to sampling from the conditional distribution, without estimating it.
threshold = 0 with many neighbours copies the TI almost verbatim; a larger threshold adds variability and noise.
n_postprocess extra passes re-simulate each non-data node with a fully informed neighbourhood, which removes the noise left by nodes simulated early from sparse data events.
Because only distances are needed, Direct Sampling handles continuous variables too.



Multiple-point co-simulation
With an exhaustive secondary variable \(y\), such as a seismic attribute or a remote-sensing image:

Direct Sampling pairs the TI with a secondary training image (secondary_ti, for example the same attribute forward-modelled on the TI). The distance becomes \[
d = (1 - w)\, d_{\text{primary}} + w\, d_{\text{secondary}},
\] with \(w\) = secondary_weight, and \(d_{\text{secondary}}\) is computed on the collocated secondary value plus n_secondary − 1 template offsets.
SNESIM combines its TI probability \(P(c \mid d_n)\) with a soft probability \(P(c \mid y)\) through the tau model (Journel, 2002). With distances \(x = (1 - P)/P\) and \(x_0\) from the prior proportions, \[
\frac{x}{x_0} = \left(\frac{x_{\mathrm{TI}}}{x_0}\right)^{\tau_1} \left(\frac{x_{\text{soft}}}{x_0}\right)^{\tau_2}, \qquad P = \frac{1}{1 + x},
\] with \(\tau = (1, 1)\) the “permanence of ratios” hypothesis. \(\tau_2 = 0\) ignores the soft data and \(\tau_1 = 0\) ignores the TI.



Diagnostics: pattern histograms and connectivity

The multiple-point histogram (pattern_histogram(image, size)) counts the frequency of every \(s \times s\) configuration. Two images are compared by the total-variation distance \(\tfrac12 \sum_p |f_1(p) - f_2(p)|\) (pattern_histogram_distance): 0 means identical pattern statistics, 1 disjoint.
The connectivity function (connectivity(image, c, max_lag, axis)) is the probability that two cells of category \(c\) at lag \(h\) along an axis belong to the same connected body, given that both are \(c\). Connected channels keep it near 1 over long lags; disconnected blobs make it decay quickly.



The GPU engines
With use_gpu=True both simulators run all realizations in lockstep with batched array operations (CuPy). SNESIM matches every realization’s data event against the pattern table in one fused kernel per step, and gives the same realizations as the CPU engine. Direct Sampling’s threads scan TI candidates in parallel. Its realizations are statistically equivalent to the CPU engine’s, not bit-identical, because candidates are visited in a different order. The GPU pays off with many realizations.


The algorithms
SNESIM, for each realization:

Place the hard data on their nearest nodes.
For each grid level, coarse to fine:

visit the uninformed nodes of the level in random order;
read the data event on the stretched template, and reduce it until at least min_replicates TI patterns match;
take \(P(c \mid d_n)\) from the stored counts; apply the tau model (soft data) and the servosystem;
draw a category.


Direct Sampling, for each realization:

Place the hard data.
Visit the nodes in random order. At each node:

take the data event;
scan the TI from a random position until a pattern is within threshold (or the scan budget runs out);
paste its centre value.

Optionally re-simulate all non-data nodes (n_postprocess).

section: Why Two-Point Statistics Are Not Enough
text:
Why Two-Point Statistics Are Not Enough
SIS is given the exact indicator variogram of the TI. A spherical model is fitted to the TI’s experimental indicator variograms along x and y, which gives a geometric anisotropy with the long range along the channels. Unconditional SIS, SNESIM and Direct Sampling realizations are then compared with the TI on three measures:

the indicator variogram along each axis;
the connectivity of channel cells along the channel direction (x);
the 3 × 3 pattern histogram.



Code
def axis_variogram(img, axis, max_lag=40):
    img = np.asarray(img, float)
    out = []
    for h in range(1, max_lag + 1):
        a = img[:-h, :] if axis == 0 else img[:, :-h]
        b = img[h:, :] if axis == 0 else img[:, h:]
        out.append(0.5 * np.nanmean((a - b) ** 2))
    return np.array(out)


p = TI.mean()
sill = p * (1 - p)
lags = np.arange(1, 41)
sph = lambda h, a: sill * (1.5 * np.minimum(h / a, 1) - 0.5 * np.minimum(h / a, 1) ** 3)
ax_x = curve_fit(sph, lags, axis_variogram(TI, 0), p0=[20])[0][0]
ax_y = curve_fit(sph, lags, axis_variogram(TI, 1), p0=[5])[0][0]
vario_ti = [90.0, 0.0, round(ax_x, 1), round(ax_y, 1), round(sill, 4), "spherical"]   # azimuth 90: major along x
print(f"TI indicator variogram: range along x {ax_x:.1f} cells, along y {ax_y:.1f} cells;  vario = {vario_ti}")

unc = {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
sis = IndicatorCoSimulator([0, 1], vario_ti, num_points=24, proportions=[1 - p, p], use_gpu=USE_GPU)   # TI proportions
unc["SIS"] = sis.fit(grid, pd.DataFrame({"X": [50.0], "Y": [50.0], "f": [0.0]}), "X", "Y", "f").simulate(

unc["Direct Sampling"] = DirectSampling(TI, use_gpu=USE_GPU).fit(grid).simulate_lattice(nsim=10, seed=1)

Two-point statistics look similar. The indicator variograms of all three simulators have the TI’s general shape: a short range across the channels (y) and a longer one along them (x). SIS’s are somewhat off; its sill is higher because its channel proportion drifted up (0.19 against 0.16). Nothing in a variogram plot says that one of these images has channels and another has blobs.
Multiple-point statistics differ completely. SIS produces disconnected, irregular patches: the connectivity of channel cells drops to 0 by 30 cells, and its 3 × 3 pattern histogram is far from the TI’s (distance 0.23). SNESIM and Direct Sampling produce continuous, sinuous channels: connectivity 0.74 and 0.68 at 30 cells (TI 0.79), and pattern distances of 0.06-0.08.
What MPS still misses. Both MPS methods let channels end more often than the TI does (connectivity falls below the TI’s beyond about 30 cells), and Direct Sampling under-produces channel cells (0.12 against 0.16). MPS reproduces patterns up to the template size; very long-range continuity depends on the multigrid (SNESIM) or the search radius (Direct Sampling).

Threshold. threshold = 0 (exact matches only) gives the most TI-like images: the best connectivity (0.76 at 30 cells) and a small pattern distance, at the highest cost. A large threshold (0.2) accepts poor matches. Background patterns are the most common partial matches, so channels die out (channel proportion 0.007): the simulation collapses.
Neighbours. Few neighbours (10) is fast and matches small patterns well (pattern distance 0.058), but long-range continuity is weaker. Many neighbours (60) costs more, and with the default threshold matching becomes harder.

Practical defaults: threshold 0-0.05, n_neighbors 20-40, and max_scan_fraction large enough that most nodes find a match.

SNESIM: Multigrid, Patterns and the Servosystem
n_patterns_ shows how many unique patterns the TI holds at each grid level. Below, the multigrid effect on the channel TI is measured: n_multigrid = 1 against the default 4, both with servo=0.

With four levels, the coarse grids lay out the channel paths with a template that spans 8 × 8 = 64 cells, and the finer levels draw them in. Each level stores more unique patterns (2,618 on the finest grid, 14,513 on the coarsest, whose stretched template sees more varied configurations). The run time barely changes.

The servosystem trade-off
The servosystem keeps proportions close to the target. Applied to every category, its additive correction would revive categories that the TI rules out, so GeoLattice corrects only categories with \(p_c > 0\) (Section 2.3). Checking this needs a training image with a strict adjacency rule. A smooth Gaussian field truncated into three ordered classes (A < B < C) has no A-C contacts at all, since every path from A to C crosses B. SNESIM is run with increasing servo, and Direct Sampling for reference.


Code
gx2, gy2 = np.meshgrid(np.arange(200.0), np.arange(200.0), indexing="ij")
g200 = np.column_stack([gx2.ravel(), gy2.ravel()])
z = FFTSimulator([0, 0, 25, 25, 1, "gaussian"]).fit(g200).simulate(1, seed=3)[0].reshape(200, 200)
TI3 = np.digitize(z, [-0.5, 0.5]).astype(float)           # 0 = A, 1 = B, 2 = C


def contact_counts(img):
    img = np.asarray(img)
    M = np.zeros((3, 3))
    for a, b in [(img[1:, :], img[:-1, :]), (img[:, 1:], img[:, :-1])]:
        ok = a != b
        np.add.at(M, (a[ok].astype(int), b[ok].astype(int)), 1)
    return M + M.T


M_ti = contact_counts(TI3)
print(f"TI3 contacts: A-B {M_ti[0, 1]:.0f}, B-C {M_ti[1, 2]:.0f}, A-C {M_ti[0, 2]:.0f};  proportions "
      f"{[round(float(np.mean(TI3 == k)), 3) for k in range(3)]}")

rows, servo_imgs = [], {}
for name, sim in [("SNESIM servo=0", SNESIM(TI3, servo=0.0, use_gpu=USE_GPU)),
                  ("SNESIM servo=0.2", SNESIM(TI3, servo=0.2, use_gpu=USE_GPU)),
                  ("SNESIM servo=0.5 (default)", SNESIM(TI3, servo=0.5, use_gpu=USE_GPU)),
                  ("Direct Sampling", DirectSampling(TI3, use_gpu=USE_GPU))]:
    r = sim.fit(grid).simulate_lattice(nsim=5, seed=1)
    servo_imgs[name] = r[0]
    Ms = [contact_counts(r[i]) for i in range(5)]
    rows.append({"method": name, "A-C contacts (forbidden)": np.mean([M[0, 2] for M in Ms]),
                 "A-B contacts": np.mean([M[0, 1] for M in Ms]),
                 **{f"prop. {c}": np.mean(r == k) for k, c in enumerate("ABC")}})
rows.append({"method": "training image", "A-C contacts (forbidden)": 0.0, "A-B contacts": M_ti[0, 1] / 4,
             **{f"prop. {c}": np.mean(TI3 == k) for k, c in enumerate("ABC")}})
servo_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("method")
display(servo_table.round(3))

axes[0].imshow(TI3[:100, :100].T, origin="lower", cmap=cm3, vmin=0, vmax=2)

    ax.set_title(k)

    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])

servo = 0 reproduces the TI’s adjacency rule, but the proportions drift.
servo > 0 pulls the proportions onto the targets and keeps the adjacency rule, because only categories the TI allows in the data event are corrected. An unmasked additive correction, which gives A or C probability where the TI says it is impossible, produced 213 (servo = 0.2) and 389 (servo = 0.5) A-C contacts per realization on this TI.
The occasional A-C contact that remains (about 3 edges over 5 realizations) is not caused by the servosystem. When fewer than min_replicates TI patterns match, the farthest data-event nodes are dropped, and the reduced event can allow A next to C. servo = 0 produces such contacts too with other seeds.
Direct Sampling, which has no servosystem, has no forbidden contacts and proportions close to the TI’s.

The servosystem can be left on when adjacency rules matter, but check contacts and proportions on the realizations. The rest of this notebook uses servo = 0 unless stated otherwise, so that SNESIM’s results reflect the TI patterns alone.

title: Multiple-Point Statistics Simulation (DirectSampling, SNESIM)
text:
Conditional Simulation against the Truth
Now the simulators are conditioned on the 60 wells and compared with the true field. A trivial “all background” map would agree with 80% of the cells, so cell agreement is a poor score. The measures used are:

channel recall and precision of the most probable map;
the Brier score of the channel probability \(P(\text{channel})\);
connectivity and pattern-histogram distance relative to the truth;
exact reproduction of the wells.

20 realizations per method; SNESIM uses servo=0.


Code
N_SIM = 20
cond = {}
times = {}
for name, sim in [("SIS", IndicatorCoSimulator([0, 1], vario_ti, num_points=24, use_gpu=USE_GPU)),
                  ("SNESIM", SNESIM(TI, servo=0.0, use_gpu=USE_GPU)),
                  ("Direct Sampling", DirectSampling(TI, use_gpu=USE_GPU))]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    cond[name] = sim.fit(grid, wells, "X", "Y", "facies").simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=5)
    times[name] = time.perf_counter() - t0

ph_truth = pattern_histogram(TRUTH, 3)
conn_truth = connectivity(TRUTH, 1, 30, 0)[-1]
rows = []
for name, r in cond.items():
    p_ch = r.mean(0)
    mode = (p_ch > 0.5).astype(float)
    tp = np.sum((mode == 1) & (truth == 1))
    rows.append({"method": name, "seconds": times[name],
                 "wells honoured": bool(np.all(r[:, well_idx] == wells.facies.to_numpy()[None, :])),
                 "channel proportion": r.mean(), "recall": tp / truth.sum(), "precision": tp / max(mode.sum(), 1),
                 "Brier": np.mean((p_ch - truth) ** 2),
                 "pattern dist. to truth": np.mean([pattern_histogram_distance(ph_truth, pattern_histogram(r[i].reshape(NX, NY), 3))
                                                    for i in range(N_SIM)]),
                 "connectivity @30": np.nanmean([connectivity(r[i].reshape(NX, NY), 1, 30, 0)[-1] for i in range(N_SIM)])})
rows.append({"method": "truth", "channel proportion": truth.mean(), "recall": 1.0, "precision": 1.0, "Brier": 0.0,
             "pattern dist. to truth": 0.0, "connectivity @30": conn_truth})
cond_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("method")
display(cond_table.round(3))
for name in cond:
    record(f"{name}: wells honoured in every realization", "PASS" if cond_table.loc[name, "wells honoured"] else "FAIL")

MPS reproduces the patterns of the true field. Pattern distance to the truth is 0.08 (SNESIM) and 0.13 (Direct Sampling), against 0.34 for SIS.
