title: Multiple-Point Statistics Simulation (DirectSampling, SNESIM)
section: Multiple-Point Co-Simulation with a Seismic-Like Secondary
text:
Multiple-Point Co-Simulation with a Seismic-Like Secondary
A secondary variable known everywhere, but blurred and noisy, is built by smoothing the facies with a Gaussian filter (\(\sigma\) = 3 cells) and adding noise, like a low-resolution seismic attribute. The same operator applied to the TI gives the secondary training image.

Direct Sampling: secondary_ti plus the secondary on the grid, with secondary_weight 0.5.
SNESIM: soft probabilities \(P(\text{channel} \mid y)\) calibrated on the TI pairs (20 quantile bins of the secondary TI), combined with the TI probabilities by the tau model.



Code
def seismic(img, seed):
    return gaussian_filter(np.asarray(img, float), 3.0) + np.random.default_rng(seed).normal(0, 0.08, np.shape(img))


SEC_TI = seismic(TI, 10)
sec_grid = seismic(TRUTH, 11).ravel()
print(f"corr(secondary, facies): TI {np.corrcoef(SEC_TI.ravel(), TI.ravel())[0, 1]:.2f}, "
      f"truth {np.corrcoef(sec_grid, truth)[0, 1]:.2f}")

# soft probabilities for SNESIM: calibrate P(channel | secondary) on the TI pairs
edges = np.quantile(SEC_TI, np.linspace(0, 1, 21))
b_ti = np.clip(np.searchsorted(edges, SEC_TI.ravel(), side="right") - 1, 0, 19)
p_bin = np.array([TI.ravel()[b_ti == b].mean() for b in range(20)])
b_grid = np.clip(np.searchsorted(edges, sec_grid, side="right") - 1, 0, 19)
soft = np.column_stack([1 - p_bin[b_grid], p_bin[b_grid]])        # columns in categories_ order: 0, 1

print("tau_model example: prior 0.16, TI 0.5, soft 0.7 ->",
      np.round(tau_model(np.array([0.84, 0.16]), np.array([0.5, 0.5]), np.array([0.3, 0.7]))[1], 3))

cosim = {
    "DS + secondary TI": DirectSampling(TI, secondary_ti=SEC_TI, secondary_weight=0.5, use_gpu=USE_GPU).fit(
        grid, wells, "X", "Y", "facies", secondary=sec_grid).simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=5),
    "SNESIM + soft (tau model)": SNESIM(TI, servo=0.0, use_gpu=USE_GPU).fit(
        grid, wells, "X", "Y", "facies", soft=soft).simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=5),
}
rows = []
for name, r in list(cond.items())[1:] + list(cosim.items()):
    p_ch = r.mean(0)
    mode = (p_ch > 0.5).astype(float)
    tp = np.sum((mode == 1) & (truth == 1))
    rows.append({"method": name, "recall": tp / truth.sum(), "precision": tp / max(mode.sum(), 1),
                 "Brier": np.mean((p_ch - truth) ** 2), "agreement per realization": np.mean(r == truth[None, :]),
                 "connectivity @30": np.nanmean([connectivity(r[i].reshape(NX, NY), 1, 30, 0)[-1] for i in range(N_SIM)])})
co_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("method")
display(co_table.round(3))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(24, 5.6))
im = axes[0].imshow(sec_grid.reshape(NX, NY).T, origin="lower", cmap="gray")
axes[0].set_title("Secondary (blurred, noisy facies)")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
show_bin(axes[1], TRUTH, "Truth", wells)
for ax, (name, r) in zip(axes[2:], cosim.items()):
    im = ax.imshow(r.mean(0).reshape(NX, NY).T, origin="lower", cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}: P(channel)")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
record("co-simulation lowers the Brier score (DS and SNESIM)",
       "PASS" if co_table.loc["DS + secondary TI", "Brier"] < co_table.loc["Direct Sampling", "Brier"] and
       co_table.loc["SNESIM + soft (tau model)", "Brier"] < co_table.loc["SNESIM", "Brier"] else "FAIL",
       f"DS {co_table.loc['Direct Sampling', 'Brier']:.3f} -> {co_table.loc['DS + secondary TI', 'Brier']:.3f}; SNESIM "
       f"{co_table.loc['SNESIM', 'Brier']:.3f} -> {co_table.loc['SNESIM + soft (tau model)', 'Brier']:.3f}")

A secondary variable changes local prediction dramatically. The secondary is blurred and noisy, with a correlation of only 0.64 with the facies.

Direct Sampling with the secondary TI recovers 77% of the channel cells with 80% precision. Its Brier score falls from 0.148 to 0.058, and connectivity at 30 cells (0.89) matches the truth’s (0.89). Matching the secondary pattern around each node uses the spatial structure of the blur, not just the collocated value.
SNESIM with tau-model soft probabilities also improves (Brier 0.093, recall 0.50), but less. Its soft probability uses only the collocated secondary value, through a calibration curve.

The tau model with \(\tau = (1, 1)\) is conditional independence in odds form. With prior 0.16, TI 0.5 and soft 0.7, it gives 0.93: two moderately informative, independent sources reinforce each other strongly. If the sources are redundant, \(\tau < 1\) tempers that.

title: Multiple-Point Statistics Simulation (DirectSampling, SNESIM)
text:
A Continuous Training Image
Direct Sampling also works for continuous variables, using the mean absolute difference as the distance. The training image here is a continuous field with a non-Gaussian pattern: the absolute value of a smooth Gaussian field. That gives sharp, narrow valleys between rounded highs, a ridge-valley structure that a variogram alone cannot describe. Unconditional realizations are compared with the TI on the histogram, the variogram along x, and the visual pattern.


Code
g150 = np.column_stack([np.repeat(np.arange(150.0), 150), np.tile(np.arange(150.0), 150)])
zc = FFTSimulator([0, 0, 30, 30, 1, "gaussian"]).fit(g150).simulate(1, seed=9)[0]
TI_C = np.abs(zc.reshape(150, 150))
dsc = DirectSampling(TI_C, kind="continuous", n_neighbors=30, threshold=0.02, use_gpu=USE_GPU).fit(grid)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
rc = dsc.simulate_lattice(nsim=5, seed=4)
print(f"continuous DS: 5 realizations in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s; kind = {dsc.kind}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(24, 5.2))
axes[0].imshow(TI_C[:100, :100].T, origin="lower", cmap="terrain")
axes[0].set_title("Continuous TI |Y| (crop)")
axes[1].imshow(rc[0].T, origin="lower", cmap="terrain", vmin=TI_C.min(), vmax=TI_C.max())
axes[1].set_title("Direct Sampling realization")
axes[2].hist(TI_C.ravel(), bins=40, density=True, alpha=0.5, label="TI")
axes[2].hist(rc.ravel(), bins=40, density=True, histtype="step", lw=2, label="realizations")
axes[2].set_title("Histogram")
axes[2].legend()
axes[3].plot(np.arange(1, 41), axis_variogram(TI_C, 0), "k--", lw=2, label="TI")
axes[3].plot(np.arange(1, 41), np.mean([axis_variogram(rc[i], 0) for i in range(5)], 0), "tab:green", label="realizations")
axes[3].set_xlabel("lag (cells)")
axes[3].set_title("Variogram along x")
axes[3].legend()
for ax in axes[:2]:
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
g1_ti, g1_r = axis_variogram(TI_C, 0)[0], np.mean([axis_variogram(rc[i], 0)[0] for i in range(5)])
print(f"TI mean {TI_C.mean():.3f}, sd {TI_C.std():.3f};  realizations mean {rc.mean():.3f}, sd {rc.std():.3f};  "
      f"lag-1 variogram ratio realization/TI {g1_r / g1_ti:.2f}")


continuous DS: 5 realizations in 9.9 s; kind = continuous









TI mean 0.932, sd 0.681;  realizations mean 0.957, sd 0.691;  lag-1 variogram ratio realization/TI 1.08


Direct Sampling reproduces the continuous TI’s histogram: mean 0.96 against 0.93, standard deviation 0.69 against 0.68. It also reproduces its spatial pattern: the narrow valleys at \(|Y| \approx 0\) between rounded highs, which a Gaussian simulator with the same variogram would not produce, since \(|Y|\) is not Gaussian. The realizations are slightly rougher than the TI at the finest lag (lag-1 variogram 1.08× the TI’s), the known Direct Sampling behaviour for continuous variables. A lower threshold or more n_postprocess passes reduce it. Continuous Direct Sampling took about 2 s per realization here.

title: Multiple-Point Statistics Simulation (DirectSampling, SNESIM)
section: Real Data: the Jura Geology Map as a Training Image
text:
Real Data: the Jura Geology Map as a Training Image
Real studies rarely have a perfect TI. Here the northern half of the Jura geology map (north of 3.0 km) is the training image, and the southern half is simulated from the Jura samples that fall in it. The true southern map is then the reference. The geology map has five units on a 50 m lattice. Its stratigraphic contacts were analysed in the PGS notebook: formations touch only their stratigraphic neighbours, with essentially no Argovian-Kimmeridgian contacts. Cells outside the study area are NaN in the TI and are ignored by both simulators.


Code
DATA = "../../../../Data/00_shared/data_geostatistics/"
jgrid = pd.read_csv(DATA + "jura_grid.csv", index_col=0)
jdata = pd.read_csv(DATA + "jura_data.csv", index_col=0)
NAMES = {1: "Argovian", 2: "Kimmeridgian", 3: "Sequanian", 4: "Portlandian", 5: "Quaternary"}
CODE = {v: k for k, v in NAMES.items()}
JG = jgrid[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
jx = np.rint((JG[:, 0] - JG[:, 0].min()) / 0.05).astype(int)
jy = np.rint((JG[:, 1] - JG[:, 1].min()) / 0.05).astype(int)
jvals = jgrid["Rock"].map(CODE).to_numpy(float)
jimg = np.full((jx.max() + 1, jy.max() + 1), np.nan)
jimg[jx, jy] = jvals
CUT = 58
y_cut = JG[:, 1].min() + CUT * 0.05
TI_J = jimg[:, CUT:]                                   # northern half (NaN outside the study area)
south = jy < CUT
SG, s_truth = JG[south], jvals[south]
s_data = jdata[jdata.Yloc < y_cut - 0.025].copy()
props = lambda v: {NAMES[k]: round(float(np.mean(v == k)), 3) for k in NAMES}
print(f"TI: {np.isfinite(TI_J).sum()} valid cells; south: {south.sum()} nodes, {len(s_data)} samples")
print("TI (north) proportions :", props(TI_J[np.isfinite(TI_J)]))
print("true south proportions :", props(s_truth))
print("south samples          :", props(s_data.Rock.to_numpy()))


def jura_contacts(values):
    im = np.full((jimg.shape[0], CUT), np.nan)
    im[jx[south], jy[south]] = values
    M = np.zeros((6, 6))
    for a, b in [(im[1:, :], im[:-1, :]), (im[:, 1:], im[:, :-1])]:
        ok = np.isfinite(a) & np.isfinite(b) & (a != b)
        np.add.at(M, (a[ok].astype(int), b[ok].astype(int)), 1)
    return M + M.T


def fit_ind(ind, xy_):
    d = pdist(xy_)
    E = np.linspace(0, 2, 17)
    hc = np.array([d[(d > a) & (d <= b)].mean() for a, b in zip(E[:-1], E[1:])])
    p_ = ind.mean()
    s_ = p_ * (1 - p_)
    g_ = 0.5 * pdist(ind[:, None], "sqeuclidean")
    e_ = np.array([g_[(d > a) & (d <= b)].mean() for a, b in zip(E[:-1], E[1:])])
    f = lambda h, nr, a: nr * s_ + (s_ - nr * s_) * (1.5 * np.minimum(h / a, 1) - 0.5 * np.minimum(h / a, 1) ** 3)
    (nr, a), _ = curve_fit(f, hc, e_, p0=[0.2, 1.0], bounds=([0, 0.1], [0.95, 4]))
    return [0.0, round(nr * s_, 4), round(a, 3), round(a, 3), round(s_, 4), "spherical"]


sxy = s_data[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
jura_sims = {
    "SIS": IndicatorCoSimulator(list(NAMES), {k: fit_ind((s_data.Rock == k).to_numpy(float), sxy) for k in NAMES},
                                num_points=16, radius=1.5, use_gpu=USE_GPU),
    "SNESIM servo=0": SNESIM(TI_J, servo=0.0, use_gpu=USE_GPU),
    "SNESIM servo=0.5": SNESIM(TI_J, servo=0.5, use_gpu=USE_GPU),
    "Direct Sampling": DirectSampling(TI_J, use_gpu=USE_GPU),
}
M_true = jura_contacts(s_truth)
rows, jura_reals = [], {}
for name, sim in jura_sims.items():
    r = sim.fit(SG, s_data, "Xloc", "Yloc", "Rock").simulate(nsim=N_SIM, seed=1)
    jura_reals[name] = r
    Ms = [jura_contacts(r[i]) for i in range(5)]
    mode = np.array([np.bincount(r[:, j].astype(int), minlength=6).argmax() for j in range(r.shape[1])])
    rows.append({"method": name, "agreement per realization": np.mean(r == s_truth[None, :]),
                 "agreement, most probable": np.mean(mode == s_truth),
                 "contact edges": np.mean([M.sum() / 2 for M in Ms]),
                 "Argovian-Kimmeridgian edges": np.mean([M[1, 2] for M in Ms]),
                 **{f"prop. {NAMES[k]}": np.mean(r == k) for k in NAMES}})
rows.append({"method": "true south map", "contact edges": M_true.sum() / 2, "Argovian-Kimmeridgian edges": M_true[1, 2],
             **{f"prop. {NAMES[k]}": np.mean(s_truth == k) for k in NAMES}})
jura_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("method")
display(jura_table.round(3))

The TI is not representative. The northern half has 29% Argovian and 26% Kimmeridgian; the true southern half has 15% and 39%. A real TI is rarely a perfect analogue, and this one also covers only 2,105 cells.
SNESIM with servo = 0 does best overall: 64% agreement per realization and 72% for the most probable unit. It has the most realistic boundary length (1,095 contact edges against the true 1,042), and its proportions follow the southern samples rather than the TI. It still produces about 29 Argovian-Kimmeridgian edges per realization, where the true south has none. Its small TI has few replicates of large data events, so they are reduced, and constraints are lost.
SNESIM with the default servo = 0.5 is close behind on agreement (63% per realization, 73% for the most probable unit), but it pulls the proportions toward the northern TI (Argovian 0.16 and Quaternary 0.14, against the true 0.15 and 0.11; Kimmeridgian 0.41). The boundaries are longer (1,192 contact edges, 35 Argovian-Kimmeridgian). Because only categories the TI allows are corrected, the servosystem itself creates no impossible patterns; an unmasked correction gave 337 Argovian-Kimmeridgian edges and twice the true boundary length here.
Direct Sampling produces large, smooth patches (774 edges). It spreads Kimmeridgian over 61% of the area against the true 39%, and Sequanian and Portlandian shrink.
SIS is competitive on cell agreement (62% and 70%), but it scatters units (71 Argovian-Kimmeridgian edges), as in the PGS notebook.

The lessons for real studies:

Check that the TI is representative (proportions, unit sizes, stationarity) before simulating.
Do not force a non-representative TI’s proportions with the servosystem; use the target area’s proportions (target_proportions) or servo = 0.
Compare several simulators on held-out information.

Here the conditioning data were dense (217 samples), so they partly compensated for the TI’s bias.

text:
CPU vs GPU Timing
Conditional simulation of the 100 × 100 channel field, for several nsim, on the CPU and the GPU. SNESIM’s GPU engine gives the same realizations as the CPU engine, which is checked. Direct Sampling’s GPU realizations are statistically equivalent rather than identical, so their channel proportion is compared instead.


Code
rows = []
for name, make in [("SNESIM", lambda g: SNESIM(TI, servo=0.0, use_gpu=g)),
                   ("Direct Sampling", lambda g: DirectSampling(TI, use_gpu=g))]:
    for nsim in [1, 8, 32]:
        row = {"method": name, "nsim": nsim}
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        out_cpu = make(False).fit(grid, wells, "X", "Y", "facies").simulate(nsim=nsim, seed=6)
        row["CPU (s)"] = time.perf_counter() - t0
        if USE_GPU:
            sim_g = make(True).fit(grid, wells, "X", "Y", "facies")
            sim_g.simulate(nsim=1, seed=0)                 # warm-up
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            out_gpu = sim_g.simulate(nsim=nsim, seed=6)
            cp.cuda.Device(0).synchronize()
            row["GPU (s)"] = time.perf_counter() - t0
            row["speedup"] = row["CPU (s)"] / row["GPU (s)"]
            row["identical"] = bool(np.array_equal(out_cpu, out_gpu))
            row["channel prop. CPU / GPU"] = f"{out_cpu.mean():.3f} / {out_gpu.mean():.3f}"
        rows.append(row)
timing = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["method", "nsim"])
display(timing.round(2))
if USE_GPU:
    record("SNESIM GPU = CPU realizations", "PASS" if timing.loc["SNESIM", "identical"].all() else "FAIL")

Two-point statistics cannot describe channels. SIS, given the TI’s own variogram, produced disconnected blobs (connectivity 0 at 30 cells), while SNESIM and Direct Sampling reproduced the sinuous, connected channels of the training image (connectivity about 0.7, pattern-histogram distance 0.06-0.08 against 0.23 for SIS).
SNESIM needs its multigrid for long structures (connectivity 0.002 with one level, 0.66 with four). Its servosystem controls proportions; because it corrects only categories the TI allows, it keeps the TI’s adjacency rules (0.6 forbidden contacts per realization with the default servo = 0.5, from data-event reduction, against 389 for an unmasked correction).
Direct Sampling needs no pattern database and handles continuous variables (TI histogram and patterns reproduced, slightly rougher at the finest lag). threshold and n_neighbors trade fidelity against speed; too large a threshold collapses the simulation.
Conditioning to 60 wells was exact for all methods. MPS gave far better pattern and connectivity reproduction than SIS but only modestly better local probabilities. A secondary variable made the difference: Direct Sampling with a secondary TI recovered 77% of the channel cells, with the true connectivity (Brier 0.148 → 0.058); SNESIM with tau-model soft data improved less (0.093).
Real data: with half of the Jura geology map as the TI, SNESIM (servo = 0) gave the best agreement per realization and boundary length, but the TI’s different proportions and small size showed. The default servosystem pulled the proportions toward the non-representative TI. Representative training images are the crux of MPS.
GPU: SNESIM’s GPU engine is identical to the CPU and 88× faster at 32 realizations; Direct Sampling’s is statistically equivalent and 11× faster.

title: Bayesian kriging
text:
Types of Bayesian kriging

Conjugate Bayesian kriging (known correlation)
If the correlation function is fixed and only β and σ² are unknown, a normal-inverse-gamma prior is conjugate. The predictive distribution is then a Student-t with a closed form (Kitanidis, 1986; Handcock & Stein, 1993). The mean looks like universal kriging, and the variance is inflated to account for the uncertain trend and sill. It is fast and exact, but leaves the range and nugget fixed, which is where most of the uncertainty usually sits.
GeoLattice: ConjugateBayesianKriging, or BayesianKriging.from_variogram when the fixed correlation comes from a fitted variogram. Tutorial: conjugate Bayesian kriging.


Bayesian kriging with a discrete posterior (model-based geostatistics)
Here the range and the relative nugget get priors as well. GeoLattice puts them on a finite grid and, at every grid point, integrates β and σ² out in closed form (Kitanidis, 1986; Handcock & Stein, 1993; Diggle & Ribeiro, 2007, the krige.bayes approach in geoR). The predictive distribution is a finite mixture of Student-t distributions, so the mean, variance, quantiles and exceedance probabilities are exact. Every prediction then reflects uncertainty in the range and nugget too. The price is one covariance factorization per grid point, which suits a few thousand observations.
GeoLattice: BayesianKriging, and the one-call wrapper bayesian_kriging. Tutorials: Bayesian kriging and the one-call function.


Bayesian transformed Gaussian kriging
Many variables are skewed: concentrations, rainfall, grades. De Oliveira, Kedem & Short (1997) put a prior on the Box-Cox transformation parameter as well, so the choice of transformation is part of the uncertainty rather than a decision made beforehand. Back-transformed predictions come from posterior draws on the data scale, which carries the median, the mean, the quantiles and the exceedance probabilities in one set of samples.
GeoLattice: BayesianTransformedKriging. Tutorial: Bayesian transformed kriging.


Bayesian generalized kriging (spatial GLMMs)
For counts, presence/absence or proportions, the Gaussian field sits inside a generalized linear model. A Poisson count has a log mean equal to a trend plus a Gaussian random field; a binomial observation uses a logit link. The posterior has no closed form, so GeoLattice samples it by MCMC (Diggle, Tawn & Moyeed, 1998; Christensen, 2004). Disease mapping and species distribution models are typical uses.
GeoLattice: BayesianGLMKriging, families "poisson" and "binomial". Tutorial: Bayesian GLM kriging.


Empirical Bayesian kriging (EBK)
EBK (Krivoruchko, 2012) accounts for variogram uncertainty without a prior and without MCMC. GeoLattice implements the global form. It fits one variogram to the data, simulates new values at the same locations, refits a variogram to each simulation, and weights those variograms by how well each one leave-one-out predicts its own simulation. Predictions are a weighted mixture of ordinary or simple kriging over that ensemble. The prediction variance splits into the usual kriging variance and a between-variogram term, which is the variogram uncertainty plug-in kriging leaves out. The predictive distribution is a mixture of Gaussians, so exceedance probabilities are available directly.
GeoLattice: EmpiricalBayesianKriging in geolattice.geostatistics.kriging.ebk. Tutorial: empirical Bayesian kriging.


The correlation function
Every class above builds its covariance from a correlation ρ(h) = 1 − γ(h), with γ a unit-sill, zero-nugget variogram. correlation_function evaluates that correlation for the six models GeoLattice supports. The Bayesian classes call it internally; it is also the right tool for building a covariance matrix or for comparing models before a fit.
GeoLattice: correlation_function. Tutorial: correlation functions.

title: Bayesian kriging
text:
Bayesian kriging in GeoLattice
The classes share a fit-then-predict pattern. Coordinates are arrays of shape (n, 2), used as given. For geometric anisotropy, transform them first with geolattice.geostatistics.transform_aniso. Continuous-data models write
\[
Z(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})^\top\boldsymbol\beta + S(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon(\mathbf{x}),
\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(Z) = \sigma^2\bigl(\mathbf{R}(\phi) + \tau\mathbf{I}\bigr),
\]
where \(\mathbf{R}(\phi)\) is the correlation matrix from correlation_function, \(\phi\) is the range in the Variogram convention of the chosen model, and \(\tau\) is the nugget relative to the partial sill. The trend \(\mathbf{f}\) is a polynomial in the coordinates (trend 0 constant, 1 linear, 2 quadratic) plus optional covariates.

correlation_function
from geolattice.geostatistics import correlation_function

rho = correlation_function(h, model="exponential", range_=1.0, nu=1.5, alpha=1.0)
rho is ρ(h), with ρ(0) = 1. model is "spherical", "exponential", "gaussian", "matern", "cubic" or "stable". range_ follows the Variogram convention of that model, so a fitted variogram’s range can be passed straight through. nu is the Matérn smoothness (default 1.5; ν = 0.5 is the exponential). alpha is the stable exponent in (0, 2] (1 is exponential, 2 is Gaussian). In the Bayesian classes the same number is passed as nu for both the Matérn smoothness and the stable exponent.


EmpiricalBayesianKriging
Module geolattice.geostatistics.kriging.ebk. An ensemble of ordinary or simple kriging models. Each member kriges the real data with its own refitted variogram. predict returns the weighted mean. predict_proba evaluates the mixture of Gaussians at one or more cutoffs.
from geolattice.geostatistics import EmpiricalBayesianKriging

ebk = EmpiricalBayesianKriging(
    model="spherical",
    kriging_type="ordinary",   # or "simple"
    n_realizations=100,
    use_gpu="auto",
).fit(coords, values)
z_hat, se = ebk.predict(grid, return_variance=True)
prob = ebk.predict_proba(grid, cutoffs=[0.8])
After fit, base_variogram_ is the variogram of the real data (used only to drive the simulations), variograms_ holds the refits, weights_ the inverse leave-one-out MSE weights, and krige_models_ the kriging models that predict actually uses. With return_variance=True, predict returns that standard error as the square root of two variances: the weighted kriging variance of the ensemble members, and the weighted variance of their means. Pass variogram_kwargs (for example n_lags, estimator, maxlag) through to every Variogram fit. The simulate-and-refit loop runs on CPU; use_gpu applies when the ensemble predicts. predict_proba returns a dictionary, one probability array per cutoff.


ConjugateBayesianKriging
Fixed range and relative nugget. Unknown trend and variance, with a conjugate normal-inverse-gamma prior and a Student-t predictive.
from geolattice.geostatistics import BayesianKriging, ConjugateBayesianKriging

ck = ConjugateBayesianKriging(
    "spherical", range_=1.2, nugget_ratio=0.2, trend=0,
).fit(coords, values)

# the same model, built from a fitted Variogram
ck = BayesianKriging.from_variogram(variogram, trend=0).fit(coords, values)

mean, sd = ck.predict(grid, return_std=True, signal=True)
beta_prior is "flat" or ("normal", mean, cov), with cov scaled by σ². sigma2_prior is "reciprocal" or ("scaled_inv_chi2", df, scale2). signal=True predicts the noise-free process. signal=False predicts a new observation, nugget included, which is the right target for a held-out sample. predict_quantiles, predict_proba and predictive_samples (with joint=True for a joint draw) use the same Student-t.


BayesianKriging
The range and the relative nugget sit on discrete grids. For every pair the conjugate prior integrates β and σ² out, and the marginal likelihood supplies the posterior weight. The predictive distribution is the corresponding mixture of Student-t distributions.
bk = BayesianKriging(
    model="exponential",
    trend=0,
    range_grid=None,                  # default: 30 values, log-spaced from 2% to 100% of the largest distance
    nugget_grid=(0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0),
    range_prior="uniform",            # or "reciprocal", "squared_reciprocal", or an array of weights
    nugget_prior="uniform",
    beta_prior="flat",
    sigma2_prior="reciprocal",
).fit(coords, values, covariates=None)

mean, sd = bk.predict(grid, return_std=True, signal=True)
quantiles = bk.predict_quantiles(grid, quantiles=(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
exceedance = bk.predict_proba(grid, threshold=0.8)
draws = bk.sample_parameters(n=1000)
posterior_ is a table with one row per grid point: range, nugget_ratio, log_prior, log_marginal, weight, dof, sigma2_mean, and one beta_* column per trend coefficient. nu is the Matérn smoothness or the stable exponent, depending on model.


BayesianTransformedKriging
BayesianKriging with a Box-Cox parameter λ on the same grid. The data must be strictly positive. The transform is the geometric-mean normalised Box-Cox, so marginal likelihoods are comparable across λ. Predictions are Monte Carlo draws, inverted back to the original units.
from geolattice.geostatistics import BayesianTransformedKriging

bt = BayesianTransformedKriging(
    "exponential",
    lambda_grid=(-0.5, -0.25, 0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0),
    lambda_prior="uniform",
).fit(coords, values)

table = bt.predict(grid, n_samples=2000)   # columns: mean, median, sd, q05, q95
lambda_posterior_ collects the posterior weight of each λ. predict_quantiles and predict_proba summarise the same back-transformed draws. For λ < 0 some draws fall outside the Box-Cox domain and are infinite, so the predictive mean need not exist; the median and the quantiles remain the summaries to report. posterior_ gains a lambda column.


BayesianGLMKriging
A spatial generalized linear mixed model, sampled by MCMC.

"poisson": \(y_i \mid \eta_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(E_i e^{\eta_i})\), with exposure or expected count \(E_i\).
"binomial": \(y_i \mid \eta_i \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_i, \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\eta_i))\), with \(n_i\) trials.

The linear predictor is a trend plus a latent Gaussian field. The sampler whitens that field and updates it with MALA, updates β and log σ² by random-walk Metropolis, and moves the range on a discrete grid. With interweave=True (the default) each iteration also updates β, σ² and the range in the centred parametrization with the linear predictor held fixed, which mixes the intercept, the variance and the range.
from geolattice.geostatistics import BayesianGLMKriging

glm = BayesianGLMKriging(
    family="poisson",          # or "binomial"
    model="exponential",
    trend=0,
    nugget_ratio=0.0,
    sigma2_prior=(1.0, 0.5),   # scaled-inv-chi2 (df, scale2)
    beta_prior_sd=10.0,
    interweave=True,
).fit(coords, counts, trials_or_exposure=expected, n_iter=6000, burn=2000, thin=4)

table = glm.predict(grid, scale="response")   # mean, sd, median, q05, q95
rate_exceeds = glm.predict_proba(grid, threshold=1.0, scale="response")
trials_or_exposure is the expected count or exposure for Poisson (default 1) and the number of trials for binomial (default 1). scale="link" returns the linear predictor; "response" returns the rate or the probability. trace_ holds the kept draws of β, σ², range and log-likelihood. acceptance_ holds the acceptance rates after burn-in.


bayesian_kriging
One call to BayesianKriging: fit, then a table of the posterior predictive mean, standard deviation and quantiles.
from geolattice.geostatistics import bayesian_kriging

table = bayesian_kriging(coords, values, grid, model="exponential", trend=0)
# columns: mean, sd, q05, q50, q95

table, model = bayesian_kriging(
    coords, values, grid,
    model="matern", nu=1.5,
    quantiles=(0.05, 0.5, 0.95),
    signal=True,
    return_model=True,
    range_grid=None,
    nugget_grid=(0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0),
)
signal=False predicts a new observation, including the nugget. return_model=True also returns the fitted BayesianKriging, so posterior_, predict_proba and sample_parameters stay available. Keyword arguments are the BayesianKriging arguments (range_grid, nugget_grid, range_prior, nugget_prior, beta_prior, sigma2_prior, nu). Covariates go in covariates at the data and covariates_pred at the prediction locations.

text:
Overview
Ordinary kriging works in two steps: estimate the variogram, then krige as if that variogram were exact. The kriging variance therefore covers only the interpolation error. It ignores how uncertain the fitted nugget, sill and range are, so it understates the total uncertainty, more so with few data or a poorly determined range.
Bayesian kriging treats the trend coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\), the variance \(\sigma^2\), the range \(\phi\) and the relative nugget \(\tau\) as unknowns with prior distributions. It predicts with the posterior predictive distribution, which averages kriging over every parameter value in proportion to how well it explains the data. GeoLattice follows the approach of geoR’s krige.bayes (Diggle & Ribeiro, 2007). The range and nugget take values on a discrete grid; for each grid point the trend and variance are integrated out exactly with a conjugate prior. The predictive distribution is then a finite mixture of Student-t distributions, so its mean, variance, quantiles and exceedance probabilities are all exact.







Object
Model




ConjugateBayesianKriging
fixed range and nugget; unknown trend and variance (Student-t predictive)


BayesianKriging
discrete priors on range and relative nugget; conjugate trend and variance


BayesianTransformedKriging
adds a Box-Cox parameter \(\lambda\) for skewed positive data


BayesianGLMKriging
Poisson or binomial data, sampled by MCMC


bayesian_kriging
one call: fit BayesianKriging, return a prediction table



On the Jura cadmium data, with the same 70/30 split as the EBK notebook, the notebook:

shows that conjugate Bayesian kriging is ordinary kriging with wider, Student-t intervals;
computes the grid posterior of range and nugget, its sensitivity to the prior, and model choice by marginal likelihood;
validates the predictive intervals at the held-out sites, against plug-in kriging and EBK;
adds the rock type as a covariate;
maps predictions and exceedance probabilities, and uses joint simulation to get the uncertainty of the contaminated area;
fits a Box-Cox transformed model to raw cadmium, and a binomial model to the guide-value exceedances.

title: Bayesian Kriging (BayesianKriging)
text:
Theory

The model
For \(n\) observations \(\mathbf{z} = (z(\mathbf{x}_1), \dots, z(\mathbf{x}_n))^\top\),
\[
\mathbf{z} \mid \boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2, \phi, \tau \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\mathbf{F}\boldsymbol\beta,\; \sigma^2 \mathbf{V}\bigr),
\qquad
\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{R}(\phi) + \tau \mathbf{I},
\]
where:

\(\mathbf{F}\) is the \(n \times p\) trend matrix: a constant (trend=0), linear (1) or quadratic (2) polynomial in the coordinates, plus optional covariates;
\(\mathbf{R}(\phi)_{ij} = \rho(\lVert\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\rVert; \phi)\) is the correlation matrix of the chosen model, with \(\rho(h) = 1 - \gamma(h)\) for a unit-sill, zero-nugget variogram (correlation_function);
\(\sigma^2\) is the partial sill, and \(\tau = \text{nugget}/\sigma^2\) the relative nugget.



Priors

Trend: flat, \(p(\boldsymbol\beta) \propto 1\) (beta_prior="flat"), or normal, \(\boldsymbol\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{V}_\beta)\) (("normal", m, Vb)).
Variance: reciprocal, \(p(\sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2\) ("reciprocal"), or scaled inverse-\(\chi^2\), \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{Scale-inv-}\chi^2(n_0, s_0^2)\) (("scaled_inv_chi2", n0, s0sq)).
Range and relative nugget: discrete priors on range_grid and nugget_grid: "uniform", "reciprocal" (\(\propto 1/\phi\)), "squared_reciprocal", or any weights.



The conjugate posterior for a fixed correlation
With \(\phi\) and \(\tau\) fixed, write \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{F}\). Under the flat and reciprocal priors, the posterior of the trend is centred at the GLS estimate and the variance has a scaled inverse-\(\chi^2\) posterior (Kitanidis, 1986):
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{z},
\qquad
S^2 = \frac{(\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{F}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top \mathbf{V}^{-1} (\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{F}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n - p},
\]
\[
\sigma^2 \mid \mathbf{z} \sim \text{Scale-inv-}\chi^2(n - p,\, S^2),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\beta \mid \sigma^2, \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta},\, \sigma^2 \mathbf{A}^{-1}).
\]
At a new location \(\mathbf{x}_0\), with \(\mathbf{r}_0\) the correlations to the data and \(\mathbf{f}_0\) its trend row, integrating out \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\) gives a Student-t predictive with \(n - p\) degrees of freedom:
\[
z(\mathbf{x}_0) \mid \mathbf{z} \;\sim\; t_{n-p}\!\Bigl(\mathbf{f}_0^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} + \mathbf{r}_0^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{F}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}),\;\; S^2\bigl[v_{00} - \mathbf{r}_0^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{g}^\top\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{g}\bigr]\Bigr),
\qquad \mathbf{g} = \mathbf{f}_0 - \mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}_0 .
\]
Here \(v_{00} = 1\) for the signal and \(1 + \tau\) for a new observation.

The location is the universal kriging predictor: ordinary kriging when trend=0.
The bracket is the universal kriging variance in correlation units. So the conjugate Bayesian predictor is kriging with the sill replaced by its estimate \(S^2\), and the Gaussian replaced by a heavier-tailed Student-t.

With the normal and scaled inverse-\(\chi^2\) priors, the same holds with updated quantities:
\[
\mathbf{V}_\beta^* = (\mathbf{V}_\beta^{-1} + \mathbf{A})^{-1}, \qquad \boldsymbol\beta^* = \mathbf{V}_\beta^*(\mathbf{V}_\beta^{-1}\mathbf{m} + \mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{z}),
\]
and the degrees of freedom \(n_0 + n\).


The marginal likelihood of the correlation parameters
Integrating \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\) out of the likelihood leaves the marginal likelihood of \((\phi, \tau)\). Under the flat and reciprocal priors (the restricted likelihood),
\[
p(\mathbf{z} \mid \phi, \tau) \;\propto\; |\mathbf{V}|^{-1/2}\, |\mathbf{A}|^{-1/2}\, \bigl[(n - p)\,S^2\bigr]^{-(n-p)/2}.
\]
With proper priors, \(\mathbf{z}\) is marginally multivariate Student-t, with scale matrix \(s_0^2(\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{F}\mathbf{V}_\beta\mathbf{F}^\top)\) and \(n_0\) degrees of freedom.


The grid posterior and the predictive mixture
The posterior weight of grid point \(k = (\phi_k, \tau_k)\) is
\[
w_k \;\propto\; p(\phi_k)\, p(\tau_k)\, p(\mathbf{z} \mid \phi_k, \tau_k),
\]
reported in posterior_. The predictive is the mixture
\[
p\bigl(z(\mathbf{x}_0) \mid \mathbf{z}\bigr) = \sum_k w_k\; t_{\nu_k}\bigl(z(\mathbf{x}_0);\, \mu_k, s_k^2\bigr),
\]
and everything follows from it exactly:

the mean \(\sum_k w_k \mu_k\);
the variance \(\sum_k w_k \bigl[s_k^2 \nu_k/(\nu_k - 2) + \mu_k^2\bigr] - \text{mean}^2\), by the law of total variance, with a within-model term and a between-model term;
quantiles, by inverting the mixture cdf (predict_quantiles);
exceedance probabilities \(\sum_k w_k\, P(t_{\nu_k} > \cdot)\) (predict_proba).



Signal or observation, and joint simulation

Signal or observation. With a nugget, signal=True (the default) predicts the noise-free process \(\mathbf{f}^\top\boldsymbol\beta + S(\mathbf{x})\), while signal=False predicts a new measurement, which adds the nugget variance. Validation against held-out measurements uses signal=False.
Joint simulation. predictive_samples(..., joint=True) draws whole fields. For each draw it picks a grid point \(k\) with probability \(w_k\), then \(\sigma^2\), then \(\boldsymbol\beta\), then a conditional Gaussian field over the prediction points with their full covariance. Joint draws are needed for any quantity that combines several locations, such as an area above a threshold or a block mean.



Transformed Gaussian kriging
For positive, skewed data, BayesianTransformedKriging adds a Box-Cox parameter \(\lambda\) to the grid (De Oliveira, Kedem & Short, 1997). It uses the geometric-mean normalised transform
\[
w = \frac{z^\lambda - 1}{\lambda\, \dot z^{\lambda - 1}} \quad (\lambda \ne 0), \qquad w = \dot z \log z \quad (\lambda = 0),
\]
with \(\dot z\) the geometric mean of the data. Its Jacobian is 1, so the marginal likelihoods of different \(\lambda\) can be compared directly, and lambda_posterior_ gives the posterior of \(\lambda\). Predictions are posterior predictive draws back-transformed to the data scale. This avoids the bias corrections that lognormal kriging needs.


Generalized linear kriging by MCMC
For counts or binary data, BayesianGLMKriging fits a spatial generalized linear mixed model (Diggle, Tawn & Moyeed, 1998):
\[
y_i \mid S \sim \text{Poisson}\bigl(E_i e^{\eta_i}\bigr) \;\text{or}\; \text{Binomial}\bigl(n_i, \text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_i)\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\eta = \mathbf{F}\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf{S},
\qquad
\mathbf{S} \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{R}(\phi) + \tau\mathbf{I})\bigr).
\]
Nothing integrates analytically, so the posterior is sampled by MCMC (Christensen, 2004). The latent field is whitened, \(\mathbf{S} = \sigma\mathbf{L}(\phi)\boldsymbol\Gamma\) with \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top = \mathbf{R} + \tau\mathbf{I}\) and \(\boldsymbol\Gamma \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\), which decorrelates it. \(\boldsymbol\Gamma\) is updated by the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA), which proposes
\[
\boldsymbol\Gamma' = \boldsymbol\Gamma + \tfrac{h}{2}\nabla \log p(\boldsymbol\Gamma \mid \cdot) + \sqrt{h}\,\boldsymbol\epsilon,
\qquad
\nabla \log p = \sigma\mathbf{L}^\top(\mathbf{y} - E[\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol\eta]) - \boldsymbol\Gamma,
\]
with the step size \(h\) adapted during burn-in toward 57% acceptance. The other updates:

\(\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(\log\sigma^2\) by random-walk Metropolis;
the range by moves to neighbouring values of its grid.

Predictions krige the latent field for each kept sample and transform to the rate or probability.


Relation to plug-in kriging and EBK

Plug-in kriging uses a single parameter value and a Gaussian.
Conjugate Bayesian kriging keeps the range and nugget fixed but accounts for the trend and sill.
BayesianKriging also accounts for the range and nugget, through their posterior.
EBK approximates the same averaging without priors: it simulates from one fitted variogram, refits, and weights the refits by cross-validation.

All of them give similar point predictions. They differ in how wide, and how honest, the intervals are, and Section 7 measures that.

title: Bayesian Kriging (BayesianKriging)
text:
Python Setup
BayesianKriging and its relatives run on the CPU with NumPy and SciPy. The cost is one Cholesky factorization of the \(n \times n\) correlation matrix per grid point, which is fine for a few thousand data points. Plug-in OrdinaryKriging and EmpiricalBayesianKriging are used for comparison.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 4 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics and geostatistics): pip install "geolattice[geostats]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
%matplotlib inline
import time
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedShuffleSplit

import geolattice.geostatistics as pygstat
from geolattice.geostatistics import (
    BayesianGLMKriging,
    BayesianKriging,
    BayesianTransformedKriging,
    ConjugateBayesianKriging,
    EmpiricalBayesianKriging,
    OrdinaryKriging,
    Variogram,
    bayesian_kriging,
    correlation_function,
)

title: Bayesian Kriging (BayesianKriging)
text:
Jura Cadmium Data
The Jura data (Atteia et al., 1994; Goovaerts, 1997) are 359 topsoil samples from a 14.5 km² area of the Swiss Jura. Coordinates are in kilometres. Cadmium is skewed, so it is modelled as \(\log(\text{Cd})\). The split is the same 70/30 stratified split by land use as in the EBK notebook (StratifiedShuffleSplit, random_state=42). Maps use every second row and column of jura_grid.csv (100 m).


Code
DATA = "../../../../Data/00_shared/data_geostatistics/"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "jura_data.csv", index_col=0)
grid_df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "jura_grid.csv", index_col=0)
g50 = grid_df[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
i50 = np.rint((g50[:, 0] - g50[:, 0].min()) / 0.05).astype(int)
j50 = np.rint((g50[:, 1] - g50[:, 1].min()) / 0.05).astype(int)
keep = (i50 % 2 == 0) & (j50 % 2 == 0)
grid_df = grid_df[keep].reset_index(drop=True)
grid = grid_df[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)

sss = StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.30, random_state=42)
tr, te = next(sss.split(df, df["Landuse"]))
train, test = df.iloc[tr].reset_index(drop=True), df.iloc[te].reset_index(drop=True)
xy, xy_test = train[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float), test[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
z, z_test = np.log(train["Cd"].to_numpy(float)), np.log(test["Cd"].to_numpy(float))
print(f"train {len(train)}, test {len(test)}, map nodes {len(grid)}")
print(f"log(Cd): mean {z.mean():.3f}, sd {z.std():.3f};  raw Cd skewness {df.Cd.skew():.2f}")

gj = np.rint((grid[:, 1] - grid[:, 1].min()) / CELL).astype(int)
EXTENT = [grid[:, 0].min() - CELL / 2, grid[:, 0].max() + CELL / 2, grid[:, 1].min() - CELL / 2,
          grid[:, 1].max() + CELL / 2]


def show_map(ax, values, title, cmap="YlOrRd", vmin=None, vmax=None, label="", points=True):
    img = np.full((gj.max() + 1, gi.max() + 1), np.nan)
    img[gj, gi] = values
    im = ax.imshow(img, origin="lower", extent=EXTENT, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, interpolation="nearest")
    if points:
        ax.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], s=5, facecolors="none", edgecolors="k", linewidths=0.4)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlabel("X (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Y (km)")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label=label, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)

title: Bayesian Kriging (BayesianKriging)
section: Plug-in Kriging vs Conjugate Bayesian Kriging
text:
Plug-in Kriging vs Conjugate Bayesian Kriging
A spherical variogram is fitted to log(Cd), as in the EBK notebook. BayesianKriging.from_variogram turns it into a ConjugateBayesianKriging with the same range and nugget ratio. According to Section 2.3:

the predictive location equals the ordinary kriging prediction;
the predictive scale is the kriging variance with the sill replaced by its posterior estimate \(S^2\);
the distribution is Student-t with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom.



Code
vg = Variogram(xy, z, model="spherical", n_lags=15, estimator="matheron", use_gpu=False).fit()
nug, psill, rng_ = vg.fitted_params[:3]
print(f"spherical variogram: nugget {nug:.3f}, partial sill {psill:.3f}, range {rng_:.3f} km "
      f"(relative nugget {nug / psill:.2f})")
ok = OrdinaryKriging(vg, use_gpu=False).fit(xy, z)
ok_mean, ok_se = ok.predict(xy_test, return_variance=True)

cbk = BayesianKriging.from_variogram(vg).fit(xy, z)
c_mean, c_sd = cbk.predict(xy_test, return_std=True, signal=False)
comp = cbk._comps[0]
print(f"conjugate posterior: S^2 = {comp['s2']:.3f} (fitted partial sill {psill:.3f}), dof = {comp['dof']:.0f}")
record("conjugate Bayesian mean == ordinary kriging", "PASS" if np.allclose(c_mean, ok_mean, atol=1e-3) else "FAIL",
       f"max |diff| = {np.abs(c_mean - ok_mean).max():.1e}")
print(f"mean predictive sd: plug-in OK {ok_se.mean():.3f}, conjugate Bayesian {c_sd.mean():.3f}")


spherical variogram: nugget 0.245, partial sill 0.210, range 1.334 km (relative nugget 1.16)
conjugate posterior: S^2 = 0.213 (fitted partial sill 0.210), dof = 250
✅ [PASS] conjugate Bayesian mean == ordinary kriging  max |diff| = 9.5e-09
mean predictive sd: plug-in OK 0.559, conjugate Bayesian 0.565


The conjugate Bayesian predictive mean equals ordinary kriging to \(10^{-8}\), as the theory says. Its spread is only slightly wider (mean sd 0.565 against 0.559):

with 251 data, the Student-t with 250 degrees of freedom is practically Gaussian;
the posterior sill estimate \(S^2 = 0.213\) is almost the fitted partial sill (0.210).

Uncertainty about the trend and the sill matters little at this sample size. It matters with few data, where the degrees of freedom are small and the t tails heavy. The larger source of uncertainty is the range and the nugget, which the next section treats.

The likelihood disagrees with the fitted variogram. The weighted least-squares fit to the binned variogram gave a long range (1.33 km) with a large nugget (relative nugget 1.16). The likelihood prefers a short range (posterior median 0.19 km) with a moderate nugget (median 0.25). Binning over 15 lags averages away the short-range structure that the likelihood, which uses every pair of data, picks up.
The range posterior is skewed. Its 90% interval runs from 0.14 to 1.9 km, and the long tail toward the fitted range keeps the mean at 0.47 km. The data cannot rule out the long-range interpretation; they just favour the short one.
The variance components are better determined. The partial sill has a 90% interval of 0.20-0.42 and the absolute nugget 0.04-0.26 (log units squared).

The posterior variogram draws show this spread directly: many plausible variograms, most rising faster than the plug-in fit.


Prior sensitivity
The same fit with the reciprocal prior on the range (\(p(\phi) \propto 1/\phi\), uniform on the log scale) and with a squared reciprocal prior on the relative nugget, which favours small nuggets.


Code
rows = []
for label, kw in [("uniform / uniform", {}), ("reciprocal range", dict(range_prior="reciprocal")),
                  ("reciprocal range, 1/tau^2 nugget",
                   dict(range_prior="reciprocal", nugget_grid=NUGGET_GRID[1:], nugget_prior="squared_reciprocal"))]:
    m = BayesianKriging("spherical", range_grid=RANGE_GRID, nugget_grid=kw.pop("nugget_grid", NUGGET_GRID), **kw).fit(xy, z)
    p_ = m.posterior_
    mean, sd = m.predict(xy_test, return_std=True, signal=False)
    rows.append({"prior": label, "posterior mean range": (p_.weight * p_.range).sum(),
                 "posterior mean nugget ratio": (p_.weight * p_.nugget_ratio).sum(),
                 "test RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((mean - z_test) ** 2)), "mean predictive sd": sd.mean()})

The prior matters for the parameters. It shifts the posterior means: the range from 0.49 km (uniform prior) to 0.22 km (reciprocal) and 0.16 km (reciprocal plus a prior favouring small nuggets), and the nugget ratio from 0.46 to 0.18. The data weakly identify the long-range tail, so a prior that downweights large ranges removes it.
The prior hardly matters for predictions. Test RMSE moves by 0.02 and the mean predictive sd by 0.015. Predictions depend on the short-range behaviour, which the data determine well.

Report the priors with the results, and check this kind of sensitivity whenever the parameters themselves are of interest.

Choosing the correlation model
Under the same priors, the marginal likelihoods of different correlation models can be compared: their sum over the grid, weighted by the prior, is the model evidence, and the ratio of two evidences is a Bayes factor. The four main models are compared.


Code
from scipy.special import logsumexp

rows, models = [], {}
for model in ["spherical", "exponential", "gaussian", "matern"]:
    m = BayesianKriging(model, nu=1.0, range_grid=RANGE_GRID, nugget_grid=NUGGET_GRID).fit(xy, z)
    models[model] = m
    p_ = m.posterior_
    rows.append({"model": model, "log evidence": logsumexp(p_.log_marginal + p_.log_prior),
                 "posterior mean range": (p_.weight * p_.range).sum(),
                 "posterior mean nugget ratio": (p_.weight * p_.nugget_ratio).sum()})
ev = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model")
ev["relative log evidence"] = ev["log evidence"] - ev["log evidence"].max()
ev["posterior model probability"] = np.exp(ev["relative log evidence"]) / np.exp(ev["relative log evidence"]).sum()

def crps_samples(s, y):
    s = np.sort(s, axis=0)
    m = s.shape[0]
    w = (2 * np.arange(1, m + 1) - m - 1) / (m * m)
    return np.mean(np.abs(s - y).mean(0) - (w[:, None] * s).sum(0))

Calibration. All are well calibrated and slightly conservative: their 90% intervals cover 93-94% of the held-out values.

title: Bayesian Kriging (BayesianKriging)
text:
A Covariate: Rock Type
Cadmium in the Jura depends on the parent rock (Goovaerts, 1997), and the geology is mapped at every grid node. Rock type enters the trend as four indicator columns, with Argovian as the reference level. The posterior of each coefficient is a contrast in log(Cd) with Argovian, after accounting for spatial correlation. The rock recorded at the samples is used for fitting, and the mapped rock for prediction.


Code
ROCKS = {1: "Argovian", 2: "Kimmeridgian", 3: "Sequanian", 4: "Portlandian", 5: "Quaternary"}
NAME2CODE = {v: k for k, v in ROCKS.items()}


def rock_dummies(codes):
    codes = np.asarray(codes)
    return np.column_stack([(codes == k).astype(float) for k in [2, 3, 4, 5]])


X_train, X_test = rock_dummies(train.Rock), rock_dummies(test.Rock)
X_grid = rock_dummies(grid_df.Rock.map(NAME2CODE))
bk_rock = BayesianKriging("spherical", range_grid=RANGE_GRID, nugget_grid=NUGGET_GRID).fit(xy, z, covariates=X_train)
names = ["intercept (Argovian)"] + [f"{ROCKS[k]} - Argovian" for k in [2, 3, 4, 5]]
draws = bk_rock.sample_parameters(4000, seed=2)
bcols = [c for c in draws.columns if c.startswith("beta_")]
coef = pd.DataFrame({"posterior mean": draws[bcols].mean().values,
                     "5%": draws[bcols].quantile(0.05).values, "95%": draws[bcols].quantile(0.95).values,
                     "P(> 0)": (draws[bcols] > 0).mean().values}, index=names)

title: Bayesian Kriging (BayesianKriging)
text:
Maps and Exceedance Probabilities
The rock-type model is used on the 1,540-node map grid. Each node gets:

the predictive median of log(Cd), shown as Cd = exp(median);
the predictive standard deviation;
the width of the 90% interval;
the probability that Cd exceeds the Swiss guide value of 0.8 mg/kg, \(P(\log \text{Cd} > \log 0.8)\), exact from the Student-t mixture.

Maps show the signal, the noise-free process.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
g_mean, g_sd = bk_rock.predict(grid, covariates=X_grid, return_std=True)
g_q = bk_rock.predict_quantiles(grid, [0.05, 0.5, 0.95], covariates=X_grid)
g_p = bk_rock.predict_proba(grid, np.log(0.8), covariates=X_grid)
print(f"predicted {len(grid)} nodes in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(15, 12))
show_map(axes[0, 0], np.exp(g_q[:, 1]), "Cd = exp(predictive median) (mg/kg)", vmin=0.3, vmax=3, label="mg/kg")
show_map(axes[0, 1], g_sd, "Predictive sd of log(Cd)", cmap="magma", label="log units")
show_map(axes[1, 0], g_q[:, 2] - g_q[:, 0], "Width of the 90% interval (log units)", cmap="magma", label="log units")
show_map(axes[1, 1], g_p, "P(Cd > 0.8 mg/kg)", cmap="RdYlBu_r", vmin=0, vmax=1, label="probability")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"nodes with P > 0.9: {np.mean(g_p > 0.9):.0%};  P < 0.1: {np.mean(g_p < 0.1):.0%}")


predicted 1540 nodes in 17.0 s









nodes with P > 0.9: 4%;  P < 0.1: 0%



Geology in the map. Because rock type enters the trend, the geology map imprints on the predictions: their level steps at unit boundaries, while the kriged residual adds local detail around the samples.
Uncertainty pattern. The predictive sd and interval width are lowest near samples and highest in gaps and along the boundary.
Exceedance. Few nodes are confidently above (4% with P > 0.9) and none confidently below (P < 0.1) the guide value. Typical cadmium is near 1 mg/kg, so most of the area sits in the uncertain middle of the probability scale. Decisions near a threshold like this one need the full predictive distribution, not just a map of predictions.


Joint simulation: the contaminated area
The fraction of the study area above 0.8 mg/kg is a quantity over many locations, so it needs joint predictive draws. For 600 random map nodes, predictive_samples(..., joint=True) draws whole fields, and each draw gives one area fraction. Two shortcuts are compared with it:

joint=False: each node is drawn separately, but all nodes in one draw share the same parameters (grid point, \(\sigma^2\), \(\boldsymbol\beta\)). Parameter uncertainty is kept; spatial correlation of the residual field is lost.
Fully independent: each node’s draws are shuffled independently across draws, which treats every node as unrelated. This is what you get by combining per-node probabilities as if they were independent.



Code
sub = np.random.default_rng(3).choice(len(grid), 600, replace=False)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
joint = bk_rock.predictive_samples(grid[sub], 1000, covariates=X_grid[sub], joint=True, seed=4)
indep = bk_rock.predictive_samples(grid[sub], 1000, covariates=X_grid[sub], joint=False, seed=4)
print(f"1000 joint draws at 600 nodes in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
shuffled = np.column_stack([np.random.default_rng(10 + j).permutation(joint[:, j]) for j in range(joint.shape[1])])
areas = {"joint": (joint > np.log(0.8)).mean(1),
         "joint=False (shared parameters)": (indep > np.log(0.8)).mean(1),
         "fully independent": (shuffled > np.log(0.8)).mean(1)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
for k, a in areas.items():
    ax.hist(a, bins=30, alpha=0.5, label=k)
ax.set_xlabel("fraction of the area with Cd > 0.8 mg/kg")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
area_tab = pd.DataFrame({k: {"mean": a.mean(), "sd": a.std(), "q05": np.quantile(a, 0.05), "q95": np.quantile(a, 0.95)}
                         for k, a in areas.items()}).T
display(area_tab.round(3))
record("joint draws give a wider area interval than fully independent draws",
       "PASS" if area_tab.loc["joint", "sd"] > 1.2 * area_tab.loc["fully independent", "sd"] else "FAIL",
       f"sd joint {area_tab.loc['joint', 'sd']:.3f}, fully independent {area_tab.loc['fully independent', 'sd']:.3f}")

title: Bayesian Kriging (BayesianKriging)
section: Transformed Gaussian Kriging of Raw Cadmium
text:
Transformed Gaussian Kriging of Raw Cadmium
Instead of choosing the log transform beforehand, BayesianTransformedKriging puts the Box-Cox \(\lambda\) on a grid, \(\lambda \in \{-0.5, -0.25, 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1\}\), and lets the data weigh the choices. \(\lambda = 0\) is the log, and \(\lambda = 1\) no transform. Predictions come back in mg/kg.


Code
cd_train, cd_test = train.Cd.to_numpy(float), test.Cd.to_numpy(float)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
bt = BayesianTransformedKriging("spherical", range_grid=RANGE_GRID, nugget_grid=NUGGET_GRID).fit(xy, cd_train)
print(f"fitted {len(bt.posterior_)} grid points in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

log_back = np.exp(bk.predict_quantiles(xy_test, [0.05, 0.5, 0.95], signal=False))
comp_t = pd.DataFrame({
    "transformed (lambda posterior)": [np.sqrt(np.mean((pt["median"] - cd_test) ** 2)), np.sqrt(np.mean((pt["mean"] - cd_test) ** 2)),
                                       cover, np.mean(pt.q95 - pt.q05)],
    "log model, back-transformed": [np.sqrt(np.mean((log_back[:, 1] - cd_test) ** 2)), np.nan,
                                    np.mean((cd_test >= log_back[:, 0]) & (cd_test <= log_back[:, 2])),
                                    np.mean(log_back[:, 2] - log_back[:, 0])]},

title: Bayesian Kriging (BayesianKriging)
section: Binomial Kriging of the Guide-Value Exceedance
text:
Binomial Kriging of the Guide-Value Exceedance
Sometimes only a binary outcome is recorded or wanted: here, whether a sample exceeds 0.8 mg/kg. BayesianGLMKriging("binomial") models the probability of exceedance through a logit-linked latent Gaussian field, with one trial per site, and is fitted by MCMC. The rock type enters the trend again.
Binary data with one trial per site carry little information about the latent variance, so the priors on \(\sigma^2\) (sigma2_prior=(df, scale2), scaled inverse-\(\chi^2\)) and on \(\boldsymbol\beta\) (beta_prior_sd) matter. Three prior settings are compared first.


Code
y_bin = (train.Cd > 0.8).astype(int).to_numpy()
o = (test.Cd > 0.8).astype(float).to_numpy()
rows, fits = [], {}
for label, kw in [("default: sigma2 (1, 0.5), beta sd 10", dict()),
                  ("moderate: sigma2 (4, 1), beta sd 2.5", dict(sigma2_prior=(4.0, 1.0), beta_prior_sd=2.5)),
                  ("tight: sigma2 (10, 0.5), beta sd 2.5", dict(sigma2_prior=(10.0, 0.5), beta_prior_sd=2.5))]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    g_ = BayesianGLMKriging("binomial", model="spherical", range_grid=np.geomspace(0.1, 4.0, 20), **kw).fit(
        xy, y_bin, covariates=X_train, n_iter=12000, burn=4000, thin=8, seed=0)
    fits[label] = g_
    p_ = g_.predict(xy_test, covariates=X_test, seed=1)["mean"].to_numpy()
    rows.append({"prior": label, "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0, "posterior mean sigma2": g_.trace_.sigma2.mean(),
                 "posterior mean range": g_.trace_.range.mean(), "test Brier": np.mean((p_ - o) ** 2),
                 "MALA acceptance": g_.acceptance_["gamma"]})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("prior").round(3))
glm = fits["moderate: sigma2 (4, 1), beta sd 2.5"]
print(f"using the moderate prior: {len(glm.trace_)} kept samples")
print("acceptance rates:", {k: round(float(v), 2) for k, v in glm.acceptance_.items()})
display(glm.trace_.describe().loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(3))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(20, 3.8))
axes[0].plot(glm.trace_["beta_intercept"], lw=0.6)
axes[0].set_title("trace: intercept")

axes[1].set_title("trace: sigma^2")
axes[2].plot(glm.trace_["range"], lw=0.6, c="tab:green")

The priors matter for binary data. The default weak prior lets the latent variance grow to about 150 on the logit scale, which is implausibly large. The latent field then pins each training site to its observed class. The test Brier score is still good (0.158), but the parameters are not meaningful.
The moderate prior (scaled inverse-\(\chi^2\) with 4 degrees of freedom and scale 1 on \(\sigma^2\), and sd 2.5 on the coefficients) gives \(\sigma^2 \approx 15\), a range of 0.37 km and a Brier score of 0.163.
The tight prior forces a smoother, longer-range field and scores worse (0.184).
Binary data alone come close to the continuous model. With the moderate prior, the binomial model predicts the held-out exceedances almost as well as BayesianKriging on the full log(Cd) values (Brier 0.163 against 0.160), and far better than a constant probability (0.241). The two probability maps correlate at 0.88.
Sampler behaviour. The rock coefficients are positive, as in the continuous model. The MALA acceptance after burn-in (0.21) is below the 0.57 target, a sign that a longer burn-in would tune the step better. The trace plots should be checked for mixing before trusting a single run.

Conjugate Bayesian kriging reproduced ordinary kriging exactly (difference about \(10^{-8}\)) and widened its intervals only slightly with 251 data: trend and sill uncertainty matter mostly for small samples.
The grid posterior of range and nugget disagreed with the least-squares variogram fit. The likelihood favoured a short range (median 0.19 km) with a moderate nugget, while the binned fit gave 1.33 km, and the posterior kept a long-range tail. Priors shifted the parameter posteriors but barely changed the predictions. Bayes factors preferred the exponential model (probability 0.87).
At the held-out sites, all methods were well calibrated (90% intervals covering 93-94%). BayesianKriging had the widest intervals and the best CRPS (0.306 against 0.314 for plug-in kriging): wider in the right places, not just wider.
Rock type as a covariate had clear posterior effects (+0.3 to +0.6 log units relative to Argovian, probability of being positive at least 0.97). It shortened the residual range and improved RMSE (0.556 → 0.540) with narrower, still calibrated intervals.
Joint simulation gave the contaminated area fraction (0.70, 90% interval 0.65-0.75). Treating nodes as independent understated its uncertainty by 40%, because parameter uncertainty moves all nodes together.
The Box-Cox model chose the log transform (posterior 0.97 at \(\lambda = 0\)). The binomial GLMM predicted exceedances nearly as well from the 0/1 data alone as the continuous model did from the full data, once the variance prior was made reasonable.

title: Bayesian Transformed Gaussian Kriging (BayesianTransformedKriging)
text:
Overview
Metal concentrations, rainfall, permeability and many other variables are positive and right-skewed. Gaussian kriging and Gaussian Bayesian kriging assume a Gaussian field, so in practice the data are transformed first, usually by a log. The prediction is then back-transformed. That routine hides two decisions:

Which transform? The log is a habit, not a law. Some variables need less (a square root), some more.
How to back-transform? \(\exp(\text{kriged log value})\) is the predictive median, not the mean. The mean needs a correction, and quantiles must be transformed one by one.

Bayesian transformed Gaussian kriging (De Oliveira, Kedem & Short, 1997) makes the transform part of the model. A Box-Cox parameter \(\lambda\) joins the range and nugget on the grid of BayesianKriging. The data then give a posterior over \(\lambda\), and predictions are posterior predictive draws back-transformed to the original units. Every summary (median, mean, quantiles, exceedance probabilities) comes from the same draws, and the uncertainty about the transform itself is included.







BayesianTransformedKriging





parameters
lambda_grid, lambda_prior, plus everything of BayesianKriging (model, trend, range_grid, nugget_grid, priors)


fit
closed-form posterior over the (λ, range, nugget) grid; lambda_posterior_, posterior_


predict
Monte Carlo back-transform: predictive_samples, predict (mean, median, sd, q05, q95), predict_quantiles, predict_proba



The notebook:

asks ten metal datasets which transformation they choose, and relates the answer to skewness;
studies Jura zinc, where \(\lambda\) is genuinely uncertain, against fixed transforms on held-out sites;
shows the bias of the naive back-transform;
uses cadmium to show that the transform matters most for exceedance probabilities;
uses lead, the most skewed metal, as a cautionary case about heavy tails;
maps zinc on the Jura grid.

title: Bayesian Transformed Gaussian Kriging (BayesianTransformedKriging)
text:
Theory

The Box-Cox family
For \(z > 0\) (Box & Cox, 1964),
\[
t_\lambda(z) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{z^\lambda - 1}{\lambda} & \lambda \ne 0 \\[6pt] \log z & \lambda = 0 \end{cases}
\]
The family is continuous in \(\lambda\) (the limit of \((z^\lambda - 1)/\lambda\) as \(\lambda \to 0\) is \(\log z\)), and increasing in \(z\) for every \(\lambda\):

\(\lambda = 1\) leaves the data essentially as they are (a shift);
\(\lambda = 0.5\) is close to a square root;
\(\lambda = 0\) is the log;
\(\lambda < 0\) compresses the upper tail even more strongly than the log.

The more skewed the data, the smaller the \(\lambda\) that makes them look Gaussian.


The transformed Gaussian model
The model says that a transformed version of the field is Gaussian:
\[
t_\lambda\bigl(Z(\mathbf{x})\bigr) = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})^\top\boldsymbol\beta + S(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon(\mathbf{x}),
\]
with the same Gaussian structure as in BayesianKriging: covariance \(\sigma^2[\mathbf{R}(\phi) + \tau\mathbf{I}]\), conjugate priors on \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\), and discrete priors on \(\phi\), \(\tau\) and now \(\lambda\) (lambda_grid, lambda_prior).


The Jacobian and the normalised transform
The likelihood of the original data \(\mathbf{z}\) includes the Jacobian of the transform:
\[
p(\mathbf{z} \mid \lambda, \cdot) = p_{\text{Gauss}}\bigl(t_\lambda(\mathbf{z}) \mid \cdot\bigr)\, \prod_i z_i^{\lambda - 1}.
\]
Without that factor, values of \(\lambda\) cannot be compared: a stronger transform shrinks the data and would always look more probable. GeoLattice uses the normalised Box-Cox transform,
\[
w_\lambda(z) = \frac{t_\lambda(z)}{\dot z^{\,\lambda - 1}},
\qquad
\dot z = \Bigl(\prod_i z_i\Bigr)^{1/n} \text{ (geometric mean)},
\]
whose Jacobian over the data is exactly 1 (Box & Cox, 1964). The \(w\) values for different \(\lambda\) are on comparable scales, and their marginal likelihoods, computed exactly as in BayesianKriging, can be compared directly.


The posterior over λ, range and nugget
For every grid point \((\lambda, \phi, \tau)\), the trend and variance are integrated out in closed form, as in Bayesian kriging, which gives
\[
p(\lambda, \phi, \tau \mid \mathbf{z}) \;\propto\; p(\lambda)\, p(\phi)\, p(\tau)\; p\bigl(\mathbf{w}_\lambda \mid \phi, \tau\bigr).
\]
The marginal posterior of \(\lambda\) is reported in lambda_posterior_, and the full grid in posterior_.


Prediction by back-transformed draws
The transform is nonlinear, so the predictive distribution in original units has no closed form. predictive_samples draws from it:

pick a grid point \((\lambda, \phi, \tau)\) with its posterior probability;
draw \(\sigma^2\), \(\boldsymbol\beta\), and the Gaussian prediction \(w_0\), as in BayesianKriging (observation scale, including the nugget);
back-transform: \(z_0 = t_\lambda^{-1}\bigl(w_0\, \dot z^{\,\lambda - 1}\bigr)\), where \(t_\lambda^{-1}(t) = (\lambda t + 1)^{1/\lambda}\), or \(e^t\) for \(\lambda = 0\).

The draws give the predictive median, quantiles, exceedance probabilities and, when it exists, the mean.


Back-transformation bias
If \(W_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, s^2)\) and \(Z_0 = e^{W_0}\) (the log case), then
\[
\operatorname{median}(Z_0) = e^{\mu}, \qquad E[Z_0] = e^{\mu + s^2/2}.
\]
So back-transforming the kriged log value gives the median, not the mean. When the predictive variance is large, the mean exceeds the median by the factor \(e^{s^2/2}\). That is the bias that lognormal kriging corrects analytically (Journel, 1980). For other \(\lambda\) no simple formula exists. Monte Carlo draws handle every \(\lambda\), and a mixture over \(\lambda\), the same way.


The domain problem and heavy tails
\(t_\lambda\) maps \((0, \infty)\) onto a half-line, not the whole real line:

for \(\lambda > 0\), onto \((-1/\lambda, \infty)\);
for \(\lambda < 0\), onto \((-\infty, -1/\lambda)\).

A Gaussian \(W\) puts some probability outside that range. For \(\lambda > 0\), draws below \(-1/\lambda\) are mapped to 0. For \(\lambda < 0\), draws above \(-1/\lambda\) correspond to \(Z = +\infty\): the transformed-Gaussian predictive with \(\lambda < 0\) has an infinitely heavy upper tail, and its mean does not exist (De Oliveira et al., 1997). GeoLattice returns those draws as inf and warns. The median and quantiles stay well defined and are the summaries to use.

%matplotlib inline

import pandas as pd

RESULTS = []
def record(section, status, note=""):
    RESULTS.append({"Feature": section, "Status": status, "Notes": note})
    marker = {"PASS": "✅", "FAIL": "❌", "BLOCKED": "⚠️"}.get(status, "?")
    print(f"{marker} [{status}] {section}  {note}")


def crps(draws, y):
    s = np.sort(draws, axis=0)
    m = s.shape[0]
    w = (2 * np.arange(1, m + 1) - m - 1) / (m * m)
    return np.mean(np.abs(s - y).mean(0) - (w[:, None] * s).sum(0))

Which Transformation Do the Data Choose?
Each of seven Jura metals and three Meuse metals is fitted with \(\lambda \in \{-1, -0.75, \dots, 1.5\}\), a uniform prior, an exponential model, 15 ranges and 5 nugget ratios. The posterior of \(\lambda\) is compared with the skewness of the data.


Code
datasets = [(f"Jura {v}", jura, "Xloc", "Yloc", v) for v in ["Ni", "Cr", "Co", "Cd", "Zn", "Cu", "Pb"]] + \
           [(f"Meuse {v}", meuse, "x", "y", v) for v in ["zinc", "copper", "lead"]]
rows, lam_posts = [], {}
for name, d, xc, yc, v in datasets:
    xy_ = d[[xc, yc]].to_numpy(float)
    z_ = d[v].to_numpy(float)
    dmax = np.sqrt(((xy_[:, None] - xy_[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)).max()
    m = BayesianTransformedKriging("exponential", lambda_grid=LAMBDA_GRID, nugget_grid=NUGGET_GRID,
                                   range_grid=np.geomspace(0.01 * dmax, dmax, 15)).fit(xy_, z_)
    lp = m.lambda_posterior_

def score_bt(model, z_test, n=3000, seed=1):
    s = model.predictive_samples(xy_test, n, seed=seed)
    med = np.median(s, 0)
    lo, hi = np.quantile(s, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
    return {"RMSE (median)": np.sqrt(np.mean((med - z_test) ** 2)), "MAE (median)": np.mean(np.abs(med - z_test)),
            "coverage 90%": np.mean((z_test >= lo) & (z_test <= hi)), "width 90%": np.mean(hi - lo),
            "CRPS": crps(s, z_test)}, s


rows, zn_draws = [], {}
for label, lg in [("posterior over lambda", LAMBDA_GRID), ("lambda = 0 (log)", [0.0]),
                  ("lambda = 0.5 (sqrt)", [0.5]), ("lambda = 1 (none)", [1.0])]:
    m = bt_zn if len(lg) > 1 else BayesianTransformedKriging(lambda_grid=lg, **BT_KW).fit(xy, zn)
    sc, s = score_bt(m, zn_test)
    rows.append({"model": label, **sc})
    zn_draws[label] = s
zn_val = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model")

       "PASS" if zn_val.loc["posterior over lambda", "CRPS"] <= 1.03 * zn_val["CRPS"].min() else "FAIL",

For point prediction, the transform hardly matters. RMSE of the predictive median is 22.5-23.5 mg/kg for every model, and CRPS is within 2%: the square root is best (11.85), then the log (11.95), the λ posterior (12.08) and no transform (12.13).

section: Back-Transformation: Median, Mean and the Naive Estimate
text:
Back-Transformation: Median, Mean and the Naive Estimate
The common shortcut is to krige \(\log z\) and report \(\exp(\hat w)\). Section 2.6 says that this is the predictive median. Here are three estimates at the held-out zinc sites:

the naive back-transform: \(\exp\) of the Bayesian kriging predictive mean of \(\log\) Zn;
the predictive median of the λ = 0 draws;
the predictive mean of the λ = 0 draws.

Their averages over the test sites are compared with the average observed zinc, and the gap is related to the lognormal factor \(e^{s^2/2}\).


Code
bk_log = BayesianKriging("spherical", range_grid=RANGE_GRID, nugget_grid=NUGGET_GRID).fit(xy, np.log(zn))
mu_log, sd_log = bk_log.predict(xy_test, return_std=True, signal=False)
s0 = zn_draws["lambda = 0 (log)"]
comp = pd.DataFrame({
    "average over test sites (mg/kg)": [np.exp(mu_log).mean(), np.median(s0, 0).mean(), s0.mean(0).mean(),
                                        (np.exp(mu_log + sd_log ** 2 / 2)).mean(), zn_test.mean()]},
    index=["naive exp(mean of log)", "predictive median (draws)", "predictive mean (draws)",
           "lognormal formula exp(mu + s^2/2)", "observed zinc"])
display(comp.round(2))
print(f"mean predictive sd of log Zn: {sd_log.mean():.3f}  ->  e^(s^2/2) = {np.exp(sd_log.mean() ** 2 / 2):.3f}")
gap = (s0.mean(0).mean() - zn_test.mean()) / zn_test.mean()
gap_naive = (np.exp(mu_log).mean() - zn_test.mean()) / zn_test.mean()
record("predictive mean closer to the observed average than the naive back-transform",
       "PASS" if abs(gap) < abs(gap_naive) else "FAIL", f"naive {gap_naive:+.1%}, mean of draws {gap:+.1%}")

The naive back-transform is the median. \(\exp(\text{mean of log})\) averages 69.5 mg/kg, exactly the median of the λ = 0 draws (69.5).
The mean is higher. The predictive mean is 72.8 mg/kg, matching the lognormal formula \(e^{\mu + s^2/2}\) (72.9). With a predictive sd of about 0.30 on the log scale, the factor \(e^{s^2/2}\) is 1.044.
Against the observed average (74.1 mg/kg), the naive estimate is 6.1% low, and the mean of the draws is 1.7% low.

The draws give the right answer for any λ, including mixtures, where no closed-form correction exists. Report the median as a robust typical value and the mean when totals or averages matter, but never present the naive back-transform as a mean.

text:
Jura Cadmium: Exceedance Probabilities
For a decision against a threshold, the tail of the predictive distribution matters, not its centre. Cadmium against the Swiss guide value of 0.8 mg/kg: about 60% of the samples exceed it, so the threshold sits in the body of the distribution, where the shape of the predictive distribution matters. The λ posterior is compared with fixed transforms by the Brier score of \(P(\text{Cd} > 0.8)\) at the held-out sites, and by its reliability (calibration curve).


Code
cd, cd_test = train["Cd"].to_numpy(float), test["Cd"].to_numpy(float)
o = (cd_test > 0.8).astype(float)
rows, probs = [], {}
bt_cd = BayesianTransformedKriging(lambda_grid=LAMBDA_GRID, **BT_KW).fit(xy, cd)
print("P(lambda | Cd):", bt_cd.lambda_posterior_[bt_cd.lambda_posterior_ > 0.005].round(3).to_dict())
for label, lg in [("posterior over lambda", LAMBDA_GRID), ("lambda = 0 (log)", [0.0]), ("lambda = 1 (none)", [1.0])]:
    m = bt_cd if len(lg) > 1 else BayesianTransformedKriging(lambda_grid=lg, **BT_KW).fit(xy, cd)
    s = m.predictive_samples(xy_test, 3000, seed=2)
    p = (s > 0.8).mean(0)
    probs[label] = p
    rows.append({"model": label, "Brier (Cd > 0.8)": np.mean((p - o) ** 2),
                 "log score": -np.mean(o * np.log(np.clip(p, 1e-3, 1)) + (1 - o) * np.log(np.clip(1 - p, 1e-3, 1))),
                 "CRPS": crps(s, cd_test)})
cd_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model")
display(cd_tab.round(4))

section: Jura Lead: Heavy Tails and a Cautionary Case
text:
Jura Lead: Heavy Tails and a Cautionary Case
Lead is the most skewed Jura metal, with a few very high values from local contamination. The survey above put its λ posterior below 0. Two things to check:

what happens to the predictive draws when \(\lambda < 0\) (Section 2.7);
whether the λ preferred by the marginal likelihood also predicts best.



Code
pb, pb_test = train["Pb"].to_numpy(float), test["Pb"].to_numpy(float)
print(f"Pb: skewness {pd.Series(pb).skew():.2f}, max {pb.max():.0f} mg/kg, median {np.median(pb):.0f}")
bt_pb = BayesianTransformedKriging(lambda_grid=LAMBDA_GRID, **BT_KW).fit(xy, pb)
print("P(lambda | Pb):", bt_pb.lambda_posterior_[bt_pb.lambda_posterior_ > 0.005].round(3).to_dict())
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    s_pb = bt_pb.predictive_samples(xy_test, 3000, seed=3)
for w in caught:
    print("warning:", w.message)
finite = np.isfinite(s_pb)
print(f"infinite draws: {np.mean(~finite):.3%};  largest finite draw: {s_pb[finite].max():,.0f} mg/kg")
print(f"'mean' of the draws at the test sites: {np.mean(s_pb, 0).mean()}  (undefined for lambda < 0)")

rows = []
for label, lg in [("posterior over lambda", LAMBDA_GRID), ("lambda = -0.5", [-0.5]), ("lambda = 0 (log)", [0.0]),
                  ("lambda = 0.5", [0.5]), ("lambda = 1 (none)", [1.0])]:
    m = bt_pb if len(lg) > 1 else BayesianTransformedKriging(lambda_grid=lg, **BT_KW).fit(xy, pb)
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        s = m.predictive_samples(xy_test, 3000, seed=3)

    lo, hi = np.quantile(s, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)

                 "coverage 90%": np.mean((pb_test >= lo) & (pb_test <= hi)), "median width 90%": np.median(hi - lo),

The likelihood wants a very strong transform. It puts λ at −0.75 (0.82) or −1 (0.15). With λ < 0, the back-transformed predictive has an infinite upper tail: 0.065% of the draws are infinite, the largest finite draw is 410,824 mg/kg, against a data maximum of 300, and the “mean” is infinite. GeoLattice warns, and the median and quantiles are the only usable summaries.
The data-chosen λ predicts the median best but is poorly calibrated. It has the best MAE of the median (15.3 mg/kg), but its 90% intervals cover only 79% of the held-out values. Coverage rises steadily with λ: 0.82 at −0.5, 0.85 for the log, 0.91 at 0.5 and 0.95 without a transform. The likelihood chooses the λ that makes the training data, dominated by a few contaminated hot spots, most Gaussian. That transform squeezes the bulk of the distribution, so the intervals around typical sites come out too narrow.
The lesson. The marginal likelihood is a good guide, not an oracle. When a few extreme values drive λ below 0:

check calibration on held-out data;
consider restricting the grid to λ ≥ 0 (or using the log);
or treat the hot spots separately, for example with an indicator or a mixture model.

Maps of Zinc
The zinc model with the λ posterior is used on a 100 m version of the Jura grid (1,540 nodes). Each node’s 2,000 back-transformed predictive draws give:

the median;
the mean;
the width of the 90% interval;
the probability of exceeding 100 mg/kg, about the 80th percentile of the data.

grid_df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "jura_grid.csv", index_col=0)
g = grid_df[["Xloc", "Yloc"]].to_numpy(float)
i50 = np.rint((g[:, 0] - g[:, 0].min()) / 0.05).astype(int)
j50 = np.rint((g[:, 1] - g[:, 1].min()) / 0.05).astype(int)
grid = g[(i50 % 2 == 0) & (j50 % 2 == 0)]
gi = np.rint((grid[:, 0] - grid[:, 0].min()) / 0.1).astype(int)
gj = np.rint((grid[:, 1] - grid[:, 1].min()) / 0.1).astype(int)
EXT = [grid[:, 0].min() - 0.05, grid[:, 0].max() + 0.05, grid[:, 1].min() - 0.05, grid[:, 1].max() + 0.05]

t0 = time.perf_counter()

    img[gj, gi] = v

    ax.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], s=4, facecolors="none", edgecolors="k", linewidths=0.4)

    ax.set_aspect("equal")

The maps come from the same draws (0.8 s for 1,540 nodes), so median, mean, interval width and exceedance probability are mutually consistent.
Mean against median. The mean exceeds the median by 6.6% on average, more where the predictive is wide (far from samples).
Intervals. Their width is largest where predicted zinc is high: on the original scale, a skewed variable’s uncertainty grows with its level, which a log-type transform builds in automatically.
Exceedance. The probability map of zinc above 100 mg/kg picks out the high-zinc areas, with graded confidence in between.
