Reading the results. The KWS row reproduces the paper closely: critical probability 0.55 (paper 0.55), 13% of validation fields misclassified, risk-α 0.21 and risk-β 0.28 at the validation fields (paper 0.20 and 0.37), 0.23 and 0.31 on the grid (paper 0.24 and 0.32), and 58% of the upazila delineated as contaminated (paper 62%), 99% of MHL-1 (paper 99%) and 30% of HL (paper 34%).
For OK, RK and OCK the delineated areas are larger than in the paper (79% to 92% against 58% to 73%). The misclassification curves of these methods are flat over a wide range of thresholds, so the critical probability, and with it the delineated area, depends on a few validation fields. With 53 fields, one field is 1.9 percentage points of misclassification. The curves also confirm the paper’s observation that the optimum lies near the marginal probability of contamination (0.63).
The risk maps show where the delineation is least certain: risk-α is highest in the patches declared contaminated within the HL north, and risk-β is highest across the central and northern HL area, where many fields lie close to 14.8 mg/kg.

title: Uncertainty of Geostatistical Risk Mapping of Paddy Soil Arsenic
section: Improvement 1: is the ranking of methods robust?
text:
Improvement 1: is the ranking of methods robust?
Table 2 rests on 53 fields. Two checks follow.

Repeated random splits. The stratified 210/53 split is repeated N_REPEATS times with different seeds.
Spatially blocked cross-validation. Fields are grouped into 2.5 km blocks and the blocks are divided into five folds, so that a validation field never has a calibration neighbour from the same block. This is closer to mapping unsampled parts of the upazila.

Four alternatives are added to the paper’s four methods:







Method
What changes




RK + land type
The global RK trend gets a land-type indicator, the simplest way to let the two strata have different means


KWS (RK / OK)
KWS with OK in place of OCK on MHL-1


RK, kriged covariates
The trend is fitted to the grid values of water As, Fe and elevation at the fields, not the measured values. The model is then calibrated on the same smooth surfaces it is applied to


RF-RK
A random forest trend on the grid covariates (coordinates, water As and Fe, elevation, soil organic C, clay, soil Fe, land type), with kriging of its out-of-bag residuals





Code
# Covariates from the grid node nearest each field, so a trend fitted at the fields can be mapped.
for c in ["WAS", "WFE", "elev", "SOC", "CLAY", "STFE"]:
    df["g_" + c] = grid[c].to_numpy()[nearest_node]
df["g_HL"] = gHL[nearest_node]
GRIDCOV = ["x", "y", "g_WAS", "g_WFE", "g_elev"]
RF_COVARS = GRIDCOV + ["g_SOC", "g_CLAY", "g_STFE", "g_HL"]
print("Correlation of measured and gridded covariates at the fields:",
      {c: round(np.corrcoef(df[c], df["g_" + c])[0, 1], 2) for c in ["WAS", "WFE", "elev"]})

# Random-forest trend, then simple kriging of the out-of-bag residuals.
def krige_rfrk(tr, cp, Xtr, Xp, seed=0):
    rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, max_features=0.5, oob_score=True, random_state=seed, n_jobs=-1)
    rf.fit(Xtr, z[tr])
    r = z[tr] - rf.oob_prediction_
    p = fit_exponential(*robust_variogram(xy[tr], r))
    rm, rse = SimpleKriging(variogram_object(xy[tr], r, p), mean=0.0, use_gpu=USE_GPU).fit(xy[tr], r).predict(cp, return_variance=True)
    return rf.predict(Xp) + np.asarray(rm), np.asarray(rse) ** 2

# The paper's four methods, plus land type, an OK stratum, gridded covariates, and a forest trend.
def all_methods(tr, te):
    out = four_methods(tr, xy[te], df.loc[te, RK_COVARS].to_numpy(float), HL[te])
    cols = RK_COVARS + ["HL"]
    out["RK + land type"] = krige_rk(xy[tr], z[tr], df.loc[tr, cols].to_numpy(float), xy[te], df.loc[te, cols].to_numpy(float))
    out["KWS (RK / OK)"] = krige_kws(tr, xy[te], df.loc[te, RK_COVARS].to_numpy(float), HL[te], mhl_method="OK")
    out["RK, kriged covariates"] = krige_rk(xy[tr], z[tr], df.loc[tr, GRIDCOV].to_numpy(float), xy[te], df.loc[te, GRIDCOV].to_numpy(float))
    out["RF-RK"] = krige_rfrk(tr, xy[te], df.loc[tr, RF_COVARS].to_numpy(float), df.loc[te, RF_COVARS].to_numpy(float))
    return out

METHOD_ORDER = ["OK", "RK", "OCK", "KWS", "RK + land type", "KWS (RK / OK)", "RK, kriged covariates", "RF-RK"]

# One hundred stratified 210/53 splits. Each row is one method on one split.
t0 = time.perf_counter()
rep_rows, pooled = [], []
for s in range(N_REPEATS):
    tr, te = stratified_split(10_000 + s)
    for k, (m, v) in all_methods(tr, te).items():
        rep_rows.append({"split": s, "method": k, **errors(z[te], m)})
        pooled.append(pd.DataFrame({"split": s, "method": k, "obs": z[te], "pred": m, "var": v, "HL": HL[te]}))
rep = pd.DataFrame(rep_rows)
pooled = pd.concat(pooled, ignore_index=True)
rep["RI_pct"] = 100 * (1 - rep["RMSE"] / rep["split"].map(rep.query("method == 'OK'").set_index("split")["RMSE"]))
print(f"{N_REPEATS} repeated splits: {(time.perf_counter() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")

# Rank within each split (1 is the lowest RMSE) and the spread of the improvement over OK.
rank = rep.pivot(index="split", columns="method", values="RMSE").rank(axis=1)
rep_tbl = rep.groupby("method").agg(RMSE_mean=("RMSE", "mean"), RMSE_sd=("RMSE", "std"), RI_mean=("RI_pct", "mean"),
                                    RI_p05=("RI_pct", lambda s: np.percentile(s, 5)), RI_p95=("RI_pct", lambda s: np.percentile(s, 95)),
                                    share_better_than_OK=("RI_pct", lambda s: 100 * np.mean(s > 0)))
rep_tbl["mean_rank"] = rank.mean()
rep_tbl["share_best_pct"] = 100 * (rank == 1).mean()
rep_tbl = rep_tbl.loc[METHOD_ORDER]
display(rep_tbl.round(2))

# How often KWS beats RK, and where the single replication split sits among the hundred.
kws_vs_rk = rep.pivot(index="split", columns="method", values="RMSE")
print(f"KWS has a lower RMSE than RK in {100 * np.mean(kws_vs_rk['KWS'] < kws_vs_rk['RK']):.0f}% of the splits")
print(f"""RI of KWS on the replication split: {table2.query('area == "All" and method == "KWS"').RI_pct.iloc[0]:.1f}%   """
      f"""percentile among the repeated splits: {100 * np.mean(rep.query('method == "KWS"').RI_pct < table2.query('area == "All" and method == "KWS"').RI_pct.iloc[0]):.0f}""")

Reading the results. The paper’s ranking does not hold up as firmly as Table 2 suggests.

The single split was favourable. Over 100 random splits, the mean improvement over OK is 3.1% for RK and 3.2% for KWS, and both fail to beat OK in about 30% of the splits. KWS beats RK in only 49% of the splits. Its 12.3% improvement on the replication split sits at the 93rd percentile of the repeated splits, and the paper’s 13.6% is at the upper end of what this data produces.
Cokriging with the loading factor does not help. OCK is worse than OK on average (-2.8%) and better in only 21% of the splits.
Spatial cross-validation favours the covariates more clearly. When whole 2.5 km blocks are held out, RK, KWS and the two simple alternatives all improve on OK by 8% to 9%, because the covariate maps still carry information where no neighbouring field exists.
The simple alternatives are at least as good. RK with a land-type indicator and KWS with OK on MHL-1 have the best mean ranks in the repeated splits and the best spatial-CV scores. They need no cross-variogram.
Training on kriged covariates costs accuracy (1.8% and 5.0%, against 3.1% and 9.0% for RK on measured covariates), so the paper’s choice of measured values at the fields was the better one. A random forest trend with four more covariates does not beat the linear trend with 263 fields.

The robust conclusion is narrower than the paper’s: secondary information improves soil As maps by a few percent at random locations and by about 9% away from sampled fields, and stratifying by land type removes bias, but no single method is reliably best.

title: Uncertainty of Geostatistical Risk Mapping of Paddy Soil Arsenic
text:
Improvement 2: are the probabilities calibrated?
A probability map is only as good as its kriging variance. The validation fields of all repeated splits are pooled (about 5,300 predictions per method) and three checks are applied:

Coverage. The share of observations inside the 90% prediction interval \(z^* \pm 1.645\,\sigma_K\). It should be close to 0.90.
Standardized errors. \((z - z^*)/\sigma_K\) should have mean 0 and variance 1.
Brier score and reliability of \(p(\mathbf u)\) for the 14.8 mg/kg threshold.



Code
# Exceedance probability and standardized residual of every held-out prediction.
pooled["p"] = exceed_prob(pooled["pred"], pooled["var"])
pooled["y"] = pooled["obs"] > Z_CRIT
pooled["std_err"] = (pooled["obs"] - pooled["pred"]) / np.sqrt(pooled["var"])
# Coverage of the nominal 90% interval, and the Brier score of the exceedance probability.
base = pooled.groupby("method")["y"].mean()
cal = pooled.groupby("method").apply(lambda g: pd.Series({
    "coverage_90": np.mean(np.abs(g.std_err) <= 1.645),
    "coverage_90_HL": np.mean(np.abs(g.std_err[g.HL == 1]) <= 1.645),
    "coverage_90_MHL1": np.mean(np.abs(g.std_err[g.HL == 0]) <= 1.645),
    "mean_std_error": g.std_err.mean(), "var_std_error": g.std_err.var(),
    "Brier": np.mean((g.p - g.y) ** 2)})).loc[METHOD_ORDER]
# Skill against a constant forecast equal to the observed exceedance rate. Zero is no skill.
cal["Brier_skill"] = 1 - cal["Brier"] / (base * (1 - base)).loc[METHOD_ORDER]
display(cal.round(3))

# Reliability diagram (bins of at least 30 predictions) and the shape of the standardized errors.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
bins = np.linspace(0, 1, 11)
for k, colr in zip(["OK", "RK", "KWS", "RF-RK"], ["tab:gray", "tab:blue", "tab:red", "tab:green"]):
    g = pooled.query("method == @k")
    b = np.clip(np.digitize(g.p, bins) - 1, 0, 9)
    px = [g.p[b == i].mean() for i in range(10) if np.sum(b == i) >= 30]
    py = [g.y[b == i].mean() for i in range(10) if np.sum(b == i) >= 30]
    axes[0].plot(px, py, "o-", color=colr, label=k)
    axes[1].hist(g.std_err, bins=np.linspace(-4, 5, 46), histtype="step", density=True, color=colr, label=k)
axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k:")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Predicted P(soil As > 14.8 mg/kg)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Observed share above 14.8 mg/kg")
axes[0].set_title("Reliability of the kriging probabilities", fontsize=10); axes[0].set_aspect("equal"); axes[0].legend()
xs = np.linspace(-4, 5, 200)
axes[1].plot(xs, norm.pdf(xs), "k:", label="N(0, 1)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Standardized error (z - z*) / σK"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Density")

Reading the results. The kriging variances are broadly honest. For all methods 86% to 91% of observations fall inside the nominal 90% interval and the standardized errors have mean zero. Two details matter for the probability maps:

Variance of the standardized errors is 1.2 to 1.4, above the target of 1. The tails are heavier than Gaussian, which reflects the skewed MHL-1 data, so probabilities near 0 and 1 are somewhat overconfident.

title: Uncertainty of Geostatistical Risk Mapping of Paddy Soil Arsenic
section: Improvement 3: uncertainty of the contaminated area by conditional simulation
text:
Improvement 3: uncertainty of the contaminated area by conditional simulation
Kriging gives a probability at each node, but the share of the upazila that is contaminated is a sum over many correlated nodes, and its uncertainty cannot be read from the probability map. Conditional simulation answers that question. The final model is refitted on all 263 fields, and each land type is simulated with the method that KWS uses for its mean:

HL. RK trend fitted to the 122 HL fields, plus conditional simulations of the residuals (simple kriging, mean 0).
MHL-1. OCK and OK give almost the same predictions on MHL-1 (Section 8), so soil As is simulated directly in normal-score space (ordinary kriging conditioning) and back-transformed. This also respects the skewness of MHL-1 soil As (1.5).

fftsim generates exact Gaussian realizations on the 86 m lattice by circulant embedding and conditions them by kriging. Each realization gives one map and one value of the contaminated area. Trend coefficients are held at their estimates, so the spread is a lower bound on the total uncertainty.


Code
# Every field, split by land type, and the grid nodes that belong to each stratum.
all_idx = np.arange(len(z))
h_idx, m_idx = all_idx[HL == 1], all_idx[HL == 0]
gh, gm = np.where(gHL == 1)[0], np.where(gHL == 0)[0]

# HL: RK trend + simulated residuals
b_hl, _, r_hl = ols_fit(df.loc[h_idx, RK_COVARS].to_numpy(float), z[h_idx])
trend_hl = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(gh)), grid.loc[gh, RK_COVARS].to_numpy(float)]) @ b_hl
p_r = fit_exponential(*robust_variogram(xy[h_idx], r_hl))
vario_hl = [0.0, p_r[0], 3 * p_r[2], 3 * p_r[2], p_r[0] + p_r[1], "exponential"]   # GSLIB convention: practical range

# MHL-1: normal scores of soil As
ns_m = nscore_forward(z[m_idx])[0]
p_n = fit_exponential(*robust_variogram(xy[m_idx], ns_m))
sill_n = p_n[0] + p_n[1]
vario_mhl = [0.0, p_n[0] / sill_n, 3 * p_n[2], 3 * p_n[2], 1.0, "exponential"]       # standardized to a unit sill

# Conditional FFT simulation: residuals on highland, normal scores back-transformed on medium highland.
t0 = time.perf_counter()
sim_res = fftsim(gxy[gh], pd.DataFrame({"x": xy[h_idx, 0], "y": xy[h_idx, 1], "r": r_hl}), "x", "y", "r", vario_hl,
                 kriging_type="simple", mean=0.0, nsim=N_SIM, seed=SEED, spacing=(DX, DY))
sim_mhl = fftsim(gxy[gm], pd.DataFrame({"x": xy[m_idx, 0], "y": xy[m_idx, 1], "z": z[m_idx]}), "x", "y", "z", vario_mhl,
                 kriging_type="ordinary", itrans=True, nsim=N_SIM, seed=SEED + 1, spacing=(DX, DY),
                 zmin=float(z.min()), zmax=float(z.max()))
sims = np.empty((N_SIM, len(gxy)))
sims[:, gh] = np.maximum(trend_hl[None, :] + np.asarray(sim_res), float(z.min()))
sims[:, gm] = np.asarray(sim_mhl)
print(f"{N_SIM} realizations x {len(gxy):,} nodes in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
print(f"HL residual variogram: c0 {p_r[0]:.1f}, c1 {p_r[1]:.1f}, a {p_r[2]:.0f} m   MHL-1 normal-score variogram: nugget share {p_n[0] / sill_n:.2f}, a {p_n[2]:.0f} m")

# Mean, spread, and exceedance rate of the realizations, set against the data.
chk = pd.DataFrame({"data_mean": [z[h_idx].mean(), z[m_idx].mean()], "sim_mean": [sims[:, gh].mean(), sims[:, gm].mean()],
                    "data_SD": [z[h_idx].std(), z[m_idx].std()], "sim_SD": [sims[:, gh].std(axis=1).mean(), sims[:, gm].std(axis=1).mean()],
                    "data_share_above_14.8": [(z[h_idx] > Z_CRIT).mean(), (z[m_idx] > Z_CRIT).mean()],
                    "sim_share_above_14.8": [(sims[:, gh] > Z_CRIT).mean(), (sims[:, gm] > Z_CRIT).mean()]}, index=["HL", "MHL-1"])
display(chk.round(2))

Reading the results. The realizations reproduce the data: the simulated mean and standard deviation in each land type are within 0.5 mg/kg of the data, and the share above 14.8 mg/kg is 43% on HL (data 43%) and 82% on MHL-1 (data 84%). Single realizations are much rougher than the kriging maps, which is how soil As varies from field to field.
The probability map from 500 realizations agrees with the KWS kriging probability (r = 0.99), so for the probability at a single location simulation adds little over Gaussian kriging. What it adds is the uncertainty of the total: the expected contaminated area is 59% of the upazila, with a 90% interval of 56% to 62% (about 18,200 ha). On HL the interval is 40% to 47%, on MHL-1 78% to 86%.
This expected area is not the same quantity as the delineated area in Section 7. Delineation counts nodes whose probability exceeds 0.55. The simulation counts the area expected to exceed 14.8 mg/kg, including the contaminated fields scattered inside areas declared clean. On HL the two differ (43% against 30%), which is the risk-β of the delineation expressed as area. The interval is a lower bound, because the trend coefficients and variogram models are held fixed.

title: Uncertainty of Geostatistical Risk Mapping of Paddy Soil Arsenic
section: Improvement 4: judging each land type against its own background
text:
Improvement 4: judging each land type against its own background
The paper used one threshold, 14.8 mg/kg, the upper baseline of MHL-1. For HL fields this threshold is well above their own background (5.2 to 8.9 mg/kg in non-rice HL soils). A HL field at 14 mg/kg is not “contaminated” under the paper’s rule, although it holds about twice its natural As. Using the upper baseline of each land type as its own threshold measures the As added by irrigation in both strata on the same footing. The same realizations are reused.


Code
# Upper end of each land type's own baseline: 8.9 mg/kg on highland, 14.8 mg/kg on medium highland.
thr_node = np.where(gHL == 1, BASELINE["HL"][1], BASELINE["MHL-1"][1])
above_own = sims > thr_node[None, :]
# Area above 14.8 mg/kg, beside the area above the land type's own baseline.
own_tbl = pd.DataFrame([{"area": name, "threshold_mg_kg": thr,

                        for name, nodes, idx, thr in [("HL", gh, h_idx, BASELINE["HL"][1]), ("MHL-1", gm, m_idx, BASELINE["MHL-1"][1])]])
display(own_tbl.round(1))

p_own = above_own.mean(axis=0)

title: Uncertainty of Geostatistical Risk Mapping of Paddy Soil Arsenic
section: Improvement 5: soil arsenic in 2020 with uncertainty
text:
Improvement 5: soil arsenic in 2020 with uncertainty
The paper projected soil As to 2020, after 16 more years of irrigation, with its land-type equations (Eq. 11 for HL and Eq. 12 for MHL-1), and found that 75% of the sites would exceed 30 mg/kg. Two refinements are made here.

Uncertainty. The projection at site \(i\) is \(z_i + 16\,\hat\beta_{yr}\): the measured value plus 16 years of the fitted annual increase. Its uncertainty comes from the standard error of \(\hat\beta_{yr}\), a 95% interval of \(\pm\, t_{0.975}\, 16\, \mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_{yr})\). Keeping the measured value avoids replacing each field by its regression estimate.
Mass balance as an independent check. The paper’s discussion gives a simple mass balance: 1 m of irrigation water per rice crop, uniform deposition into the top 15 cm and a bulk density of 1.2 g/cm³. One crop then adds \(1000\,\text{L/m}^2 \times \text{WAs} / 180\,\text{kg/m}^2 = 5.56 \times \text{WAs}\) mg/kg with WAs in mg/L, if all As is retained. Sixteen crops add \(89 \times \text{WAs}\) mg/kg.

The HL slope is taken from the four-variable HL model refitted in Section 2. The coefficients printed as Eq. 11 in the paper are those of the MHL-1 model (Section 2), so the paper’s slope of 1.01 mg/kg per year is also shown.


Code
# Years from the 2004 sampling to the paper's 2020 horizon.
YEARS_AHEAD = 16
m_hl, m_mhl = models["HL fields"], models["Eq. 12, MHL-1, STW years only"]
# Slope of soil As on years of tubewell use, with its standard error and residual degrees of freedom.
slopes = {"HL, refitted (Section 2)": (m_hl["coef"]["yr"], m_hl["se"]["yr"], m_hl["dof"]),
          "HL, paper Eq. 11 as printed": (1.01, m_hl["se"]["yr"], m_hl["dof"]),
          "MHL-1, Eq. 12": (m_mhl["coef"]["yr"], m_mhl["se"]["yr"], m_mhl["dof"])}

# Point projection, and a 95% interval from the standard error of the slope.
def project(idx, slope, se, dof):
    add = YEARS_AHEAD * slope
    half = student_t.ppf(0.975, dof) * YEARS_AHEAD * se
    return z[idx] + add, z[idx] + add - half, z[idx] + add + half

# Apply each slope to the fields of that land type.
proj_rows = []
proj = {}
for name, idx in [("HL, refitted (Section 2)", h_idx), ("HL, paper Eq. 11 as printed", h_idx), ("MHL-1, Eq. 12", m_idx)]:
    c, lo, hi = project(idx, *slopes[name])
    proj[name] = c
    proj_rows.append({"model": name, "slope_mg_kg_per_yr": slopes[name][0], "SE": slopes[name][1],
                      "mean_2004": z[idx].mean(), "mean_2020": c.mean(), "mean_2020_95lo": lo.mean(), "mean_2020_95hi": hi.mean(),
                      "pct_sites_above_30": 100 * np.mean(c > 30), "pct_above_30_lo": 100 * np.mean(lo > 30), "pct_above_30_hi": 100 * np.mean(hi > 30)})
# Upper bound if each crop retains all the As it receives: 0.15 m soil depth, bulk density 1200 kg/m3.
mass = 1000.0 / (0.15 * 1200.0)          # mg/kg added per crop per mg/L of WAs
mb = z + YEARS_AHEAD * mass * df["WAS"].to_numpy(float)
for name, idx in [("HL, mass balance (full retention)", h_idx), ("MHL-1, mass balance (full retention)", m_idx)]:
    proj_rows.append({"model": name, "slope_mg_kg_per_yr": mass * df["WAS"].to_numpy(float)[idx].mean(), "mean_2004": z[idx].mean(),
                      "mean_2020": mb[idx].mean(), "pct_sites_above_30": 100 * np.mean(mb[idx] > 30)})
proj_tbl = pd.DataFrame(proj_rows)
display(proj_tbl.round(2))

# Share of fields above 30 mg/kg, the level highlighted on the paper's 2020 figure.
all_2020_refit = np.r_[proj["HL, refitted (Section 2)"], proj["MHL-1, Eq. 12"]]
all_2020_paper = np.r_[proj["HL, paper Eq. 11 as printed"], proj["MHL-1, Eq. 12"]]
print(f"Sites above 30 mg/kg in 2020:  paper equations {100 * np.mean(all_2020_paper > 30):.0f}%   refitted HL slope {100 * np.mean(all_2020_refit > 30):.0f}%   "
      f"mass balance {100 * np.mean(mb > 30):.0f}%   (paper: 75%)")
print(f"Retention implied by the regression slopes (slope / mass-balance input):  HL {m_hl['coef']['yr'] / (mass * df.loc[h_idx, 'WAS'].mean()):.2f}   "
      f"MHL-1 {m_mhl['coef']['yr'] / (mass * df.loc[m_idx, 'WAS'].mean()):.2f}")

# Measured 2004 values, the regression projection, and the mass-balance projection.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8), sharey=True)
for ax, (lt, idx, key) in zip(axes, [("HL", h_idx, "HL, refitted (Section 2)"), ("MHL-1", m_idx, "MHL-1, Eq. 12")]):
    bins_ = np.linspace(0, 80, 33)
    ax.hist(z[idx], bins=bins_, alpha=0.6, label="2004 (measured)", color="tab:blue")
    ax.hist(proj[key], bins=bins_, alpha=0.6, label="2020 (regression)", color="tab:red")
    ax.hist(mb[idx], bins=bins_, histtype="step", lw=1.6, label="2020 (mass balance)", color="k")
    if lt == "HL":
        ax.hist(proj["HL, paper Eq. 11 as printed"], bins=bins_, histtype="step", lw=1.2, ls="--", color="tab:orange", label="2020 (paper Eq. 11 slope)")
    ax.axvline(30, color="0.4", ls=":")
    ax.set_title(f"{lt}: soil As in 2004 and 2020", fontsize=10); ax.set_xlabel("Soil As (mg/kg)")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)

Reading the results.

The paper’s figure of 75% depends on the mislabeled HL slope. With the slope printed in Eq. 11 (1.01 mg/kg per year), 68% of sites exceed 30 mg/kg in 2020, close to the paper’s 75%. With the refitted HL slope (0.41 mg/kg per year) the share falls to 49%. MHL-1 is unaffected: 87% of its sites exceed 30 mg/kg either way.
The uncertainty is large for HL. Within the 95% interval of the slopes, the share of MHL-1 sites above 30 mg/kg is 67% to 97%. For HL it is 3% to 12% with the refitted slope.
Mass balance gives a similar answer. Retaining all As from 1 m of irrigation water per year raises soil As by 0.63 (HL) and 0.80 (MHL-1) mg/kg per year at the mean water As, and puts 52% of sites above 30 mg/kg in 2020.
The implied retention is plausible on HL but not on MHL-1. The regression slope is 65% of the mass-balance input on HL, consistent with strong but incomplete retention. On MHL-1 it is 125% of the input, which is physically impossible if 1 m of water is the only source. Years of operation is a cross-sectional proxy here: older wells may sit in areas with higher background, receive more water, or the field nearest the STW may receive more than the average deposition. The MHL-1 projection should therefore be read as an upper estimate.

Either way, soil As keeps rising wherever As-rich groundwater is used, and a substantial share of rice fields is projected to pass 30 mg/kg, the level the paper associates with yield loss.

title: Uncertainty of Geostatistical Risk Mapping of Paddy Soil Arsenic
text:
Conclusions and limitations
Replication

Summary statistics, correlations and the main regression model (Eq. 10, R² 0.43) reproduce the paper exactly from the archived data.
The validation scores and contaminated areas of the paper are reproduced on a split that matches its validation statistics: KWS improves RMSE over OK by 12% (paper 13.6%) and delineates 58% of the upazila as contaminated, 99% of MHL-1 and 30% of HL (paper 62%, 99% and 34%).
The coefficients printed as Eq. 11 (HL) belong to the MHL-1 model. The HL model has a yearly increase of 0.41 mg/kg, not 1.01.

What the extensions add

On average over 100 splits, the gain from secondary information is about 3% at random locations and about 9% when whole blocks are held out. KWS is not reliably better than RK, and cokriging with the loading factor does not beat OK.
A land-type indicator in a single RK model, or KWS with OK on MHL-1, are at least as accurate as the paper’s KWS and simpler to fit.
Kriging variances are reasonably calibrated (coverage 86% to 91% of a nominal 90%), with somewhat heavy tails.
Conditional simulation puts the area with soil As above 14.8 mg/kg at 56% to 62% of the upazila (90% interval), and shows that the delineated map understates contamination on HL.
Against its own baseline, 85% of HL is enriched, as much as MHL-1.
With the corrected HL slope, about half of the sites, not three quarters, are projected to exceed 30 mg/kg by 2020. MHL-1 remains at about 87%.

Limitations

The calibration/validation split of the paper is not archived; the split used here was matched on summary statistics.
The 74 non-rice soils are not in the data files, so the baseline values are taken from the paper.
The kriging systems use all calibration data, not the paper’s 50 neighbours.
One exponential structure is fitted to every variogram, and the LMC shares a single range.
The simulations hold the trend and variogram parameters fixed, so the intervals of the contaminated area are lower bounds.
The 2020 projection assumes a linear build-up and uses years of operation, a cross-sectional proxy, to estimate it.

title: Uncertainty of Geostatistical Risk Mapping of Paddy Soil Arsenic
text:
Exercises

Replace the 4 km lag limit by 8 km. How do the range of the soil As variogram and the Table 2 scores change?
Use 50 nearest neighbours instead of all data in each kriging system, as the paper did, and check whether any RMSE moves by more than 0.1 mg/kg.
Add STW years to the RK trend by kriging a map of years of operation from the fields. Does the gain justify the extra uncertainty of an interpolated covariate?
Repeat Section 9 for the spatially blocked folds. Are the kriging variances still well calibrated when the nearest calibration field is far away?
In Section 10, draw the HL trend coefficients from their sampling distribution in each realization. How much wider does the interval of the contaminated area become?
Choose the critical probability by minimizing a cost, for example a false “clean” decision costing three times a false “contaminated” one, and redraw the delineation map.

title: Diabetes and Obesity in US Counties: Multivariate Poisson Cokriging
text:
Overview
A county rate is a count divided by a population. Its reliability depends on that population: a rate from 2,000 adults scatters far more around the true risk than a rate from 2 million. Poisson kriging (Monestiez et al., 2006; Goovaerts, 2005) builds this into kriging. It treats each count as Poisson given the underlying risk, removes the population-dependent noise from the semivariogram, and adds an error term of size m*/n to the diagonal of the kriging matrix, so small counties get less weight and are smoothed more.
Payares-Garcia et al. (2024) extended this to several diseases at once. Each count is modelled as multivariate Poisson, so two diseases share a joint risk at the same location. The risks are linked by a linear model of coregionalization (LMC), and the cokriging system carries Poisson terms for the variances and for the covariances between diseases measured in the same area. Their application predicted HIV incidence in 66 Pennsylvania counties, where 30% of the counts were suppressed, from HIV prevalence, chlamydia and gonorrhea.
Diabetes and obesity are a natural pair for this method. Obesity is the strongest modifiable risk factor for type 2 diabetes, and physical inactivity adds to both. If the three risks share spatial structure, counties with obesity and inactivity data carry information about diabetes, even where diabetes itself is missing.

Objectives








Objective
Question
Sections




1. Prepare the data
What do the counts and populations look like, and which counties have gaps?
1


2. Describe the data
How noisy are the rates, and how strongly are the three risks related?
2


3. Model the spatial structure
What are the Poisson semivariograms and cross-semivariograms, and what LMC fits them?
3 and 4


4. Smooth
How much does cokriging improve the leave-one-out estimate of diabetes risk in every county?
5


5. Predict
How well is diabetes predicted where it is hidden, at random or for whole states?
6


6. Test the choices
How sensitive are the results to the neighbourhood, model and error term?
7


7. Report
Where is risk high, how does it relate to social conditions, and where is the estimate least reliable?
8 and 9





Design notes

Crude risk. Poisson cokriging models crude risk, cases over adults. USDSS age-adjusted percentages are kept only for comparison.
The counts are model-based estimates. USDSS county numbers come from small-area models of survey data (BRFSS), not from registers. Section 2 compares their reported standard errors with Poisson noise, and Section 7 repeats the analysis with those standard errors as the error term.
Inactivity counts are approximate. USDSS gives inactivity only as an age-adjusted percentage, so the count is that percentage times the adult population.
Local neighbourhoods. With 3,108 counties and three variables, every prediction uses the k nearest counties of each variable (number_of_neighbors). Leave-one-out smoothing drops the county’s own diabetes count and keeps its own obesity and inactivity counts.
Rates in percent. All rates are in percent (pop_rate = 100), so semivariances are in squared percentage points.

Reading the results.

Size. 3,108 counties hold 258.0 million adults, 26.0 million of them with diagnosed diabetes (a national crude rate of 10.1%), 76.8 million with obesity (29.8%) and 52.1 million physically inactive (20.2%).
Population. County adult populations range from 37 (Loving County, Texas) to 7.8 million (Los Angeles County). The median is 20,600, and one county in ten has fewer than 3,900 adults. That range is why a Poisson model is needed.
Diabetes. Crude rates are highest across the Southeast, the Mississippi Delta, Appalachia (West Virginia and eastern Kentucky), and parts of Arizona and New Mexico (Apache County, Arizona, 15.5%; McKinley County, New Mexico, 15.2%). They are lowest in Colorado, the northern Rockies and parts of the upper Midwest and New England.
Obesity and inactivity. Both follow the southern and Appalachian pattern of diabetes, but obesity is also high across the Midwest and the northern Plains, where diabetes is moderate.
Gaps. 357 counties average fewer than five years: the 349 counties of Florida, Kentucky, Pennsylvania and Tennessee, and the eight former Connecticut counties (2020 and 2021 only). The adult share is imputed in 196 counties (120 in Kentucky, 67 in Pennsylvania, 8 in Connecticut and one in Texas), so the population at risk in those states is less certain than elsewhere.

title: Diabetes and Obesity in US Counties: Multivariate Poisson Cokriging
text:
Exploratory analysis

How noisy are the rates?
If every county had the same risk, the rates would scatter only by Poisson chance, and that scatter shrinks as the population grows. A funnel plot shows the rates against population with Poisson control limits around the national rate. Counties outside the limits differ by more than chance.
The second plot compares two measures of the error of a county estimate: the Poisson standard deviation of the crude rate, 100 √(m/n), which the Poisson cokriging model assumes, and the USDSS standard error of the count expressed as a rate, 100 se/n, which comes from the small-area model.


Code
# National crude rates, and a population grid for drawing the funnel limits
m_nat = {v: CASES[v].sum() / POP.sum() for v in VARS}
nn = np.logspace(np.log10(POP.min()), np.log10(POP.max()), 200)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.5))
for ax, v in zip(axes[:2], ["diab", "obes"]):
    p = m_nat[v]
    ax.scatter(POP, RATE[v], s=4, alpha=0.4)
    # 1.96 and 3.09 are the 95% and 99.8% normal limits around the national rate
    for z, ls in [(1.96, "--"), (3.09, ":")]:
        half = PR * z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nn)
        ax.plot(nn, PR * p + half, "k", ls=ls, lw=1); ax.plot(nn, PR * p - half, "k", ls=ls, lw=1)
    ax.axhline(PR * p, color="red", lw=1)
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("adults"); ax.set_ylabel("crude rate (%)")
    ax.set_title(f"{LABEL[v]}: funnel plot (95% and 99.8% limits)")

# Poisson standard deviation of the diabetes rate, set beside the USDSS standard error

Reading the results.

Real differences between counties, far above Poisson noise. 64% of counties lie outside the 99.8% Poisson limits for diabetes, and 73% and 74% for obesity and inactivity. The variance of the county rates is 24 times the mean Poisson variance for diabetes, 33 times for obesity and 44 times for inactivity. Most of the variation between counties is variation in risk, not chance. The Poisson term matters only in the smallest counties.
The data carry much more error than Poisson implies. The median USDSS standard error of a county diabetes rate is 1.65 percentage points, about seven times the Poisson standard deviation (0.22 points). Most counties form an upper band in the third plot; a smaller group has standard errors close to the Poisson line.

So the Poisson reliability term understates how uncertain the input estimates are. It is kept as the main model, because it is the method under study, and Section 7 repeats the analysis with the USDSS standard errors as the error term.

Pearson correlations of the crude rates and of the USDSS age-adjusted percentages, and the empirical Bayes rates (eb_risk), which shrink each crude rate towards the national rate according to its population. Because the populations are large, the empirical Bayes z-scores keep the rank order of the crude rates.

title: Diabetes and Obesity in US Counties: Multivariate Poisson Cokriging
text:
Population-weighted Poisson semivariograms
The semivariogram of risk is estimated from rates whose noise depends on population. Payares-Garcia et al. (2024, Eq. 12) weight each pair of counties by w = nᵢnⱼ/(nᵢ+nⱼ) and subtract the Poisson bias term, so pairs of small counties count less and the nugget created by Poisson noise is removed:
γ(h) = [Σ w (rᵢ − rⱼ)² − N(h) · bias] / (2 Σ w).
The cross-semivariogram (Eq. 13) uses the product of the two rate differences, and its bias term is the mean joint risk of the two diseases, r_lk = ρ √(R_l R_k) (shared_risk). Here ρ is the correlation of the two crude rates, as an estimate of the Poisson correlation of the counts within a county.

Package fix. Before this capstone, pck_variogram, poisson_cokrige and poisson_krige scaled the Poisson bias and reliability terms by pop_rate instead of pop_rate², which is correct only for pop_rate = 1. The terms now use the variance of a Poisson rate on the pop_rate scale, pop_rate² m*/n, so results in percent are exactly 100 times the results in proportions. The check below confirms this.



Code
# Scale check: percent (pop_rate = 100) against proportions (pop_rate = 1)
g1 = mpk.pck_variogram(XY, CASES["diab"], POP, pop_rate=1, maxd=MAXD, nbins=NBINS)[1]
g100 = mpk.pck_variogram(XY, CASES["diab"], POP, pop_rate=PR, maxd=MAXD, nbins=NBINS)[1]
print("max |gamma(percent) - 100^2 gamma(proportion)| =", float(np.abs(g100 - PR**2 * g1).max()))


max |gamma(percent) - 100^2 gamma(proportion)| = 8.881784197001252e-16




Code
# Three outcomes. Their crude-rate correlation is the within-county Poisson correlation.
P_ALL = len(VARS)
PAIRS = [(a, b) for a in range(P_ALL) for b in range(a + 1, P_ALL)]
RHO = np.corrcoef([RATE[v] for v in VARS])

# Population-weighted Poisson semivariograms for a chosen set of counties
def empirical_variograms(idx_by_var, maxd=MAXD, nbins=NBINS):
    # idx_by_var: one index array per variable (the counties where it is observed).
    # Direct variograms use each variable's own counties, cross-variograms the shared ones.
    dv, cv, shared = [], [], {}
    for l, v in enumerate(VARS[:len(idx_by_var)]):
        o = idx_by_var[l]
        dv.append(mpk.pck_variogram(XY[o], CASES[v][o], POP[o], pop_rate=PR, maxd=maxd, nbins=nbins))
    P = len(idx_by_var)
    for a, b in [(a, b) for a in range(P) for b in range(a + 1, P)]:
        o = np.intersect1d(idx_by_var[a], idx_by_var[b])
        va, vb = VARS[a], VARS[b]
        rlk = mpk.shared_risk(RATE[va][o], RATE[vb][o], RHO[a, b])
        shared[(a, b)] = float(np.mean(rlk))
        cv.append(mpk.pck_crossvariogram(XY[o], CASES[va][o], CASES[vb][o], POP[o], rlk,
                                         pop_rate=PR, maxd=maxd, nbins=nbins))
    return dv, cv, shared

# All counties out to 800 km for the fit, and out to 1,600 km for the longer plot
ALL = np.arange(len(gdf))
t0 = time.time()
DV, CV, SHARED = empirical_variograms([ALL] * P_ALL)
DV_LONG, CV_LONG, _ = empirical_variograms([ALL] * P_ALL, maxd=1600, nbins=32)
print(f"Empirical (cross-)semivariograms in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")
print("Mean shared risk r_lk (percent):", {f"{VARS[a]}-{VARS[b]}": round(s, 2) for (a, b), s in SHARED.items()})
print("Pairs in the first lag class:", int(DV[0][2][0]))

title: Diabetes and Obesity in US Counties: Multivariate Poisson Cokriging
text:
Linear model of coregionalization
The LMC uses one spatial structure with a common range for all three risks, plus a nugget:
C_lk(h) = B0_lk · 1(h = 0) + B_lk · exp(−h/a).
fit_lmc fits each entry of the nugget matrix B0 and the sill matrix B by weighted least squares (weights are the numbers of pairs), chooses the common range a by a grid search over all six semivariograms, and projects B0 and B to the nearest positive semi-definite matrices, which is what makes the model valid for cokriging. The fit uses lags up to 800 km, where the neighbourhoods used for kriging lie. The paper used a stable model with no nugget; the package offers exponential and spherical structures, and the county data need a nugget (see below).


Code
# Common range on a 25 km grid. The exponential model with a nugget is the one used below.
RANGE_GRID = np.arange(100, 1501, 25)
lmc_exp = mpk.fit_lmc(DV, CV, PAIRS, P_ALL, 300, model="Exp", fit_range=True, nugget=True, range_grid=RANGE_GRID)
lmc_sph = mpk.fit_lmc(DV, CV, PAIRS, P_ALL, 600, model="Sph", fit_range=True, nugget=True, range_grid=RANGE_GRID)
lmc_nonug = mpk.fit_lmc(DV, CV, PAIRS, P_ALL, 300, model="Exp", fit_range=True, nugget=False, range_grid=RANGE_GRID)
LMC = lmc_exp
for name, m in [("Exponential + nugget (main model)", lmc_exp), ("Spherical + nugget", lmc_sph),
                ("Exponential, no nugget", lmc_nonug)]:
    extra = f" (practical range {3 * m.range:.0f} km)" if m.model == "Exp" else ""
    print(f"{name}: range parameter {m.range:.0f} km{extra}")

# Nugget B0, structured sill B, and the correlations each matrix implies

tabs = {

    "structured sill B": pd.DataFrame(LMC.B, lab, lab),

tabs["nugget correlation"] = pd.DataFrame(LMC.B0 / np.outer(d0, d0), lab, lab)
display(pd.concat(tabs, axis=0).round(3))

Reading the results.

Shape. All six semivariograms rise steeply over the first 200 km and then slowly. Inactivity and the diabetes-inactivity cross-semivariogram keep rising beyond 800 km, which reflects the broad contrast between the South and the West. The LMC is fitted up to 800 km, the scale that matters for local kriging, and the long-range rise is left to the local neighbourhoods.
Main model. The exponential model with a nugget fits best, with a common range parameter of 325 km (practical range about 975 km). The spherical model gives almost the same curves with a range of 725 km. Without a nugget, the fitted range drops to the lower end of the search grid (100 km) and the model misses the semivariograms near the origin.
A large nugget. The nugget is 57% of the total sill for diabetes, 77% for obesity and 68% for inactivity. The Poisson noise has already been removed from the semivariograms, so this is variation between neighbouring counties that the 50 km lag classes cannot resolve, plus the error of the USDSS estimates.
Correlation sits in both parts. The structural correlation of diabetes is 0.48 with obesity and 0.71 with inactivity. The nugget correlations are about 0.69 for every pair. So a county’s own obesity and inactivity carry information about its diabetes even where its neighbours do not, which is what co-located cokriging uses.
Valid model. All eigenvalues of B and B0 are positive, so the fitted LMC is positive definite.

title: Diabetes and Obesity in US Counties: Multivariate Poisson Cokriging
section: Smoothing: leave-one-out estimates of diabetes risk
text:
Smoothing: leave-one-out estimates of diabetes risk
For every county, diabetes risk is estimated from the k = 32 nearest diabetes counts of the other counties, and, for cokriging, from the 32 nearest obesity and inactivity counts, including those of the county itself. Comparing the estimate with the county’s own rate is a leave-one-out cross-validation. Three estimators are compared:

PK: univariate Poisson kriging of diabetes.
PCK-2: Poisson cokriging with obesity.
PCK-3: Poisson cokriging with obesity and inactivity.

The scores follow the paper: mean error (bias), mean absolute error, mean squared prediction error (MSPE) and Pearson’s ρ between estimate and observed rate. The z-scores, error divided by kriging standard deviation, should have a mean near 0 and a standard deviation near 1 if the kriging variance is right, and 90% of rates should fall inside the 90% intervals.


Code
# Coregionalization of the first P variables, in the order diabetes, obesity, inactivity
def sub_lmc(lmc, P):
    return mpk.LMC(lmc.B[:P, :P], lmc.range, lmc.model, lmc.B0[:P, :P])

# One record per variable: coordinates, counts, and population where that variable is observed
def datasets(P, target_idx=ALL, aux_idx=None, noise=None):
    # Target (diabetes) at target_idx; auxiliaries at aux_idx (default: all counties).
    aux_idx = aux_idx or [ALL] * (P - 1)
    idx = [target_idx] + list(aux_idx)
    out = []
    for l in range(P):
        o, v = idx[l], VARS[l]
        d = dict(x=XY[o, 0], y=XY[o, 1], cases=CASES[v][o], pop=POP[o])
        if noise is not None:
            d["noise_var"] = noise[v][o]
        out.append(d)
    return out

# Bias, absolute and squared error, correlation, and coverage of the 90% interval
def scores(pred, var, obs):
    e = pred - obs
    sd = np.sqrt(np.clip(var, 1e-12, None))
    z = e / sd
    return {"ME": e.mean(), "MAE": np.abs(e).mean(), "MSPE": np.mean(e**2),
            "rho": np.corrcoef(pred, obs)[0, 1], "z mean": z.mean(), "z SD": z.std(),
            "cover 90%": np.mean(np.abs(e) <= norm.ppf(0.95) * sd)}

# Leave-one-out Poisson kriging, or cokriging with obesity and optionally inactivity
def smooth(P, lmc=None, k=K, mean_rate="global", noise=None):
    lmc = sub_lmc(lmc or LMC, P)
    return mpk.poisson_cokrige(datasets(P, noise=noise), 0, lmc, pop_rate=PR, shared_mean=SHARED,
                               smooth=True, number_of_neighbors=k, mean_rate=mean_rate, use_gpu=USE_GPU)

# PK is diabetes alone, PCK-2 adds obesity, and PCK-3 adds inactivity as well
SM, rows = {}, {}
for P, name in [(1, "PK"), (2, "PCK-2"), (3, "PCK-3")]:
    t0 = time.time()
    SM[name] = smooth(P)
    rows[name] = scores(SM[name]["rate_pred"], SM[name]["rate_var"], RATE["diab"])
    rows[name]["seconds"] = time.time() - t0
smooth_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
smooth_tab["MSPE drop vs PK (%)"] = 100 * (1 - smooth_tab["MSPE"] / smooth_tab.loc["PK", "MSPE"])
smooth_tab.round(3)

Reading the results.

Cokriging improves the estimate a lot. The MSPE falls from 1.89 for PK to 1.44 with obesity (24% lower) and 1.29 with obesity and inactivity (32% lower). The correlation with the observed rate rises from 0.63 to 0.74 and 0.77, and the mean absolute error falls from 1.04 to 0.88 points. All three are almost unbiased (mean error −0.02 points).
The maps show why. PK can only borrow from neighbours, so its map is a regional surface. PCK-3 also uses the county’s own obesity and inactivity, so it recovers county detail, for example high single counties in the Dakotas (Todd, Dewey and Rolette), southeastern Missouri and southern Ohio.
Cokriging intervals are slightly too narrow. The z-scores have a standard deviation of 0.92 for PK and 1.11 for PCK-3, and 92% and 86% of rates fall inside the 90% intervals. The single common range and the PSD projection make the LMC tie diabetes to the auxiliaries a little more tightly than the data support in some regions (Section 6 shows Florida).
Speed. With k = 32 neighbours per variable, smoothing all 3,108 counties takes about one second for PCK-3.

title: Diabetes and Obesity in US Counties: Multivariate Poisson Cokriging
text:
Prediction where diabetes is missing
The paper’s main use of Poisson cokriging is prediction where the target is not observed: counties with suppressed counts, or areas outside a survey. The USDSS data are complete, so missing data are created by hiding diabetes:

Random masks. Diabetes is hidden in 30%, 50% or 65% of counties, chosen at random; obesity and inactivity stay observed everywhere. Each design is repeated with different masks.
The paper’s design. Diabetes observed in 35% of counties, obesity in 70% (including those 35%) and inactivity in all, as in the simulation of Payares-Garcia et al. (2024).
State holdouts. Diabetes is hidden for a whole state: Kentucky, Tennessee, Florida and Pennsylvania, the four states with a year missing in USDSS. Predictions there must come from neighbouring states and from the state’s own obesity and inactivity.

In every replicate the semivariograms and the LMC are refitted from the observed data only, so the hidden counties play no part in the model. The predicted risk is compared with the hidden crude rate.


Code
# Refit the semivariograms and the LMC using only the counties still observed
def fit_from(idx_by_var):
    dv, cv, shared = empirical_variograms(idx_by_var)
    P = len(idx_by_var)
    pairs = [(a, b) for a in range(P) for b in range(a + 1, P)]
    lmc = mpk.fit_lmc(dv, cv, pairs, P, 300, model="Exp", fit_range=True, nugget=True, range_grid=RANGE_GRID)
    return lmc, shared

# Predict the hidden counties. Obesity and inactivity can still be observed there.
def predict_hidden(hidden, idx_by_var, lmc, shared, P, k=K):
    obs_idx = [idx_by_var[0]] + list(idx_by_var[1:P])
    ds = datasets(P, target_idx=obs_idx[0], aux_idx=obs_idx[1:])
    r = mpk.poisson_cokrige(ds, 0, sub_lmc(lmc, P), pop_rate=PR, shared_mean=shared,
                            coords_pred=XY[hidden], number_of_neighbors=k, mean_rate="global", use_gpu=USE_GPU)
    return r["pred"], r["var"]

# Random masks, the paper's 35/70/100 design, and four whole-state holdouts
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
pred_rows, keep_preds = [], {}
t0 = time.time()

designs = [(f"random {int(100 * f)}% hidden", f) for f in (0.30, 0.50, 0.65)] + [("paper: 35 / 70 / 100%", None)]
for name, frac in designs:
    for rep in range(N_REPS):
        # Hide a random share of diabetes counts. Obesity and inactivity stay observed everywhere.
        if frac is not None:
            hidden = np.sort(rng.choice(len(gdf), int(round(frac * len(gdf))), replace=False))
            obs_t = np.setdiff1d(ALL, hidden)
            idx_by_var = [obs_t, ALL, ALL]
        else:
            # Paper design: diabetes in 35% of counties, obesity in 70%, inactivity in every county
            perm = rng.permutation(len(gdf))
            obs_t = np.sort(perm[: int(0.35 * len(gdf))])
            obs_o = np.sort(perm[: int(0.70 * len(gdf))])
            hidden = np.setdiff1d(ALL, obs_t)
            idx_by_var = [obs_t, obs_o, ALL]
        lmc_r, shared_r = fit_from(idx_by_var)
        for P, est in [(1, "PK"), (2, "PCK-2"), (3, "PCK-3")]:
            pr_, va_ = predict_hidden(hidden, idx_by_var, lmc_r, shared_r, P)
            pred_rows.append({"design": name, "rep": rep, "estimator": est, "range": lmc_r.range,
                              **scores(pr_, va_, RATE["diab"][hidden])})

# Hide diabetes for one whole state and predict it from the rest of the country
for st in HOLDOUT_STATES:
    hidden = np.flatnonzero(gdf["state"].to_numpy() == st)
    obs_t = np.setdiff1d(ALL, hidden)
    idx_by_var = [obs_t, ALL, ALL]
    lmc_r, shared_r = fit_from(idx_by_var)
    for P, est in [(1, "PK"), (2, "PCK-2"), (3, "PCK-3")]:
        pr_, va_ = predict_hidden(hidden, idx_by_var, lmc_r, shared_r, P)
        keep_preds[(st, est)] = (hidden, pr_, va_)
        pred_rows.append({"design": f"state: {st}", "rep": 0, "estimator": est, "range": lmc_r.range,
                          **scores(pr_, va_, RATE["diab"][hidden])})
print(f"Prediction experiments: {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
PRED = pd.DataFrame(pred_rows)

Reading the results.

Random masks. PCK-3 lowers the MSPE by 30% to 32% at all three masking levels (PK 1.94 to 2.07, PCK-3 1.34 to 1.44), and raises ρ from about 0.60 to about 0.75. The gain hardly changes as more counties are hidden, because obesity and inactivity are still observed in every hidden county.
The paper’s design. With obesity missing in 30% of counties, PCK-2 gains only 13%, but adding inactivity, which is observed everywhere, brings the gain back to 31%. The auxiliary that is observed at the prediction location matters most.
Intervals. PK covers 91% to 92% of the hidden rates with its 90% intervals; PCK-3 covers 85% to 86%.
States. Cokriging lowers the MSPE by 41% in Kentucky (2.61 to 1.53) and 47% in Pennsylvania (2.97 to 1.59). PK overestimates both states (by 0.61 and 1.09 points), because their neighbours have higher rates; the auxiliaries cut that bias roughly in half. The Kentucky maps show PCK-3 recovering county highs in the east and west that PK smooths away.
Florida and Tennessee need care. In both, PCK-2 beats PCK-3 (Florida 3.49 against 3.91, Tennessee 1.48 against 1.55). Florida is underestimated by about one point by every estimator: its crude rate is high because its population is old, and the inactivity count, built from an age-adjusted percentage, does not carry that age effect.
Pennsylvania. Even with cokriging, ρ within Pennsylvania is only 0.22. Its adult shares are imputed (Section 1), which adds error to the crude rates the predictions are compared with.

title: Diabetes and Obesity in US Counties: Multivariate Poisson Cokriging
text:
Sensitivity
The leave-one-out smoothing of Section 5 is repeated with one choice changed at a time. PK and PCK-3 are shown, so the gain from cokriging can be seen under each choice.

Neighbourhood size: k = 8, 16, 64 and 128 instead of 32.
Covariance model: spherical instead of exponential, and exponential with no nugget.
Range: the fitted range halved and doubled.
Mean rate in the Poisson term: the local rate of the neighbours (the package default) instead of the national rate.
Error term: the USDSS standard error (100 se/n)² instead of the Poisson variance.
Rounded counts: the five-year means rounded to integers.



Code
# Same coregionalization with the range rescaled
def with_range(lmc, factor):
    return mpk.LMC(lmc.B, lmc.range * factor, lmc.model, lmc.B0)

# Extra variance from the published USDSS standard errors, on the percent scale
USDSS_NOISE = {
    "diab": (PR * gdf["diab_cases_se"].to_numpy() / POP) ** 2,
    "obes": (PR * gdf["obes_cases_se"].to_numpy() / POP) ** 2,
    "inact": (gdf["inact_pct_aa_se"].to_numpy()) ** 2,     # USDSS gives inactivity as a percentage with its SE
}

# One change at a time: neighbourhood, covariance, range, mean rate, or the USDSS error term
runs = [("main: Exp + nugget, k = 32", dict())]
runs += [(f"k = {k}", dict(k=k)) for k in (8, 16, 64, 128)]
runs += [("spherical + nugget", dict(lmc=lmc_sph)), ("exponential, no nugget", dict(lmc=lmc_nonug)),
         ("range x 0.5", dict(lmc=with_range(LMC, 0.5))), ("range x 2", dict(lmc=with_range(LMC, 2.0))),
         ("local mean rate", dict(mean_rate="local")), ("USDSS SE as error term", dict(noise=USDSS_NOISE))]
# Leave-one-out scores for PK and PCK-3 under each setting
sens = []
for name, kw in runs:
    for P, est in [(1, "PK"), (3, "PCK-3")]:
        r = smooth(P, **kw)
        sens.append({"setting": name, "estimator": est, **scores(r["rate_pred"], r["rate_var"], RATE["diab"])})

# Rounded counts: five-year means are fractional, so the scores are repeated on whole cases
saved = {v: CASES[v].copy() for v in VARS}
for v in VARS:
    CASES[v] = np.round(saved[v])
for P, est in [(1, "PK"), (3, "PCK-3")]:
    r = smooth(P)
    sens.append({"setting": "rounded counts", "estimator": est, **scores(r["rate_pred"], r["rate_var"], RATE["diab"])})
CASES.update(saved)

SENS = pd.DataFrame(sens)
sens_tab = SENS.pivot(index="setting", columns="estimator", values=["MSPE", "rho", "z SD", "cover 90%"])
sens_tab[("MSPE drop (%)", "")] = 100 * (1 - sens_tab[("MSPE", "PCK-3")] / sens_tab[("MSPE", "PK")])
sens_tab.reindex([n for n, _ in runs] + ["rounded counts"]).round(3)

Reading the results.

Neighbourhood. Results are the same for k = 16 to 128 (MSPE 1.29 to 1.30 for PCK-3). Only k = 8 is slightly worse (1.32).
Model and range. The spherical model and a halved or doubled range change the MSPE by less than 0.03, and the gain from cokriging stays between 29% and 32% in every setting.
The nugget is needed for honest variances. Without it, the MSPE rises to 1.39 and the z-score SD to 1.74, and only 70% of rates fall in the 90% intervals.
The Poisson term is small here. The local or global mean rate and rounding the counts to integers make no difference, because the Poisson variance is small next to the nugget in all but the smallest counties.
USDSS standard errors as the error term. The MSPE of PCK-3 rises slightly (1.35), because large standard errors push each estimate further towards its neighbours. But the intervals become honest: the z-score SD is 0.93 and coverage is 92%. When the inputs are model-based estimates, their own standard errors are the better error term.

title: Diabetes and Obesity in US Counties: Multivariate Poisson Cokriging
text:
Risk patterns and social context
The PCK-3 leave-one-out estimate is the diabetes risk expected in a county from its neighbours and from its own obesity and inactivity. Two quantities are mapped from it:

Probability of high risk. P(risk > national crude rate), from a normal approximation with the PCK-3 estimate and kriging variance. Counties with a probability above 0.9 are flagged.
Local excess. The z-score of the observed rate against the PCK-3 estimate, (observed − estimate)/SD. A positive value means more diabetes than the neighbours, obesity and inactivity predict.

Both are then related to the social and economic covariates with Spearman correlations, and summarized by state.

Reading the results.

High risk. 954 counties, home to 24.7% of adults, have a probability above 0.9 that their diabetes risk exceeds the national crude rate of 10.1%. 691 of them are in the South, covering most of the Southeast, the Mississippi Delta and Appalachia, and 183 in the Midwest. West Virginia, Mississippi, Alabama, South Carolina, Arkansas and Louisiana have the highest population-weighted risk (12.3% to 13.4%).
Expected risk follows social disadvantage. The PCK-3 risk correlates with poverty (0.50), the Social Vulnerability Index (0.49), the share of non-Hispanic Black residents (0.42) and the uninsured share (0.38), and negatively with median household income (−0.47) and the food environment index (−0.44).
The local excess is about age. 130 counties have more diabetes than PCK-3 expects (z above 2), and 104 less. The excess correlates most with the share aged 65 and over (0.54) and the rural share (0.39), and hardly at all with poverty or SVI. Counties older than their neighbours have more diabetes than neighbours, obesity and inactivity predict, because crude risk depends on age and the inactivity input is age-adjusted. Age is the next variable to add (Exercise 5).

Reading the results.

A floor set by the nugget. The PCK-3 standard deviation lies between 0.96 and 1.48 points, with most counties close to 1.0. That floor is the nugget: variation between neighbouring counties that neither the neighbours nor the auxiliaries can predict.
Where reliability is lowest. The largest standard deviations are in the sparsely populated Great Plains and the interior West, in counties with a few hundred adults or fewer (Loving, King and Kenedy in Texas; McPherson, Arthur and Blaine in Nebraska). The standard deviation falls with population (Spearman −0.54) and rises with the distance to the neighbours (0.84).
Cokriging roughly halves the variance. PCK-3 has 52% to 55% less kriging variance than PK in most counties, with the smallest reductions along the Great Plains.
Two different uncertainties. The kriging standard deviation is almost unrelated to the USDSS standard error (Spearman 0.09). The first measures how well a county’s risk can be predicted from the others; the second measures the uncertainty of the USDSS estimate itself. Both are needed to judge a county value.

title: Diabetes and Obesity in US Counties: Multivariate Poisson Cokriging
text:
Summary

Data. Five-year means of USDSS diabetes, obesity and inactivity counts for 3,108 counties, with adult populations from 37 to 7.8 million. Between-county differences in risk are far larger than Poisson noise, and the USDSS standard errors are about seven times the Poisson standard deviation.
Spatial structure. One exponential structure (range parameter 325 km) plus a large nugget (57% of the diabetes sill) fits all six Poisson semivariograms. Diabetes is correlated with obesity and inactivity both in the structured part (0.48 and 0.71) and in the nugget (about 0.69).
Smoothing. Trivariate Poisson cokriging lowers the leave-one-out MSPE of diabetes risk by 32% against univariate Poisson kriging (1.29 against 1.89) and raises ρ from 0.63 to 0.77.
Prediction. With diabetes hidden in 30% to 65% of counties, the gain is 30% to 32%. For whole states it is 26% to 47%. The gain comes mainly from the auxiliary data at the prediction location.
Limits of the auxiliaries. Florida and Tennessee show that an age-adjusted auxiliary can mislead for a crude target. The local excess of diabetes is explained mostly by age.
Uncertainty. Cokriging roughly halves the kriging variance, but its 90% intervals cover 86% of rates. Using the USDSS standard errors as the error term gives honest intervals (92%).
Package. The k-NN leave-one-out smoothing, heterotopic k-NN prediction, the LMC nugget, user-supplied error variances and the pop_rate scaling fix were added to multi_poisson_kriging for this capstone.


Limitations

Modelled counts. The USDSS county counts are small-area model estimates. The Poisson model describes sampling noise in registered counts, which these data do not have, and the USDSS standard errors describe a different kind of uncertainty. The method is shown on realistic risk surfaces, but the reliability terms are not the true error of the data.
Crude against age-adjusted. Crude diabetes risk depends strongly on age, while the inactivity count was built from an age-adjusted percentage. Counties with many older adults, such as much of Florida, are therefore harder to predict from inactivity.
One structure. The LMC has one structure with a common range plus a nugget. The semivariograms keep rising beyond 800 km (the South against the West), which a local neighbourhood absorbs but a single global model does not describe.
Point support. Counties are treated as points at their geometric centroids. The paper used population-weighted centroids; area-to-area Poisson kriging would use the population distribution inside each county.
Five-year means. Averaging 2020 to 2024 hides trends, and four states have a year missing.
Shared risk. The joint risk r_lk uses the correlation of county rates as the Poisson correlation within a county. Its effect is small here, because the Poisson terms are small next to the nugget.



Exercises

Make obesity the target and diabetes and inactivity the auxiliaries. Is the gain from cokriging symmetric?
Fit the models to each year separately and predict the missing state-years (FL 2021, KY 2023, PA 2023, TN 2024), which are real missing data. Compare with the five-year model.
Add diabetes mortality as a fourth variable. Where is it missing, and does it help?
Replace the inactivity count with a crude count, for example by applying the age-adjusted percentage to the age structure of each county, and repeat the Florida holdout.
Use the share aged 65 and over as an external drift (regression with Poisson cokriging of the residual risk). How much of the PCK-3 gain remains?
Compute population-weighted centroids from census tracts and repeat Section 5.

title: Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV in California Counties: Poisson Kriging in Space, Time and Across Diseases
text:
Overview
County rates of rare infections are unreliable in small counties. A county of 1,200 people with one case of early syphilis has a rate of 83 per 100,000; with none, its rate is zero. Poisson kriging (Goovaerts, 2005, 2006) treats each count as Poisson given an underlying risk, removes the population-dependent noise from the semivariogram, and adds an error term B·m*/n to the diagonal of the kriging system, so that small counties are smoothed towards their neighbours.
Three extensions are compared:

Area-to-area (ATA) and area-to-point (ATP) Poisson kriging represent each county by a set of points inside it instead of its centroid. ATA accounts for the size and shape of counties, which matters in California, where San Bernardino County is 400 times larger than San Francisco. ATP turns county rates into a continuous risk surface whose population-weighted average reproduces the county estimate.
Poisson cokriging (Payares-Garcia et al., 2024) uses other diseases counted in the same counties. HIV shares transmission routes and risk groups with syphilis and gonorrhea, so their counts carry information about HIV, including in counties where HIV counts are suppressed.
Space-time Poisson kriging uses the same counties in other years. Rates of sexually transmitted infections change over years but county rankings are persistent, so the county’s own history may be the best neighbour.

for d_ in DISEASES:
    c5, p5 = np.nansum(CASES[d_][:, -5:], 1), np.nansum(POP_STD[:, -5:], 1)
    r5 = B * c5 / p5
    sp, sp_log = neighbour_corr(r5, p5)
    yr = np.mean([np.corrcoef(RATE[d_][:, t], RATE[d_][:, t + 1])[0, 1] for t in range(len(YEARS) - 5, len(YEARS) - 1)])
    rows[d_] = {"space: 5 nearest counties": sp, "space, log rates": sp_log, "time: consecutive years": yr,
                "time: 2011 vs 2021": np.corrcoef(RATE[d_][:, YEARS == 2011][:, 0], RATE[d_][:, -1])[0, 1]}
info = pd.DataFrame(rows).T

# Cross-disease correlation with HIV in 2020-2021, using only counties where HIV is reported.
hiv_cases_2021 = chr_[chr_["year"].isin([2020, 2021])].groupby("fips")["hiv_cases"].mean().reindex(FIPS).to_numpy()
pop2021 = POP_STD[:, -2:].mean(1)
hiv_rate = B * hiv_cases_2021 / pop2021
ok = np.isfinite(hiv_rate)
for d_ in DISEASES:
    info.loc[d_, "across: with HIV (2020-21)"] = np.corrcoef(hiv_rate[ok], (B * CASES[d_][:, -2:].mean(1) / pop2021)[ok])[0, 1]

Reading the results.

Early syphilis rose 15.8-fold between 2001 and 2021, gonorrhea 3.4-fold and chlamydia 1.7-fold. In 2021, 17 counties had fewer than 12 early syphilis cases and 3 had none. Their rates are dominated by chance, as the funnel plot shows.
Space carries little information. A county’s rate correlates with the mean of its five nearest counties at 0.41 for chlamydia, 0.20 for gonorrhea and 0.02 for early syphilis. On log rates the correlations are about 0.4 for all three. A metropolitan core and its suburbs often differ more than counties far apart.
Time carries a lot. Rates in consecutive years correlate at 0.92 for all three infections, and even rates ten years apart correlate at 0.85 (chlamydia), 0.87 (gonorrhea) and 0.60 (early syphilis).

The kriging results in Sections 4 to 6 follow this ranking: time first, other diseases second, space last.

title: Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV in California Counties: Poisson Kriging in Space, Time and Across Diseases
text:
Poisson semivariograms with 58 counties
Two estimators of the risk semivariogram are compared, each averaged over the five annual maps 2017 to 2021 to reduce noise:

Population-weighted (Monestiez et al., 2006; pck_variogram): each pair is weighted by nᵢnⱼ/(nᵢ+nⱼ) and the Poisson bias B²m* is subtracted.
Unweighted, bias-corrected: the ordinary semivariance of the rates minus the Poisson noise of the pair, ½B²m*(1/nᵢ + 1/nⱼ).

With only 58 counties, the population weights concentrate on a handful of metropolitan pairs, so the weighted estimator mainly describes the Bay Area and Los Angeles. An exponential model with nugget is fitted to the unweighted estimator by weighted least squares (weights: number of pairs).


Code
# Centroid distances, binned every 40 km out to 640 km.
D_PAIRS = pdist(XY)
II, JJ = np.triu_indices(len(XY), 1)
EDGES = np.arange(0, 640, 40)

# Semivariance of the rates after the Poisson sampling variance has been removed.
def unweighted_poisson_variogram(cases, pop, xy_idx=None, edges=EDGES):
    idx = np.arange(len(cases)) if xy_idx is None else xy_idx
    D = pdist(XY[idx]); ii, jj = np.triu_indices(len(idx), 1)
    c, n = cases[idx], pop[idx]
    r = B * c / n
    m = np.nansum(c) / np.nansum(n)
    g = 0.5 * (r[ii] - r[jj]) ** 2 - 0.5 * B * B * m * (1 / n[ii] + 1 / n[jj])
    b = np.digitize(D, edges) - 1
    k = range(len(edges) - 1)
    return (np.array([D[b == q].mean() for q in k]), np.array([g[b == q].mean() for q in k]),
            np.array([(b == q).sum() for q in k], dtype=float))

# Exponential fit weighted by the square root of the pair count. The sill starts from the last four bins.
def fit_exp(h, g, n, a0=100.0):
    v = max(np.nanmean(g[-4:]), 1e-6 * np.nanmax(np.abs(g)) + 1e-9)
    f = lambda p: np.sqrt(n) * (p[0] + p[1] * (1 - np.exp(-h / p[2])) - g)
    r = least_squares(f, [0.4 * v, 0.6 * v, a0], bounds=([0, 1e-9, 5], [np.inf, np.inf, 2000]))
    return tuple(float(x) for x in r.x)                       # nugget, partial sill, a (km)

def exp_gamma(h, p):
    return p[0] + p[1] * (1 - np.exp(-np.asarray(h) / p[2]))

# Average 2017-2021, and compare the unweighted bins with the population-weighted estimator.
VG, VPAR = {}, {}
last5 = [list(YEARS).index(y) for y in range(2017, 2022)]
for d_ in DISEASES:
    un = [unweighted_poisson_variogram(CASES[d_][:, t], POP_STD[:, t]) for t in last5]
    pw = [mpk.pck_variogram(XY, CASES[d_][:, t], POP_STD[:, t], pop_rate=B, maxd=600, nbins=15) for t in last5]
    VG[d_] = {"unweighted": (un[0][0], np.mean([u[1] for u in un], 0), un[0][2]),
              "population-weighted": (pw[0][0], np.mean([q[1] for q in pw], 0), pw[0][2])}
    VPAR[d_] = fit_exp(*VG[d_]["unweighted"])

# Binned estimates, the fitted exponential, and the plain variance of the rates as a reference line.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4))
hh = np.linspace(1, 620, 200)
for ax, d_ in zip(axes, DISEASES):
    for est, mk in [("unweighted", "o"), ("population-weighted", "x")]:
        h, g, n = VG[d_][est]
        ax.plot(h, g, mk, label=est)
    ax.plot(hh, exp_gamma(hh, VPAR[d_]), "r-", label="exponential fit (unweighted)")
    ax.axhline(np.nanvar(RATE[d_][:, last5]), color="k", ls=":", lw=1, label="variance of rates")
    ax.set_xlabel("distance (km)"); ax.set_title(d_); ax.set_ylim(0, None)
axes[0].set_ylabel("semivariance (per 100,000)²"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
pd.DataFrame({d_: {"nugget": VPAR[d_][0], "partial sill": VPAR[d_][1], "a (km)": VPAR[d_][2],
                   "practical range (km)": 3 * VPAR[d_][2],
                   "nugget share": VPAR[d_][0] / (VPAR[d_][0] + VPAR[d_][1])} for d_ in DISEASES}).T.round(2)

Only chlamydia has spatial structure. Its unweighted semivariogram rises from about 19,500 at short distances to a sill near 33,000, with a practical range of about 420 km. The nugget is 60% of the sill.
Gonorrhea and early syphilis are pure nugget. Their semivariograms are flat, and the fit puts all the variance in the nugget. Neighbouring counties are no more alike than distant ones.
The population-weighted estimator is unstable here. Its first lag is far above the sill for all three infections. The few pairs of large neighbouring counties (San Francisco and its neighbours, Los Angeles and Orange) dominate it, and those pairs differ strongly, so the estimator mainly describes the urban core against its suburbs.

title: Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV in California Counties: Poisson Kriging in Space, Time and Across Diseases
section: Poisson kriging in space: centroid, area-to-area and area-to-point
text:
Poisson kriging in space: centroid, area-to-area and area-to-point

Point support
Area-to-area kriging needs each county as a set of points with weights. Population points (for example census blocks) are not in the data folder, so each county is filled with a regular grid of about 150 points and its population is spread evenly over them. This captures size and shape, but not where people live within a county, a limitation discussed at the end. PointSupport stores the points by county.


Code
# Support points inside each county. Spacing is at least 1.5 km, and wider in large counties so a county gets about 150 points.
rows = []
for _, row in ca.iterrows():
    geom = row.geometry
    sp = max(1500.0, np.sqrt(geom.area / 150))
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = geom.bounds
    gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(x0 + sp / 2, x1, sp), np.arange(y0 + sp / 2, y1, sp))
    pts = gpd.GeoSeries(gpd.points_from_xy(gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()), crs=ca.crs)
    pts = pts[pts.within(geom)]
    if len(pts) == 0:
        pts = gpd.GeoSeries([geom.representative_point()], crs=ca.crs)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({"fips": row["fips"], "x": pts.x.to_numpy() / 1000, "y": pts.y.to_numpy() / 1000}))
SUPPORT = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
print(f"Support points: {len(SUPPORT):,}; per county {SUPPORT.groupby('fips').size().min()} to {SUPPORT.groupby('fips').size().max()}")

# Split the county population equally across its support points.
def point_support(pop):
    w = SUPPORT["fips"].map(pd.Series(pop, index=FIPS)) / SUPPORT["fips"].map(SUPPORT.groupby("fips").size())
    return PointSupport(SUPPORT[["x", "y"]].to_numpy(), w.to_numpy(), SUPPORT["fips"].to_numpy())


Support points: 8,653; per county 58 to 155




Leave-one-out comparison
Each county’s 2021 rate is predicted from its 8 nearest counties, without its own data, by centroid Poisson kriging (PoissonKriging.predict_id) and by area-to-area Poisson kriging (AreaPoissonKriging.predict_area). The baselines are the statewide rate and the population-weighted mean of the same 8 neighbours. Because the observed rates of small counties are themselves noisy, errors are weighted by population, as in Goovaerts (2006), and also shown unweighted.


Code
# Turn the fitted nugget, partial sill, and range into an exponential variogram.
def make_variogram(params, xy, z):
    return Variogram(xy, z, model="exponential").set_params(*params)

# Leave-one-out at one year: the statewide rate, eight neighbours, centroid kriging, and area-to-area kriging.
def spatial_loo(d_, t=-1, k=K_SPACE):
    cases, pop = CASES[d_][:, t], POP_STD[:, t]
    rate = B * cases / pop
    vg = make_variogram(VPAR[d_], XY, rate)
    pk = PoissonKriging(vg, rate_base=B, use_gpu=False).fit(XY, rate, pop, ids=FIPS)
    apk = AreaPoissonKriging(vg, rate_base=B).fit(point_support(pop), pd.Series(rate, index=FIPS))
    out = {"statewide rate": np.full(len(rate), B * cases.sum() / pop.sum())}
    _, nb = cKDTree(XY).query(XY, k=k + 1)
    out["mean of 8 neighbours"] = np.array([np.average(rate[nb[i, 1:]], weights=pop[nb[i, 1:]]) for i in range(len(rate))])
    out["centroid PK"] = np.array([pk.predict_id(f, number_of_neighbors=k)["zhat"] for f in FIPS])
    out["ATA PK"] = np.array([apk.predict_area(f, number_of_neighbors=k)["zhat"] for f in FIPS])
    return rate, pop, out, pk, apk

# 2021 scores. Population-weighted mean squared error is reported against the statewide rate.
LOO = {}
rows = []
for d_ in DISEASES:
    rate, pop, out, _, _ = spatial_loo(d_)
    LOO[d_] = out
    for m, p in out.items():
        e = p - rate
        rows.append({"disease": d_, "method": m, "pop-weighted MSE": np.average(e ** 2, weights=pop),
                     "MSE": np.mean(e ** 2), "pop-weighted ME": np.average(e, weights=pop),
                     "Spearman": stats.spearmanr(p, rate)[0]})
loo_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["disease", "method"])
loo_tab["pop-weighted MSE vs statewide (%)"] = 100 * loo_tab["pop-weighted MSE"] / loo_tab.groupby(level=0)["pop-weighted MSE"].transform("first")

Reading the results.

Kriging does not beat the statewide rate in population-weighted MSE. For chlamydia, centroid PK and ATA have 22% and 16% higher population-weighted MSE than the statewide rate. For gonorrhea and early syphilis, whose models are pure nugget, kriging reduces to the population-weighted mean of the 8 neighbours and is 46% to 52% worse. The large counties dominate this score, and their rates are close to the statewide rate, which they largely determine.
Unweighted, kriging helps chlamydia. Its unweighted MSE falls from 45,071 (statewide rate) to 19,330 (centroid PK) and 19,463 (ATA), and the rank correlation with the observed rate is 0.59.
ATA and centroid PK give almost the same answers. ATA is slightly better in population-weighted MSE for chlamydia (17,033 against 18,018), but the difference is small next to the differences between counties.

With 58 counties, a weak spatial structure and very unequal populations, spatial Poisson kriging is mainly a smoother for small counties, not a predictor of unobserved ones.


Filtered county rates and the area-to-point surface
For the maps, each county keeps its own rate in the system, with its Poisson error term on the diagonal (exclude_self=False, added to the package for this capstone). The result is the noise-filtered county risk of Goovaerts (2006): close to the observed rate in large counties, pulled towards the neighbours in small ones. The area-to-point surface is computed on a 5 km grid, each node using the kriging system of the county that contains it. The coherence check compares the population-weighted average of each county’s point estimates with its area-to-area estimate.


Code
# Chlamydia in 2021. Keeping each county in its own system produces a filtered rate rather than a blank-county prediction.
d_ = "Chlamydia"
rate, pop, _, pk_c, apk_c = spatial_loo(d_)
t0 = time.time()
ata = pd.DataFrame([apk_c.predict_area(f, number_of_neighbors=K_SPACE, exclude_self=False) for f in FIPS]).set_index("id")
cent = pk_c.predict(XY, number_of_neighbors=K_SPACE)[0]

# Coherence check: the population-weighted mean of the point predictions should match the area prediction.
coh = []
for f in FIPS:
    pp = apk_c.predict_points(f, number_of_neighbors=K_SPACE, exclude_self=False)
    coh.append(np.average(pp["zhat"], weights=pp["population"]))
print(f"ATA and coherence check: {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")
print(f"Coherence: max |population-weighted ATP mean - ATA| = {np.nanmax(np.abs(np.array(coh) - ata['zhat'].to_numpy())):.2e}")

# 5 km grid for the ATP surface
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(*ca.total_bounds[[0, 2]], 5000), np.arange(*ca.total_bounds[[1, 3]], 5000))
grid = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()), crs=ca.crs)
grid = gpd.sjoin(grid, ca[["fips", "geometry"]], predicate="within").drop(columns="index_right").reset_index(drop=True)
t0 = time.time()
atp = []
for f, g in grid.groupby("fips"):
    tg = np.column_stack([g.geometry.x, g.geometry.y]) / 1000
    pp = apk_c.predict_points(f, number_of_neighbors=K_SPACE, exclude_self=False, targets=tg)
    atp.append(pd.DataFrame({"x": tg[:, 0], "y": tg[:, 1], "zhat": pp["zhat"].to_numpy(), "sig": pp["sig"].to_numpy(), "fips": f}))
ATP = pd.concat(atp, ignore_index=True)
print(f"ATP surface: {len(ATP):,} nodes in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")

# Smallest and largest counties, where filtering moves the rate the most.
small = pd.DataFrame({"county": ca["name"], "population": pop.astype(int), "observed": rate, "centroid PK": cent,
                      "ATA (filtered)": ata["zhat"].to_numpy(), "ATA SD": ata["sig"].to_numpy()})
display(small.sort_values("population").head(10).round(1))
display(small.sort_values("population").tail(5).round(1))

Reading the results.
